The correlations between depression and smartphone use are strong enough to suggest that more parents should be telling their kids to put down their phone. As the technology writer Nick Bilton has reported, it’s a policy some Silicon Valley executives follow. Even Steve Jobs limited his kids’ use of the devices he brought into the world.

What’s at stake isn’t just how kids experience adolescence. The constant presence of smartphones is likely to affect them well into adulthood. Among people who suffer an episode of depression, at least half become depressed again later in life. Adolescence is a key time for developing social skills; as teens spend less time with their friends face-to-face, they have fewer opportunities to practice them. In the next decade, we may see more adults who know just the right emoji for a situation, but not the right facial expression.

I realize that restricting technology might be an unrealistic demand to impose on a generation of kids so accustomed to being wired at all times. My three daughters were born in 2006, 2009, and 2012. They’re not yet old enough to display the traits of iGen teens, but I have already witnessed firsthand just how ingrained new media are in their young lives. I’ve observed my toddler, barely old enough to walk, confidently swiping her way through an iPad. I’ve experienced my 6-year-old asking for her own cellphone. I’ve overheard my 9-year-old discussing the latest app to sweep the fourth grade. Prying the phone out of our kids’ hands will be difficult, even more so than the quixotic efforts of my parents’ generation to get their kids to turn off MTV and get some fresh air. But more seems to be at stake in urging teens to use their phone responsibly, and there are benefits to be gained even if all we instill in our children is the importance of moderation. Significant effects on both mental health and sleep time appear after two or more hours a day on electronic devices. The average teen spends about two and a half hours a day on electronic devices. Some mild boundary-setting could keep kids from falling into harmful habits.

In my conversations with teens, I saw hopeful signs that kids themselves are beginning to link some of their troubles to their ever-present phone. Athena told me that when she does spend time with her friends in person, they are often looking at their device instead of at her. “I’m trying to talk to them about something, and they don’t actually look at my face,” she said. “They’re looking at their phone, or they’re looking at their Apple Watch.” “What does that feel like, when you’re trying to talk to somebody face-to-face and they’re not looking at you?,” I asked. “It kind of hurts,” she said. “It hurts. I know my parents’ generation didn’t do that. I could be talking about something super important to me, and they wouldn’t even be listening.”

Once, she told me, she was hanging out with a friend who was texting her boyfriend. “I was trying to talk to her about my family, and what was going on, and she was like, ‘Uh-huh, yeah, whatever.’ So I took her phone out of her hands and I threw it at my wall.”
I couldn’t help laughing. “You play volleyball,” I said. “Do you have a pretty good arm?” “Yep,” she replied.

This article has been adapted from Jean M. Twenge's forthcoming book, iGen: Why Today’s Super-Connected Kids Are Growing Up Less Rebellious, More Tolerant, Less Happy—and Completely Unprepared for Adulthood—and What That Means for the Rest of Us.

politico.com/news/2026/11/18/haaland-new.headline: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
politico.com/news/2026/11/18/haaland-new.author: Alec Hernandez

paragraphs.text: Deb Haaland is about to take the helm of a newly-minted Democratic presidential primary battleground. She has thoughts for her party’s White House hopefuls on how to win there.

Haaland, New Mexico’s incoming governor, told POLITICO that immigration will be a “top issue” in the presidential election — one that she’s “anxious” to see how future candidates plan to address — and said that engaging with rural voters in her state will be key to any successful primary campaign.

“New Mexico is the fifth largest state, and we are largely rural,” Haaland told POLITICO’s Erin Doherty in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. “There are far more rural communities than there are large cities in our state, and so this will be important for New Mexicans to to really understand or to really know that any presidential candidate understands the challenges that they're facing.”
Immigration is “going to be a top issue with the 2028 presidential election,” she added. “New Mexico is an early primary state, and it happens that we're a border state, too.”

Haaland’s ascension to the governor’s mansion coincides with a major change in New Mexico’s place in the Democratic Party's presidential nominating calendar pecking order. The state will now be fourth in the voting calendar behind South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. The move gives New Mexicans — and their new governor — significant influence in shaping the kind of nominee the party selects to take back the White House. It’ll also pose a significant test for candidate’s engagement with Latino voters, as New Mexico ranks first nationwide in its population share of Latino residents.
Some of those potential candidates have already come calling.

“Rahm Emanuel was in New Mexico, and he did quite a bit of traveling around,” Haaland said, noting that several senators made their own sojourns to the state for an event hosted in October by Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján in Alberquerque. Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg made his own trip to the state in September. “Whether all of them are running for president, I can't tell you, but I am really anxious to see who does.”

Haaland, a former Secretary of the Interior and the first Native American woman elected to a governorship, is ready to wield her own influence in the process as well, flexing her new power broker status. “I would love to endorse, but I'll wait and see who throws their hat in the ring,” she said.

Haaland was swept into office with a historic number of fellow Democrats across the country on a mandate to deliver on affordability. It’s the “biggest issue” in New Mexico, Haaland said, adding that her priority to deliver lower costs for New Mexicans will start with expanding access to affordable health care.
“Right now we're talking with some of the leaders in the legislature about health care, a public option for people in New Mexico,” she said. “Health care is a top top priority.”

politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-t.headline: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-t.author: Casey He and Jonathan Martin

paragraphs.text: Bo French, the far-right firebrand who centered his losing campaign for the Texas Railroad Commission on his anti-immigration stance, lost his membership at a Fort Worth country club, according to a letter obtained by POLITICO.

The letter from River Crest Country Club, dated Nov. 10 and addressed to French, said the club’s board of directors voted to terminate French’s membership immediately “for reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.”

The country club, founded in 1911, is the eighth to open in the state and boasts being a “who’s who” of Fort Worth. It hosts a 6,368-yard golf course that has been a training ground for top golfers, according to its website.
River Crest declined to comment, citing its policy of not doing so about “past, present and prospective members” and club operations, its general manager said in an email.

French, who has a history of making controversial statements on immigration issues like the H-1B visa program, made headlines in September after going viral on social media for a post he made that appeared to disparage Asian American students at the University of Texas at Austin.
His remarks capitalized on the growing anti-Indian sentiment sweeping Texas and across the nation, particularly against holders of the high-skilled worker visa, a majority of whom are from India.

The post quickly drew rebukes from Democrats and some Texas Republicans, who denounced it as racist. But French stood by the post. He said he was criticizing admission and hiring policies at UT, the state’s public flagship, that he claimed discriminated against Texas residents. (State law requires a majority of admitted students at the school to be residents of the state.)

French lost by 677,000 votes in his bid to sit on the influential statewide body that regulates Texas’ oil and gas industry two months later amid a statewide wipeout for the GOP. He previously led the Tarrant County Republican Party and also had two unsuccessful state House bids.
French did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent to multiple email addresses associated with him.

politico.com/news/2026/11/18/spencer-cox.headline: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
politico.com/news/2026/11/18/spencer-cox.author: Lauren Fedor

paragraphs.text: Utah’s Republican governor wants his party to move beyond President Donald Trump heading into the next presidential election.

“It’s time for the next thing,” Gov. Spencer Cox said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah.
Cox called on his fellow Republicans to start looking for new leadership in the wake of this month’s midterm election defeats.
“This is how this works when presidents move on. We should be looking for the next leadership in our party and what that looks like,” Cox told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson.

“We’ve got JD Vance and Marco Rubio, and those seem to be kind of the two choices now,” Cox said, referring to the Vice President and Secretary of State, respectively. “But I think you’ll see a lot of people step up … there are a lot of really interesting folks.”
“I’m a fan of governors,” Cox added. “I think governors with executive experience are the best to lead the country.”

Vance told Fox News earlier this week that he would decide “sometime next year” whether he will run for president in 2028. Rubio has dismissed suggestions that he would launch his own bid, and has said he would support Vance if the Vice President ran for the White House.
“I am hopeful that there are some Republican governors that will throw their hat in,” said Cox, a two-term governor. “We can have a competition of ideas heading in to find out what's next.”

Cox said that Trump still has a “really important role to play” in leading the party over the next two years, adding that the president still had an “opportunity” to strike bipartisan deals on permitting reform and other policy areas in his last two years in office.
Cox called the president “unique,” adding: “He’s someone who has the attention of the country in a way that almost no president has had in my lifetime.”
“People really love him or really don’t like him, but everybody’s paying attention to him,” he said.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/pete-h.headline: Hegseth boasts of Maduro’s capture while vowing to deepen US military cooperation with Venezuela
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/pete-h.author: Tom Phillips

paragraphs.text: Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/18/flor.headline: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/18/flor.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/israel.headline: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/israel.author: Lorenzo Tondo

paragraphs.text: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The military has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

politico.com/news/2026/11/18/oklahoma-go.headline: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
politico.com/news/2026/11/18/oklahoma-go.author: Lauren Fedor

paragraphs.text: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.”

“A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.”
When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums..
“When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said.

“When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.”
Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic.

“We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy.

“To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.”
Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform.

“It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.headline: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.author: Sarah Johnson

paragraphs.text: One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/buttigieg-a.headline: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/buttigieg-a.author: Adam Wren

paragraphs.text: Allies of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are launching an independent, grassroots effort urging him to undertake a second presidential campaign ahead of 2028.

Team Pete PAC will be led by Jennifer Holdsworth, the former national campaign manager of Buttigieg’s unsuccessful 2017 bid for DNC chair, and Mohsin Syed, his former chief of staff at the Transportation Department. The PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid.
“Mohsin and I have traveled the country this year, and everywhere we go, people ask us the same question: how can I help Pete?” Holdsworth said in a statement.
Team Pete PAC is independent and has no ties to Buttigieg’s Win the Era PAC, nor is it a presidential committee.
Through Win the Era, Buttigieg campaigned with 102 candidates across the map for the midterms, visiting 38 states (19 of them twice).

Asked on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday whether he had a timeline to make a decision, Buttigieg said he would be “surprised” if he was the first potential 2028 presidential candidate “to make news” and said he’s “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.”

Even as it forms to press Buttigieg to mount a second presidential campaign, Team Pete PAC is urging potential backers to take part in community service — a nod to Buttigeig’s proposed national service program he proposed as a candidate.
“I’ve seen up close what Pete can do,” Syed said. “He has a unique ability to bring people together and inspire action.”

theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/19/.headline: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/19/.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe

paragraphs.text: Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/19/car-ra.headline: Car rams into Palestinian residents four times in Israeli city, injuring eight
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/19/car-ra.author: Lorenzo Tondo

paragraphs.text: Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.

Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and added that “as of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”

The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.

Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”
Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”.
“Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”

In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/19/china-.headline: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/19/china-.author: Rebecca Bailey

paragraphs.text: China, Russia and the US have said they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran triggered by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and a “mutual understanding” had taken place.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed advances by Trump to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued before by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK. “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had warned that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”

However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he warned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/jd-vance-sl.headline: JD Vance slams GOP governor’s call for immigration reform as ‘morally and electorally disastrous’
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/jd-vance-sl.author: Lauren Fedor

paragraphs.text: Vice President JD Vance took aim at Kevin Stitt, calling the Republican governor of Oklahoma’s push for bipartisan immigration reform “morally and electorally disastrous.”
“I like Kevin, but what does ‘bipartisan immigration reform’ mean?” Vance wrote on X on Thursday morning.

“If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I'm all ears,” Vance wrote. “But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws. It is morally and electorally disastrous.”

The vice president was responding to comments the Oklahoma Republican made at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Park City, Utah, on Wednesday.
“We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt said.
Stitt described President Donald Trump as a “businessperson” who “understands the need for a workforce.”
“He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy,” the Oklahoma governor said.
But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform.

“It’s not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they’re winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That’s why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

Stitt has long called for sweeping changes to immigration policy, including enabling state governors to issue work permits to unauthorized immigrants. Vance — who is weighing a run for the White House in 2028 — has been a staunch defender of the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration.

theguardian.com/law/2026/nov/19/myanmar-.headline: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
theguardian.com/law/2026/nov/19/myanmar-.author: Julian Borger

paragraphs.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/sus.headline: Susan Smith denied parole 32 years after drowning sons in S.C. lake
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/sus.author: Brady Dennis

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Critic covering digital arts and entertainment
What I saw playing 170 hours of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ before everyone else

Playing “Grand Theft Auto VI” three weeks early felt like I’d shown up too early for the biggest concert festival in human history. Like SZA, the Weeknd and Travis Scott had new music, but I was required by a nondisclosure agreement to not even whisper it to another soul.

Since “GTA VI” was unveiled in 2023, people have been making whole essays about of a few minutes of footage. The game was impossibly beautiful and realistic. It looked like the future. But since late last month, I felt like I was living in that future. I had all the answers of how the game works and all the shocking plot twists throughout its 50- to 100-hour storyline to write my review where I called it the most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed.

I wondered what it must’ve felt like to see the “Star Wars: A New Hope” before anyone in 1977 saw it. There must have been a moment where you realized film could do something beyond the limits of imagination at the time. I wondered how long you could sit with that.
On Wednesday, as the game finally released worldwide, I spent hours watching streamers play the opening of “GTA VI.” Even after the 170 hours I spent in the game, I saw things I’d never seen.

I’d been waiting three weeks to tell people what I saw — and now the rest of the world is showing up for the same thing, a rare flash of modern monoculture. I can finally turn to the person in the next seat and ask, “Did you see that?”
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Officials on Thursday unanimously denied parole to Susan Smith, who was convicted of killing her two young sons in 1994 by strapping them into her car and rolling it into a South Carolina lake.
The case gripped the nation at the time, after Smith’s false claim that a Black man had abducted 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alex. She later confessed to drowning them.

“I’m not the same person I was 32 years ago. I have changed. I have grown up. I have matured,” Smith, who was first denied parole in 2024, told the board Thursday. Now 55, she said she carries deep remorse over the “unbearable pain” she caused.
The boys’ father, David Smith, was among a litany of people who pleaded for her to remain behind bars.

“It’s been 32 years since I buried Michael and Alex,” he said, wearing a picture of his sons on the lapel of his suit and fighting back tears. “I know for some of you 32 years is a long time, but for me it was yesterday.”
Setting her free, he said, “would be a huge injustice.”
On Thursday, members of the parole board agreed, by a 6-0 vote.
Reporter covering the business, culture and politics of sports
A ticket to the NWSL final? Be ready to pony up.

Saturday’s NWSL Championship between the Washington Spirit and the Kansas City Current at D.C.’s Audi Field is set to be the most expensive ever. It’s the latest example of an explosion in playoff ticket prices in women’s sports.

According to TickPick, a ticket resale platform, the average ticket has sold for $318, a 212 percent increase from last year’s $102 average for the final, in which Gotham FC beat the Spirit. It also tops the $307 average ticket for the 2025 MLS Cup Final, which Inter Miami CF won over Vancouver Whitecaps FC.

And the prices have only increased since the matchup, which features American stars Trinity Rodman and Croix Bethune, was set on Sunday. As of Wednesday evening, the cheapest ticket cost $328. A fan could have attended all 15 regular season Spirit home games at Audi Field for a combined $312.
Reporter covering the U.S. House of Representatives
Absent Republicans are a problem for House leaders in the lame-duck session
House Republican leaders have a pretty packed to-do list during this lame-duck period.
They have 13 legislative days left.
They also have an attendance problem. Fourteen members missed votes on Wednesday. On Thursday morning, votes trickled in slowly. Twenty-one Republicans didn’t vote.
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) recognized that this is a challenge.

“Attendance is a great frustration for me right now. We’ll be addressing that with members,” he told reporters Thursday morning. “It’s not possible for us to … advance our legislative agenda unless the members are here doing their job.”
Many of the missing lawmakers lost in this month’s midterm elections, and their tenures in Congress will end in early January.
Johnson said he’ll be having individual meetings with members to address the issue “because we have important weeks ahead of us.”
Congress is seeking to stave off a government shutdown (funding ends on Dec. 11), and lawmakers want to pass a major defense policy in coming weeks.
House Republicans also want to push through a spending bill answering President Donald Trump’s demand for $350 billion in funds for the Pentagon to address the ongoing war in Iran.
Reporter covering Florida
Extreme flooding sets records in Florida, with more rain to come
Parts of Florida remained underwater Thursday, with schools closed, residents stranded and little relief in sight as forecasters warned of more downpours.

Along the Space Coast, the National Weather Service warned of life-threatening flash flooding in central Brevard County as bands of heavy rain continued to move ashore. Videos showed cars stranded in floodwaters and neighborhoods submerged. In Palm Bay, emergency crews used boats to evacuate residents.
After days of heavy rain, the St. Johns River, Florida’s longest river, rose to a record 18.1 feet at a gauge west of Cocoa on Thursday morning.

Farther south, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Broward County had recorded nearly 17 inches of rain over two days by Thursday morning, according to preliminary National Weather Service totals.
The flooding kept public schools in Broward, Miami-Dade and Brevard counties closed Thursday.
A flood watch remained in effect for parts of southeast Florida through Thursday evening, while most of east-central Florida was under a watch through Friday evening.

Forecasters warned that some areas from Indian River County north to Volusia County could see an additional 4 to 8 inches of rain through Friday night, with totals potentially topping 15 inches near the coast.
Reporter covering issues in national K-12 education
Proposed change to SNAP threatens free school meals for 1.7 million children

The Trump administration’s changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, cut more than 5 million people off from federal food benefits and eliminated free school meals for some students.
Now, a newly proposed rule threatens free school meals for nearly 2 million children.

The Agriculture Department wants to limit a provision called “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows families that receive certain public benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP, commonly known as food stamps.

The department, which runs SNAP, estimates the change could drop 6.3 million people from the food assistance program because they exceed income limits. Because SNAP recipients are automatically eligible for free school meals, the families of more than 1.7 million children affected by the change would have to fill out paperwork to apply for the free meals — or lose access to them.

Most of those children — 1.66 million — would still be living in households that qualify for free meals, according to USDA. School districts have said automatic enrollment has been helpful because many families don’t complete the paperwork. Districts end up footing the bill for those children’s meals.
USDA said the rule change would ensure SNAP can be accessed only by the households that need it most. Nutrition advocates argue it would exacerbate food insecurity.
The public can comment on the proposal until Dec. 10. If adopted, the rule will take effect in fall 2028.
Reporter covering breaking news from London
Van Gogh painting nets record $190.4M after dispute over its history

A Vincent van Gogh painting fetched a record-breaking $190.4 million at auction after a last-minute agreement between the sellers and the heirs of the painting’s former Jewish owners allowed the sale to proceed.
“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) went under the hammer at Sotheby’s on Wednesday evening, and secured the highest price ever paid for a Van Gogh artwork.
The 1890 painting “dates from the extraordinary period of creative intensity that marked the final two months of the artist’s life,” the auction house said.
The sale appeared uncertain last week, as descendants of the painting’s former owners, Samuel and Hedwig Fischer, said the family sold the painting in the 1930s due to Nazi persecution.

On the day of the auction, Sotheby’s confirmed that a deal between the Fischer heirs and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting for more than 50 years, would allow the sale to proceed. “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history … the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution,” Sotheby’s said in a statement.
Gunnar Schnabel, an attorney for the Fischer heirs, said the family hopes the resolution “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era.”

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/nevada-aaro.headline: Nevada's new governor promises legislative blitz on affordability
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/nevada-aaro.author: Jason Beeferman

paragraphs.text: Nevada Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford is vowing to immediately pass a trifecta of measures that he says will drive down the cost of living when he enters office in the key swing state.

“Those are concrete things that immediately can bring some level of effect to this cost-of-living crisis that we're experiencing right now,” Ford told POLITICO’s Megan Messerly in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah.

The legislative blitz includes a bill to make school breakfast and lunch free for public school students, legislation that would limit the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicare-negotiated price for everybody and new rules aimed at lowering housing costs that would limit the number of homes corporations can purchase.

“I've been working with my colleagues already in the Legislature, and we're going to sign bills beginning on Day 1,” Ford said. “We'll be signing bills within the first 30 days to ensure that we can start effectuating some of the promises that I made on the campaign trail.

“You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses — cut regulations and make it easier to do business — I think that’s cool, that’s fine, and that’s dandy. But if you could do it for businesses, you could do it for people too,” he also said.

The incoming Nevada governor and former state attorney general also emphasized his willingness to work across the aisle — even though the massive Democratic wins in his state earlier this month make it so “I don't need one Republican vote to get something done in my state right now,” he said.
Nevada will be the second state to vote in the Democratic primaries in 2028, and Ford said candidates need to come and travel up and down the state before staking out policy positions.

“You need to come to Nevada. Period. Point blank,” Ford said. “We’re one of the most diverse states in the nation. If you can convince a Nevadan that you’re worth your salt, you may very well be able to convince the rest of the nation that you are.”

And he cautioned Democrats against making assumptions on what Nevadans want and need. “Don’t presume you know what their issues are,” he said. “Don’t be high and mighty and highfalutin and sitting in some ivory tower putting out ideas when you haven’t heard them say to you what their concerns are.”

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/josh-stein-.headline: ‘They should be subsidizing the ratepayers’: NC governor says data center subsidies should be rolled back
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/josh-stein-.author: Jessica Piper

paragraphs.text: North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein said his state needs to roll back subsidies for data centers, telling POLITICO that Big Tech companies should be “paying their own way.”

“I think the idea that this industry needs any public incentive is laughable. These are the wealthiest companies in the history of humanity. They have more resources than many nations. So we, little North Carolina, should not be giving subsidies,” Stein said in an interview Thursday at the POLITICO Pub at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah.

The Democratic governor pointed to subsidies in North Carolina for electricity for data centers that were rolled back earlier this year, along with ongoing subsidies for the purchase of new equipment, which he said ought to be phased out.
“For new data centers, why are we giving them any public dollar when they should be subsidizing the ratepayers?” he said.

Stein, elected in 2024, will be governing with a divided Legislature next year after Democrats flipped North Carolina’s House of Representatives this year and broke the Republican supermajority in the state Senate amid a nationwide blue wave. Republicans are likely to maintain narrow control of the upper chamber pending a recount in a pivotal race.

The first-term governor, who won by nearly 15 points in 2024 despite President Donald Trump also winning the state that year, didn’t commit to running again in 2028 but said he “cannot think of any” reasons not to.

Stein touted bipartisan work in the state to address recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated western North Carolina in 2024. But he faulted “one of the most ineffectual Congresses in history” for failing to deliver for the state. The $60 billion in damages North Carolina suffered, he noted, are nearly as large of a sum as the state’s two-year budget — making it impossible for the state to allocate enough funds for recovery.
He said that he spoke to Trump earlier this year and was told that hurricane recovery was a priority for the president, but the necessary federal funds have not come through.
“The state stepped up,” Stein said. “The people of Western North Carolina have truly stepped up, and it's time for the federal government to step up.”

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/19/n.headline: Nvidia scandal could be tipping point toward tougher export control enforcement
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/19/n.author: David J. Lynch

paragraphs.text: The Nvidia scandal is the latest episode in a decades-long debate within the United States over which products should — and should not — be sold to China, a rising economic power and formidable U.S. strategic rival.

The Trump administration this week belatedly closed regulatory loopholes that may have enabled some of Nvidia’s best artificial intelligence chips to skirt U.S. export controls and reach customers in Beijing, including elements of the Chinese military. One day later, Nvidia’s board announced the establishment of a new export control oversight committee staffed by independent directors, outside specialists and lawyers.

In the nearly half-century since China launched its economic opening, Washington has struggled to reconcile corporate America’s desire to profit from the enormous Chinese market with the imperatives of U.S. national security. The widening Nvidia scandal, which is drawing scrutiny from multiple congressional committees and the Securities and Exchange Commission, may mark a turning point in that campaign.

“You’re going to have more laws that are passed to tighten export controls. But it’s ultimately the Department of Justice and the Commerce Department that have to get on board,” said Edward Fishman, a former State Department sanctions official. “And it would take a little time. You have to reshape the risk calculus of the whole tech sector.”

New export-control powers are likely to be included in an annual must-pass defense spending bill that Congress will take up before year’s end. Among them are provisions that would expand controls to cover remote access to sensitive technologies via cloud computing services and tighten restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment, analysts said.

The U.S. government has been reluctant to punish major tech companies because of their importance to government efforts in both the Trump and Biden administrations to reinvigorate domestic semiconductor production, Fishman said.

Tougher enforcement also could trigger Chinese retaliation. When Commerce last year expanded its export blacklist to include majority-owned foreign affiliates of targeted companies, China struck back by restricting shipments of vital rare earth minerals. The two governments ultimately agreed to a trade truce, deferring enforcement of these measures.

“One of the results of the Nvidia crisis is clearly going to be significant pressure for Commerce to increase enforcement. Obviously, the big question then becomes ‘How does China react?’” said Daniel Bahar, a managing director with Rock Creek Global Advisors in Washington.

Major tech companies so far have escaped the sizable financial penalties that incentivized big banks to prioritize compliance with U.S. rules governing their work with foreign customers. In 2014, BNP Paribas, for example, pleaded guilty to violating U.S. financial sanctions and paid a nearly $9 billion penalty to settle the case,

The French bank “deliberately disregarded U.S. law” in processing payments for customers subject to U.S. sanctions in Sudan, Cuba and Iran, the Justice Department said at the time. The massive fine caused the bank’s profits to shrink by 97 percent compared with the previous year.

Punishments are typically less severe for export violations. In February, when Applied Materials in Santa Clara, California, settled charges of violating U.S. export controls by illegally routing shipments of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China via South Korea, it paid a fine of just $252 million.
Commerce Department officials hailed the penalty at the time, noting it was the second-highest ever. But it was dwarfed by Applied Materials’s annual profits of more than $10 billion.

Commerce officials have pushed lawmakers to increase the maximum penalties allowed by law, according to a department spokesman who spoke on the condition of anonymity in accordance with department policy.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that if Nvidia were a bank with similar compliance failures, federal regulators would have intervened and “a lot of the executives would be removed.”

Indeed, over many years, major banks devoted significant staff resources, often including a chief compliance officer, to ensuring that their operations conform with extensive regulations. Silicon Valley companies whose leaders often were indifferent to or disdainful of government have been slow to develop similar competencies, said Geoffrey Gertz, senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security in Washington.

“There’s a real need to build up the broader culture of compliance around these issues. It did take banks some time to build up these very strong compliance systems. Similar incentive structures need to be in place for advanced chip controls,” Gertz said.

Even before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials describe as a Chinese intelligence asset, there were questions about the company’s adherence to U.S. export controls.

In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) wrote to Nvidia saying that recent chip-smuggling cases filed by the Justice Department “allege troubling facts that raise serious questions about NVIDIA’s compliance practices.”

To date, there is no public evidence that Nvidia directly sold its advanced chips to China, and Huang, before resigning, had denied that chips were being diverted there. But one of Nvidia’s customers in Singapore, a cloud computing company called Megaspeed, reportedly purchased several billion dollars worth of the company’s advanced chips. Some analysts have suggested that some of those could have been diverted to Chinese end users, in defiance of U.S. law.
Federal prosecutors have documented the extensive diversion of Nvidia chips to China through networks of shell companies in Asia.

Companies such as Megaspeed also may have exploited an export control loophole by selling Chinese companies remote access to top Nvidia chips that they were prohibited from buying themselves, U.S. officials have said.

The Justice Department last year took the lead in an ongoing Commerce investigation of Megaspeed for “potential export control violations” involving “sensitive semiconductor diversion,” according to a joint statement from the two agencies.

In May 2025, Commerce requested records from Nvidia of any sales to Megaspeed. One month later, the chipmaker put Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Commerce investigators, along with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site investigation of Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive and Jason Huang’s mistress. (Though they share a surname, the two are unrelated.
U.S. limits on exports to China have evolved over time.

In the 1980s, the Reagan administration approved sales to China of an array of military hardware, including anti-submarine torpedoes, artillery-locating radars, jet fighter avionics and General Electric engines for naval destroyers. At the time, the U.S. and China were partners in an informal alliance against the Soviet Union.

Washington halted the provision of military goods after the June 1989 pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square were violently suppressed. But overall U.S. exports climbed rapidly from around $12 billion that year to more than $100 billion when China joined the global trading system in 2001 and were more than four times that amount when Joe Biden became president.

“We were very open to buying and selling to China. But over time, that changed as our relationship deteriorated, trust decreased and suspicions grew,” said Wendy Cutler, a former U.S. trade negotiator who is now senior vice president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

The Biden administration began restricting sales to China of advanced chips and chip-making equipment in October 2022, adopting an approach that then-national security adviser Jake Sullivan described as “small yard, high fence.”
The idea was that the U.S. would maintain tight restrictions on a limited set of advanced technologies that China might use to build a more powerful and sophisticated military.
As the relevant technologies continued to advance, the Biden administration updated its export regulations in 2023 and 2024, Sullivan said in an interview next week.
“By the time we left, we had built an architecture of export controls that were quite effective in giving the U.S. a really considerable compute advantage over China,” he said.
One area — how to regulate Chinese remote access to top U.S. chips — was left unaddressed until last week. On Monday, Commerce issued a new regulation closing that loophole.

But in a sign of an open split within the Trump administration over the matter, the Commerce Department announcement said that the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”

Commerce had delayed enacting the tighter rules for months, despite support for them from other powerful Cabinet agencies, including Treasury. After Jensen Huang’s ouster, Bessent was publicly critical of Commerce for dragging its feet.
Meanwhile, Nvidia this week brushed aside the new regulations’ potential impact, saying demand for its AI-related hardware is “far exceeding” supply.
“We expect our performance to remain strong,” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s acting CEO, told investors on Tuesday.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/cyb.headline: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/cyb.author: Violet Jira

paragraphs.text: Cyberattackers may have accessed the names and email addresses of some JPMorgan Chase and Mastercard customers, the financial giants said Thursday. Visa in a statement also said it was aware of claims that its customers’ data had been affected, but it did not confirm any exposure.

Chase, Mastercard and Visa said that their own systems were not impacted. None of the companies have reported a disruption in service associated, and the companies said payment data, such as card numbers, was not affected.
All three companies said the incident involved a third-party service provider. None of the companies have named the vendor, and it is unclear whether the breaches were the result of the same attack.

The attacks arrived on the heels of incidents in which several other companies saw their systems affected by technological issues, though not cyberattacks in each instance. A global Microsoft outage disrupted access to Outlook and Microsoft 365 last week, and a nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration was attributed to a telecommunications failure.

But those and a string of other disruptions in recent weeks — some of which have been linked to artificial intelligence — have put customers on edge and prompted institutions globally to take steps to brace themselves against cyberthreats.

Mastercard said in a statement Thursday that an incident at a third-party provider resulted in the exposure of a “limited amount of email addresses” of a small subset of customers enrolled in a specific program.

Chase said in a statement on X that a breach affecting third parties that work for the firm may have allowed attackers to access marketing data held by the vendors, which may have included names and emails.
Chase declined to comment further on who the vendors are, when the company became aware of the attack and how many customers’ data had been accessed.
Mastercard said that “the exposure has been contained” and that the company was working to support affected cardholders. Chase said affected customers would be contacted directly.

On Tuesday, Chase customers across the country couldn’t access some online banking services after a disruption in service that the company said was caused by “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and not a cyberattack.
