Service was restored Tuesday. That incident and the one Chase reported Thursday are unrelated, according to the company.

cnbc.com/2026/11/19/gap-gap-q3-2026-earn.headline: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
cnbc.com/2026/11/19/gap-gap-q3-2026-earn.author: Laya Neelakandan

paragraphs.text: Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.
The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.
"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."

Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.
While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.
Third-quarter earnings

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.
Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.
Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.
"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.
Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
• Earnings per share: 82 cents adjusted vs. 78 cents expected
• Revenue: $4.01 billion vs. $4.02 billion expected

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.
Brand sales

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing.

The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.
"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.
Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/after-texas.headline: Leader of Democratic AG group to step down after Texas triumph
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/after-texas.author: Shia Kapos

paragraphs.text: CHICAGO — The head of the Democratic Attorneys General Association is stepping down after a successful 2026 cycle in which their party flipped Republican-held attorney general offices in five states, including the conservative legal powerhouse of Texas.

Sean Rankin started as executive director at the group — known as DAGA — in 2016, and oversaw its operations as Democratic attorneys general banded together to challenge the first Trump administration over a range of issues. He became president of the group in 2022 and is credited with raising nearly $250 million for DAGA and its affiliated entities over the past decade.
“Since Sean joined DAGA in 2016, the committee has won the majority of their competitive races” against Republicans, “reshaping the map for Democrats,” the group said Thursday.
Rankin will stay at DAGA as it conducts a search for his successor.
Democrats will take control of at least five additional attorney general offices in January, following wins in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.
Alaska, which just elected a Democratic governor, is also expected to have a Democratic attorney general, since the governor appoints the state's top lawyer.

“On Texas, we took the head of the snake. So fundamentally, there will be a change in how the Republican attorneys general have to engage nationally if they do not have Texas at the front,” Rankin told POLITICO in a wide-ranging interview after the midterms earlier this month. “Texas has played an outsized role in the actions taken, in my opinion, against many of the issues that I care about, that the AGs fight for, that we believe the American people support — having Texas not on the other side, that’s a game changer.”

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear defended his decision not to invest more in Gina Hinojosa’s successful race for Texas governor in an interview with POLITICO, amid criticism that could derail his own potential presidential ambitions.

Beshear, the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, took heat this month when Latino Democratic operatives and Hinojosa allies publicly maligned him for failing to do enough to help Hinojosa over the finish line.
“There might have been frustration by folks who just really wanted to win that race, but they did, and she did, and we're very excited to have her a part of the DGA room,” Beshear said Thursday.
“Did we spend a little more money, say, in Kansas, where we were trying to protect the seat? Yes, but we only won that race by 7,000 votes," he said.

In a stunning victory, Hinojosa won Texas by 7 percentage points. Hinojosa’s allies’ say that their calls for the DGA to support her campaign went unanswered for months. Ultimately, the DGA contributed $1.4 million — a far cry from the $19 million the organization invested in Keisha Lance Bottoms’ successful bid to win Georgia’s governorship.
But Beshear said the context matters. When the budget for this campaign cycle started at the end of 2024, Democrats had suffered brutal losses.

“We built out our map protecting our incumbents,” Beshear said. “We were going to be lucky to get [Arizona Gov.] Katie Hobbs and [Oregon Gov.] Tina Kotek reelected, and we were going to have tough elections, even in places potentially like Pennsylvania.”

Democrats Abigail Spanberger in Virginia and Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey both won gubernatorial victories in 2025 on affordability platforms, which helped propel them to victory at a time when the economy had become a key pressure point for voters.

Heading into 2026, Beshear said, "what came online were the first set of flips, where the earliest polling indicated it was possible, and those were Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. And so at that point, we already had the largest DGA map ever."

“We had a size 10 budget with a size 14 map, and then what happened? Alaska, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas and Florida all became or seemed competitive as well, which meant we had a size 10 budget with a size 16 map," Beshear said.
The party flipped six governorships in states that President Donald Trump won. In January, Democrats will control 30 governorships and the majority of state legislative chambers.
“So at the end of the day, I think we're judged by results,” Beshear said. “And I get that every campaign wants as much funding as they can, but Gina won in Texas, and I'm excited for her.”
While Beshear hasn’t publicly announced a run for president in 2028, he’s already crafting his pitch.

“If you look at what we've done in Kentucky, the ability to do that all across this country would be special for so many other communities that deserve better jobs, more accessible health care and a better life for our people,” he said.
Despite his role as chair of the DGA, Beshear argues that of all the rumored candidates out there, he would be the “ultimate outsider.” He’s not from “inside the Beltway” or either coast.
He would be “a candidate from where the South meets the Midwest,” he said — a governor who has helped “improve and revive a place that the country for many years left out.”
Beshear says that Bottoms’ victory in Georgia showed Democrats can win in the South.

“I am a Southern governor that has won in a red state, and so I knew a great candidate when I saw one,” he said. “And together, our financial support plus her grassroots campaign that turned out voters sent a message that the South is winnable and that the Deep South is winnable.”
Next up? Mississippi and Louisiana, Beshear said.

“You look at Mississippi, where three years ago the election was close and will be again,” he said. “And then, depending on the candidate we get in Louisiana, the governor there has incredibly low approval ratings, and so even though that's going up against an incumbent, I think the seat is very much in play.”
In 2023, Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves defeated his Democratic nominee Brandon Presley by 3.24 percentage points. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry took office in January 2024.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/want-to-see-yo.headline: Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac’s icons? This clever new app lets you
techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/want-to-see-yo.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!

Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.

Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.

Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!)

Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.)
Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.

There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.

Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.

He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.
Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.

“The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said.

That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.
“That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.
The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: US Lawmakers Near Deal to Ban Chinese Cars in Lame Duck Session
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Josh Wingrove, Gabrielle Coppola, David Welch and Steven T. Dennis

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, according to people familiar with the matter, following last-minute negotiations aimed in part at sparing Mercedes-Benz Group AG, which is nearly 20% owned by Chinese entities.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Republicans and Democrats from auto-producing states driving the effort aim to send a bill to President Donald Trump's desk by the end of the year, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private. If enacted, the profitable US car market would be walled off to automakers such as BYD Co. and Geely Automobile Holdings Inc., whose low-cost, technology-packed electric vehicles have rapidly gained market share in Europe and South America.

Details about the measure are still being hammered out. Republican Senator Bernie Moreno on Wednesday briefed automaker representatives on changes under consideration to earlier legislation that aimed to block Chinese connected vehicles from the US, including provisions that would shield Mercedes from an outright ban, said the people.

Automaker representatives were broadly supportive of the effort Moreno described, though a Mercedes official voiced reservations and negotiations remain underway, the people said. Proponents are working to pass the measure before the next Congress begins in January, the people said.
"We continue to meet with all stakeholders who have a shared interest in ensuring this important legislation becomes law in this Congress," Mercedes said in a statement.

Chinese cars are effectively shut out of the US because of steep tariffs and restrictions on Chinese vehicle technology imposed by the Commerce Department. Enshrining a ban into law would take those measures a step further to address growing concerns about national and economic security threats posed by China's ambition to dominate the global auto industry.

A bill advanced by a Senate panel earlier this year would have prohibited manufacturers that are more than 15% owned by Chinese entities from selling cars equipped with technology that can transmit data. Mercedes, which has lobbied for changes to that bill, is nearly 10% owned by China's BAIC Motor Corp., a state-owned carmaker.
Li Shu Fu, the billionaire founder of Chinese carmaker Geely, also holds nearly 10% of Mercedes' shares, putting the company above the earlier bill's 15% threshold.

Lawmakers are in talks with multiple parties, including Mercedes, and have expressed optimism that an agreement could be reached as early as this week, said one person close to the talks who asked not to be identified. Provisions under discussion include looser rules for companies with passive ownership stakes that lack voting power and how such an approach would be structured and verified.
The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Republican Senator Katie Britt of Alabama, a major hub of Mercedes' sport utility vehicle production, said she has worked through the bill with Moreno and believes both Mercedes and Alabama will be protected.
"We understand that there will be some adjustments that have to be made, but feel good about Mercedes continuing to be able to thrive in our state and across the country," she said.

Banning Chinese cars would also run counter to a more permissive approach taken by Europe and Canada. Chinese automakers have quickly made inroads in Europe, in particular, leading to intense competition with homegrown brands. The EU has started to pull back after Chinese automakers rapidly expanded their share of the market there, reaching an agreement last month with China to curb imports of hybrid vehicles into the bloc.
--With assistance from Amy Stillman.

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/massachuset.headline: Massachusetts gov says Dems want ‘a uniter and a fighter’ for 2028
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/massachuset.author: Lisa Kashinsky

paragraphs.text: Democrats want fighters. Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey believes they want healers, too.

Healey, a Democrat who easily won a second term in the deep-blue state earlier this month, told POLITICO on Thursday that she’d like to see her party’s next presidential nominee show “decency” and “humanity.”

“It’s really important that we have leaders who genuinely see people, understand their situation. If you don't see people, if you don't understand people, you're never going to be able to deliver for them,” Healey said during an interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah.
“Having leaders who have that, and who have a strong moral compass, I think that's really important,” she told POLITICO’s Adam Wren.

Healey suggested the midterms offered a “resetting” as the nation moves toward a post-Donald Trump era. Pressed on whether it’s more important for Democrats to nominate a fighter or a healer, Healey — who burnished her national profile as a hard-charging state attorney general who sued the first Trump administration dozens of times and urged Democrats to more aggressively oppose his second — insisted good leaders can do both.
“You can be a uniter and a fighter; you can be a fighter and a healer,” she said.

It’s a debate that’s already driving the earliest stages of Democrats’ shadow 2028 primary as the party’s rising stars try to discern whether voters who powered their midterm wave want a brawler or a uniter after candidates of both stripes won difficult races.
Healey ruled out a 2028 presidential bid of her own on Thursday. And she deflected when asked whether Democrats should nominate a governor.

But the Massachusetts governor, who has close relationships with several likely contenders and routinely hits the campaign trail for Democrats in the early primary state of New Hampshire, could play a role in shaping the primary.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-19/.headline: California subpoenas Nvidia as questions about CEO affair, AI chips mount
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-19/.author: Kevin Rector

paragraphs.text: California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta on Thursday subpoenaed the AI chip manufacturer Nvidia — asking whether its advanced chips or other confidential information went to China and whether it had misled investors and the public on the issue.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The subpoena follows Nvidia co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s resignation after it was revealed he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and after Bonta’s office sued OpenAI — another AI company — over similar claims that it had misled the public about its advanced AI capabilities.
Bonta’s office said information gleaned from the subpoenas “will help the California Department of Justice evaluate whether Nvidia’s actions violated California law.”
Bonta said both Nvidia’s and Jensen’s conduct raise “bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” and his office intends to determine if it did so.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta said.
The shake-up at Nvidia has rattled markets.
This article will be updated.

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/keisha-lanc.headline: Keisha Lance Bottoms says Democrats better spend big on the South
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/keisha-lanc.author: Erin Doherty

paragraphs.text: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said the midterm election results “have spoken for themselves” in showing the need for the Democratic Party to invest more in the South.

“I would hope that in two years, we're not having to beg and borrow to be able to run successful campaigns,” Bottoms said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah.

Democrats had a historically strong cycle in Georgia this year: Bottoms became the first Democrat to win her state’s governorship in more than a quarter-century, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection handily, and the party flipped the state House for the first time in more than two decades. But it wasn’t just Georgia. Democrats also won Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, three states that have long been out of reach for the party, and just missed in Louisiana.
“The numbers have been there for Democrats to flip that seat in Mississippi for a while, but the investment has not been there,” Bottoms said.
She said that her campaign was a lean operation, particularly in contrast to her GOP opponent’s. Rick Jackson spent nearly $200 million of his own money on his campaign.

“During the primary it was the shoestring, dental floss campaign, we were holding it together with every single thing that we had because we weren't getting in the resources and some people have written Georgia off,” she said.

“But also even when those resources come from our friends nationally: Trust us. Nobody knows their community, nobody knows their electorate better than the people who are living and breathing it every single day.”
Bottoms made history as the first-ever Black woman ever elected governor to in the U.S. earlier this month. But on her campaign trail, she did not focus on the historic nature of her candidacy.

“I wake up as a Black woman every day,” she said. “So it was not something that I felt compelled to talk about, it was never top of mind, so it was not even a conscious decision for me not to talk about it. I just didn’t think about it.”
She said she instead focused on voters’ cost of living concerns that dominated the cycle.

“For me, it was about focusing on the issues. I can't hide, and don't want to hide, that I'm a Black woman,” she said. “To the extent that the conversations were organic with me as a mother or as a woman or whatever the case may have been, then it was a part of the discussion. But I can tell you, as I moved around the state of Georgia, people were focused on, ‘what are you gonna do about this cost of living? How are you going to make my life better?’”

techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/elon-musk-says.headline: Elon Musk says SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones
techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/elon-musk-says.author: Kirsten Korosec

paragraphs.text: CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.
These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

“We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”

The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”
Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”
The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.
SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.
Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid celluar-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

“I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-se.headline: Oil Set for Third Weekly Drop as Ample Supply Counters Iran Risk
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-se.author: Kanoko Matsuyama

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 19, 2026 at 3:05 PM PST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Oil edged higher after a volatile session on Thursday, with futures on track for a third weekly decline as traders weigh the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran against signs of ample supply.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The most-active contract for West Texas Intermediate traded near $83 a barrel after swinging in a range of more than $2 in the previous session, while Brent settled near $92.

US President Donald Trump told Axios he was "not rushing into any decision" on Iran, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Fox News played down concerns about regional supplies, saying flows through the Strait of Hormuz reached a record. The comments tempered concerns after Western officials said that the chances of the US launching another round of mass strikes against Iran had risen in recent days.

Global benchmark Brent has retreated about a fifth this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed strikes. Still, there's been a flare-up in low-level fighting across the region in recent days, including a spate of attacks on vessels transiting the critical Strait of Hormuz and strikes by Tehran-backed Houthis in Riyadh.

"While the near-term rise in geopolitical tensions is bringing some buying back to crude, the overall fundamentals are still moving more bearish," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc., pointing to Iraq selling physical crude at steep discounts.

Elsewhere, the leaders of the US, China and Russia agreed to "increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations" at a meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, according to a joint statement. They didn't spell out what that would entail.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Treasury Official Renews Warning on Wave of Tax-Saving Trades
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Justina Lee

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 19, 2026 at 2:31 PM PST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- A senior US Treasury official reiterated concerns Thursday about Wall Street's tax-efficient investing boom, saying firms should win clients on the merits of their investments, not on how far they'll go to minimize a tax bill.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Kevin Salinger, acting assistant secretary for tax policy at the Treasury, spoke at a Wall Street Tax Association conference in New York. His comments come after the department in late September issued a ruling on a strategy that uses exchange-traded funds to avoid capital gains taxes, along with a notice warning of possible action on other tactics.

"Businesses should be competing on investment performance, on fees, and on service," said Salinger, who is also acting chief counsel for the Internal Revenue Service. "Businesses should not be competing on who can take most tax risk and expose their investors to the most tax risk."

Salinger offered few new details on what action might be in store following the September notice, which identified tactics ranging from hedge funds that cut income tax to exchange-traded funds that turn interest income into capital gains. The rhetoric from government has been steadily increasing, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying last week that eliminating what he called "tax gimmicks" could help reduce the US budget deficit, without raising tax rates.

The recent IRS notice is "not necessarily exhaustive" and the government continues to "learn about new transactions that taxpayers are engaging in," Salinger added, without naming any additional trades. He reiterated the government has a range of tools at its disposal, including guidance and enforcement actions.

The business of tax-aware investing has proved highly lucrative for Wall Street, as it lures assets and earns fees from the growing ranks of wealthy Americans. Most are in products that harvest capital losses to offset gains from selling investments like a private business or equity holding, but a small group of firms has even found ways to generate ordinary losses that can offset income such as wages.

AQR Capital Management, the quant investing giant co-founded by Cliff Asness, has been at the forefront of the industry. A spokesperson for the firm didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

politico.com/news/2026/11/19/rob-sand-io.headline: Rob Sand shuts down any talk of 2028
politico.com/news/2026/11/19/rob-sand-io.author: Aaron Pellish

paragraphs.text: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand isn’t indulging any consideration of him as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

Sand, who cemented himself as a rising star in the party by flipping the governor’s seat in Iowa with a commanding 11-point victory, said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum that he’s unlikely to ever consider running for president.
“Are you completely taking 2028 off the table?” POLITICO’s Adam Wren asked Sand.
“Yes,” he replied.
When asked if he would ever consider running for president, Sand curtly replied, “Doubt it.”
Sand offered a tongue-in-cheek rebuttal to the suggestion that he could position himself as an influential voice and a power broker in the national conversation ahead of the next election.
“Ooh, that sounds exciting,” Sand quipped sarcastically before adding, “I expect to be a governor in 2027 and in 2028.”

Sand also declined to weigh in on his preference for who Democrats should nominate in the presidential primaries. Asked to choose between Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — all of whom campaigned for Democrats in Iowa in the midterms — Sand refused to take the bait.

“We have forever to go on all of this,” he said. “The people who want to do that, they're going to get in the race. They're going to do things. They're going to say things. We'll learn a lot more. Then we'll have a clear opinion about who should be doing what.”

Sand reiterated that he intends to keep Iowa’s Democratic caucuses as the first nominating contest on the calendar despite the Democratic Party removing Iowa from its early state lineup and encouraged Democratic presidential candidates to continue the tradition of visiting Iowa’s state fair next year.
“I'm pretty confident that we'll figure something out that means we're following Iowa law, and they're going to be able to do that,” he said.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/anthropic-riva.headline: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/anthropic-riva.author: Connie Loizos

paragraphs.text: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open-source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI and other heavyweights and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke on stage toward the end of the day.

Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “early talks” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
How far behind are open models right now?
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v2d8q879eo.headline: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v2d8q879eo.author: Orla Guerin

paragraphs.text: Senior international correspondentReporting fromIstanbul
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/apple-may-be-d.headline: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/apple-may-be-d.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/anthropics-7-f.headline: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/anthropics-7-f.author: Julie Bort

paragraphs.text: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”
With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.
Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.
Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.
The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.
All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/cin.headline: Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo, Fiona, dead at 9 years old
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/19/cin.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: Fiona, the beloved 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus, has died after ingesting a knit hat that fell into her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo last week.
Her many fans had been following her treatment, which included medication, a colonoscopy and time on a vibration plate, through updates posted by the zoo.
“We are in shock at the moment,” zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”

Born six weeks premature in 2017 at just 29 pounds — normal birth weight, her keepers said, ranges from 55 to 120 pounds — she became an internet sensation as the zoo documented her growth and progress online. Her first birthday celebration, for which she was served a tower of tropical fruits, was broadcast to thousands of fans on Facebook Live.
Hippos typically live 35 to 50 years.
The hat was flung into her habitat accidentally, the zoo said. There had been no sign that it had passed through her digestive system and out of her body.
Fiona was initially asymptomatic, the zoo said, but within a few days her appetite started to decline. She was sedated, examined and given medications, but the hat was not retrieved.

She was sedated again this week, the zoo said, for an evaluation that included a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. She was given fluids and medications to help her pass the hat. She was also given her favorite foods to encourage digestion.
On Wednesday, zoo staff members encouraged her to stand on a vibration plate borrowed from a nearby horse farm to help move the hat through her intestines.

Surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, the zoo said. Veterinary staff members tried everything they could to help her, the zoo said. “Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.”
“The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo said.
Before Fiona’s death was announced, the news station WCPO reported Thursday that students at local schools were making get-well cards for her.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.headline: Dollar Heads for Fourth Week of Gains Following Anthropic IPO
finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.author: Melos Ambaye

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The dollar is headed for a fourth straight weekly gain as demand tied to the Anthropic PBC IPO further lifts the currency that has been supported by expectations of further Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes and elevated US Treasury yields.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 0.7% this week — on track for its longest winning weekly streak since Oct. 9. The advance comes as artificial intelligence lab Anthropic shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday. The biggest-ever public debut created more demand for the dollar as investors across the globe converted their currency to buy shares in the company. Anthropic stock jumped 17% on its first day of trading.

"A fair estimate of foreign take-up of the IPO is probably in the $10 billion to $15 billion range," Brent Donnelly, president of Spectra Markets, wrote in a note Thursday. "Those US dollar buyers are racing against corporates who are trying to get their US dollar buying done before Thanksgiving."

While Anthropic is seen as a bellwether for the future of AI, the boom in the technology has already influenced Wall Street's long-term dollar forecasts. Barclays Plc, Deutsche Bank AG and Standard Chartered Bank expect the dollar to extend its rally into 2027, citing US dominance in AI and its potential to lift productivity and interest rates. Anthropic's listing adds to the appeal of the US equity market and positions the company to become one of the world's most important stocks in the space.

Foreign inflows into US stocks jumped 43% to $670 billion in the January-September period, the highest since at least 2016, according to data from the Department of the Treasury compiled by Bloomberg.
The dollar gauge is up more than 3% this year, strengthening against most of its major peers.

Nomura strategist Dominic Bunning said the world's reserve currency is benefiting from other sources of support this week. Treasury yields near recent highs are keeping carry trades in the dollar's favor, Bunning added. The US 10-year yield is poised for its longest stretch above 5% since 2007.

Meanwhile, Wednesday's Fed minutes from its latest meeting showed nearly all officials agreed the central bank would likely need to raise rates "in the months ahead" to return inflation to their 2% target in a timely manner. And concerns that violence in the Middle East could escalate added to inflation worries and lifted oil prices.

"This week's been all about de-risking," said Alex Cohen, a strategist at Bank of America Corp. "US data and Fed speakers have delivered a message that further rate hikes are coming and justified. That's a good mix for the US dollar."

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/20/race-t.headline: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/20/race-t.author: Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.headline: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.author: Tom Levitt

paragraphs.text: The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”

The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Catie McLeod

paragraphs.text: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials have said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

wsj.com/world/uk/u-k-government-borrowed.headline: UK Government Borrowed More in October, But Is on Track for Smaller Deficit

paragraphs.text: The U.K. government borrowed more in October than a year earlier, but it remained on course to reduce its budget deficit in the current fiscal year.
The Office for National Statistics on Friday said government spending exceeded its revenues by 17 billion pounds in October, an increase of 800 million pounds from the same month of 2025.
Over the first seven months of the fiscal year that will end in early April, borrowing was 111.3 billion pounds, down 7.3 billion pounds from the same period a year earlier.
At 3.5% of gross domestic product, the budget deficit for the fiscal year to October was lower than the 3.8% recorded a year earlier.
The government's total debt stood at 3.1 trillion pounds, or 95.8% of GDP, up from 93.9% in October 2025.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Bond Sales Hit €2 Trillion Europe Record as AI Surge Takes Hold
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Olga Voitova and Tasos Vossos

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Bond sales in Europe have topped €2 trillion ($2.2 trillion) for the first time, as unrelenting government borrowing collides with the vast funding needs of the artificial intelligence boom.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Tech companies are the biggest driver of the annual record, with US hyperscalers including Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. raising vast sums to finance the data centers and infrastructure needed for AI. With the tech race still gaining speed, borrowing is set to keep European bankers busy.

"Most of the growth in non-financial borrowing is driven by US firms seeking to tap funding from numerous bond markets," HSBC Holdings Plc strategists led by Song Jin Lee wrote this week in their outlook for 2027.

The surge materialized even as higher global interest rates pushed up financing costs, with euro high-grade corporate yields rising to levels last seen in 2023. Investor appetite for corporate debt has remained relatively strong, however, keeping the additional premium companies pay to borrow contained.

The €2 trillion milestone for the publicly syndicated debt market was reached on Thursday, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The record covers syndicated sales in euros, pounds and dollars issued under Regulation S, which allows securities to be sold outside the US without being registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Corporate borrowing is up about €49 billion from 2025, with roughly €37.5 billion of that increase coming from hyperscalers. Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. each rank among the top four non-financial bond issuers in European currencies this year.

Syndicated sales by governments, multinational institutions and government-backed organizations — which account for roughly 40% of the market — are at record levels but tracking close to last year's figures.

The borrowing binge has downsides. The constant stream of mega-deals by hyperscalers has made investors demand large premiums to invest in new issues. Secondary market trading levels of hyperscalers' euro bonds are in line with bonds rated several steps below their actual scores.

Syndicated sales form part of a larger trend in Europe. Governments, which also borrow via auctions, are using debt to fund spending on defense and infrastructure. Elevated issuance coincides with an increase in yields driven by higher energy costs.

France is contending with growing political and fiscal risks ahead of next year's presidential election, which may usher in a populist leader. Germany is set to be the largest gross issuer of debt among euro area peers next year, according to strategists at Commerzbank AG, who estimate the region as a whole could sell a record amount in excess of €1.5 trillion.
