finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Tech Valuation Plunge Brings Some Opportunities
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Michael Msika

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The sharp drop in the valuations of technology stocks, especially those linked to the artificial intelligence trade, is fueling debate over whether too much negativity has already been priced in.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Nasdaq 100, S&P InfoTech and Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index are all trading at multiyear lows relative to expected earnings. While AI enablers such as semiconductors have taken the biggest hit, companies spending heavily on data centers did also suffer. Some more signs of capitulation this week are making the timing difficult. Yet, after strong results from Nvidia Corp., a blockbuster debut for Anthropic PBC, and an overall washed-out positioning on tech, some investors see an opportunity.
"I think we're going to have a nice AI rebound," said Louis Navellier, founder of Navellier & Associates Inc. "Earnings remain strong, but it's shocking how the valuations are so cheap right now."
Stocks including Micron Technology Inc. and Super Micro Computer Inc. are trading less than four times forecast earnings, making them "an incredible buying opportunity," he said.

The divergence between share prices and earnings expectations has been striking. Analysts are still upgrading estimates after the latest reporting season. While firms still need to deliver on those expectations, it remains to be seen how long investors can stay on the sidelines if downgrades fail to materialize.

A capex cut from hyperscalers could be a trigger for further downside, but for now their spending commitments remain firm. While the Democratic sweep in the US midterms has revived debate over the AI buildout, the shift in political control seems unlikely to halt it, even if it could slow the pace. Since the start of the year, earnings estimates for tech stocks have sharply outpaced those for the broader market, especially so for semiconductors and hardware.

"Despite these uncertainties, recent results show continued strength in cloud services and AI computing demand," said Johan Van der Biest, co-global head of equity management at Candriam, who sees potential for tech to outperform the broader market.

"Investment is translating into revenue growth, while semiconductor and equipment suppliers have issued encouraging outlooks for 2027," he said. "The current earnings picture therefore remains supportive, even as investors question the longer-term returns."

It's not just valuations that look tempting. All profits generated through leveraged exchange-traded funds this year, which have been a popular way to bet big on AI, have now nearly been erased, according to calculations by Societe Generale SA.

Derivatives strategist Jitesh Kumar looked at SOXL and TQQQ, which offer three-times leveraged exposure to chipmakers and the Nasdaq-100, respectively. A situation at the end of July when the aggregate capital invested in South Korean leveraged single-stock ETFs began losing money, "subsequently proved to be a local bottom for the underlying stocks," he said.

Both ETFs have pretty much erased all their gains for the year, even though their unleveraged underlying instruments remain up. Looking at the SOXL in particular, the 84% drawdown it has just suffered is comparable to the biggest plunges seen over the past 10 years, which were followed by sharp rebounds.

Risks to tech stocks have not disappeared. A jumbo Federal Reserve interest-rate hike in December will likely derail any rally, while three hikes are expected over the next seven months. Yet, US crude is down more than 20% in November alone, and even signs of renewed escalation have failed to push prices up meaningfully.

With valuations this low, fundamentals still strong, a global economy set to accelerate in 2027 and a full rate hike already priced in for December, investors may experience some fear of missing out. That's not even accounting for a seasonality, which is typically on equities' side in November and December.

"We think positioning is cleaner and thus entry points are more attractive," said JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s market intelligence desk led by Andrew Tyler, who sees a Fed rate hike of 50 basis points in December as highly unlikely. "While the AI trade has given the market more to think about, demand is insatiable but the pace of the build out may be slower, which is not necessarily a bad thing as the commercial adoption rate and productivity gains increase."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Give UK Your Data, Nobel Economist Tells Anthropic and OpenAI
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Jacob Reid

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The UK's fledgling AI Economics Institute is aiming for what its chairman calls the "holy grail:" linking data from companies and AI labs with everything the government knows about individuals and businesses.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Having all of that information — including tax records and the HMRC business register — will help the institute work out how artificial intelligence is actually changing the economy, according to Simon Johnson, the Nobel prize-winning economist who chairs it.

"You can have a level of detail and texture that nobody else has, including the big labs, because they don't have the administrative data," Johnson told Bloomberg. That will help his institute gauge "what's happening to total jobs, who's losing a job, who's gaining a job, how does this match up with skills and experience," he said.

The UK government is trying to understand how AI is altering the economy as ministers seek to avoid stifling the development of the quickly-advancing technology while managing the risks associated with it.

"The range of plausible economic outcomes from AI is wide," the government said in June, setting out the institute's role. "AI is widely expected to raise productivity, but evidence of firm-level or aggregate effects remains limited."

Johnson's institute was set up by the government to build the evidence base ministers need to inform policy decisions and is modeled directly on the UK's AI Security Institute, which has become the world leader in testing cutting edge models before they're released. Last month Britain also announced an AI Biosecurity Lab to detect and monitor biological threats.

AI labs including Anthropic PBC — which held an initial public offering on Thursday — and OpenAI, have been "very positive" about working with the institute and haven't yet turned down a request for data, Johnson said. They already publish some usage data, but it's generally aggregated and excludes enterprise accounts.
Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to a request for comment.

Companies have also been "pretty open and thoughtful and candid" in confidentially sharing information about what they're using AI for and how tasks, roles and wages are changing, Johnson said. "Nobody is closing their ears, nobody says, 'Don't talk to me, I want to bury my head in the sand'."

The proliferation of institutes reflects the UK's broader approach to research, monitor and use the technology, rather than passing new regulations. Britain is trying to position itself as an "honest broker" on AI between the US, which has so far refrained from passing federal legislation, and the European Union, which quickly passed sweeping AI laws that are unpopular in the industry.

Explaining the similarities with the model-testing institute, Johnson said: "You have expertise, and you have some people who are established civil servants, and some people who are data nerds, and then you bring them together and you elevate them within Whitehall in such a way as they have access and they're available to answer questions."

AI helped the UK economy to grow at its fastest pace in two and a half years in the third quarter, Office for National Statistics data show. It will boost productivity by 0.2 percentage points a year in the medium term, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility, although it notes the scale and timing of that uplift is highly uncertain.
AI minister Kanishka Narayan has said how much the country adopts AI will be "the biggest driver" of whether the government has a surplus or needs to make cuts to meet its fiscal rules.

Johnson, who is from the UK but has lived in the US for 40 years, said the relationship between AI labs and the government is better in Britain. "This whole discussion or thinking around the social license to operate is much more salient here," he said. "And the EU is more on the lines of 'the answer is no, so what's the question?'"

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Anthropic Slumps 5% Post-Market After Record $107.3 Billion IPO
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Natasha Mascarenhas, Carmen Reinicke and Sangmi Cha

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC shares were down about 5% in post-market trading as the artificial intelligence developer wrapped up its first day as a public company after a record-setting $107.3 billion offering.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The late moves pared a debut pop of 17% on Thursday, which provided a rare bright spot as the Nasdaq fell 2.2%. The broader market continued on a downward trend into the Asian day, with global stocks poised for their longest losing streak in more than three years, as the AI trade cratered.

While the bright open for the Claude chatbot maker reflected massive investor appetite after a heavily oversubscribed initial public offering, the steep valuation — combined with fresh competitive threats — weighed heavily in after-hours trading, highlighting jitters over how long that momentum can hold.

"With what appeared to be the final pillar supporting the AI rally now giving way, market sentiment is now very pessimistic," said Gerald Gan, chief investment officer at Singapore-based Reed Capital. "While I am preparing to accumulate quality stocks at more attractive valuations, I am equally mindful of the risks of catching a falling knife."

MSCI Inc.'s Asia Pacific equities index fell 3.4%, extending its decline to a seventh session, and is poised for its lowest close since April. That pushed the MSCI All Country World Index — a key barometer of global stocks — on course for its longest losing streak since September 2023.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic's IPO had attracted global demand for seven times the shares available for sale, with investors outside the US pouring in billions of dollars, including those in Japan securing $3 billion in stock after seeking $9.4 billion in shares and $1.1 billion of stock bought by mom-and-pop investors in the UK and continental Europe.

The IPO vaulted Anthropic to the status of unrivaled AI industry leader — at least for the moment — and delivered billions of dollars in returns to its backers and pushed up the combined wealth of its seven founders to $166 billion. The record raise blasted by the $75 billion IPO record set in June by SpaceX, which ultimately totaled $86.25 billion with the so-called overallotment shares sold by the underwriters. Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record $550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic's IPO.

Anthropic's Nasdaq debut followed weeks of shaky trading in US stocks, which has left investors grappling with worries over Nvidia Corp.'s role as a major backstop of the AI ecosystem following its longtime chief's ouster and a Democratic sweep in midterm elections that promises to change the industry's regulatory landscape.

"You've seen sentiment sort of continue to worsen around AI and it has not let up today," said Jordan Watson, managing director of investments at Tandem Investment Advisors. "What's important for markets now is Anthropic is the most transparent real-time signal of the AI risk trade."

Anthropic closed at $97.17 Thursday in New York, paring an opening surge that took it as much as 39% above the IPO price of $83. It ended the day as the world's seventh-biggest public company with a fully diluted market value of about $1.8 trillion.

In a blow to sentiment, Apple Inc. said it is developing its own autonomous AI agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta Platforms Inc. and others.

Thursday's broader market weakness was "just a continuation of what we've seen for the last several weeks, and that is a lot of nervousness around the semiconductor space," said Gina Martin Adams, chief market strategist at HB Wealth. "The financing of the AI ecosystem is certainly a question that investors are asking and it's weighing on the market at large."
Some of the broader selloff may have also been fueled by investors selling positions in other companies to buy Anthropic shares, she added.

The company won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualized from a shorter period — to $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.

Claude Code, the company's coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering $100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.
The company aims to expand its footprint in more professions from law to healthcare. Anthropic counts Novartis AG CEO Vas Narasimhan as one of its board members.

A major challenge will be taming ballooning costs for AI infrastructure and reliably delivering operational profitability. Anthropic reported a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, primarily driven by $5 billion of computing costs under short-term commitments and $2 billion of non-cash charges related to the company's charitable donation-matching program.

"It popped like any other IPO on the first day but we will need to see solid results in the coming quarters, new use cases for AI, accelerating monetization etc to dispel the gloom in the AI trade," said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. "Investors don't have very many fundamental drivers to go on for Anthropic for now. A large part of the value is in the future, which is uncertain, so the share price movements will reflect that."

Goldman Sachs Group Inc. research analysts expect the company to take until 2030 to generate positive free cash flow on an annual basis, Bloomberg News reported. That said, they are modeling Anthropic's annual revenue to soar to roughly $685 billion by 2030, Bloomberg News has reported. To pull off that feat, it will need to fend off AI pricing pressures from cheaper open-weight models, including from Chinese developers.

Anthropic is expected to see a lift from index-tracking funds generating billions of dollars in demand. If it qualifies for early inclusion, it could join the Russell 1000 and the Nasdaq 100 as soon as December. FTSE Russell and Nasdaq changed their rules this year to speed the inclusion of large new listings.

finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/a.headline: The Anthropic IPO Is Adding to a Real Estate Frenzy in Major Tech Hubs
finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/a.author: Paulina Cachero and Francesca Maglione

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC's IPO is turning billions of dollars of paper fortunes into real ones. In the housing market, wealth from AI startups has already arrived.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Homes in San Francisco are drawing offers that can go for millions over asking. Buyers in New York and Miami are swooping in with all-cash deals, even when their wealth isn't yet liquid.

The wave of AI money is washing over major tech hubs as employees holding richly valued stakes in private companies find ways to unlock that wealth rather than waiting for an IPO or having to sell shares. Many are turning to specialty lenders for cash to compete in already heated housing markets, fueling bidding wars and soaring prices.

For startup workers, the arrangement can offer lower rates than conventional mortgages while turning paper wealth into attractive all-cash offers. For financial institutions racing to win the business of newly minted millionaires, advancing cash against private shares can help get these clients — and their assets — in the door.

"I've never seen anything like this," said David Cohen, the founder of City Real Estate, who has worked as a broker for more than two decades in San Francisco. He recently helped an AI company employee buy a five-bedroom home in Pacific Heights for $6 million, financed with a conventional mortgage that took his private stakes into account.
"We're not seeing bids over $100,000," Cohen said. "We're seeing millions of dollars overbid. It's the wild, wild west."

The median price of a single-family home in San Francisco — where major AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks and Scale AI are based — soared 29% last month from a year earlier to $2.39 million, the brokerage Compass reported this week. Forty homes sold for more than $5 million, the highest monthly total in records going back more than three decades.
A type of housing FOMO is playing out as wealthy buyers race to ink home deals before prices climb even higher, according to local real estate agents and wealth managers.

"There's a paranoia in SF that you have to buy a house before the AI companies go public, especially when people can pay all cash with 20% over asking," said Brooks Schaffer, a managing partner of wealth advisory firm Waypoint West, who recently helped a founder secure a $10 million loan to buy a home in cash.

The success of Anthropic's IPO, which raised more than $107 billion, means that the money will likely keep flowing. The stock soared 17% above its offering price Thursday, giving the company a fully diluted market value of about $1.8 trillion. That makes it one of the 10 biggest public companies in the world by market capitalization.

The tech housing boom is particularly striking at a time when elevated mortgage rates have brought much of the US real estate market to a crawl, pricing out would-be buyers and discouraging homeowners with cheaper existing loans from selling. The market at the higher end has been more resilient, fueled in part by wealthy buyers who are less constrained by conventional financing.

Borrowing against equity creates a risky link between artificial intelligence and housing at a time when fears are already mounting about the tech boom fizzling out. If private company valuations fall, these home borrowers could see their net worth and the value underpinning their loans shrink, said Deniz Kahramaner, founder of data-driven brokerage Atlasa.

"Even if it's not in a location that's backed by any fundamentals, they still pay what their budget affords — sometimes five or six million — which I've been warning my clients against," said Kahramaner. "If there's ever a correction, you could be in a lot of trouble."

Pledging private stakes to get cash without selling lucrative shares has long been a playbook for billionaire tech executives such as Elon Musk and Larry Ellison. During the pandemic's low-interest-rate fueled venture capital spending spree, specialized lenders began assessing private shares to dole out loans as tech valuations soared. After the 2023 collapses of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic Bank, which catered heavily to startups, Wall Street banks have stepped in with more of this type of lending.

Now, the AI boom is creating giant equity fortunes not just for founders, but for rank-and-file employees. In the third quarter, the median new job offer for software engineers at frontier AI labs hit more than $650,000, with equity for about 60% of the total compensation, according to crowdsourced data from Levels.fyi, a tech compensation platform.

Workers can tap specialty companies such as Secfi, which effectively provides cash upfront to employees with vested shares at certain companies. The terms vary based on factors including the valuation of their holdings and the amount they want to access. Secfi gets paid when the employer goes public or is acquired, at which point the worker owes the borrowed amount plus a percentage of the returns and a portion of shares, or the cash equivalent.

The firm saw a 40% increase in the volume of financing requests in the first half of 2026 compared with last year, representing billions of dollars. The "lion's share" of clients are using their credit option to fund home purchases, said Chief Operating Officer Jaime Moreno de los Rios.

For banks including JPMorgan Chase & Co., Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc., the terms and structures of private share financing vary widely by firm and borrower. Some are structured like traditional securities-backed lines of credit, where borrowers are typically required to make monthly interest-only payments based on a variable rate while the principal repayment is flexible. If the pledged stock's valuation tanks, the employee could face a margin call, requiring them to sell shares, pledge additional assets or pay cash to satisfy the balance.

JPMorgan, which purchased First Republic's assets, offers short-term, unsecured recourse loans where payment is due anywhere from 12 to 18 months. Lending from its asset and wealth-management business — which includes both secured and unsecured loans — hit $313.2 billion in the third quarter, up 21% from a year earlier. The bank assesses borrowers based on their full financial picture, including the value of private shares.

At Citizens Private Bank in San Francisco, Garret Spiecker has been working on this type of lending since before he moved over from First Republic Bank in June 2023. The underwriting is tied to a vetted list of companies and takes into account the value of the client's vested shares and their personal financials.

Lenders have gotten more comfortable with the financing given the enormous valuations of top AI companies and the many ways to monetize private shares, such as through tender offers or secondary sales, Spiecker said.
"They're just categorically private because they just haven't done an IPO, but everything else really is, looks, smells, feels like a public company," Spiecker said.
'Avalanche' of Wealth

The new liquidity is reaching high-end housing markets across the country. In New York, Compass real estate agent Philip Scheinfeld said he has helped close at least two deals this year with all-cash offers provided by lines of credit against private stock. A buyer in Miami purchased a five-bedroom, six-bathroom home for $4 million in cash, using financing secured by private company equity, said Miltiadis Kastanis, who also works as a broker for Compass.

"The most sophisticated buyers are not selling their investments to purchase a home, because they are taking a bet on the future growth of these investments," Kastanis said. "And securing this type of loan is faster, it's less paperwork, way less intrusive, and less intense than traditional real estate mortgages."

In San Francisco, a home near the Presidio recently listed for $8 million and went into contract at $15 million. A $4 million condo nestled in the affluent Cow Hollow neighborhood went to the highest bidder at 75% over asking. In September, buyers who work at a frontier AI lab overbid by more than $2 million on a nearly $7 million five-bedroom in Noe Valley within five hours of it being listed on the market. All were cash offers.

The founder of an AI startup recently made a nearly $4 million all-cash bid on a home that was listed at just $2.5 million, said Compass agent Michael Bellings, who represented the buyer. Armed with a flexible budget thanks to a cash advance from a bank that leveraged his private stakes, the founder took a "whatever it takes" strategy to finding a home, he said.

"There are all these buyers trying to get into the market before the IPO unleashes an avalanche of wealth," said Bellings, who is working with three 20-something founders with as much as $10 million sitting in their bank accounts. "I've never worked with clients who have a somewhat unlimited budget. For them, half a million to one million dollars is a rounding error in their home offers."
Rachel Swann, an agent for Coldwell Banker said one client who estimated their newfound wealth to be around $30 million to $50 million, casually set their home budget at $10 million.

"Just because you can go to 10 doesn't mean you should," said Swann, who says she's been making a lot of referrals to wealth managers. "You've got these kids who are making $5 million and half of them are like, 'what's a credit card?'"

It's a marked turn for San Francisco, which just a few years ago was written off as being in a post-pandemic "doom loop." Given the history of the boom-and-bust city, some type of correction is inevitable, said Cohen of City Real Estate.
"These prices seem frothy and it's unclear if it's going to last," said Cohen. But "even if it drops, prices will still be higher than where we started."
--With assistance from Sophie Alexander.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: SpaceX Sells $32 Billion of AI Chip Debt at Yields Topping 8%
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Brian Smith, Davide Barbuscia and Caleb Mutua

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- SpaceX sold $32 billion of bonds to fund its purchase of artificial intelligence chips on Thursday, in a complicated and relatively high-yielding transaction that may serve as a model for a wave of similar financings to come.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The debt offering was designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX's balance sheet, and is part of a more than $40 billion financing that also includes bank loans. The deal will effectively allow SpaceX to buy Nvidia Corp. chips that the rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company will lease for about five years.

The debt was sold on Thursday in three parts, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Apollo Global Management Inc. ran the transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified as they're not authorized to speak publicly. Representatives for the firms and SpaceX didn't respond to requests for comment.

The biggest of the three portions sold on Thursday, about $25.2 billion of Class A3 notes, were priced at a yield of 8.259%, a relatively high level for an investment grade security. The average US high-grade note yielded 5.95% on Thursday, according to Bloomberg index data. The bonds also offered a premium over SpaceX's existing debt from its June offering, which tanked in the secondary market after the securities started trading.

Investors had already committed to buy about $26 billion of the bonds earlier, with the final $6 billion, part of the Class A3, offered on Thursday. Many of the securities were sold to investors that focus on blue-chip corporate bonds.

The chips will be bought through a special-purpose vehicle known as Saturn Funding Trust and managed by an Apollo-backed entity. SpaceX is leasing from the vehicle, and has committed to make the payments even if the equipment fails or there's an extraordinary occurrence like a natural disaster, known as a "force majeure" event.

The financing structure is expected to help SpaceX maintain investment-grade credit ratings — a critical competitive advantage for many of the biggest companies competing in the AI space, because it allows them to borrow more money, faster.

Bret Johnsen, SpaceX's chief financial officer, highlighted the company's "strong investment-grade balance sheet" on a conference call with investors after posting results last month. SpaceX sold $86.2 billion of stock in a June initial public offering and priced $25 billion of high-grade corporate bonds days later.

Companies will need some $1.5 trillion to pay for computer chips driving the artificial intelligence buildout, and deals to finance these purchases will probably become more commonplace, Scott Goodwin, co-founder of hedge fund manager Diameter Capital Partners, said at a conference this week.
"It's a new asset class," Goodwin said.

Tech companies are tapping all corners of capital markets to raise the trillions of dollars needed for data centers and other AI infrastructure, testing the depths of investor demand and risking indigestion. Thursday's debt sale came one day after AI giant Anthropic PBC completed the largest-ever initial public offering, exceeding SpaceX's own IPO.

After investors lost money on SpaceX's earlier unsecured bond offering, "we've definitely had concern from clients that are very skeptical about how is this deal going to go," said Davis Hebert, head of technology, media and telecom at research firm CreditSights. "I do think that's why the pricing on this is really wide to try and attract participation for more traditional investors."

The latest deal structure was complex for investment-grade investors to analyze, particularly as financing deals tied to AI graphics processing units, or GPUs, are relatively new, with investors still assessing risks related to the lifecycle and valuation of the chips.
BlackRock Inc., Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR & Co. accounts were among the anchor investors in the latest transaction, the company said in October.

SpaceX is raising a total of more than $40 billion through the broader transaction, which includes the bonds priced Thursday and a senior secured loan. The debt package will be used to pay for about $47.3 billion of GPU equipment, namely Nvidia's latest Rubin chips, earlier documents showed. Delivery of the chips is expected to begin in January.
