theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/20/c.headline: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/20/c.author: Mark Sweney

paragraphs.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/cali.headline: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/cali.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/the-u-s-nation.headline: The U.S. national cyber director is stepping down
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/the-u-s-nation.author: Dominic-Madori Davis

paragraphs.text: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.
We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/20/spac.headline: Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit
theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/20/spac.author: Ian Sample

paragraphs.text: After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world.

The BepiColombo mission will become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit.

For researchers, the €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission is the best hope yet of understanding how Mercury formed so close to the sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what makes up the frozen ice that lurks in the planet’s permanently shadowed craters.
“We’re very excited, it’s been a long wait,” said Prof Emma Bunce at the University of Leicester, who has worked on the project for 20 years.

Getting to Mercury poses unusual difficulties. Because the planet is near the centre of the solar system, spacecraft accelerate under the sun’s gravity and must spend much of their time braking to avoid shooting straight past. “It’s a very complex and challenging mission,” said Bunce, the principal investigator on an instrument called the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer, or MIXS, which will analyse the geochemical composition of the planet’s surface.

It will be some months before scientists can start observing Mercury. In early December, the spacecraft will separate into two orbiters, one European, the other Japanese, which will manoeuvre to different polar orbits around the planet. Science operations are due to start in April next year.

The European probe, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter or MPO, will map the planet’s surface and composition at high resolution, and study Mercury’s interior to shed light on its unusually large core. Its Japanese partner will measure the planet’s magnetic field and its sodium exosphere, the extremely thin layer of gas and atoms that surrounds the planet. Mercury is only 50% larger than the moon but has four times its mass. One question the mission will explore is why the rock is so dense.

Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist on BepiColombo at the European Space Agency, said anticipation of the scientific results had kept everyone enthused during the spacecraft’s eight-year journey.
“We’re expecting to learn a huge amount, bringing more powerful instruments on two spacecraft to study all aspects of the planet – its interior, surface, and the space around it,” he said.

Mercury is a planet of extremes. The tiny world takes 58 Earth days to rotate on its axis, meaning any given spot on the surface can experience daylight for three months and then night-time for three months. It is little more than a third of Earth’s distance from the sun, at only 36m miles. In the day, ground temperatures reach 450C while at night they drop to -180C.

Jones said: “As well as cameras covering a wide range of wavelengths to study the surface, we’ll be ‘tasting’ the gases around the planet, sensing the magnetic field, probing the interior with ultrasensitive instruments, and mapping the shape of the whole planet with a laser.”

The spacecraft are expected to orbit Mercury for about three years, after which they will run out of fuel, lose altitude and ultimately slam into the surface. “Sadly, they are not coming back,” said Bunce.

theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/20/pill.headline: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/20/pill.author: Helena Horton

paragraphs.text: A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.

In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.

Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.

Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.

He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”
Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.
There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.

Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.

“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/20/when.headline: When Nazis were held responsible for war crimes
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/20/when.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: The camera lights in Courtroom 600 were so bright that the defendants were issued sunglasses.

World War II was over, and the victorious Allies — the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France — had gathered in Nuremberg, Germany, to convene history’s first international war crimes tribunal.

More than 20 surviving leaders of the Third Reich stood accused of war crimes, crimes against peace and crimes against humanity, and the U.S. Army Signal Corps was filming the proceedings for newsreels to show in movie theaters around the world.

The choice of venue was symbolic. Nuremberg was where the Nazi Party had orchestrated its annual mass rallies, as captured in Leni Riefenstahl’s propaganda film “Triumph of the Will.” At the 1935 edition, the party announced rules stripping German Jews of their citizenship, public offices, professional licenses and other legal rights — the Nuremberg Laws — laying the foundation for the Holocaust.
Allied bombers had destroyed much of the Bavarian city, but its Palace of Justice and adjacent prison remained largely intact. The first trial opened on Nov. 20, 1945, 81 years ago Friday.

Chief among the Nazis’ crimes was the extermination of 6 million European Jews and millions more Poles, Roma, homosexuals and others. In the indictments, prosecutors pioneered a new legal term: genocide. The accused, they charged, had committed “murder and ill-treatment of civilians” in a “deliberate and systematic genocide, viz., the extermination of racial and national groups.”

The first defendants, all men, included Deputy Führer Rudolf Hess, Luftwaffe commander Hermann Göring, foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and war production minister Albert Speer. All pleaded not guilty. (Adolf Hitler, propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels and SS chief Heinrich Himmler killed themselves before the German surrender.)

The International Military Tribunal included one judge from each of the four European Allies. President Harry S. Truman appointed former attorney general Francis Biddle the U.S. judge and named Supreme Court associate justice Robert Jackson the chief U.S. prosecutor.

The courtroom held hundreds of members of the international media. The proceedings were translated into several languages and fed live to participants’ headsets, the first major use of simultaneous translation.

The prosecutors presented documents, witness testimony, including from the commandant of the infamous Auschwitz death camp, and graphic footage showing the Allied liberation of Nazi concentration camps — one of the first uses of film as trial evidence.

Defendants argued that they had merely done what they were told by their superiors, their actions had been legal under German civil and military authorities and they should not be held responsible for violations that weren’t clearly defined before the war.

The tribunal rejected the just-following-orders defense, ruling that individual conscience and international law supersede obedience to command, an important precedent. The judges found that the charges were based on existing principles in the conduct of war, not new concepts.
Of the first group of defendants, 19 were convicted and three acquitted. Twelve were sentenced to death; 11 were hanged. Göring killed himself by taking cyanide on the eve of the scheduled execution.

Trials of Axis leaders would continue in Nuremberg and Tokyo, where the panel included judges from the four European allies plus China, the Philippines, India, Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands, as the colonial ruler of the Dutch East Indies, much of which is now Indonesia.
Through 1951, the Allies tried and convicted thousands of defendants and sentenced nearly 1,000 to death.

Nuremberg was the first time multiple countries had come together to prosecute defendants jointly, and the first time individuals were personally held accountable under international law. It’s remembered as a key step in the development of international law and the law of war, and a model for the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
Photo Almanac is an occasional series from The Washington Post, using photo archives to understand where we are today by examining where we’ve been.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/17/r.headline: Rich people are spending 13 times more than poor on their kids
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/17/r.author: Julie Z. Weil

paragraphs.text: The gap between how much the rich and the poor spend on their children is widening dramatically.

That’s the conclusion of a new analysis of highly detailed federal data on consumer spending. Orestes P. Hastings, a sociologist at Colorado State University, found that since 1980, the poorest Americans have slightly decreased their spending on their children’s education, care and extracurriculars — while the richest Americans have quadrupled what they spend.

Nearly 50 years ago, Hastings found, rich people spent three times as much as poor people on their children’s care and schooling, and twice as much as middle-income parents. Now, the top 10 percent of earners spend 13 times as much as low-income families and five times as much as the middle 50 percent.

“We attribute a lot of it to the rising pressure,” said Hastings, himself a father who is home-schooling his three children. “It feels more important to the parents for the kids to do well, so they increase their investment in higher quality extracurriculars and schooling. … Families at the top end who have the resources are feeling pressure to dedicate even more of these resources toward their children.”

It’s not that lower-income families don’t feel the same pressure to prepare their children for a highly competitive higher education landscape and uncertain future job market, Hastings added. But at a time of rising costs for necessities such as health care and housing, they simply don’t have the discretionary income to put toward education that rich people do.

“The most surprising was the finding that among the lower-income parents, there is a decline,” said Mariana Amorim, a Washington State University sociologist not involved in the research. “Budgets are more squeezed now than they were in the past. … The price of everything else is going up, so they don’t have the money in their budget.”

Hastings’ analysis of the Bureau of Labor Statistics’s Consumer Expenditure Survey examined only parental spending on child care, education and extracurricular activities, not shorter-term spending on goods like toys and technology.
He found not just that wealthy people spent more money, but that the percentage of their household budget that they devoted to child care and education climbed.

Nina Bandelj, whose recent book “Overinvested” discusses the increased pressure on parents to spend on their children’s development, said companies have worked to persuade rich parents to spend more, including private equity firms that have bought day care chains and gotten into the high-cost children’s sports business.

“With the big parenting economy, all of these things involve a lot of money. Things have become much more expensive both because we value them so much and also because there’s an economy that feeds on parental ideas of what’s best for their children,” she said. “It’s very easy to do that: sell something to a parent who’s exhausted and wants to do the best for their kid.”
For child care, one reason wealthy families are spending more now than in the 1980s is that more mothers are working rather than solely taking care of their young children.

One reason poor families are spending less is that subsidized care has become more widely available. Public preschool is offered in 45 states and covers close to half the 4-year-olds in the U.S. for some part of the day.

Amorim said costlier care often tracks with better care, but not always. Families who aren’t spending anything on child care might have kids enrolled in a great public program, or might be struggling to cobble together a plan.
“Grandma could be great child care … or it could be spotty and unpredictable,” she said. “We just see the amount that’s being spent. We have no measure of quality.”
Hastings said it’s difficult to assess how much unequal spending on children drives future inequality.

“It’s not clear to me,” he said. “Is it really the case that children who go to a more expensive private education or tutoring, are they really going to turn out better than children who don’t? It’s usually parents who already have a lot of resources.”

Amorim said that while spending “probably” matters for children’s futures, “it’s really hard to separate the amount of money” from other benefits that rich parents can often offer, like connections through social networks.
“We can’t say that each dollar buys better outcomes,” she said.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/big.headline: Bigfoot believers get a boost from an unlikely ally: the U.S. Forest Service
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/big.author: Annie Gowen

paragraphs.text: For decades, the U.S. Forest Service has been officially mum on Bigfoot, beyond the occasional cheeky social media post treating the hairy cryptids as little more than a fun bit of folklore.
But in recent weeks, while the federal government released its latest batch of UFO files, it has taken a similar, albeit far more limited, tack on the age-old mystery of its terrestrial domain.

Last month, the agency quietly posted three historical documents from its archive that included accounts of Bigfoot encounters in Montana and Washington state dating to 1941. And in a California national forest, the agency hosted a forum near Yosemite called “Bigfoot in Your Backyard,” with presentations from two Forest Service employees who spoke about them matter-of-factly.
“He smells bad, he screams, he howls, wood knocks and whistles,” said Kathy Marquez, a visitor information services employee. “All sizes from little to big, male and female, have been seen.”
Kathy Strain, the Stanislaus forest’s archaeologist, said there have been 65 recorded sightings in her patch of the Western Sierra Nevada over the years.

Strain is a true believer. Years ago, when she was out with other Bigfooters, Strain says she saw two of the furry humanoids moving through the underbrush of the Ouachita Mountains in Oklahoma — a sight that gave her a “mild panic attack.”

Bigfoot aficionados are hoping the agency’s actions are a sign of a new approach — like the Trump administration’s new program to unseal and release government documents related to UFOs (or as they call them “Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena”). But the Forest Service won’t say for sure.

As part of the UFO program, the Defense Department released a 2010 investigation into reported paranormal goings-on at a ranch in Utah that included witness reports of “dog-like creatures” over 6 feet tall that walked on two legs. (Hair samples collected from the ranch matched dogs and a raccoon.)
“Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?” Jeremiah Byron, the host of the podcast Bigfoot Society, asked in an interview.
His voice dropped, low and conspiratorial.

“I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information about Bigfoot,” he said. “People need to be aware it’s the right time to come forward and talk about what you’ve seen, if the government’s starting to talk about it.”

For the uninitiated into this world of cryptozoology, Bigfoot is not thought to be one single creature, like Godzilla, but a humanoid species roaming forests across North America. (Its name doesn’t use an “s” to make it plural, like deer or sheep.)

Stories of hairy creatures that walk on two legs, emit eerie growling and a foul smell and live in the remote woods have persisted for centuries from cultures all over the world, including from Native American tribes in the United States. The native Me-Wuk in the Sierra foothills have an oral tradition about “Yayali”— a giant, hirsute creature that is best avoided.
A big year for Bigfoot
It must be said that most scientists reject the existence of Bigfoot, noting that credible proof — remains, scat or a clear video, even with modern trail cams — does not exist.
Still, it’s been a notable few months in Bigfoot Country.

On Oct. 20, the release of the documentary “Capturing Bigfoot” shook believers to their core. The filmmakers used archival footage and family interviews to debunk the most famous Bigfoot video ever recorded, a glimpse of a hulking being with brown matted fur loping along a creek bed in a forest in Northern California in 1967.
The nearly one-minute video clip has been debated, discussed and analyzed in the Bigfoot community for decades, a Zapruder film for enthusiasts.
But according to the film, the Bigfoot clip was an elaborate fake, a ruse sustained for decades.

The man who filmed the video, Roger Patterson, was a down-on-his-luck cowboy with an artistic streak who was trying to raise money to complete a Bigfoot movie, one of his accomplices told filmmaker Marq Evans. Patterson likely constructed the Bigfoot costume in a shed in his backyard, using fur coats.
The documentary — which has a 100 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes — dropped like a bomb in the thriving online community of amateur sleuths, conspiracy theorists and trackers, Byron said.
“It will blow your mind,” said Byron. “It’s pretty clear we’re looking at a hoax.”

The U.S. Forest Service document post on Oct. 15 was less explosive but no less significant in Byron’s view. The documents appeared without warning in its Freedom of Information Act reading room under the heading “Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records.”

The first details a Forest Service investigation into tracks found by a part-time ranger in the Washington part of the Umatilla National Forest in 1982. Two others were in Montana, where locals detailed encounters with foul-smelling creatures crashing through the underbrush and finding other tracks.

A spokesman said the agency had little to share about why the documents were posted, except to note that that the USDA — which oversees the service — weighs several factors when deciding to release records online — including if the records are likely to attract attention from the media, researchers, historians, businesses or the general public.

“Stories of Bigfoot, Sasquatch, and other legendary creatures have long been part of the cultural fabric of the Sierra and continue to add to the rich tradition of folklore that surrounds our public lands,” the spokesman said.

The Washington investigation stemmed from a report by a part-time forest patrolman, Paul Freeman, who told his superiors that he saw a Bigfoot in a remote biological research area in the forest near Walla Walla. Days later, he claimed to have discovered tracks.

A wildlife biologist and a tracker for the U.S. Border Patrol investigated those tracks and ruled out Bigfoot as the source, saying they were isolated and constructed by something that had rocked from side to side, the documents show.

Grover Krantz, a late anthropology professor at Washington State University who researched Bigfoot and advocated its existence, disagreed. He studied the casts of the footprints and claimed they were authentic, because the dermal ridges of the foot would have been impossible to fake.

Freeman’s son Michael, an Amazon warehouse employee who frequently speaks of his late father’s record, defended him in an interview, saying that after the negative controversy his dad left the Forest Service and moved the family away to another part of the state.
But he never stopped looking for Bigfoot and in 1992 produced a shaky video that captured a glimpse of a dark creature in the trees.
Michael Freeman recalled that he was home playing video games with his friends when his father returned from the excursion, pale, shaky and yelling, “I got it!”
He then played a video of what he said he had found for the teens, of which Freeman says now, “I can tell you what it’s not, it’s not a bear. I’m 99 percent sure it’s not a man in a suit.”
“My dad was like Superman,” he continued. “It was the only time in my entire life, including the day he died, I ever saw him scared of anything.”
The video spread and soon became yet another slice of Bigfoot lore, eternally debated and analyzed by the faithful, inspiring deep skepticism in others.
Freeman said he did not know why the Forest Service had released the documents now, but he welcomed it.
“Any and all information should be released. Nobody is trying to hide anything,” he said.
Strain was heavily influenced as a child by the “Hairy Man,” prehistoric pictographs on the Tule River Indian Reservation, near where she grew up, that depict humanoid figures that resemble Bigfoot.

Now she’s a member of the North American Wood Ape Conservancy, a group of scientists dedicated to studying the creature they call the “North American wood ape,” or Bigfoot. She was out “Bigfooting,” as she calls it, with the group when she claims she had her sighting of two young creatures in 2012.
She said the moment left her both elated and deeply shaken, as the two creatures scrambled speedily away over rocky terrain.
“I had been told before they were fast but when you really see it you’re kind of shocked. I had no idea they could move like that,” she said.

On Oct. 8, a standing-room-only crowd gathered in a meeting room in the Stanislaus forest, where Marquez opened up the presentation and then played a video of Strain explaining the history of Bigfoot in the area and making a pitch for Bigfoot tourism.

“If you’re interested in seeing Bigfoot, or having an adventure or maybe catch a little glimpse or seeing some footprints, come to the Stanislaus National Forest ... Tuolumne County has the second-most Bigfoot sightings in all of California,” she said.
Marquez played tapes of supposed Bigfoot howls and displayed a map of numerous sightings along Route 108, which passes through the forest crossing the Sierras.

But she ended the program with a caveat: “While the forest cannot confirm or deny the existence of Bigfoot, we recognize his cultural impact, his place in tribal lore and his significance on the Stanislaus.”
Razzan Nakhlawi contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/20/glo.headline: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/20/glo.author: Lauren Almeida, Graeme Wearden

paragraphs.text: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/ice-.headline: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/ice-.author: José Olivares

paragraphs.text: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.
Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/business/anthropi.headline: Anthropic Shares Slip as AI and Tech Stock Sell-Off Continues

paragraphs.text: The blockbuster market debut for Anthropic, one of the biggest players in artificial intelligence, was not enough to turn the broader tide for stocks, with major indexes slumping at the end of another tumultuous week for investors.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq benchmarks were on course for their worst weeks in well over a year, dragged down by technology stocks as traders question the durability of the A.I. boom.

The S&P 500 has fallen over 5 percent through Thursday, the worst week for the index since April 2025, when the market convulsed in response to the announcement of President Trump’s sweeping global tariffs. Futures markets suggested that stocks would continue to slide when U.S. trading opens on Friday.
Anthropic’s stock, after surging by double-digit percentages in its trading debut on Thursday, itself slipped 8 percent premarket.

The declines have persisted despite generally favorable reactions from analysts and investors to the week’s major events, billed ahead of time as pivotal to the A.I. trade that has powered the market for months but has faltered more recently.

Nvidia’s earnings report on Tuesday helped to calm fears of a slowdown in growth of the A.I. build-out, with the giant chip maker raising its profit forecast. It was a brief respite for the company, which is reeling after the resignation of its larger-than-life chief executive, Jensen Huang, following revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials determined was feeding information to Beijing.

Then on Thursday, Anthropic jumped more than 17 percent in its first day of trading, achieving a trillion-dollar valuation after setting a record for the largest public offering in history. Robust demand for the shares of the maker of the Claude chatbot suggested that investors were still optimistic about aspects of the A.I. industry.

But the rest of the market has continued to slide. The S&P 500 has fallen for six straight trading days, its longest losing streak since April 2024. Every sector of the index is lower for the week, led by tech shares. The Nasdaq Composite is on course for a loss of 5 percent this week.

“Unfortunately, there isn’t an obvious catalyst or event to improve sentiment as we head into year-end,” said Stuart Kaiser, an analyst at Citi, adding that “there are no clear signposts to swing the pendulum.”

Traders tend to book profits in the run-up to Thanksgiving, mindful that markets slow into the end of the year, which can make it harder to move in and out of positions. There is also typically trepidation around this time about holding large positions through year’s end.

Nvidia has fallen nearly 40 percent since the S&P 500 peaked in early October, accounting for roughly half of the 8 percent drop in the index over that period, according to Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist for LPL Financial. Nvidia has been “the big factor” weighing on the market, he said, emblematic of “the broader fear over an A.I. slowdown.” The chip maker’s stock was down, again, in premarket trading on Friday.

Chip makers and related stocks were also weighed down by a report released on Thursday by Hunterbrook, a short-selling firm that profits from bets against companies, that claimed Advanced Micro Devices had supplied U.S.-blacklisted Chinese companies with updates to keep its chips running. (AMD said that the claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships.”)

Anthropic’s newly listed stock soared as much as 38 percent in early trading on Thursday, but as the day progressed, the air came out of the company’s ballooning price. Its shares ended the day up 17 percent, at $97 a share.
That’s still a healthy rise from its I.P.O. price of $83 per share, but suggested a more restrained optimism for the company’s prospects than the initial flurry of trades.

Still, analyst recommendations for the Anthropic, collated by the market data firm FactSet, show bullish expectations for the future. Ben Reitzes at Melius Research represents the high-water mark, with an initial price target of $155 per share. At the other end of the spectrum is Patrick Walravens at Citizens, with a target of $125.

But the CBOE Vix Volatility index, a measure known as the market’s “fear gauge,” which measure investors’ expectations of volatility over the next 30 days, recently rose just above its peak in the whipsaw aftermath of the midterm elections, a sign of market jitters.

“There’s been a lot of talk about whether the A.I. trade had gotten ahead of itself,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, who pointed to Nvidia’s strong earnings and the initial rise in Anthropic’s shares as “notable” signs for investors. “That doesn’t settle every valuation debate,” he added, “but it’s pretty strong affirmation that the market is not ready to walk away from the trade just yet.”

technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149371/.headline: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149371/.author: Thomas Macaulay

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

• Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

• AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”
• Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”
• It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”
• There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”
To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/behind-jensen-.headline: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/behind-jensen-.author: Connie Loizos

paragraphs.text: Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”

Well, maybe not everyone does. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, and also by humiliating people.

According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate them with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him, and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-greens.headline: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-greens.author: Ashley Capoot

paragraphs.text: Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release on Friday.
The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and net an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."
Shares of the Claude maker closed 17% higher in their first day of trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday, but they've fallen more than 11% in pre-market trading on Friday as a tech selloff intensifies.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/california-ag-.headline: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/california-ag-.author: Ram Iyer

paragraphs.text: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of the company’s former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The state is investigating the company to find out if Nvidia’s advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government itself is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent thinks Nvidia’s board should hire an outsider to replace Huang as CEO, saying on Fox News earlier this week that the company “needs a dramatic shake-up.”
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/6-ai-powered-g.headline: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/6-ai-powered-g.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.
From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159)
If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, Flowtica’s Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.
You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.
The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
Anker Soundcore Work ($159)
Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work, is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

Priced at $159, the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to five meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.
The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.
If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).
Logitech MX Keypad ($99)

Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.

The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.
Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($629)
Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital note-taking lineup, and also offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

Starting at $629, the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.

Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.
Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249)
If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.

Priced at $249, this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.

The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.
Autonomous Desk Pro ($599)
Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.

Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.

The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Anne Davies

paragraphs.text: The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.
Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.
“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.
Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.
Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.
Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.
The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.
“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.
This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.
Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.
But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.
If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.
Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.
• Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

paragraphs.text: What to know about the Iran war today:
• President Trump told an Israeli TV network on Thursday that he is "not rushing" and could wait until 2027 to make a decision on his next move in the war with Iran.

• Despite Mr. Trump's remark, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, with the Netanyahu administration concerned about how rapidly Iran is rebuilding its weapons production capacity.

• Iran on Thursday rejected Mr. Trump's accusation that it may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, with the foreign ministry saying U.S. allegations "keep changing" and are following "the same fraudulent script" as the justification for the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq.
U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.

Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions.
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.

The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.

For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.

Iran's foreign ministry rejected on Thursday President Trump's accusation that the country may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, comparing the claims to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting to the United Nations that Iraq had obtained weapons of mass destruction.

Baqaei cited the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, which Washington justified with the claim of weapons of mass destruction being developed by Saddam Hussein's government, and asked why Americans would fall for it again.

paragraphs.text: Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo, Fiona, dead at 9 years old
Fiona, the beloved 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus, has died after ingesting a knit hat that fell into her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo last week.
Her many fans had been following her treatment, which included medication, a colonoscopy and time on a vibration plate, through updates posted by the zoo.
“We are in shock at the moment,” zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”

Born six weeks premature in 2017 at just 29 pounds — normal birth weight, her keepers said, ranges from 55 to 120 pounds — she became an internet sensation as the zoo documented her growth and progress online. Her first birthday celebration, for which she was served a tower of tropical fruits, was broadcast to thousands of fans on Facebook Live.
Hippos typically live 35 to 50 years.
The hat was flung into her habitat accidentally, the zoo said. There had been no sign that it had passed through her digestive system and out of her body.
Fiona was initially asymptomatic, the zoo said, but within a few days her appetite started to decline. She was sedated, examined and given medications, but the hat was not retrieved.

She was sedated again this week, the zoo said, for an evaluation that included a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. She was given fluids and medications to help her pass the hat. She was also given her favorite foods to encourage digestion.
On Wednesday, zoo staff members encouraged her to stand on a vibration plate borrowed from a nearby horse farm to help move the hat through her intestines.

Surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, the zoo said. Veterinary staff members tried everything they could to help her, the zoo said. “Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.”
“The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo said.
Before Fiona’s death was announced, the news station WCPO reported Thursday that students at local schools were making get-well cards for her.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.author: Jeffrey Sparshott

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- US consumer sentiment picked up in November as gasoline prices fell, the outlook for business conditions improved and inflation expectations plunged.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The University of Michigan's final sentiment index increased to 51.5 from 48 in October, according to the survey released Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists projected November sentiment would rise to 51.6.

The university conducted its survey from Oct. 20 through Nov. 16, a span that saw Democrats take the House, the Senate and flip governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada during midterm elections.
The economy and affordability were key issues during the contest. Democrats' sweeping victory in part reflected voter frustrations with high costs for food, gasoline, healthcare and housing.

Inflation expectations in the year ahead plummeted, the survey showed. Consumers expect prices to rise 3.7% over the next year, the lowest since February and down from 4.7% in October. They saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.3% over the next five to 10 years, also down from last month.
Consumer views of current conditions and expectations for the future both improved.

"Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come," Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement. "Accordingly, the expectations index surged for independents."
Following the election, expectations for gas prices sank and are now "broadly comparable to pre-Iran readings," Hsu added.
A gauge of current personal finances also rose to the highest since July.

US households still face elevated inflation, with economists estimating that consumer prices rose about 4% from a year earlier in October. Borrowing costs are also high, with interest rates on a 30-year mortgage running above 7% since mid-September.
Relentless price increases helped push consumer sentiment to a record low in May and to the second-lowest level on record in October.
More recently, households have gotten some relief on at least one front: gasoline prices.

The national average price of a gallon of gasoline was above $4 at the beginning of the month, according to data from AAA, but had dropped to about $3.75 when the University of Michigan survey concluded.
