finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/sa.headline: Sanofi Lines Up Takeover Target to Fix Pharma’s Lowest Valuation
finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/sa.author: Margaryta Kirakosian

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- To understand why Sanofi is pursuing what would be the biggest takeover in the pharmaceutical industry in years, look no further than one number.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Even after a surge since early October, the stock trades at 9 times estimated earnings, making Sanofi the cheapest among the world's 10 biggest pharmaceutical companies by sales. The multiple is below the group average of 17.3. The stock is underperforming many of its big rivals this year.

Investors aren't willing to pay up for Sanofi because — while it's posting booming sales now of its skin and asthma drug Dupixent — they can see the dreaded patent cliff coming. Dupixent will begin to lose patent protection in 2031, and skeptics aren't convinced the company has the experimental treatments in its pipeline to replace the revenue.

That leaves the option of acquiring promising drugs: Sanofi is considering an acquisition of US drugmaker Insmed Inc., people familiar with the matter said this week. The company has a market value of $31.6 billion and has two approved drugs for respiratory diseases on the market.

"Bold moves rarely come without risks, and it might be the right time for Sanofi's management to take some calculated chances," Abhishek Raval, an analyst at Alphavalue in Paris, said by email. Buying Insmed "would certainly be a massive step in answering the market's pressing question around Sanofi's life after Dupixent."

Both companies have declined to comment on a potential deal, which would be the biggest in the industry since Pfizer Inc. bought Seagen Inc. for $43 billion in late 2023. Sanofi shares fell 2.9% Thursday on the report, though they pared some of that drop on Friday.
Chief Executive Officer Belén Garijo has made it clear she knows investors are looking ahead.

"The whole organization is focused on managing Sanofi's post-Dupixent trajectory over the next decade," she said in the company's earnings statement last month. "Our priority is to protect earnings through Dupixent's loss of exclusivity." Sanofi raised its full-year sales and profit forecasts for a second straight quarter on strong demand for Dupixent.
Garijo took charge of Sanofi this year after previously working at Merck KGaA, and investors are still assessing her ability to pull off the kind of acquisition Sanofi may need.

The company probably can afford to spend more than €25 billion ($27.5 billion) without jeopardizing the dividend or its credit rating, analyst Michael Leuchten at Jefferies said in a note Thursday, and the Insmed deal might be within reach.

"A sizeable M&A transaction should provide greater stability through the Dupixent patent cliff and, hence, create time for Sanofi to reload its pipeline," he wrote. "Bottom line for us is that whilst this looks big on paper, it is doable, digestible and directionally seems consistent with what management was aiming for."
Sanofi shares, meanwhile, have returned 8.9% this year including reinvested dividends, underperforming the 11% return for the Stoxx Europe 600 Health Care Index.

Even before the Insmed report, some analysts were arguing the market was pricing in the Dupixent problem too early and giving Sanofi too little credit for the cash the drug can generate before the patent expiration. Intron Health's Naresh Chouhan raised the stock to buy from hold this month and set the highest price target among analysts tracked by Bloomberg, implying a 41% gain from current levels.
Some of that thesis is already playing out. The shares have surged 12% since Sanofi's better-than-expected earnings and higher forecast on Oct. 30.

Chouhan expects Dupixent sales to jump to €34 billion in 2031 from €15.7 billion last year. He's also upbeat about its M&A prospects. These are among key factors behind his call that Sanofi will be the best EU pharma stock by the end of 2027.

BNP Paribas analyst Peter Verdult upgraded the shares to outperform this month, arguing that concerns over the weak pipeline are already reflected in the valuation, while investors underestimate Dupixent's near-term earnings potential.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/warsh-fed-forward-gu.headline: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/warsh-fed-forward-gu.author: Jeff Cox

paragraphs.text: In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void.
Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake.

Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time.

Largely on the sidelines in the debate is Warsh, who has expressed disdain for that sort of forward guidance and argued that it handcuffs policymakers long before they actually have to make a decision. But that hasn't stopped most of the other 18 officials who sit in on Federal Open Market Committee meetings.
In fact, according to a Bank of America analysis, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025.
"Warsh's refusal to guide markets might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less," Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note Thursday.

"There is always a range of views across the 19 FOMC participants. Typically, the Chair would weigh in, indicating to markets whether the hawks or doves are in ascendence," he added. "Absent this leadership, however, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully."
The increasingly vocal debate comes at a critical time for the Fed and has myriad policy implications.
Threading a needle

Bhave noted "a deepening divide" on the FOMC. The Fed's decision not to increase its benchmark rate at its October meeting "increasingly looks like a mistake," and as a result "the hawks have been very vocal of late," he wrote. Leading the charge is Waller, who has raised the possibility of hiking by half a percentage point when the committee next meets in December.
Minutes from the October meeting hint at the tension, particularly when it comes to Warsh's refusal to provide guidance.

The summary related that some officials who were looking for a hike in October "could have supported no change in the federal funds rate provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely" — a statement that points toward the forward guidance that Warsh has insisted the Fed avoid.

The minutes "revealed that some officials favoring a hike would have accepted a hold if the Fed had clearly communicated further tightening," market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday. "Warsh's communication philosophy may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most."
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point hike, tiptoed around the forward guidance issue during a recent public appearance.

Prefacing some observations she made about where she sees policy headed, Hammack noted that, "Those are not promises. Those are not commitments. They're not forward guidance, which is a hot-button topic. But what they are are a conditional set of expectations of where I think the economy can go, based on what I'm seeing."

Hammack's comments illustrate a needle that Fed officials have been trying to thread: continuing to be transparent about their thinking without appearing locked into a future policy that changing economic conditions could render obsolete.
Speaking Thursday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee framed the argument around credibility.

"I am sympathetic to the view that [Warsh] has expressed that let's not be so, in in our language, forward guidance-oriented, saying here is what I think rates are going to be at the next meeting," Goolsbee said, calling such pronouncements "falsely precise."
However, he quickly separated forward guidance from transparency.

"I think central banks should be careful about doing anything that undermines credibility," Goolsbee said. "That said, I also think that it's pretty important [that] each person who sits around that table explain how they see the world. What do you see in business conditions? You don't want to surprise everybody."

Taking a slightly different tack, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, in a speech Thursday on policy communication, insisted that markets can figure out where policymakers are going without specific guidance so long as they understand how economic developments will influence decisions.
Paulson also defended the variety of voices coming from the Fed.

"But volume is not the same as clarity," she said. "The measure is not how much we say. It is whether we are understood." The mixture of voices "guards against any single communication becoming the only one that matters."
Markets take their own view
Financial markets have taken the plethora of Fed communications and interpreted it in a fairly hawkish way.

Traders are implying a 100% chance of at least a quarter percentage point hike in December, with a very small probability of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. From there, odds are high for a follow-up increase in January, then perhaps one more before the end of 2027.
While current inflation indicators are running above 3%, compared to the Fed's 2% target, market measures of longer-term inflation have declined.

Five-year forward expectations, as indicated through the Treasury market, are at their lowest since April. That suggests investors could be less concerned about inflation over the longer term, even as policymakers warn that current price pressures remain elevated.
Still, a sclerotic communications strategy from the Fed amid volatile economic and geopolitical currents could prove dangerous ahead.
"The result of this back-and-forth is undue rates volatility in already turbulent times," BofA's Bhave said.
For his part, Warsh has been advocating for a "family fight" atmosphere inside the Fed, arguing that competing viewpoints deserve a full airing as the committee works towards decisions.

"There are benefits to shaping the market's future expectations. Perhaps this is part of the 'family fight' that Warsh keeps referencing in his pressers," said Tom Graff, chief investment officer at advisory firm Facet. "That family fight seems to be happening out in public."

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/20/fed.headline: Federal health panel reshaped by RFK Jr. faces political interference concerns
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/20/fed.author: Daniel Wu

paragraphs.text: A top federal health task force that issues guidance on cancer screenings, infectious diseases and other health services is meeting this week for the first time in over a year amid concerns that staff cuts, procedural changes and the appointment of new members has made the influential panel less reliable and more open to conflicts of interest.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, a panel of independent physicians and scientists whose recommendations determine what preventive services are covered by health insurance, normally meets three times a year, but had not convened to discuss health guidelines since March 2025.

In the interim, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took major steps to overhaul the group, firing its vice chair and chair, and appointing new members who have received waivers for conflicts of interest for owning stock in pharmaceutical companies. Kennedy has said reforming the task force will strengthen its expertise and pledged it will remain scientifically independent.

But the upheaval has disrupted the work of a group relied upon by physicians for impartial medical guidance, and whose recommendations can have major financial implications for health care providers and biotech companies, public health experts said.
“I think that there’s a huge erosion of trust,” said Aaron Carroll, president and CEO of health policy nonprofit AcademyHealth. “And it’s going to take time to earn it back.”
The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The task force convened Thursday to discuss updates to guidelines on cervical cancer screening and counseling for unhealthy alcohol use and perinatal depression. It is meeting again today to hear presentations from medical experts on colorectal cancer, kidney disease and lung cancer.
In an unusual change, part of the meetings are being broadcast on a public live stream. The task force generally has not made its meetings public in the past.
On Thursday concerns about the task force’s independence and impartiality loomed over some discussions.

Some task force members said that Health and Human Services officials made edits to proposed guidelines for cervical cancer screening, including adjusting language describing tumors and health care professionals and removing references to race and ethnicity.

“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the top line may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” said Sei Lee, a task force member and professor of medicine in the division of geriatrics at the University of California, San Francisco.
Mike Silverstein, a professor of health services, policy and practice at Brown University and former USPSTF chair, said allowing that precedent would severely compromise the task force’s reliability.
“For a political appointee to be editing task force recommendations means the task force is effectively no longer independent and under political control,” Silverstein told The Washington Post.

Several task force members also criticized plans to focus Friday’s meeting on expert presentations. The task force usually relies on systematic reviews of bodies of research on a subject to inform its recommendations, and panel members said that individual medical experts could give potentially incomplete or biased opinions on their areas of study.

Joel Tsevat, a task force member and a physician and professor of medicine at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, called the expert presentations “unprecedented” in task force meetings.
“I fear that they stand to infringe on the task force’s scientific independence,” Tsevat said.
Carroll said much of the discussion Thursday still involved reliable, evidence-based analysis.

But the objections raised by task force members were notable, he added, and he remains concerned about how members will manage conflicts of interest. Four task force members appointed by Kennedy to serve on the panel were granted conflict-of-interest waivers despite owning stock in pharmaceutical companies, the New York Times reported.

Several task force members recused themselves from discussing certain topics due to conflicts of interest during Thursday’s meeting. Silverstein said that in previous years, it was unusual for members to recuse themselves during meetings because physicians with many conflicts of interests would not have been appointed to the group.
“All those things make me very concerned for the future of this task force,” Silverstein said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/gm-ceo-succession-ma.headline: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/gm-ceo-succession-ma.author: Michael Wayland

paragraphs.text: Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough."

He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."

His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.
"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.
Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.
GM succession planning
Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's annual proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.
That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."
Selecting Barra as CEO
When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.

Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.
"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."
Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.
Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Tether Insiders Seek to Turn Gold Into a 4% Yield Machine
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Ryan Weeks and Jack Ryan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Two executives with close ties to stablecoin giant Tether are raising money for a fund which will offer yield on digital assets backed by gold, at a time when the cryptocurrency issuer extends its reach in the bullion market.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Kintsugi Capital has been set up to offer yield on XAUt, Tether's gold-backed token, through strategies including hedged staking and lending, as well as basis and options trades, according to investment materials reviewed by Bloomberg News. Hedged staking involves earning rewards by locking up cryptocurrencies to help operate a blockchain network while using derivatives to reduce the risk of price swings.

Kintsugi, which has a direct partnership with Tether, will target a net yield of around 4% above returns from simply holding gold, according to the materials. It aims to grow to more than $100 million in assets under management within its first 12 months of operations, the materials show.

Alessandro Giori, who from 2024 served as global senior strategic partnership manager and head of Middle East and North Africa for Tether, leads the fund as chief executive officer, alongside Tether adviser Koh Onozawa Martinez, the materials show.
Kintsugi and Tether didn't respond to requests for comment.

Tether, issuer of the world's largest stablecoin USDT, has aggressively expanded into commodities markets in recent years, amassing gold reserves worth more than $19 billion by the end of September, one of the world's largest private stockpiles of the precious metal. It has simultaneously emerged as a bullion lender, providing about $1.5 billion in financing to a top US gold dealer.

Stablecoins such as USDT are designed to maintain a price closely correlated to a traditional asset like the US dollar, typically achieved by managing a reserve of cash-like assets. In a recent assessment of USDT's backing, S&P Global Ratings noted that the stablecoin's exposure to risky assets has increased over the past year. After a rally in gold prices, bullion holdings in the reserve accounted for about 10% of USDT in circulation, compared with 7% in September 2025.

Tether cut some of those gold holdings for the first time since 2024 in the most recent quarter, reducing them by 3.4 tons after a period of rapid accumulation, according to figures in its latest attestation report.
Tether also issues XAUt, a digital asset backed by physical gold. It is the largest of its kind, with a market capitalization of roughly $3 billion.

Kintsugi was named after the Japanese art of fixing broken pottery with gold, the materials show. Its fund will be regulated in the Cayman Islands, and overseen by a British Virgin Islands division of Further Asset Management, an Abu Dhabi-headquartered asset management group.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/a-transcriptio.headline: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors and tech giants exposed customer data online
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/a-transcriptio.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, Sen, 30, has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.
Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.
Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president Adam Goldberg said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”
“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.
The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.
It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.
‘Basic human error’

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.
Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multi-step warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.
“Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/rei.headline: Reporter says lengthy Texas execution was ‘like no other’ he’d seen
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/rei.author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering breaking news from London

Texas prisoner Reinaldo Dennes cried out in pain as he was executed Thursday, in a procedure that extended over an hour as staff struggled to find veins suitable for intravenous needles, the Associated Press reported.
Dennes, 70, faced the death penalty for a 1996 murder and robbery, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

Associated Press reporter Michael Graczyk, who witnessed the execution in Huntsville, said it was “dramatically different” from the hundreds of other executions he had witnessed. In Texas, access to witness death penalty proceedings is tightly controlled.

Once a lethal dose of pentobarbital had been delivered, Graczyk said, Dennes “moaned in excruciating pain” for almost three minutes, crying out, asking God to take him, and at one point saying: “I don’t think this is normal.” The execution was “like no other” he had witnessed before, Graczyk added.

Prison officials said the correct procedures were followed and suggested Dennes was “exaggerating or even faking his pain,” Graczyk said. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice did not immediately reply to an overnight request for comment.
The death penalty, particularly death by lethal injection, has been the spotlight since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September.
Reporter covering international breaking news
Four men guilty of assaulting woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
Four British men have been convicted of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged her and invited strangers online to use her for sex, in the first case of its kind to go to trial in England.
Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity, told reporters after the trial ended Thursday: “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.”
Philip Young, 50, whom she divorced last year, pleaded guilty to multiple sexual offenses in January.

Young, who served as a Conservative local government councillor in the town of Swindon between 2007 and 2010, was caught after police discovered he uploaded extreme bestiality images online. Police then uncovered other images, including of Joanne Young being raped.
A sixth man pleaded guilty to rape and assault before the trial began.

The couple’s daughter has called for a change in England’s consent laws, writing: “We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone … This is simply unacceptable.”
The case had echoes of that of Gisèle Pelicot in France. Her then-husband was found guilty of repeatedly drugging and raping his wife and orchestrating her abuse by dozens of men.
Owl survives 45-mile drive stuck to front of truck after collision

Ashley Moffitt was driving on a Pennsylvania highway recently when an owl collided with the front of her freight truck. It wasn’t until she arrived at her destination about 45 miles away that she saw the owl’s head was trapped above the windshield.
Somehow, the owl was alive.
“When you’re going 65 miles an hour and it hits, I honestly didn’t think that anything like that could survive,” said Moffitt, a line-haul driver for Old Dominion Freight Line.
Employees from the freight company removed the owl, which had been stuck in a fiberglass panel, and called a wildlife rehabilitation center that night, Nov. 6.
Tracie Young, founder of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Washington Boro, Pennsylvania, said she struggled to believe the owl was alive until she saw photos of him standing.
“How he didn’t break his neck is just beyond me,” Young said. “I have honestly never heard of a bird of prey even surviving that.”

If birds do survive car collisions, Young said, they’re typically severely injured. When wildlife rehabilitators inspected the great horned owl that night, Young said, his only injury was damage to his left eye, which was swollen and bleeding.

The owl, which Young said was probably born this year, is recovering at the center. When the owl shows he can fly and forage on his own, Young said, the center will release him in Franklin County, near where he collided with Moffitt’s truck.
Reporter covering brain health and writer of the Brain Matters column
Video games like ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ may have surprising brain benefits

“Grand Theft Auto VI” has taken the world by storm. Many people are reportedly taking time off from their jobs to immerse themselves in the crime epic. In doing so, they may actually be putting their brains to work.

Researchers have found that action video games similar to “Grand Theft Auto VI” may help improve cognitive skills by challenging the brain to make split-second decisions. A 2022 study reported that people who played at least five hours of action video games a week — including previous editions of “Grand Theft Auto” — performed better than non-gamers at a task that involved mentally visualizing rotating objects.

In another study, scientists had non-gamers play action video games about five hours a week for three months. By the end of the study, the participants had boosted their learning speed. They picked up two unrelated skills faster than people who played a slower type of game.
But of course, moderation is key.

“I cannot say that playing video games for hours and hours and hours is going to be good for your brain health,” Carlos Coronel, a research fellow at Trinity College Dublin and Adolfo Ibañez University in Santiago, Chile, previously told me. “You need to find a balance.”
Agriculture Secretary’s religious emails are unconstitutional, judge rules

A federal judge ruled Thursday that religious messages Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins sent to her department amount to a violation of the Constitution, stressing that “the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.”

The case, filed by a labor union and six employees, took issue with emails Rollins sent, particularly a Christmas video message and an Easter message of several paragraphs that was sent to about 100,000 USDA employees.

“Happy Easter — He is Risen indeed! Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind,” Rollins wrote in the email, which was reviewed by The Washington Post. Several employees told The Post the message unnerved them, and legal experts said the message defied a norm of officials steering clear of overtly religious language.

Judge Trina L. finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.headline: Jimmie Johnson’s Nascar Team Valuation Reaches $450 Million
finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.author: Randall Williams

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 20, 2026 at 10:44 AM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Legacy Motor Club, the auto racing organization owned by seven-time Nascar Cup Series Champion Jimmie Johnson, has closed an $85 million investment round led by Knighthead Capital Management.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The raise values Legacy at $450 million, according to a person familiar with the matter who wasn't authorized to speak publicly about the deal.
The money will be put toward growing the team's operation and the development of a new headquarters in Moorseville, North Carolina, which is expected to open in 2028.

In July, Legacy announced a funding round with celebrity investors including Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper, tennis champion Andy Roddick, Grammy-award-winner Darius Rucker and celebrity chef Guy Fieri.
Johnson said Legacy went back to raise more funds to continue to scale and grow, including adding a third race team.
With this investment, "we can truly hit our objectives to be a tier one racing operation in the Nascar series," Johnson said in an interview.
Legacy has three chartered Nascar teams that all use a Toyota Camry XSE. Drivers for this coming season will be Josh Berry, Erik Jones and Riley Herbst.
Knighthead Capital is led by its co-founder Tom Wagner, who founded the firm in 2008. Wagner owns stakes in the Las Vegas Raiders and Birmingham City Football Club.

Knighthead originally acquired minority interest in Legacy in January 2025, buying out much of the stake owned by Maury Gallagher, an airline entrepreneur. The transaction also made Johnson the majority owner of the racing organization.
"Investing and immediately deploying growth capital was part of the plan," Kyle Kneisly, a partner at Knighthead and Legacy board member, said in an interview.

The investment comes nearly a year after Nascar resolved a federal antitrust lawsuit by a settling with Michael Jordan's 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports. The settlement allowed Nascar teams to have permanent charters, potentially unlocking value for clubs.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/data-center-construc.headline: Property Play: Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/data-center-construc.author: Diana Olick

paragraphs.text: A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors.

All that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average.
The report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets. It also included a survey of 400 experts in the global data center industry.
While there was some stabilization in cost inflation this year, it was not enough to offset the huge growth in not just demand but speed of construction and delivery.

"More aggressive schedules tie to contractors in particular and subcontractors baking in more risk allowances in their pricing," said Paul Barry, North America data center lead for Turner & Townsend. "So whether that's acceleration allowances, whether that's more overtime and labor attraction allowances, even just higher fees for taking on the risk of delivering at a faster pace than what they would traditionally take on."
All of those things, combined with the spike in demand and the strain on the supply chain, translate into higher costs, he added.

Capital expenditure on global data centers is projected to rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion per year in 2050, according to a recent report from PwC. The U.S. is expected to capture almost half of all global investment in AI infrastructure, which includes both data centers and chips.

Power is, of course, key to all data centers, and 56% of those surveyed by Turner & Townsend globally said it was a major obstacle to delivery. Just over half said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and almost a third reported timeframes of over two years. Costs for power vary regionally — from $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley to $10.51 per watt in Dallas, based on a typical 60-megawatt design.As with every type of construction in the U.S., labor continues to be a significant headwind. Just over one quarter of respondents said their contractor capacity, that is, the ability to manage construction backlogs, was sufficient.

Going forward, Barry said he expects costs to moderate somewhat, with cost increases in the 6% to 10% range in the next year. A lot of the major projects have already started or are starting now, so cost risk has been baked into those contracts.

"If this demand continues, then there'll be more continued flow of project starts and so on, but I think we've hit a big surge in 2026, especially of new big major projects that have been procured," said Barry.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/bending-spoons.headline: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68 billion
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/bending-spoons.author: Russell Brandom

paragraphs.text: Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/mam.author: Amy B Wang

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Friday proposed pushing back by five years the legal deadline to close Rikers Island, the city’s infamous and long-troubled jail complex, and outlined his plan to replace the facility with smaller jails based in each borough.

Mamdani’s proposal moves the deadline from 2027 to 2032 to allow time to build the borough-based jails, starting with a facility in Brooklyn slated to open in 2029. The plan calls for reducing the jail population from more than 6,000 to about 4,100.

New York City officials argue that creating smaller, borough-based jails will make it easier for incarcerated people to maintain family relationships and access support and legal services, leading to better outcomes once they are released.
Officials also plan to more than triple the number of outpatient therapeutic housing units across the city where prisoners with serious mental health issues can be transferred.

Efforts to close Rikers Island have been years in the making, and the New York City Council first voted to close the notorious jail and build new borough-based facilities in 2019, under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio (D).
Mamdani, who promised in his campaign to close Rikers Island once and for all, hailed the plan he unveiled Friday as a victory, even with the delayed closure.

“The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. … What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through, to chart a new path of public safety that endures and to keep our promises where so many have been broken before,” Mamdani said at a news conference.
Reporter covering breaking news from London
Reporter says lengthy Texas execution was ‘like no other’ he’d seen

Texas prisoner Reinaldo Dennes cried out in pain as he was executed Thursday, in a procedure that extended over an hour as staff struggled to find veins suitable for intravenous needles, the Associated Press reported.
Dennes, 70, faced the death penalty for a 1996 murder and robbery, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

Associated Press reporter Michael Graczyk, who witnessed the execution in Huntsville, said it was “dramatically different” from the hundreds of other executions he had witnessed. In Texas, access to witness death penalty proceedings is tightly controlled.

Once a lethal dose of pentobarbital had been delivered, Graczyk said, Dennes “moaned in excruciating pain” for almost three minutes, crying out, asking God to take him, and at one point saying: “I don’t think this is normal.” The execution was “like no other” he had witnessed before, Graczyk added.

Prison officials said the correct procedures were followed and suggested Dennes was “exaggerating or even faking his pain,” Graczyk said. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice did not immediately reply to an overnight request for comment.
The death penalty, particularly death by lethal injection, has been the spotlight since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September.
Reporter covering international breaking news
Four men guilty of assaulting woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
Four British men have been convicted of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged her and invited strangers online to use her for sex, in the first case of its kind to go to trial in England.
Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity, told reporters after the trial ended Thursday: “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.”
Philip Young, 50, whom she divorced last year, pleaded guilty to multiple sexual offenses in January.

Young, who served as a Conservative local government councillor in the town of Swindon between 2007 and 2010, was caught after police discovered he uploaded extreme bestiality images online. Police then uncovered other images, including of Joanne Young being raped.
A sixth man pleaded guilty to rape and assault before the trial began.

The couple’s daughter has called for a change in England’s consent laws, writing: “We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone … This is simply unacceptable.”
The case had echoes of that of Gisèle Pelicot in France. Her then-husband was found guilty of repeatedly drugging and raping his wife and orchestrating her abuse by dozens of men.
Owl survives 45-mile drive stuck to front of truck after collision

Ashley Moffitt was driving on a Pennsylvania highway recently when an owl collided with the front of her freight truck. It wasn’t until she arrived at her destination about 45 miles away that she saw the owl’s head was trapped above the windshield.
Somehow, the owl was alive.
“When you’re going 65 miles an hour and it hits, I honestly didn’t think that anything like that could survive,” said Moffitt, a line-haul driver for Old Dominion Freight Line.
Employees from the freight company removed the owl, which had been stuck in a fiberglass panel, and called a wildlife rehabilitation center that night, Nov. 6.
Tracie Young, founder of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Washington Boro, Pennsylvania, said she struggled to believe the owl was alive until she saw photos of him standing.
“How he didn’t break his neck is just beyond me,” Young said. “I have honestly never heard of a bird of prey even surviving that.”

If birds do survive car collisions, Young said, they’re typically severely injured. When wildlife rehabilitators inspected the great horned owl that night, Young said, his only injury was damage to his left eye, which was swollen and bleeding.

The owl, which Young said was probably born this year, is recovering at the center. When the owl shows he can fly and forage on his own, Young said, the center will release him in Franklin County, near where he collided with Moffitt’s truck.
Reporter covering brain health and writer of the Brain Matters column
Video games like ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ may have surprising brain benefits

“Grand Theft Auto VI” has taken the world by storm. Many people are reportedly taking time off from their jobs to immerse themselves in the crime epic. In doing so, they may actually be putting their brains to work.

Researchers have found that action video games similar to “Grand Theft Auto VI” may help improve cognitive skills by challenging the brain to make split-second decisions. A 2022 study reported that people who played at least five hours of action video games a week — including previous editions of “Grand Theft Auto” — performed better than non-gamers at a task that involved mentally visualizing rotating objects.

In another study, scientists had non-gamers play action video games about five hours a week for three months. By the end of the study, the participants had boosted their learning speed. They picked up two unrelated skills faster than people who played a slower type of game.
But of course, moderation is key.

“I cannot say that playing video games for hours and hours and hours is going to be good for your brain health,” Carlos Coronel, a research fellow at Trinity College Dublin and Adolfo Ibañez University in Santiago, Chile, previously told me. “You need to find a balance.”
Agriculture Secretary’s religious emails are unconstitutional, judge rules

A federal judge ruled Thursday that religious messages Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins sent to her department amount to a violation of the Constitution, stressing that “the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.”

The case, filed by a labor union and six employees, took issue with emails Rollins sent, particularly a Christmas video message and an Easter message of several paragraphs that was sent to about 100,000 USDA employees.

“Happy Easter — He is Risen indeed! Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind,” Rollins wrote in the email, which was reviewed by The Washington Post. Several employees told The Post the message unnerved them, and legal experts said the message defied a norm of officials steering clear of overtly religious language.

Judge Trina L. Thompson in California said Rollins’s emails breached the establishment clause of the Constitution, designed to prevent the government from influencing a person’s faith, and USDA’s own rules, given Rollins’s position of authority, the use of her official email and language alienating to those who did not share her beliefs.
A USDA spokesperson called the ruling an “unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6808ym10vzgo.headline: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6808ym10vzgo.author: Rachel Clun, Jemma Crew

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

We’ve all now seen the photos of Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin at their trilateral meeting yesterday in Shenzhen, China. These images have been broadcast on TV and printed in newspapers all over the world.

But summits like this involving the U.S. president should be about more than just a photo op. They should deliver tangible outcomes that advance the security and prosperity of the American people. That is their purpose. This meeting produced nothing good for American national interests.

Maybe Putin, Trump, and Xi negotiated outcomes that we have yet to learn about that benefit American interests and values. The short joint “Declaration toward Peace” released after the meeting, however, communicated nothing of the sort. Instead, it listed only four short and very general points of agreement: a commitment to “reform the UN” (with no details given); nuclear nonproliferation; criticism of the International Criminal Court and affirmation of “the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials”; and a pledge to ramp up the supply of refined petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations.”

Persuasion is a registered nonprofit that relies on reader support to pay our staff and keep our content free for everyone. If you value our work and want to fight for liberal values wherever they are threatened, please become a paying subscriber today!

The summit’s most important outcome, however, had nothing to do with this statement. I’m talking about the giant gift to Vladimir Putin—a photo with two of the most powerful leaders in the world, which created the impression that Putin, too, is the respected leader of a third great power.

That is a shame. Putin is a man who has waged a full-scale war on a democratic partner of the United States for nearly five years. He has systematically targeted Ukrainian civilians to try to break their morale. He has locked up, chased out, or killed Russian citizens who have dared to speak out against him in their own country. This man should be vilified, not welcomed, on the global stage.

And if representatives of the United States have to engage with Putin, they should have a clear purpose that advances American national interests and values. Nothing I’ve seen or read about Trump’s interactions with Putin leads me to believe this was the case in Shenzhen. Shockingly, Trump even referred to Putin as his “friend.” In doing so, he was speaking in a personal capacity, not as a representative of the American people. More than 80 percent of Americans say they have little or no confidence in Putin to do the right thing in world affairs. And a new poll released by the Pew Research Center this week found that two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

More broadly, Americans still value our democratic alliances, still support NATO, and still believe that the promotion of democracy and the defense of human rights should have a place in American foreign policy. In contrast to Trump, Americans value friendships abroad with democratic leaders.

U.S. leaders sometimes need to meet with dictators to advance American national interests. During the Cold War, American presidents met with Soviet and Chinese communist leaders. While I worked for President Obama, first at the National Security Council at the White House, and then as the U.S. ambassador to the Russian Federation, I participated in meetings with Putin and other senior Russian officials working for that autocratic regime.

These meetings were always a means to a larger objective. A “good” meeting was never an end in itself. For instance, President Obama met with then-Russian President Dmitry Medvedev several times to negotiate the terms of the New START Treaty, a nuclear arms control agreement, which they eventually signed in April 2010. In every one of these bilateral meetings—including on the sidelines of multilateral conferences—our goal was to make progress on getting this treaty done.

Attending the same summits as our Russian counterparts afforded us opportunities to conduct diplomacy on the sidelines. We used these meetings to negotiate transit routes through Russia to support our soldiers in Afghanistan, secure agreement on multilateral sanctions on Iran, and obtain Russia’s acquiescence not to block UN Security Council resolutions authorizing the use of force in Libya. At every meeting, we had a list of concrete outcomes we sought to achieve.

The trilateral meeting in Shenzhen yesterday was the first of its kind. I also hope it is the last. We should not mistake it for the emergence of a new international order—a “G3,” or worse yet, a “Yalta 2.0.” Trump is a lame-duck president whose foreign policies are extremely unpopular at home. Putin is bogged down in a war he is losing after nearly five years of fighting and enormous cost to his country’s people and economy. Xi has done little to end either the war in Ukraine or the war in Iran. None of these men are demonstrating strong global leadership right now. They most certainly are not forging a new international system based on three spheres of influence.

In the wake of the “Blue Tsunami” we saw in the midterms, the Trump era is winding down. The next American president is unlikely to befriend Putin or embrace autocrats more broadly. Yesterday’s trilateral meeting, which some breathlessly described as historic, pivotal, and unprecedented, will soon be forgotten as just another crazy but ephemeral moment of the Trump era.
That’s a good thing.

Michael McFaul, a columnist for American Purpose, is a professor of political science and a senior fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute and Hoover Institution, all at Stanford University. washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/flo.headline: Child begged for life in 911 call as father killed family, sheriff says
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/flo.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: A Florida county sheriff’s office is investigating the killing of three young children and their mother in Plant City, in which one of the children appears to have called 911 while the shooting was taking place.
The gunman, whom authorities identified as the father of the children, then took his own life, Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said.
Chronister told reporters on Thursday that authorities received a 911 call around 3:30 p.m. and heard what appeared to be gunshots.
“It’s an open line, and we can hear a male’s voice say, ‘Sorry, buddy.’ And we hear a loud bang,” he said.
“In the distance, we can hear a small child begging for his life. … Three or four times before we hear another loud bang,” Chronister added.
The sheriff said deputies arrived at the property about 10 minutes later and forced their way inside.
Five people, including a man, a woman and three children, ages 1, 3 and 5, were found dead from gunshot wounds, the sheriff said.
He identified the man as the father of the children and said authorities believe he killed them and their mother before taking his own life.
The victims’ identities have not been disclosed. Chronister said the family was not known to authorities in Plant City, which is in central Florida, east of Tampa.
The incident has left deputies and the dispatcher traumatized, he said.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/20.headline: Jonathan Yardley, Pulitzer-winning book critic at The Post, dies at 87
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/20.author: Matt Schudel

paragraphs.text: Jonathan Yardley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning book critic whose assertive and sometimes snappish reviews were a staple of The Washington Post for more than three decades, died Friday at 87 at an assisted-living facility in Washington, his son Jim Yardley confirmed.

Mr. Yardley considered himself a workaday journalist who approached the world of books with the vigor and practiced eye of a sportswriter covering a ballgame. He wrote several books of his own, including literary biographies and an unsentimental memoir of his parents. But his most far-reaching impact came in the thousands of reviews he published in The Post and, before that, in the Washington Star and Miami Herald.
Often described as prickly, acerbic and curmudgeonly — terms he did not disavow — Mr. Yardley had a blunt, plainspoken style that sometimes reached rhapsodic heights when he was moved by a book.
Not one to mince words, he believed that a critic who wrote only favorable reviews had no credibility.

“I have high literary standards and delight in the expression of strong opinion, literary and otherwise,” he wrote in his farewell column in 2014, “but I also read a book as if I were a reporter: looking for what it is ‘about’ in the deepest sense of the word, determining what matters about it and what doesn’t, trying to give the reader a feel for what it is like as well as passing judgment on it.”

For most of his 33 years at The Post, beginning in 1981, Mr. Yardley wrote two reviews a week, one for the Book World section on Sunday and another for Style. He also penned a wide-ranging column on politics and cultural affairs, with a title — “Prejudices” — borrowed from one of his journalistic heroes, the gruff and opinionated H.L. Mencken.

“Jonathan was a tough critic,” Donald E. Graham, The Post’s longtime publisher and chief executive, said in an interview for this obituary. “But when he praised a book, you could be sure that it was excellent. I owe him for many hours of reading pleasure.”
Mr. Yardley deplored the clubby worlds of New York publishing and faculty lounges, but his reviews were widely influential in helping shape the views of readers and writers in Washington and beyond.
He was an enthusiastic champion of novelists Peter Taylor, Anne Tyler, Edward P. Jones and Michael Chabon, all of whom went on to receive the Pulitzer Prize for fiction.

In a glowing review of Chabon’s 1995 novel “Wonder Boys,” Mr. Yardley called Chabon “the young star of American letters” but added: “It is time for him to move on, to break away from the first person and explore larger worlds. His apprenticeship is done; it has been brilliant, but the books as yet unwritten are the ones in which we will learn just how far this singular writer can go.”

“When I read those words,” Chabon later wrote, “the hair stood up on the back of my neck, and it was at that moment that I decided to take a chance on this comic book novel I had been thinking about writing.” His “comic book novel” was “The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay,” which became a bestseller, won the Pulitzer Prize in 2001 and is now recognized as Chabon’s masterpiece.

Although he was based in the nation’s capital for most of his career, Mr. Yardley said that he had little interest in “politics and power,” the typical themes of the Washington novel. He often reviewed political memoirs and biographies in withering terms, memorably lambasting “The Last Brother” — Joe McGinniss’s 1993 biography of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy — as “a genuinely, unrelievedly rotten book, one without a single redeeming virtue.”

In 2005, Mr. Yardley charged former senator Bob Dole with “trying to climb aboard the highly lucrative ‘Greatest Generation’ bandwagon” with a memoir about his experiences in World War II, which Dole and his supporters had recounted “over and over and over again.” Dole responded, according to the Hill, by faxing a brief note to Yardley along with a copy of the review: “Some damn fool wrote this piece and attached your name to it.”

It was far from the only time one of Mr. Yardley’s reviews provoked an angry reaction. Author Pete Dexter, whose novel “Paris Trout” was excoriated by Mr. Yardley as being “almost entirely devoid of literary interest,” called him a “worn-out old whore” in a 2007 essay collection. And a longtime friendship with novelist Doris Grumbach was shaken by a public dispute over whether Mencken, whom Mr. Yardley had defended in print (with qualifications), was an antisemite.

Perhaps the most pointed response to one of Mr. Yardley’s reviews came in a Gucci gift box wrapped in gold ribbon, not long after he published a blistering critique of Washington writer Kitty Kelley’s 1981 biography of actress Elizabeth Taylor.
“Inside,” Mr. Yardley told Time magazine, “was a bag of fish heads and a postcard of Liz Taylor giving me the finger.” An enclosed card was signed, “From the friends of Kitty Kelley.”
A life in books

Jonathan Yardley, the oldest of four children, was born Oct. 27, 1939, in Pittsburgh. His father was an educator who became an Episcopal clergyman and the rector of Chatham Hall, a private girls’ school in Virginia. His mother managed the home and was a bookkeeper. Both were avid readers, with a collection of Trollope first editions and other rare books.

Both his parents traced their ancestry back to Jonathan Edwards, the 18th-century theologian for whom Mr. Yardley was named. He chronicled their marriage, and offered a broader social history of the American WASP, in his 1989 memoir “Our Kind of People.”

Mr. Yardley wrote that while the WASP ascendancy was ending, he was “proud of those from whom I am descended, and reluctant to see our kind of people reduced to mere caricature. So it is that the more I thought about my parents’ lives the more I became convinced that they represented traditions and beliefs deserving of praise rather than censure.”

Educated at boarding schools, he attended the Woodberry Forest School in Virginia before graduating from Groton in Massachusetts. He edited the student newspaper at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, received a bachelor’s degree in 1961 and later spent a year at Harvard on a Nieman journalism fellowship.

Mr. Yardley launched his journalism career at the New York Times, working as an assistant to James Reston, the columnist and Washington bureau chief, before moving to the paper’s New York office to compile weekly news summaries.

At age 24, he became an editorial writer for the Greensboro Daily News in North Carolina, where he began to write and edit book reviews. He joined the Miami Herald in 1974, serving as the paper’s book editor and critic, and four years later moved to the Washington Star, a scrappy afternoon newspaper that folded not long after he won the 1981 Pulitzer Prize for criticism.

Mr. Yardley’s Pulitzer-winning reviews included pieces celebrating John Kennedy Toole’s novel “A Confederacy of Dunces” and Ronald Steel’s biography of journalist Walter Lippmann, which he called “a magisterial book: scrupulous, reflective, balanced, comprehensive, admiring yet never fawning.”

By then, Mr. Yardley was writing books of his own, beginning with a well-received 1977 biography of sportswriter and humorist Ring Lardner. His other books included “Misfit,” a biography of author Frederick Exley; “States of Mind,” a travelogue about the Mid-Atlantic; and essay collections such as “Second Reading,” drawn from a Post series in which he reexamined literary works from the past.

Not all of those reconsiderations were warm strolls down memory lane. In his lacerating reappraisal of J.D. Salinger’s “The Catcher in the Rye,” Mr. Yardley mused, “Why do English teachers, whose responsibility is to teach good writing, repeatedly and reflexively require students to read a book as badly written as this one?”
Mr. Yardley’s marriages to Rosemary Roberts and Susan Hartt ended in divorce. In 1999, he married Marie Arana, a deputy editor at Book World who was later promoted to run the section.

He had two sons from his first marriage, William and Jim Yardley, who both became New York Times journalists. Complete information on survivors was not immediately available. In addition to his wife, survivors include two sons from his first marriage, William and Jim Yardley; two stepchildren, Hilary Walsh and Adam Ward; two sisters; a brother; six grandchildren; and 5 step grandchildren.

When he retired from The Post, stepping down after some 3,000 reviews, Mr. Yardley wrote that he was most looking forward to a life of reading “for pleasure rather than duty.” He said he wanted to give James Joyce’s “Ulysses” another shot (he had never been able to finish it) and revisit some of his favorites (P.G. Wodehouse, Peter Taylor).
“People long to be told stories,” he had written in 2002, explaining why he found books so endlessly rewarding. “The need is essential to human nature.”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Trump Officials Met Privately With Hedge Funds on Mega Rail Deal
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Leah Nylen, Crystal Tse, Yiqin Shen and Josh Sisco

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- In a highly unusual gathering, White House officials met privately this week with a group of hedge fund investors betting on whether the $72 billion tie-up between Union Pacific Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. will win approval from the Trump administration, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The gathering included investors from several major hedge funds and multiple officials from President Donald Trump's administration, and the participants discussed the prospects for the rail deal, said the people, who asked not to be named describing the meeting.

Stakes are high for the proposed merger of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, which would create the country's first true transcontinental railroad. The deal requires approval from the Surface Transportation Board, a relatively obscure independent regulator. The Justice Department is expected to weigh in with its views on the merger in the coming weeks. During the second Trump administration the White House has also played a larger role in the antitrust review process.

The investors who attended the meeting specialize in merger arbitrage, a strategy that seeks to profit from the gap between the offer price on an announced deal and the target company's share price. Because merger arbs can make — or lose — large amounts of money depending on the outcome, they pay close attention to the government's regulatory review as they place their bets.
Attendees were invited to the meeting based on their financial relationships with the private-sector organizers, who advertised it to arbitrage traders, said some of the people.

Administration officials didn't share non-public information with the group, according to people familiar with the meeting. Attendees were able to ask officials questions in the private meeting, which wasn't made public by the Trump administration.

In response to questions about the meeting and its attendees, a White House official said in a statement that a junior staffer who no longer works at the White House attended a lunch off the White House complex and that his attendance wasn't authorized by the White House. The STB, which evaluates rail deals, declined to comment.

The $72 billion railway deal has become a major focus for merger arbitrage investors since it was announced last year. As one of the largest transactions pending, it offers the prospect of substantial gains and steep losses, depending on whether traders bet for or against the deal and whether it's completed or falls apart.

The proposed tie-up has also engendered a high-level lobbying push. Trump met in the Oval Office with Union Pacific Chief Executive Officer Jim Vena last year. This summer a coalition of shippers and labor unions sought to persuade Trump's previous chief of staff, Susie Wiles, that the administration should oppose the deal. The battle became even more pitched after the rail regulator forced Union Pacific to publish a video of remarks Vena made in March threatening to raise rates on shippers opposing the deal.
Vena apologized for the comments at an industry conference this week, and said they were meant in jest.
A bipartisan group of senators including New York Democrat Chuck Schumer came out against the deal Wednesday.

The deal's complexity, with multiple layers of regulatory scrutiny and political pressure, gives arbs opportunities to analyze developments and trade around the shifting odds. Hedge funds collectively owned roughly $10 billion worth of Norfolk Southern stock — or about 15% of the total shares outstanding, as of the end of September, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from securities filings.

Merger arbitrage traders closely follow news related to announced deals and attend conferences and public appearances involving key government officials to try and interpret their comments and what they mean for the outcomes of particular deals. They also often hire law firms or consultants to provide insight into how federal agencies or courts might decide in close cases.

Even relative minutiae can be of interest: during the Biden administration, some were focused on the due date of then-FTC Chair Lina Khan's first child and whether it might impact the timing of the agency's decision on Microsoft Corp.'s acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

The DOJ and the Federal Trade Commission, which share antitrust authority to review deals, have for years provided ethics guidance advising senior officials against speaking with arbs outside of public settings. US insider trading laws prohibit government officials from providing material, non-public information to third parties for trading purposes.

Concerns about the rail merger's prospects have intensified in recent weeks. The spread on the rail deal — the gap between the value of Union Pacific's offer and Norfolk Southern's share price — widened to a record of more than $65 a share earlier this week, from roughly $50 a month ago. At current prices, the market is pricing in less than a 50% chance of the deal closing.
"Teach You a Lesson"

Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern announced their plans to merge last year, heralding the tie-up as the first coast-to-coast railway to provide better reach for shippers and move millions of truckloads of goods off congested highways. The agriculture and chemical industries, however, have opposed the deal, arguing it would raise the cost of moving goods across the US.

The DOJ's antitrust division is due to offer preliminary comments on the competitive impact of the transaction by Dec. 3. Those comments are likely to indicate the administration's position on whether the deal should receive a green-light.

The STB, which has sole authority to determine whether railroad mergers are in the public interest, isn't expected to make a final decision until next year. The STB's rules don't just require it to find that a merger doesn't hurt competition; they also require the board to find that a merger would enhance competition in the industry.
While that presents an uphill climb for Union Pacific before the STB, neither the DOJ nor state attorneys general have authority to challenge the combination should it go through.
"We're pleased to see so much participation in the process and value our customers' perspectives," Union Pacific said in a statement.

Union Pacific's Vena touted the benefits of the deal at an industry conference in March, ending his remarks by saying "I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by three or four extra percent to teach you a lesson."

The company said his remarks were offhand comments and not intended as a threat. The STB, however, ordered Union Pacific to make a copy of his comments available to the public and expressed concern that shippers might be less inclined to offer candid views as part of the proceeding.
"Retaliation, whether perceived or actual, can seriously undermine the integrity" of the agency's review, the board wrote in a Nov. 4 decision.
--With assistance from Lydia Beyoud and Ted Mann.
