finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: JPMorgan Warns Long Tail of El Niño Will Hurt Crops, Water Supplies
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Leslie Kaufman and Eric Roston

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The current El Niño could keep pushing up food prices and straining water supplies well into 2027, even after the Pacific Ocean warming that drives it begins to fade, according to a new JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysis provided to Bloomberg News.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The problem isn't simply El Niño itself. The natural warming of the tropical Pacific is occurring on top of long-term climate change and colliding with drought, wars and other disruptions to food and commodity markets.

"It's going to be inflationary," said Sarah Kapnick, global head of JPMorgan's climate advisory, and it could produce a longer tail of impacts on agriculture and commodities than historical experience would suggest.
El Niño typically develops in spring, peaks during late fall or winter and dissipates the following spring or summer. But the heat it releases into the atmosphere takes longer to disappear.

Think of the ocean as a giant heat battery, said Kapnick, a former chief scientist of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Even if Pacific Ocean temperatures shift from El Niño to cooler La Niña conditions by June or July, the heat may linger until fall or later. The second year of an El Niño is typically when the planet experiences the most heat, she said.
And this time the starting point is already exceptionally warm. Scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest year on record so far and for 2027 to measure even hotter.

Seasonal climate models cited by JPMorgan forecast average global temperatures at about 1.8C above preindustrial levels next February and March, with some model runs exceeding 2C for the first time. Temperatures are expected to remain unusually high into the summer.

The risks aren't only to crops. Extreme heat was found to have contributed to more than 50,000 excess deaths in Europe this past summer, when repeated heat waves also strained infrastructure and transportation. Scientists have warned that rising temperatures are increasing the health burden even as countries adapt.
Recent heat waves are "a test for the floor, not the ceiling, for temperatures in future years," Kapnick wrote in the report.

Commodity markets are already responding. Since El Niño was declared in June, futures prices have climbed 40% for cocoa, 37% for rice, 25% for sugar and 17% for coffee. Cocoa and coffee are particularly vulnerable because they're grown in tropical regions and require narrow ranges of temperature and rainfall, Kapnick said.

A strong El Niño has historically raised global food commodity prices by as much as 9%, with the peak arriving roughly 16 months after the event begins. But Kapnick said current forecasts may not fully account for the possibility of severe heat next summer further reducing supplies.

Water is another concern. On Germany's Rhine River, unusually low water has restricted coal deliveries to power plants. In the western US, the Colorado River is entering winter with reservoirs already depleted by years of drought. Lake Powell stood about 92 feet below its historical same-date median at the beginning of November, and Lake Mead, about 88 feet below.

The Colorado illustrates how the effects can compound. A warmer, drier winter could prevent enough mountain snow from accumulating to replenish the river before another hot summer. Because of the existing drought, normal snowfall may no longer be enough.
More broadly, Kapnick said the current El Niño offers businesses a preview of a warmer planet and a chance to adapt in advance.

"El Niño is a near-term stress test for a hotter world," she said. "Today's conditions can help identify vulnerabilities, anticipate future needs, and make more informed decisions about where investment in adaptation and resilience may be needed."

You have, by now, read something about the Enhanced Games, the steroid-fueled athletic spectacle held this year in Las Vegas. (Perhaps we even recommended it.) But there’s nothing quite like seeing the event through Kent Russell’s eyes as he sneaks high-proof whiskey from his ThermoFlask, considers the physical demands of parenting and his own life’s onrushing decline, and concedes that a drug-enhanced life sounds “pretty fucking dope.”

As of this moment, the sprinters are clean, the Erth bleachers are searing the backs of my thighs, and Michael Bryan is overawing me through the act of locomotion. I sip from my thermos and bask in wonderment that a human body can be made to move that way. Beauty of this kind, which eighteenth-century types correctly filed under the category of the sublime, requires that it exceed me. A thing I could do myself is admirable; a thing that no effort of mine could ever accomplish, that lives permanently past my ceiling, is awesome in the old, strong sense of the word, in which awe is part fear, part love, part recognition that I am small and soft. The unfairness is the source of the wonder. To resent that Bryan is gifted beyond me is to resent that the thing I’m watching is beautiful, which is insane and would require that I demand the world contain nothing larger than myself.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/chips-can-surv.headline: Chips can survive the space environment. Can their financing?
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/chips-can-surv.author: Tim Fernholz

paragraphs.text: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and re-sell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Research Index, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above the Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the company in the near-term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that buildout by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center buildout. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, how when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Company, Sophia Space, Orbital and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terrafab, in the US, but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

Tim Fernholz is a journalist who writes about technology, finance and public policy. He has closely covered the rise of the private space industry and is the author of Rocket Billionaires: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and the New Space Race. Formerly, he was a senior reporter at Quartz, the global business news site, for more than a decade, and began his career as a political reporter in Washington, D.C. cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-a.headline: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-a.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will either be banned from building data centers in other countries, or will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here."

The remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global issues.
Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump said, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better.

technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149399/.headline: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149399/.author: Grace Huckins

paragraphs.text: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, due to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than the tasks in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt the task many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential to AI systems automating research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month weeks ago, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI capabilities progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to incorporate some of these fuzzier, judgment-laden tasks that could be most relevant to AI research and development into their new suite. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about the extent to which the task is relevant for AI R&D automation. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even more so to determine what these scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into their work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees ask them to do as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original task suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising research questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck to AI R&D automation, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the tasks most relevant to AI R&D automation. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people to complete tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move towards open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq702ez8d4lwo.headline: Indian man gets 19-plus years in assassination plot of Sikh leader
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq702ez8d4lwo.author: Kayla Epstein

paragraphs.text: A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."
Nadine Yousif contributed to this report.

politico.com/news/2026/11/20/dem-govs-hu.headline: Dem govs huddle to address living costs
politico.com/news/2026/11/20/dem-govs-hu.author: Samuel Benson and Erin Doherty

paragraphs.text: PARK CITY, Utah — Cost-of-living concerns fueled Democrats to victory this month. Now they’re preparing to do something about it.

As newly elected governors gathered for a job training conference hosted by the National Governors Association, conversations among the Democrat-heavy group often turned to the economic woes in their states — and the necessity to get something done quickly.

“What are the things that we can do — not in the first 100 days, but in the first 100 hours — that can start bringing some relief to the American people?” Wes Moore, the National Governors Association chair and Maryland governor, said in an interview with POLITICO.

Health care and home costs topped the target list. Several newly elected Democratic governors — Jocelyn Benson in Michigan, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Deb Haaland in New Mexico and Rob Sand in Iowa — plan to take action to lower health costs, ranging from caps on prescription drug prices to expanding Medicaid coverage, within days of taking office. California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to spur affordable housing construction. His Nevada counterpart, Aaron Ford, said he plans to limit corporations purchasing private homes, and is preparing a day-one executive order to task every state agency with “finding ways to put money back in people's pockets.”

“You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses, cut regulations, and make it easier to do business. I think that's cool, that's fine, that's dandy,” Ford said in an interview. “But if you can do it for businesses, you can do it for people, too.”

Affordability was, far and away, the top issue for voters this cycle. Results from The POLITICO Poll, conducted just days after the midterm elections, found a 47% plurality of Americans — including 59% of Democratic voters and 41% of Republicans — said affordability and the economy were among the main issues driving their vote.

Democrats’ tsunami washed over governors’ mansions across the nation: They won 24 of the 36 governor’s races held this month, flipping red states like Texas, Alaska and Ohio, and will hold 30 of the 50 governorships nationwide next year — the most in three decades.

These governors and soon-to-be governors will be buoyed by a boon of Democrats in their statehouses: Democrats won unified control of government in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada and Wisconsin; in North Carolina, Democrats flipped the House for the first time in 16 years and broke Republicans’ supermajority in the Senate.

As several inches of snow descended on the Wasatch Front and blanketed the glitzy ski resort in Park City this week, the newly elected governors sheltered inside the NGA’s New Governors Leadership Forum — colloquially called “baby governors’ school.” At the two-day seminar, the incoming state executives and their teams attended seminars and workshops, mingled over hors d'oeuvres and heard from current and former governors on what to expect.

Former President Bill Clinton, sitting spread-legged in a Team USA sweater Thursday, dished to a room full of governors on his book recommendations (“The Social Conquest of Earth” by E.O. Wilson), fun facts (“The combined weight of ants on earth exceeds the combined weight of all the people on earth!”) and political predictions (“I think if President Trump gets closer to leaving, he may get more interested in leaving actual legacies in forms other than buildings.”)

Clinton, who chaired the NGA when he served as governor of Arkansas, also offered some advice to the newly electeds: “The most important thing is that you and your Cabinet and your office and your organizations out in the state know what your priorities are and know what your progress is.”

Governors will face a steep climb to deliver immediate relief to Americans. Economic forces are national and international, and much of the past year’s price spikes, from fuel to food to energy, can be tied to the Iran war.

Bottoms said she will immediately begin to prepare Georgia agencies for Medicaid expansion, and expects the state legislature — with Democrats now in control of the state House, while Republicans still control the state Senate — to cooperate.
“I do believe this is an issue we will get bipartisan support on,” she told POLITICO.

In addition to his Day-One executive order, Ford says he plans to work with the Nevada legislature to sign bills in his first 30 days on expanding free public school meals, lowering the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicaid negotiated price and limiting corporations’ ability to buy private homes.

Benson said she has already reached out to the Trump administration about tariffs, which includes a 50% tariff on most Canadian exports and have disproportionately impacted Michiganders. She said she has not yet heard back, but “the point is I have reached out, and I do hope to have that conversation.”
She also emphasized her focus on lowering health care costs. “That's life or death for so many families,” Benson said.
Megan Messerly and Adam Wren contributed reporting.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/super-hot-rock.headline: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes
techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/super-hot-rock.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.
The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.
An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop to refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.
XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.
Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.
That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2026/11/20/s.headline: Stefanik family’s D.C. home sells to mystery buyer for $900K over list price
washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2026/11/20/s.author: Joe Heim, Jon Swaine, Aaron Schaffer

paragraphs.text: Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-New York) was struggling to find a buyer.
The Capitol Hill rowhouse she had bought years earlier with her parents and brother was listed for sale in September 2025 for $2.195 million.
Just six blocks from the U.S. Capitol, the three-bedroom home on Independence Avenue SE was ideally located for someone hoping to live in the nation’s power corridor. The house, however, sat unsold.
Two months later, in November, the list price was cut to $1.99 million. In February of this year, five months after it was initially listed for sale, the home was taken off the market altogether.

But in June the property — still off the market — sold in an all-cash transaction for $2.9 million, or $910,000 more than its most recent list price, according to property records examined by The Washington Post. Only two homes on Capitol Hill are publicly listed as having sold for more in the past year.

The buyer was AFS Real Estate Holdings, a limited liability company formed in Delaware about a month before the sale. The company has no online presence, and a search of public records revealed no information about who owns it.

In a statement to The Post, Stefanik’s office said the home was publicly listed for sale during a government shutdown and “a slow holiday season” and was later sold in a “commercially reasonable transaction.” Her office said that she was a minority owner of the property and that off-market sales are increasingly common in Washington.
“The offer to buy the investment property was made and accepted within the range of prices for comparable historic townhouse sales in the neighborhood that range from $2-$4 million,” her office said.
Stefanik, who leaves office when her term expires in January, did not answer written questions asking if she knows who owns and operates AFS.

A half-dozen real estate agents and estate lawyers, none involved with the Stefanik property and each with decades of experience in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, told The Post they could recall no other transactions where a buyer paid so much more than what a seller had only recently been asking. Nor could they see why the Independence Avenue SE home would be so expensive.

“There may be outlying factors I’m not aware of, but from what I can see on the listing and the property records, it seems to be a very unusual purchase price,” said Patrick Tangney, a settlement attorney with two decades of experience with residential and commercial properties in the Washington region.

The Post found no records or work permits indicating that changes had been made to the home in the four-month period between when it was taken off the market and when it was sold. Records do not indicate there was any mortgage on the property at the time of the sale.

Stefanik, 42, announced in December that she would not seek reelection. Before this year she was chair of the House Republican Conference, a position to which she was elected by fellow GOP members and one that made her the fourth-highest-ranking Republican in the House. She was briefly seen as a possible vice-presidential candidate for Donald Trump in his 2024 White House bid.

The Independence Avenue SE home was recorded on June 24 as having been sold by EMS DC Properties, the limited liability company in which Stefanik and her family members were shareholders. EMS then purchased a newly built house in McLean, Virginia, for $3.3 million. Stefanik signed a document recording a $434,425 mortgage on that property. The document identifies her as “managing member” of EMS.

Janis M. Penman, the lawyer who filed papers to form AFS Real Estate Holdings, did not respond to a request for comment. Penman is a partner in the Washington office of the Cleveland-based firm BakerHostetler.

In response to questions from The Post, Stefanik’s office provided a list of 34 properties in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, “many” of which it said were comparable to hers. Records confirm that 13 of those properties fetched prices that were higher than Stefanik’s and the others sold for roughly similar amounts.

All but three, however, had more bedrooms than the Independence Avenue SE property and all but two had more living space. One of the properties with a similar sale price had a swimming pool and almost twice the square footage. Others were in particularly desirable locations, such as directly across from the Supreme Court. All but five had either a garage or one or more parking spaces.

To be considered comparable, real estate agents said, properties should have broadly similar features and sales ought to have been completed within months of each other. A majority of the properties on the list from Stefanik’s office were sold more than a year before hers.

At The Post’s request, Tom Faison, a real estate broker with more than three decades of experience on Capitol Hill, identified comparable properties through the Multiple Listing Service, or MLS, a database used by real estate brokers and agents.
“A reasonable appraiser looking at six months of sales in my opinion would not be able to justify $2.9 million for this house,” he said of the property on Independence Avenue SE.

Faison said that the home’s recent history on the market, and the fact that it did not sell at a lower price, revealed more about its value than any analysis of comparable properties. “I’ve never known a $3 million buyer, or any buyer, who would overlook the history,” he said.

Real estate listings describe the house as having 3.5 baths, three fireplaces and 2,700 square feet. It was not listed as having a garage or private parking spot, often a must for high-end buyers on Capitol Hill.

Developers and those who purchase rental properties sometimes do so through limited liability corporations, in part because such arrangements can simplify ownership among multiple partners. D.C. law requires the disclosure of owners of LLCs formed in the District but not of those formed elsewhere.

Stefanik, after graduating from Harvard in 2006, moved to Washington during the George W. Bush administration. She eventually took a job working for Joshua Bolten, then Bush’s White House chief of staff.

EMS DC Properties — “M” is both Stefanik’s middle initial and the initial of her brother’s first name — purchased the home on Independence Avenue SE in August 2010 for a little over $1.2 million. The property description for the listing that year touted the home as a one-of-a-kind renovation that “will knock your socks off.” It highlighted features including a “huge” chef’s kitchen, designer baths, a finished basement with bar and a rear deck and patio.

Stefanik’s father, Kenneth, signed a loan agreement for the house as a member of the company. Her mother, Melanie, later signed New York corporate registration paperwork as EMS’s chief financial officer, and her brother, Matthew Stefanik, signed loan documents as a company member.
Efforts to contact Stefanik’s parents and brother were not successful.

At the time of the purchase, Elise Stefanik was working for the leadership PAC of Tim Pawlenty, then the governor of Minnesota, who went on to explore a run for the Republican presidential nomination. Federal campaign records of Stefanik’s salary and expenses gave her address as the Independence Avenue SE house. Politico reported in September 2011 that Stefanik hosted a Pawlenty fundraiser at what it called “her Hill townhouse.”

In April 2013, Stefanik changed her voter registration from her parents’ home in Upstate New York to a lakeside house owned by her mother in that state’s 21st Congressional District. She ran for the seat the following year.

In a required financial disclosure filing during her 2014 campaign, Stefanik reported owning “residential rental property” in Washington via EMS DC Properties. Records do not show EMS owning any other properties in the capital. Stefanik valued her holding at between $250,001 and $500,000 and reported that it brought in rent of between $15,001 and $50,000.

Stefanik drew heat in the 2014 Republican primary from critics who accused her of living in a $1.2 million home purchased by her parents. Stefanik’s campaign responded that she was a New York resident and that she “owns 20 percent of a rental property in Washington, DC.”
Stefanik won her race and, at 30, was at the time the youngest woman ever elected to Congress.

Originally billing herself as a moderate Republican, Stefanik became a staunch ally of Trump during his first term. In 2025, on his first day back in office, Trump nominated her to be U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. He later withdrew the nomination to preserve the GOP’s slim majority in the House.

Stefanik had hoped for Trump’s endorsement in the Republican primary race for New York governor, but it never came. In December 2025, she dropped out of the contest and announced that she wouldn’t run again for her House seat.

By then her house was already on the market. In a Wall Street Journal story about the listing in September 2025, Stefanik described growing tomatoes in the yard, hosting family cookouts and cooking “Sunday sauce” in the kitchen of the open-layout first floor. She also said she liked to buy groceries from the butcher and cheese stand at Eastern Market, just steps from her home.
“One thing people may not know about me is I love to cook,” Stefanik told the Journal. “I come from a family of cooks.”

Earlier this year she published her first book, “Poisoned Ivies: The Inside Account of the Academic and Moral Rot at America’s Elite Universities,” an examination of top-tier universities becoming what she describes as “hotbeds of radical ideology, groundless elitism, intellectual laziness and anti-American hatred.”
Stefanik said in April that she had not ruled out running for any political office.

thebignewsletter.com/p/a-700-price-hike-.headline: A 700% Price Hike on A Key Component in Gaming Consoles? Blame A 25-Year Cartel.
thebignewsletter.com/p/a-700-price-hike-.author: Lee Hepner

paragraphs.text: By the end of its first day of availability, Grand Theft Auto VI sold over 19 million copies, more than doubling the previous one-day sales record held by its predecessor GTA V. Cumulative revenue at the end of launch date has neared $2 billion, a huge event for the largest segment of the entertainment industry and for consumer electronics writ large. Even if you aren’t excited about GTA VI, you probably know someone who is. Employers are lamenting “GTA flu” as employees stay home.
But there was another earth-shaking event in consumer electronics just five days prior to the release of GTA VI, and this one happened in court.

That development relates to another startling data point, which is the 700% price increase since 2022 of a core component of gaming consoles, like the Xbox and PS5 devices running GTA VI, and billions of other consumer electronic devices around the globe. Five days ago, a federal judge in the Northern District of California allowed a price-fixing case to proceed against Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix, the three dominant trillion dollar memory chip makers, whose collective pricing power in the $130 billion per year memory chip industry has raised the price of consumer electronics, including video games.

The specific product line at issue is called Dynamic Remote Access Memory, or “DRAM,” and the market share of this oligopoly is roughly 90%. And memory goes into pretty much every consumer electronics product now. If you bought a PlayStation 5 since April 2026 or an Xbox after August 2026, you paid more than $150 in additional cost because of the memory-price shock. A few months ago, in June, Microsoft announced that it would be increasing Xbox prices by $100-150 – that’s a 33% increase on the Series S – which it attributed to a 2.5x increase in memory costs. Microsoft anticipates another doubling of its memory costs in 2027. In its 2026 Investor Q&A, Sony said that while it had secured memory to get through 2026, rising memory costs might delay its next-generation PlayStation platform. Like its competitor Microsoft, Sony didn’t foresee conditions improving in 2027.

As for other consumer goods, one estimate suggests increased DRAM prices are responsible for an 8-10% increase in smartphone prices in 2025 alone, and a 5-15% increase to the price of laptops. Based on monthly sales figures, the extra amount consumers paid amounts to about $200 million just in the month of September. Extrapolated across the billions of consumer electronic devices that also run on DRAM yearly, that number reaches into the tens of billions.

There are other factors involved in this pricing change, notably the white hot demand for generative artificial intelligence products to go into data centers, of which memory is a key component. But we shouldn’t overlook price-fixing, because part of the story of why there isn’t enough productive capacity might be a restraint of investment as a result of such a conspiracy.

Once you start delving into the history here, the more eye-raising the behavior in the industry seems to be. After all, two decades ago, the very same major DRAM companies minting money pled guilty to criminal charges for their participation in a global memory-price cartel. And several executives went to jail. But it’s clear they were unchastened by the experience.

In 2006, Sun Woo Lee, Samsung’s then-Senior Manager of DRAM Sales, was one of five Samsung executives sentenced to 8 months in prison in connection with his participation in the early-2000s DRAM cartel. What did Mr. Lee do after serving his debt to society? Well, he went right back to working at Samsung. Not only that, he was promoted to President of Samsung Germany in 2009. In 2014, he was again promoted to President of Samsung Europe.
There are very few jobs that will hire you back after you committed a crime at work. But one of the lessons of the 25-year DRAM cartel is that crime pays.
Who Pays the Price of DRAM Price Hikes?

DRAM is a type of semiconductor capable of temporarily storing information, or “memory.” A single 16-gigabit DRAM chip can store approximately 16 billion “bits” of information and is smaller than a typical adult index fingernail. A high-end smartphone requires about 8 of them. A souped-up desktop computer rigged for gaming might include 32 of them, which corresponds with 64 GB of memory capacity.

DRAM is the backbone of nearly every computational device on earth. The videogame GTA VI is played on either an Xbox or PlayStation console. Well over 100 million of these devices sold since 2022 require DRAM. So do the 7.68 billion smartphones used worldwide, and 1.8 billion computers, another 750 million tablets, and about a half billion smart watches. So does every fancy Nvidia chip powering AI.

When the cost of DRAM goes up, those costs get passed through. Smartphones and notebooks aren’t just consumer products; they are also essential infrastructure for much of the modern economy. Increased unit prices also represent increased operational costs for businesses, reduced access to computers in schools, a drain on taxpayer dollars, delayed government modernization projects, higher manufacturing costs for automobiles, telecom devices, medical equipment, and so on. And that’s not even getting to the AI bubble.
Hawks Don’t Fly In Formation

The antitrust laws were intended to apprehend price-fixing cartels and enhance price competition. For most of the history of American antitrust law, cases against price-fixing were more or less straightforward, if challenging to detect.

Historically, price-fixing conspiracies have been most common in highly-concentrated markets. Algorithmic pricing software has changed that calculus dramatically, but the basic idea is that at the root of every conspiracy is an agreement between participants in the conspiracy. It’s easier to arrive at such an agreement when there are fewer players in the market, and its also easier to make sure everyone is sticking to the plan. The DRAM market is a classic example.

In June of this year, a group of 17 consumers and small business brought a class action lawsuit against Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung alleging they had cut production of DRAM, coordinated a pivot toward “high bandwidth memory,” and locked up DRAM supply – all contrary to sound economic and business logic.

The alleged cartel emerged in the middle of the “DRAM Winter” of 2022-2023, when demand was weak and prices were falling. Samsung, Hynix and Micron each reported multibillion-dollar losses at the fiscal year ending in 2023.

In late 2022 and early 2023, each of the companies announced that they would be reducing their production in DRAM, in response to the weak demand for DRAM across the board. But then came 2023, and with it, the AI boom.

Now, I’m going to lay out the allegations in a little bit of detail, because I think it’s useful for understanding how a cartel might be inferred from circumstance. After all, people don’t typically make illegal agreements out in the open.
According to the allegations in the case, here’s what happened:
• As the AI boom hit, all three companies redirected their manufacturing capacity from “commodity DRAM” to “High Bandwidth Memory,” a high-margin DRAM product sold exclusively to AI accelerators.
• As each company cut DRAM production, DRAM prices started going up. By January 2024, a global DRAM shortage began to materialize, and by mid-2025, DRAM prices had increased 171.8% in one year.
• Despite the shortage and rapidly increasing prices, for some reason, the three companies committed to restraints on DRAM output lasting beyond 2026.

• In 2024, all three companies announced in succession that they would wind down “DDR4,” a generation of DRAM chip that was still widely being used, causing DDR4 prices to surge amid “panic buying” by major customers.

• As prices for conventional DRAM continued to soar, by 697% over an 18-month period according to one estimate, not one of the three companies announced plans to expand DRAM production capacity, even after DRAM profitability had overtaken that of the accelerator chips.

• In October 2025, Samsung and SK Hynix locked up 40% of total worldwide DRAM output for a single customer, OpenAI, again with no plans to expand DRAM output to meet the strongest supply signal in the market’s history.
• In December 2025, Micron announced it would close its multibillion-dollar direct-to-consumer DRAM brand, Crucial, again foregoing any expansion of DRAM output.

• Then, in January 2026, all three companies introduced eerily similar customer vetting procedures for DRAM orders, allowing each of the companies to exchange customer information and monitor their agreed-upon restrictions.

Considered holistically, the allegations depict three companies not acting in their own self-interests, but a series of “perilous decisions that locked away” DRAM, a collective “refusal to cash-in on a nearly 700% price increase,” near-identical customer-vetting practices – and all of it performed by three companies with a decades-long history of conspiratorial behavior.

It’s possible that this behavior was purely coincidental. One famous quote from a Chicago School judge is that “competitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks.” That does not mean they are price-fixing, even if it results in closely-timed parallel moves, but that they are closely monitoring the competition and adjusting to market trends.

According to the judge in this case, the above allegations had “gone beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”
DRAM Price-Fixing 2.0

What’s fascinating about this particular case is that the judge let the case proceed. But in 2018, a similar class action lawsuit was filed against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron alleging industry price-fixing. That case was dismissed, even though you’d have to parse hairs to distinguish it from the current case that was just allowed to proceed. Had the 2018 case moved along to completion, it’s unlikely we would see the current crisis in DRAM pricing. Indeed, the fact this collusive arrangement has existed for more than 25 years is suggestive of a structural problem with the enforcement of antitrust laws.

Today’s DRAM oligopoly was already coming into focus by the end of the late 1990s, when the dot-com boom produced an enormous wave of business investment in computers and telecommunications infrastructure. One of the themes of the DRAM oligopoly is its orientation around boom-bust cycles of capital investment in the broader tech industry, which drives the demand for DRAM in good times, then causes the bottom of the industry to fall out in bad times, leading to consolidation. (Intel was once a memory chip maker, but pulled out because of this pricing dynamic.)

By 2002, the dot com bust fostered a standard pricing collapse in memory chips. Amid U.S. trade disputes with South Korea, government restructuring of failing firms, and other fallout, rumors began to circulate that the U.S. Justice Department was pursuing an antitrust investigation of all four leading DRAM producers – Micron, Samsung, Hynix, and Infineon. Of the Big Four, Micron was the only American company, and is still based out of Boise, Idaho.

Why Idaho? Here’s a fun detour: Micron’s principal early financier was one J.R. “Jack” Simplot. Simplot wasn’t a technologist, but an agribusiness entrepreneur who had built a food processing empire that ended up providing McDonald’s with its french fries. A real potato man, in 1980, his $1 million investment at 40% equity in Micron made him one of the richest men in America.

Another curiosity, the J.R. Simplot Company is itself defending against allegations of another illegal price-fixing scheme among frozen potato processors involving the data-sharing system “PotatoTrack.” It became a bit of an inside joke last year during committee hearings on algorithmic price-fixing when someone would list off industries rattled by price-fixing and conclude with, “even frozen potatoes!”
Jack Simplot was in his mid-90s back in 2004, when then-Micron CEO Steve Appleton offered a public admission:

“Although a recent Electronics Weekly article suggested that I believe it is not possible to control prices in this industry and that the DOJ’s investigation is theoretical, neither is the case. The DOJ’s investigation revealed evidence of price fixing by Micron employees and its competitors on DRAM sold to certain computer and server manufacturers.”

Micron agreed to cooperate with the Justice Department under its Corporate Leniency Policy, and by 2007, each of the other major DRAM manufacturers had entered guilty pleas. In total, 18 executives were charged, and 15 agreed to serve actual prison sentences ranging from four to 14 months. Total criminal fines were $730 million, against an industry that was pulling in $34 billion per year at its then-peak.

What we know about this earlier DRAM price-fixing scheme is gleaned from high-level fact summaries in various plea deals. The Defendant DRAM producers had participated in a conspiracy to fix the price of DRAM sold to equipment manufacturers, like Dell, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, and Apple. They’d done so by communicating with their competitors about the price of DRAM, agreeing to charge prices for DRAM at certain levels, issuing price quotes consistent with those agreements, and exchanging information about DRAM sales to certain customers to monitor and enforce adherence to the agreements.

In other words, more or less the same conduct the same companies are accused of today. Normally, this criminal arrangement would have led to successful civil suits and scrutiny on the industry. There was in fact one follow-on case brought by California and a coalition of states, which settled, but then the Supreme Court intervened.
A Cartel Economy

In 2007, the law of price-fixing fundamentally changed with the Supreme Court opinion in Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, or just “Twombly.” For decades, courts had sought to distinguish between, on the one hand, competing companies responding in the same rational manner to the same market pressures and, on the other hand, two competitors agreeing with each other to rig the market.

But where that dispute was mostly left to a judge or jury after all of the evidence had been presented, Twombly forced that dispute to occur at the outset of the case. Today, if a plaintiff doesn’t have evidence of an agreement on day 1, they get kicked out of court.

Twombly is the reason why a 25-year price-fixing scandal in the market for DRAM still exists today. When plaintiffs can hardly get their foot in the door, markets are rigged with near impunity. From RealPage to Rainmaker, and for a cottage industry of “cartel management services,” we have Twombly to thank.

To make an even finer point of it, the 2018 class action case against the memory cartel was dismissed because of Twombly. Reasonable minds can disagree, but the overarching problem is that judges have too much discretion and end up making line calls based on incomplete evidence that result in inconsistent policing of rigged markets. It’s a vibes-based approach to enforcement.

There’s a bill in Congress to fix this legal problem foisted on us by the Supreme Court. It’s called the Competitive Prices Act. The point of that law is to put the burden on competitors to avoid engaging in conduct that stacks the marketplace against consumers, rather than on outgunned consumers.

There’s a lot of anger among gamers about the high price of DRAM; people understand they are getting ripped off, and they get who is doing it. What is a bit more difficult is to show that the way around it is to fix the pleading standards for antitrust conspiracy cases. But if just a fraction of the 20 million people who are playing GTA VI this weekend understand this is the fix to their higher console prices, well, that would be a strong start.
To put it differently, what if I told you with this one little trick, Sony might release its next-gen PlayStation next year, after all?
