cnbc.com/2026/11/19/anthropic-ipo-ai-sto.headline: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?
cnbc.com/2026/11/19/anthropic-ipo-ai-sto.author: Tobias Burns

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.
The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.
It wasn't supposed to play out this way.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.
But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.
"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."
While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.
Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.
"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.
"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."
For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.
Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.
Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.
— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/hat.headline: Hat had traveled too far into Fiona’s intestines to safely remove, zoo says
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/hat.author: Amy B Wang

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news

A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo who died Thursday, showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff “tried everything they could” after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.

“Open incision in a hippo that size — with an incision that’s that long — would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasn’t enough for her,” Wenninger said in a video Friday.

Fiona’s unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons — a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday — at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.
Reporter covering consumer economics
Men made up most of Vanguard’s self-directed investors in Anthropic debut
Men made up 71 percent of the self-directed Vanguard investors who bought shares in Anthropic on the artificial intelligence company’s first day of trading on the Nasdaq.

The major investment company said about 15,400 people, or 0.22 percent of the roughly 7 million self-directed investors who have used Vanguard for more than four months, purchased Anthropic on its first day of trading.
Of those, nearly three-fourths were men, though men make up only 55 percent of all Vanguard investors.
Still, SpaceX outpaced newcomer Anthropic — nearly 0.5 percent of self-directed investors bought shares in Elon Musk’s space company on its first day of trading in June.
The median buyer in Anthropic invested about 1 percent of their portfolio in the AI company, which makes the chatbot Claude. And the median amount of stock bought was about $1,950, Vanguard said.
Some buyers wagered heavily on the company’s success: About 2 percent of them put more than half their portfolio into the stock.
Anthropic is one of the first of the new generation of AI companies to hit the public markets, raising about $79 billion from new investors in its initial sale.
Critic covering digital arts and entertainment

“Grand Theft Auto VI” generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day Thursday, Rockstar Games said Friday. The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games.

Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.”
Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it “an astonishing American epic.”

The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, “Grand Theft Auto V” hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, “Avengers: Endgame” took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” reached that mark in three weeks this summer.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, the studio’s president and founder, said in a statement.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
Trump defends Jensen Huang after alleged Chinese spy affair

President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

“He’s a good man. By the way, he’s a man — while we’re at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. “… I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.”
The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump.
The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its “brilliant people,” like Huang.
“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said.
He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI.

“You know, I came to Elon’s defense in my first term very strongly,” Trump said, without elaborating on the reason for his intervention. “I’m not sure that Elon would be with us right now if I didn’t. And I said, ‘We have to protect our brilliant people because no country has too many of them.’”
Reporter covering criminal justice in the D.C. region
Another judge blocks Trump’s arch construction in second blow to project
A second federal judge on Friday said she would block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, according to statements from the lawsuit’s parties.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said from the bench that she intended to issue a preliminary injunction, granting a request from Arlington County to halt work on the project while the case continues in the Eastern District of Virginia, according to Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy nonprofit and party to the case.
The White House on Friday said the ruling came from “another activist district court.”
“The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement.

Earlier this week, a different federal judge blocked construction of the arch for an additional two weeks while she weighs legal arguments. Brinkema’s injunction, however, would extend until the Virginia-based case is over.
Opponents of the arch include the D.C. government, the Commonwealth of Virginia, historic preservationists and some military veterans.
In a statement, an attorney with Democracy Forward said they were pleased that the judge ruled to stop what it called a “massive vanity project.”
Feature writer
Following the death of Fiona the hippo, grief has given way to outrage

On Thursday afternoon, in the hours after the Cincinnati Zoo announced the sudden death of Fiona — the world-famous, 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus who first became an internet celebrity as a premature newborn calf — legions of her fans took to social media to share their sense of shock and grief.

But the discourse has quickly spiraled into outrage, fueled by the spread of unsubstantiated accounts of what led to Fiona’s death. According to the Cincinnati Zoo, a child threw a knit hat into the air while standing in an enclosed observation area; a ceiling fan caught and flung the hat through a narrow opening, into the hippo’s enclosure. In a statement, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as an accident, noting: “We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried.”

This didn’t satisfy those who voiced fury over Fiona’s loss — focusing their ire on the child who threw the hat and the parent (or parents) who were present at the time. Some called for the family to be doxed, “charged,” “prosecuted” or far worse. In the absence of verified details, unconfirmed accounts spread wildly — sharing conflicting reports about the child’s age, their intention in throwing the hat, the conduct of the parents and whether or not zoo officials were notified when the hat entered the enclosure.

The death of the beloved hippo soon morphed into a referendum on permissive parenting and the dangers of being too lenient with misbehaving children — even as many others emphasized the impossibility of anticipating such an unlikely tragedy, and expressed concern for the safety and well-being of the child and their family who were involved in the incident.
Reporter covering arts, culture and the way we live now
‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ includes unreleased song by late singer D’Angelo

As players worldwide dive into the complex world of “Grand Theft Auto VI” this week, several have noticed a never-heard-before song playing on one of the in-game radio stations: an unreleased track by the late R&B soul visionary D’Angelo.

The song “Kamikazi” by D’Angelo — who died last year of cancer at 51 — appears in the official music credits from “Grand Theft Auto” maker Rockstar Games. Some players have posted videos of the song played by the in-game radio station, “WorldWide FM.”

This is notable because D’Angelo song releases are major musical events; the elusive godfather of neo-soul would allow years to pass between music releases. His most recent album was 2014’s “Black Messiah.”

And while his brother publicly has said there is a posthumous album on the way, it’s fitting that the first new D’Angelo song to be released since his death would be in a video game. D’Angelo was an avid gamer; in 2018 he contributed a song, the haunting “Unshaken,” to Rockstar Games’ “Red Dead Redemption 2,” a game he tested out at the company’s offices ahead of its release.
The new song is credited to “courtesy of RCA.” The record label did not immediately respond to an inquiry on whether “Kamikazi” will be released as a single elsewhere.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/as-anthropic-shares-.headline: As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/as-anthropic-shares-.author: Oliver Renick

paragraphs.text: As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.
Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/zscaler-crowdstrike-.headline: Zscaler stock jumps 20% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/zscaler-crowdstrike-.author: Samantha Subin

paragraphs.text: Zscaler shares surged 20% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor.
CrowdStrike shares fell 4% after the bell.
CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The talks between the two cyber vendors are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter.

CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the AI boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.
The potential deal would create one of the largest cybersecurity companies to date, behind cyber consolidator Palo Alto Networks, which closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
Like its rival, CrowdStrike has made a slew of acquisitions in recent months to beef up security offerings in the AI era.
Most recently, CrowdStrike announced plans to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.headline: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Sells $3.79 Billion, Making It Biggest Entertainment Launch Ever
finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/arti.author: Jason Schreier

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Take-Two Interactive Software Inc. said its new release Grand Theft Auto VI has generated $3.79 billion in revenue worldwide through the end of the day on Thursday's launch, making it the most successful entertainment property in history.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The company said it sold 32.5 million units in presales, also a record. A PC version of the game is expected to be released at a later date, as is an online component. The game costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for a package that includes a bonus vehicle, weapons, outfits and other in-game items.
Take-Two shares reversed losses earlier in the day and were up about 2.7% in New York trading.

Anticipation was significant going into Thursday's release. It's been 13 years since the last fully new addition to the Grand Theft Auto franchise, one of the most popular ever. The new game allows players to explore and rob their way through a fictional version of Miami called Vice City. Take-Two's subsidiary Rockstar Games, which now has more than 4,700 employees, spent more than eight years developing the game. The reviews have been the highest ever for a video game, with Bloomberg calling it "a masterpiece."

"This is a new platform for Rockstar to build more games and build on top, with really high fidelity," Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese said in a Bloomberg TV interview on Friday before the sales were announced. "This should benefit Take-Two for years to come."

The release has turned into a popular culture moment. Take-Two paid for a marketing takeover of Miami, which celebrated the release even as it faced backlash from some residents. The NBA's Miami Heat played a game Wednesday in an arena bedecked with references to the game. Take-Two plans a concert Saturday in the city. Online influencers have been streaming marathon sessions of their gameplay on sites like Amazon.com Inc.'s Twitch and Alphabet Inc.'s YouTube.
Many fans of the game took Thursday off of work to play the game, which is also expected to eat into family time over the coming Thanksgiving weekend.
Grand Theft Auto V, the previous game in the franchise, generated sales of $800 million in its first 24 hours and $1 billion over three days after its 2013 debut.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/trum.headline: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/trum.author: Ben Doherty

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/20/ben.headline: Bengals’ winding path offers Commanders a road map back to prominence
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/20/ben.author: Tashan Reed

paragraphs.text: The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books.

That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window.
The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since.

It wasn’t until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons.
When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals’ winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same.

The adversity hit right away for Cincinnati. After getting drafted first overall in 2020, Burrow suffered a torn ACL and MCL in his left knee. While there weren’t questions about his health by the time he signed an extension in September 2023, that wouldn’t last long.

Burrow suffered a season-ending wrist injury later that season. Although he was healthy in 2024, he missed nine games because of turf toe last season. Amid his inability to stay on the field, his cap hit ballooned from about $19.5 million in 2023 to $29.5 million in 2024 and $45.9 million in 2025.

That led to some difficult decisions for Duke Tobin, the Bengals’ director of player personnel. Burrow’s increasingly expensive contract — along with new deals for wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins — led them to lose several core players from their Super Bowl run.
That increased the pressure on Tobin to build the team through the draft. He proved to be capable — of their 22 starters, 14 were drafted or signed by Cincinnati as undrafted free agents.

With that base of homegrown talent, Tobin was freed up to take some risks. He signed left tackle Orlando Brown Jr., defensive end Boye Mafe, defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and safety Bryan Cook to significant free agent contracts in recent years and made a splashy trade for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence this past offseason.

Throughout the roster reconstruction, the Bengals remained committed to head coach Zac Taylor. There were plenty of questions about his job security last winter after they missed the playoffs for the third consecutive season.

Cincinnati made coordinator changes, but they stuck with Taylor. As the franchise reshaped itself around Burrow, the Bengals maintained continuity in the front office and coaching staff. They were criticized at times, but the patience paid dividends.

“With Joe being out, that was obviously a big piece of it for them — he’s such an incredible player,” Commanders Coach Dan Quinn said. “But I think, starting with him, there’s a lot of resiliency and toughness that come throughout the entire team.”

Washington got off to a much faster start with its magical run to the NFC championship game during the 2024 season, when Daniels was a rookie, but they’ve since plummeted. Daniels — and many others throughout the roster — suffered major injuries and doomed a 2025 season that ended with a 5-12 record.

This season also presented challenges. Although Daniels missed just two games after re-dislocating his left elbow in Week 2, several key teammates — Laremy Tunsil, Terry McLaurin, Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw — have gone down with injuries. The Commanders remain alive in the playoff hunt, but their chances of advancing (if they manage to get there) are low.

Changing that will probably require another offseason retooling. The question is whether the tandem of General Manager Adam Peters and Quinn will be handling that. Owner Josh Harris hasn’t made any public decisions, but it’s worth looking ahead, anyway.

To mirror what Cincinnati has pulled off, the Commanders must draft better. Quinn’s game management issues and failure to consistently close out contests have drawn criticism this season, but the roster is flawed. They simply don’t have enough young, ascending talent.

Peters has hit on picks such as Daniels, linebacker Sonny Styles and wide receiver Antonio Williams, but the overall results have been underwhelming. Only six of Washington’s 22 starters were drafted by Peters. The roster also lacks quality depth.
The Commanders have leaned heavily on veteran acquisitions throughout Peters’ tenure. That’s not a recipe for continuous growth.

In the short term, it’s largely on Quinn and Daniels to ensure this regime gets another crack at improving in the offseason. Harris didn’t give Quinn a win total he needs to hit, but he wants to see progress. Given the state of the roster, Daniels will have to play at an elite level for that to happen.

“You don’t really know what you’ve learned until you get into the next season and the next opportunity,” Quinn said. “So, for us, having him playing now and getting back into that over an extended time, that’s winning football.”
It remains to be seen whether that’ll translate to results. Knocking off the Bengals would make their hopes of gaining ground in the NFC East a lot more realistic.
“The proof is in, ‘Can you do it again? Can you do again?’” Quinn said. “That’s what I’m looking for.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/sp-500-8000-kalshi-o.headline: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/sp-500-8000-kalshi-o.author: Davis Giangiulio

paragraphs.text: As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/20/t.headline: Texas governor-elect and Trump agree to work together on border security
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/20/t.author: Molly Hennessy-Fiske

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
“It was a very productive call,” Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa, adding, “I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall.

“He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,” said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. “I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.”

On Thursday, Hinojosa met the state’s border sheriffs and told Fox News, “We need the federal government to put more resources along the border,” noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICE’s violent interior immigration enforcement “needs to end.”
“We have had people killed in the streets,” she said. “I will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Hat had traveled too far into Fiona’s intestines to safely remove, zoo says

A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo who died Thursday, showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff “tried everything they could” after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.

“Open incision in a hippo that size — with an incision that’s that long — would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasn’t enough for her,” Wenninger said in a video Friday.

Fiona’s unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons — a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday — at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.
Additional Coverage
Reporter covering consumer economics
Men made up most of Vanguard’s self-directed investors in Anthropic debut
Men made up 71 percent of the self-directed Vanguard investors who bought shares in Anthropic on the artificial intelligence company’s first day of trading on the Nasdaq.

The major investment company said about 15,400 people, or 0.22 percent of the roughly 7 million self-directed investors who have used Vanguard for more than four months, purchased Anthropic on its first day of trading.
Of those, nearly three-fourths were men, though men make up only 55 percent of all Vanguard investors.
Still, SpaceX outpaced newcomer Anthropic — nearly 0.5 percent of self-directed investors bought shares in Elon Musk’s space company on its first day of trading in June.
The median buyer in Anthropic invested about 1 percent of their portfolio in the AI company, which makes the chatbot Claude. And the median amount of stock bought was about $1,950, Vanguard said.
Some buyers wagered heavily on the company’s success: About 2 percent of them put more than half their portfolio into the stock.
Anthropic is one of the first of the new generation of AI companies to hit the public markets, raising about $79 billion from new investors in its initial sale.
Critic covering digital arts and entertainment

“Grand Theft Auto VI” generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day Thursday, Rockstar Games said Friday. The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games.

Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.”
Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it “an astonishing American epic.”

The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, “Grand Theft Auto V” hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, “Avengers: Endgame” took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” reached that mark in three weeks this summer.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, the studio’s president and founder, said in a statement.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
Trump defends Jensen Huang after alleged Chinese spy affair

President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

“He’s a good man. By the way, he’s a man — while we’re at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. “… I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.”
The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump.
The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its “brilliant people,” like Huang.
“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said.
He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI.

“You know, I came to Elon’s defense in my first term very strongly,” Trump said, without elaborating on the reason for his intervention. “I’m not sure that Elon would be with us right now if I didn’t. And I said, ‘We have to protect our brilliant people because no country has too many of them.’”
Reporter covering criminal justice in the D.C. region
Another judge blocks Trump’s arch construction in second blow to project
A second federal judge on Friday said she would block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, according to statements from the lawsuit’s parties.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said from the bench that she intended to issue a preliminary injunction, granting a request from Arlington County to halt work on the project while the case continues in the Eastern District of Virginia, according to Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy nonprofit and party to the case.
The White House on Friday said the ruling came from “another activist district court.”
“The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement.

Earlier this week, a different federal judge blocked construction of the arch for an additional two weeks while she weighs legal arguments. Brinkema’s injunction, however, would extend until the Virginia-based case is over.
Opponents of the arch include the D.C. government, the Commonwealth of Virginia, historic preservationists and some military veterans.
In a statement, an attorney with Democracy Forward said they were pleased that the judge ruled to stop what it called a “massive vanity project.”
Feature writer
Following the death of Fiona the hippo, grief has given way to outrage

On Thursday afternoon, in the hours after the Cincinnati Zoo announced the sudden death of Fiona — the world-famous, 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus who first became an internet celebrity as a premature newborn calf — legions of her fans took to social media to share their sense of shock and grief.

But the discourse has quickly spiraled into outrage, fueled by the spread of unsubstantiated accounts of what led to Fiona’s death. According to the Cincinnati Zoo, a child threw a knit hat into the air while standing in an enclosed observation area; a ceiling fan caught and flung the hat through a narrow opening, into the hippo’s enclosure. In a statement, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as an accident, noting: “We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried.”

This didn’t satisfy those who voiced fury over Fiona’s loss — focusing their ire on the child who threw the hat and the parent (or parents) who were present at the time. Some called for the family to be doxed, “charged,” “prosecuted” or far worse. In the absence of verified details, unconfirmed accounts spread wildly — sharing conflicting reports about the child’s age, their intention in throwing the hat, the conduct of the parents and whether or not zoo officials were notified when the hat entered the enclosure.

The death of the beloved hippo soon morphed into a referendum on permissive parenting and the dangers of being too lenient with misbehaving children — even as many others emphasized the impossibility of anticipating such an unlikely tragedy, and expressed concern for the safety and well-being of the child and their family who were involved in the incident.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Lawmakers On Verge of Deal to Ban Chinese Cars, Moreno Says
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Steven T. Dennis

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- US lawmakers are closing in on an agreement to shut China's fast-growing automakers out of the US market that avoids entangling Mercedes-Benz Group AG, Senator Bernie Moreno said.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Ohio Republican spearheading the effort said in an interview Friday that all major issues have been resolved, including changes to protect the German automaker, which is about 20% owned by Chinese entities.
"We're super, super, super close," Moreno told Bloomberg at the Capitol. "All the big issues are resolved."

If enacted, the measure would wall off the world's second-largest auto market from China's automakers such as BYD Co., which have rapidly grown around the world with technology-packed electric vehicles that often undercut Western competition on price. Although tariffs and technology restrictions already effectively block Chinese cars from the US, enshrining a ban into law would go a step further.
Bloomberg reported Thursday that lawmakers were nearing an agreement to ban Chinese cars.

Carmakers in the US have urged Congress to adopt the ban, citing economic and national security threats posed by subsidized Chinese cars equipped with software and hardware that can transmit data about American drivers and infrastructure.

Moreno said negotiators are still working out some technical details about the legislation. The goal is to ensure the same bill can pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate, either on its own or packaged with another bill like the annual defense policy legislation.
Earlier legislation under consideration would have prohibited sales of connected vehicles by automakers that are more than 15% owned by Chinese entities.

That risked jeopardizing Mercedes' business in the US. The German carmaker is nearly 10% owned by China's BAIC Motor Corp., a state-owned carmaker. Li Shu Fu, the billionaire founder of Chinese carmaker Geely, also holds nearly 10% of Mercedes' shares, putting the company above the earlier bill's 15% threshold.

"The Mercedes issue is not even on the table anymore," Moreno said. "The bill is about banning Chinese predatory vehicles that affect national security, economic security. Mercedes doesn't affect either one of those."
Moreno also said there is agreement on language regarding battery technology.
"We're down to the final technical details, and hopefully we'll get it across the finish line when we get back," he said.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/se.headline: Secret Board Talks, Big Payday: Inside GM’s CEO Succession Plans
finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/se.author: David Welch

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- General Motors Co.'s strategy was clear: bring on a tech executive with software and self-driving smarts, and give them a shot at earning the automaker's top job.
Most Read from Bloomberg

It's a plan that has put Sterling Anderson in a strong position to succeed Mary Barra, GM's chief executive officer since 2014, when the moment is right. People familiar with the board's thinking say the prevailing idea is GM's next leader should be savvy in the very areas that Anderson concentrates on as global product chief.

The question is whether Anderson, who's 43 and been with GM for just shy of 18 months, is ready to step up and lead its tens of thousands of engineers and union workers into a highly uncertain future for the global auto industry. Barra and GM's board have been mulling the timing of naming a new CEO and transitioning to new leadership, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. The courses of action could include Barra staying on beyond this year as CEO or becoming GM's executive chair.

People familiar with the matter say Anderson recently did a round of one-on-one meetings with board directors, though the exact purpose is unclear. The company also has been working for more than a month with the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help evaluate potential external candidates, the people said.
A GM spokesperson declined to comment.

Anderson has been busy since GM poached him from Aurora Innovation Inc., the startup he co-founded with the former head of Google's self-driving car project. He's led an initiative to cut GM's vehicle development cycle in half. He rehired key personnel from Cruise, the robotaxi operation GM shuttered months before he joined the company, and revived efforts to build autonomous vehicles. By 2028, the goal is to deliver a Cadillac that can safely coast on its own without a driver's hands on the wheel or eyes on the road.

GM's board, chaired by Barra since 2016, is weighing that early record against a range of factors. For one, there's no rush to usher Barra out of the CEO seat she's occupied since January 2014. While the company's normal retirement age is 65, and Barra will celebrate that birthday on Christmas Eve, there's no mandate for her to bow out.

The board also has internal alternatives. Chief Financial Officer Paul Jacobson is interested in the top job and could be considered if the board opts to give Anderson more time to settle in, people familiar with the matter said. While the 54-year-old former Delta Air Lines Inc. CFO is well liked by Wall Street, financial proficiency is a lesser priority. Barra and GM's directors are more interested in finding leadership with command of the role software is playing in controlling modern vehicles, as well as how advances in artificial intelligence will define transportation for years to come, the people said.
President Mark Reuss, a 63-year-old GM lifer, may also play a major role in a transition, but at his age is less likely to be CEO.

"I'm not convinced she is going to leave, nor do I think she should," Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a Yale School of Management professor, said of Barra. The two speak roughly half a dozen times a year. "She has done very well and we have other successful companies being led by leaders past 65."

This is a critical juncture for GM to be working out who will lead the carmaker into a next era. Chinese manufacturers have been flooding virtually all major auto markets other than the US with millions of vehicles, further crowding an already congested industry that's long grappled with chronic overcapacity.

While GM has been able to count on refuge from Washington, which has put up barriers to Chinese imports, President Donald Trump has on multiple occasions indicated a willingness to let the likes of BYD Co. or Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd. in, as long as they manufacture locally. Even if China's automakers end up steering clear or are kept at bay, GM and its peers are increasingly reliant on a US new-car market that has never been more expensive and is close to peak levels of demand.

GM's answer to these challenges has been to try to match its Chinese counterparts on costs and speed to market. Anderson has played a lead role in the company's push to use AI and digital tools to reduce its vehicle development time to two years, down from four.

The automaker also is trying to get back into the automated driving game after its robotaxi unit Cruise imploded two years ago. Anderson, who as a direct report to Elon Musk led the team that delivered Tesla Inc.'s Autopilot, has invigorated GM's development of Super Cruise, a hands-free system now generating billions of dollars of subscription revenue.

While Anderson may have the technology background GM seeks, less than two years ago he was the second-in-command at Aurora, an autonomous trucking startup with only around 2,000 employees. GM has single factories with double that staff.

Auto industry succession has always been thorny, in part due to the breadth of expertise required spanning product, sales, engineering, manufacturing and more. It can also be a tough sell nowadays, because with the exception of Tesla, carmakers' market valuations pale in comparison to tech giants.

Anderson was brought in with an annual pay package set at $16 million, the majority of which is stock-based and vests over time. He also was awarded one-time cash and at-risk stock awards totaling $24 million as part of his new-hire package. This meant Anderson's compensation package exceeded $40 million last year, surpassing Barra's total, which was just shy of $30 million.

Barra has been opening up lanes for her direct reports to shine. When GM has hosted new vehicle and tech showcases in New York the past two years, the CEO has kicked off festivities, then handed off the mic to Anderson to do most of the talking. She's taken a similar approach to earnings calls, with Jacobson getting most of the airtime with Wall Street analysts.
Anderson also has planted a flag in Michigan. He moved to the Detroit area this year and no longer commutes in from Silicon Valley.

Barra is preparing to hand over the reins having racked up major achievements, most notably getting GM in the game with electrification and hands-free driving. She also navigated a faulty ignition switch crisis that erupted almost immediately after she started as CEO.
There also have been some major missteps.

The company's electric vehicle program is in a strong position if Americans start to shift to plug-ins anytime soon, but this has come at great cost. GM has shelled out some $35 billion on EVs and autonomous driving, with little in the way of early return on investment.

GM was far from alone in plowing billions into EVs that have sold in underwhelming volumes, but Barra went long by developing a dozen models and aiming to sell 1 million a year. The company's sales have come nowhere near that level, even before Trump pulled the rug out from the EV market by ending incentive programs and gutting fuel economy and emissions regulations.

The company has written down more than $11 billion of its EV investments, and after spending over $10 billion to acquire and grow Cruise, shut the operation down after one if its cars dragged a woman and regulators grounded its fleet.

GM's stock price was static for much of Barra's tenure. Over the past three years, it has more than doubled as the automaker bought back $29 billion in shares. GM has taken some political heat from progressive Democrats including Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed for recently authorizing another $20 billion worth of repurchases.
Those moves largely came under the direction of Jacobson. If he pushes for the job, GM's recent share performance bolsters his case.
When asked at a Barclays investor conference this week about potential leadership transition, Jacobson reiterated comments Barra has made about still being invigorated by the job.

"As Mary has said very publicly, she's got a lot of energy for this," Jacobson said. "I can vouch for that. Some day she has more energy than I do, and that's evidenced by the grilling that I get from time to time. She's here, she's fully engaged, and I expect that to continue."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Goldman Says Stock Selloff Has Legs as Panic Index Nears Maximum
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Natalia Kniazhevich

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Goldman Sachs Group Inc.'s panic gauge climbed near its maximum level as US stocks tumbled Friday, signaling that another substantial wave of selling will follow over the coming week, according to the bank's traders.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Goldman's trading desk said the selloff has spread across the so-called systematic investors, as the bank's Panic Index rose to 9 out of 10. Momentum traders, such as commodity trading advisers, sold $57 billion in equities over the past month, with their net positioning in US stocks turning short by $19 billion, according to Goldman estimates.
The bank's models are projecting that CTAs could offload another $65.8 billion in a flat market, $28.6 billion if stocks rise and as much as $80.6 billion if equities continue to decline.

The market's latest leg lower reflects growing investor reluctance to buy the dip in technology stocks, even as Anthropic PBC's blockbuster initial public offering was seen as a potential catalyst for a broader recovery in risk appetite. Instead, the listing has failed to deliver the anticipated market-wide boost.

Many investors were looking for the world's biggest offering "to act as a clearing event to usher a 'risk-back-on' trade into year end," Goldman traders wrote in a note. "Without this force it has been a tough pill to swallow."

The selling threatens to reinforce an already difficult market environment, as falling prices trigger further reductions in exposure by trend-following strategies, which adjust their positions based on the stock market direction and volatility.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending on AI infrastructure, chips and computing capacity will generate returns sufficient to justify the valuations across the sector. The concerns were compounded by the turmoil at Nvidia Corp., which led to the ouster of chief executive Jensen Huang.

Crowded positions and momentum-driven strategies have exacerbated volatility, with technology shares at the center of the selloff. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6% Friday in its worst week since March 2020 and the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index tumbled 11%, dragged by losses in Nvidia, which has plunged nearly 50% from its Oct. 6 peak after a 14% slump Friday.

The retreat is also spreading beyond institutional portfolios into more speculative corners of the market. Goldman's basket of retail investor favorites fell 8.9%, while its Bitcoin-sensitive basket dropped 11%. The rotation into defensive stocks was also evident, with the bank's cyclical-versus-defensive basket declining 3.2%.
