npr.org/2026/11/20/g-s1-154797/nasdaq-sp.headline: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
npr.org/2026/11/20/g-s1-154797/nasdaq-sp.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/treasury-secretary-s.headline: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/treasury-secretary-s.author: Kevin Breuninger, Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.
Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating.

A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.

Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.

"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."
Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.
The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.
Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.
Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.
"We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.

The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.

Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.
Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.

The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.

They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.

In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.

Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.

Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."

"I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.
Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.
Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde1lj4yjxno.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde1lj4yjxno.author: Wedaeli Chibelushi

paragraphs.text: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-lutnick-commer.headline: Trump says he still has confidence in Lutnick
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-lutnick-commer.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday said he has not lost confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, pushing back on growing pressure from bipartisan lawmakers and even members of his own administration.

Trump, at a wide-ranging White House press conference, was asked about Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., telling The Wall Street Journal that, if Lutnick is to be ousted, it should happen soon enough for the Republican-led Senate to confirm his replacement before Democrats take over the chamber.

"Well, Tom's right," Trump replied, saying he would agree with taking swift action if he had indeed lost confidence in Lutnick. "But I have not lost confidence," Trump said in response to a question from CNBC's Eamon Javers.
"He's a different kind of a guy, very good businessman. He's not traditional," Trump said, praising Lutnick's involvement in the U.S. taking an equity stake in Intel.

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/politics/train.headline: Officials Find Cascade of Problems With ICE Training in Trump’s Immigration Crackdown

paragraphs.text: The Department of Homeland Security went too far last year in loosening training standards for thousands of immigration officers hired to support President Trump’s mass deportation push, an internal department watchdog has found.

The findings, in a 19-page draft report that has not been finalized or released, amount to a sweeping critique of the plan carried out under Kristi Noem, the homeland security secretary at the time, to rapidly hire and deploy 10,000 new officers with the help of tens of billions of dollars provided by Congress.
One recruit instructor quoted in the draft report, which was obtained by The New York Times, called the rollbacks in training standards a “catastrophic failure.”

Among the changes highlighted was a decision to allow more than 3,500 recruits with prior law enforcement experience to complete their basic training virtually. Previously, the training was done fully in person at a training center over the course of a month. Using the online option, some officers completed the training in less than a day.

The draft report also criticized the relaxing of a policy that had given the recruits only two chances to pass a training test. As the department staffed up, it allowed them to take the test an unlimited number of times. One officer took the training test 32 times before passing.

The draft noted that the current secretary, Markwayne Mullin, restored the more robust training standards in July. However, it said, “despite increasing training hours and days for future recruits, ICE has not fully addressed training gaps born of the reductions and revisions.”

The rush to hire officers and get them onto American streets came after months of pressure from the White House to increase deportations and arrests. While Immigration and Customs Enforcement has long said that the training was adequate, several shootings and other incidents have led to concerns that underqualified and improperly vetted people were being given ICE badges.

The draft report, from the Homeland Security Department’s Office of Inspector General, did not consider whether lax training had contributed to problems on the ground. But at least one officer involved in a recent incident is known to have joined ICE while lower standards were in place: David Brouillette, who was hired last December and fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant, in Maine this summer during a vehicle stop.
Representatives for Ms. Noem did not respond. Mr. Brouillette did not respond to a message to his personal email address.
In a statement, the Homeland Security Department said that Mr. Mullin had acted quickly upon taking office and that ICE officers were getting extra training.

“A significant portion of officers brought on during the hiring surge have law enforcement experience and have already successfully completed a law enforcement academy,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement.
Asked at a hearing this week about training changes, Mr. Mullin told Congress that “there were some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we are having to undo.”

ICE officer training has come under scrutiny as viral videos documenting rough tactics have proliferated online, and the agency has been involved in a series of shootings of immigrants and a U.S. citizen. The agency has faced a downturn in public support and intensifying criticism from Democrats, including numerous candidates who won in the midterm elections promising reforms.

One whistle-blower previously reported that the agency had “improperly vetted” new recruits. Top ICE officials believed that the training changes were a mistake, according to a former senior official who spoke to The Times on the condition of anonymity to discuss the findings in the draft report.

The Homeland Security Department’s inspector general, Joseph V. Cuffari, is one of the few internal agency watchdogs Mr. Trump did not dismiss after retaking office. Mr. Cuffari, who was nominated by Mr. Trump during the president’s first term, has been aggressive in examining agency practices. His office is also scrutinizing contracting, ICE hiring and compensation.

“We strongly condemn the premature release of draft reports before the department has had the opportunity to complete its review and provide formal comments,” Mr. Cuffari’s office said in a statement. “Such disclosures undermine the integrity of the oversight process, risk presenting incomplete or misleading information, and compromise the fairness and accuracy essential to credible oversight.”
Truncated training for thousands of officers

In-person basic training historically has included firearms instruction, de-escalation techniques, use-of-force lessons, techniques for handcuffing and ways of identifying the immigration status of targets, among other topics. But from August 2025 to around July this year, nearly 6,000 officers went through a sharply curtailed training model, according to the draft.
Among those hires were many with law-enforcement backgrounds.

The more than 3,500 deportation officers with prior law enforcement were hired under the more lax training standards, the inspector general draft report found. That is equivalent to about 35 percent of the active force of deportation officers across the country. Deportation officers work in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, or ERO.

The draft report found the online training provided recruits a way to speed through the training. More than 80 percent of those completed the training within 10 days. Some went even quicker: More than 10 percent completed it within 24 hours. At least five recruits did it within two hours.
An ICE official who spoke with inspector general agents said it should have taken the recruits the same amount of time as before — about a month.

“Another graduate told us that some students clicked through the learning modules without absorbing content,” the draft report said. “An ERO official stated that the virtual training appeared ineffective for many recruits, and they would have preferred that those recruits (even with prior law-enforcement experience) take in-person training instead.”
ICE told the inspector general’s office that additional in-person trainings were offered to these officers.

ICE officials cut the training hours for recruits with no law enforcement experience from 543 hours to around 300 hours, and the number of days of training went down from 72 to 42 days. The cuts were made beginning in November 2025 until February 2026.

ICE officials cut training hours on “law enforcement handguns,” how to control detainees during deportation flights, driving maneuvers, and “arrests and determining citizenship.” More than 2,000 recruits — or more than 20 percent of its deportation officers — went through the condensed training, the document says.

The agency also withdrew from Federal Law Enforcement Training Accreditation, which vets federal training standards. The U.S. Secret Service and the Department of Veterans Affairs have been accredited by the organization.
ICE officials believed the changes to the training made them ineligible, according to the draft report. One official said that without the accreditation the training could “become a crisis.”
ICE has reapplied, but the process takes three years.
No explanation given to watchdog agents

The draft report said inspector general agents struggled to determine the rationale of department leaders in justifying the slimmed-down training because the leaders “did not leave behind any written explanation for their decision.”

The watchdog agents spoke with the former head of training, who told them he was ordered to make the changes. The official indicated “that course reductions were dictated to him by then ICE deputy director and strongly supported by former Secretary Kristi Noem and former senior adviser Corey Lewandowski.”
Mr. Lewandowski did not respond to a request for comment.
ICE instructors found the changes alarming.

“Several ERO instructors shared concerns that students were not adequately trained or tested on critical material,” the draft report said. “One instructor characterized the revised training as a ‘catastrophic failure.’ Another instructor noted that undertrained students could become liabilities.”

Earlier this year, Ryan Schwank, a former ICE lawyer who quit the agency in February, publicly detailed some of the changes to the courses for new recruits. ICE officials at the time said that on-the-job training would be a supplement.
In March, The Washington Post reported on documents it obtained backing the claims made by the whistle-blower.

“The training does not stop after graduation from the academy — recruits are put on a rigorous on-the-job training program that is tracked and monitored,” read an agency statement following Mr. Schwank’s disclosures.
But officials with inspector general’s office also found problems with the on-the-job training, in which ICE officers are supposed to build on academy knowledge with the help of coaches.

“ICE could not demonstrate that its field offices consistently implemented” on-the-job training “as intended,” the draft report found, “raising significant concerns about the completeness and effectiveness of employee training.”
Nearly 90 percent of ICE officials managing the program who filled out a questionnaire sent to them by the inspector general’s office said the on-the-job training was “not successful.”

In some places, like Dallas, the push for more arrests meant that the training became a secondary thought. A supervisor there said that the push to get “nearly every officer” out doing arrests and deportations made it impossible to do more advanced training.

In Baltimore, new recruits were assigned to follow more senior officers instead of getting a coach to train them formally. And in San Francisco, the draft report said, on-the-job training was more informal because there were not enough people to carry it out.
The inspector general officials had a stark warning to ICE leadership.
“It is imperative,” the draft report said, “that steps be taken to promptly ensure all new ICE hires are fully prepared to perform their law enforcement duties and responsibilities.”

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-20/ca.headline: California adds 47,000 jobs in October, as unemployment drops to three-year low
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-20/ca.author: Laurence Darmiento

paragraphs.text: The California economy surprisingly added 47,100 jobs in October, defying expectations and dropping the state’s unemployment rate to its lowest level in three years, according to jobs figures released Friday.
The economy added jobs broadly, including in professional and business services, while prior gains were largely limited to health care to meet the growing needs of the state’s aging population.

The job growth accounted for 28.5% of the nation’s increase of 165,000 jobs for the month, even as California’s unemployment rate of 5% remained second-highest among states — and well above the national mark of 4.1%, according to the state Employment Development Department.
With the gains, the state has added 148,700 jobs this year. By comparison, California lost 9,300 jobs in September, the agency said.
“You don’t want to read too much into a single month, but this could not have been a much more positive report,” said economist Manfred Keil, a professor at Claremont McKenna College.

He noted that unlike past months when the unemployment rate dropped due to a shrinking number of people looking for work, in October the state reported the civilian labor force grew by nearly 5,000 people.

The latest employment data counters a state economic picture that some have characterized as a “jobless boom,” with little job growth despite California’s 2.5% real second quarter GDP growth outpacing the national average.

Through the second quarter, California companies received $366 billion in venture capital, three times more than every other state combined. It also has benefited from huge initial public offerings, including SpaceX $75 billion IPO in June, a record until Anthropic raised $107 billion this week, netting a huge windfall for L.A. investors.

Still, the state has experienced a series of high profile layoffs in Silicon Valley amid the wrenching AI revolution, and in Hollywood, where runaway production and disruption in the streaming industry have caused job losses.

Just last month, the quarterly UCLA Anderson School of Management forecast said that the state’s economic growth should exceed the nation’s for the rest of the year due to AI investments, a revitalized aerospace industry and a growing U.S. defense budget, but not result in significant job gains.

However, the latest job figures show that eight of 11 industry sectors added jobs in October, with professional and business accounting for 11,600, and leisure and hospitality another 8,100. Other notable job gains include government at 5,100 and manufacturing at 3,400.
Keil said that the gains in leisure and hospitality indicate more people are eating out and booking hotel rooms, while it appears the huge AI investments are finally generating job growth.

Michael Bernick, a former director of the Employment Development Department, said that the data indicate AI is not causing the job destruction that some feared, while growth in the aerospace and defense, as well as large public infrastructure projects, is creating strong demand for engineers.

He added that the large initial public offerings creating huge wealth for investors will also create job demand, though it will take some time for that money to percolate through the economy. He noted the state is doing well in creating startups with 57,316 new business applications in September alone — though he added a caveat regarding California’s business environment.

“The Census Bureau also identifies applications likely to become employer firms and those that report a planned date for paying wages. On these measures, California is more to the middle of the state rankings, reflecting the disincentives to hiring that have been built up in the state over the past four decades,” he said in a statement.
Keil added that the state’s economy may unexpectedly gain from the mid-term election results if projected cuts in Medicaid funding are either trimmed or rolled back.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9d7e9wvvweo.headline: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9d7e9wvvweo.author: Hugh Schofield

paragraphs.text: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/la-.headline: L.A. train heists net thieves more than $22 million in goods, feds say
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/20/la-.author: N. Kirkpatrick

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Visual correspondent covering California and the Southwest
The freight train was still clattering down the tracks when a masked man using a red Milwaukee angle grinder sawed through the lock of a shipping container filled with Nike Air Max sneakers.

By the time the crew filmed this heist in October 2024, it had already allegedly stolen more than $167,000 in Nike shoes in another train job. According to a federal indictment released Thursday, they were just getting started.

The Southern California crew is charged with breaking into more than 70 shipping containers over 31 months, stealing more than $22 million in electronics, tools, sneakers and other apparel to be sold on the black market.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the indictment. The 14 men were arrested Thursday and a federal grand jury charged each of them with one count of conspiracy, 14 counts of theft and two counts of violence against railroad carriers.

Federal prosecutors say the crew was led by Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, and included his father and two uncles. They allegedly identified trains hauling high-value cargo from overseas and were moving through Southern California rail yards headed to distribution centers out of state. The thieves allegedly climbed aboard and cut air hoses to trigger the emergency brakes at predetermined locations, where they loaded rental trucks and vans with stolen goods.

The indictment comes during concerns about rail heists around the country. According to the Association of American Railroads there were more than 75,000 thefts nationally last year with a 50 percent increase year over year. In Los Angeles, a string of thefts in 2022 left hundreds of boxes strewn on the tracks.
“The images looked like a Third World country,” Gov. Gavin Newsom told reporters at the time. “What you saw here in the last week is just not acceptable.”
Reporter covering Latin America from Mexico City
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
El Salvador’s popular and ironfisted president, Nayib Bukele, formally registered his candidacy for a third term Thursday, setting the stage for elections in February that he is expected to win.

Since entering office in 2019, Bukele, 45, has found widespread support at home and from some quarters abroad for his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and a steep reduction in homicides. But he has been widely criticized for curtailing civil liberties, sweeping up alleged gang members without due process, repressing political dissent and dismantling democratic institutions.

He has successfully consolidated his power in what has become a de facto one-party state. Last year, Bukele’s allies in the legislature changed the country’s constitution to allow a president to serve an unlimited number of terms. If he wins next year’s elections, he would remain president until 2033.
Speaking before cheering crowds Thursday after registering his candidacy at the country’s electoral tribunal, Bukele said that “some international media say there isn’t democracy in El Salvador.”
“I tell them, no, no, no, there wasn’t democracy in El Salvador before,” he said.

Bukele is launching his candidacy as he pursues a gang battle abroad, in Haiti, where he has deployed about 2,500 Salvadoran troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing during a gang ambush while supporting a United Nations-backed international force. This week, large crowds poured into the streets in Haiti to praise and thank Bukele.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
Texas governor-elect and Trump agree to work together on border security
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
“It was a very productive call,” Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa, adding, “I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall.

“He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,” said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. “I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.”

On Thursday, Hinojosa met the state’s border sheriffs and told Fox News, “We need the federal government to put more resources along the border,” noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICE’s violent interior immigration enforcement “needs to end.”
“We have had people killed in the streets,” she said. “I will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Hat had traveled too far into Fiona’s intestines to safely remove, zoo says

A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo who died Thursday, showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff “tried everything they could” after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.

“Open incision in a hippo that size — with an incision that’s that long — would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasn’t enough for her,” Wenninger said in a video Friday.

Fiona’s unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons — a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday — at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.
Additional Coverage
Reporter covering consumer economics
Men made up most of Vanguard’s self-directed investors in Anthropic debut
Men made up 71 percent of the self-directed Vanguard investors who bought shares in Anthropic on the artificial intelligence company’s first day of trading on the Nasdaq.

The major investment company said about 15,400 people, or 0.22 percent of the roughly 7 million self-directed investors who have used Vanguard for more than four months, purchased Anthropic on its first day of trading.
Of those, nearly three-fourths were men, though men make up only 55 percent of all Vanguard investors.
Still, SpaceX outpaced newcomer Anthropic — nearly 0.5 percent of self-directed investors bought shares in Elon Musk’s space company on its first day of trading in June.
The median buyer in Anthropic invested about 1 percent of their portfolio in the AI company, which makes the chatbot Claude. And the median amount of stock bought was about $1,950, Vanguard said.
Some buyers wagered heavily on the company’s success: About 2 percent of them put more than half their portfolio into the stock.
Anthropic is one of the first of the new generation of AI companies to hit the public markets, raising about $79 billion from new investors in its initial sale.
Critic covering digital arts and entertainment

“Grand Theft Auto VI” generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day Thursday, Rockstar Games said Friday. The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games.

Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.”
Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it “an astonishing American epic.”

The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, “Grand Theft Auto V” hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, “Avengers: Endgame” took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” reached that mark in three weeks this summer.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, the studio’s president and founder, said in a statement.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
Trump defends Jensen Huang after alleged Chinese spy affair

President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

“He’s a good man. By the way, he’s a man — while we’re at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. “… I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.”
The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump.
The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its “brilliant people,” like Huang.
“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said.
He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI.

“You know, I came to Elon’s defense in my first term very strongly,” Trump said, without elaborating on the reason for his intervention. “I’m not sure that Elon would be with us right now if I didn’t. And I said, ‘We have to protect our brilliant people because no country has too many of them.’”

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Penry Buckley, Lisa Cox

paragraphs.text: The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.
At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT by 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.
Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.
“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”
She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.
“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.
The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.
She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.
‘Serious corruption risk’

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent changes from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.
The Law Society of NSW said on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jre8xd83qgo.headline: Nepal PM Balendra Shah to meet India PM Modi on first trip abroad
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jre8xd83qgo.author: Anbarasan Ethirajan

paragraphs.text: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.headline: Retrial ends with conviction of man accused of sparking Palisades fire
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.author: Brittny Mejia

paragraphs.text: Following a mistrial over the summer, a federal jury on Friday convicted a 30-year-old former Uber driver accused of intentionally setting a blaze that later became the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

Federal prosecutors accused Jonathan Rinderknecht of using a lighter to ignite the Lachman fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — a fire they said burned underground for days and reignited as the deadly Palisades fire. Rinderknecht’s defense attorney argued there was no evidence proving his client set the fire and offered fireworks as an alternate cause.
The jury deliberated for just over two days before returning its verdict of guilty on both counts he faced.

Rinderknecht was being tried for a second time, after a federal jury in June deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal. U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang ordered that there be no reference to the first trial and instructed the second jury to disregard a defense witness’ mention of it during his testimony.

Despite the jury’s lean toward acquittal over the summer, prosecutors vowed to retry Rinderknecht, who has remained in custody since his arrest in October 2025. Earlier this year, prosecutors obtained a revised indictment that narrowed the scope of one charge to focus solely on damage from the initial Lachman fire, while a second count still sought to hold him responsible for both the Lachman and Palisades fires.
The secondary inferno erupted on Jan. 7, 2025, killed 12 people, destroyed 6,500 structures across the Palisades and Malibu, and caused billions of dollars in damage and insurance claims.

Rinderknecht’s second trial was contentious, with prosecutors accusing a defense witness of perjury, the defense attempting to introduce a new witness at the eleventh hour to bolster their theory of fireworks, and constant sniping between the two sides.

In closing arguments Wednesday, Assistant U.S. Atty. Mark Williams told jurors that Rinderknecht was “mad at everything and frustrated” when he hiked to a clearing overlooking Pacific Palisades and set a fire on New Year’s Eve 2024. Williams said investigators ruled out fireworks as a cause “because there was no evidence to prove it.”
“This fire was an incendiary fire started by an open flame,” he said. “The defendant is the only one who could have started it ... He was angry that night and he set the fire and watched it burn.”

Williams also reminded the jury that they were not to consider the adequacy of the Los Angeles Fire Department’s fire suppression efforts, something jurors raised following the June mistrial. In a civil lawsuit against the city and the state, Los Angeles firefighters testified about a series of communication failures and questionable decisions by higher-ups that led crews to leave the area of the New Year’s Day fire prematurely.
“This case is about arson, the fire that the defendant started — not about first responders who responded to it,” Williams said.

In his closing argument, Steve Haney, Rinderknecht’s defense attorney for both trials, said jurors were “to decide the case based on the evidence” not on anything his client did “outside of the act of arson.” He argued that no one saw his client start the fire and that the ignition wasn’t captured in thousands of photos and videos reviewed by investigators.

Haney said investigators concluded in August 2025 that an open flame started the fire. Rinderknecht was charged that October, but Haney said authorities didn’t request lab tests to prove a lighter could have ignited the fire until the following year.
“The decision came first, the test came 11 months later,” Haney said. “Decided, charged and tested. That’s backwards.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn502ek17yvo.headline: Philippines pet dumping: These dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn502ek17yvo.author: Gavin Butler

paragraphs.text: The livestream begins.
A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.
It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."
"Purebreds," says the woman filming.
Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.
Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.
One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.
170 carcasses found

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.
"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."
In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.
"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.
"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.
Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.
There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.
"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."
'God knows what was inside those urns'
The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.
As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."
These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.
Or not, as the case may be.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.
When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.
"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.
One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.
But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.
The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".
Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."
Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."

In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.
Animal-cruelty law 'doesn't apply'

On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."

Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.
"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.
But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.
Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".
The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.
Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.
One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".
"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.
Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.
"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.
"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.
"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."
Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.
Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.
"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling. "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."
Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."
She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."
With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pqr2g7w059o.headline: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pqr2g7w059o.author: Kali Hays

paragraphs.text: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/histor.headline: Historic Winner of Texas Oil Regulator Seat Wants Faster Permits
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/histor.author: David Wethe

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The first Democrat in 36 years to win a seat on the commission that governs the oil and gas industry in Texas said he plans to work with his Republican colleagues to speed up permitting in the state.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Texas Railroad Commission member-elect Jon Rosenthal said he aims to find ways to incentivize the industry to expand "responsibly" and did not express plans to reduce oil production in the state.

"We should be partnering with folks in the industry because they're the ones who understand this intimately," Rosenthal said Friday in an interview with Bloomberg. "I've talked to folks out there in the real world who have been working on this permit or that permit for months or even years. They're way behind."

The three-member commission is responsible for overseeing the $200 billion Texas oil and gas industry. Its purview expanded from managing freight rates more than 100 years ago to handling drilling permits and well inspections as well as enforcing safety and pollution rules. The agency provided the template for OPEC's founders in 1960.

Rosenthal defeated Republican firebrand Bo French on Nov. 3 amid a so-called blue wave that saw Texas Democrats sweep the governor's office, a US senate seat and a host of down-ballot races in the state.

A self-described "drill-baby-drill Democrat," Rosenthal is no stranger to the energy industry. He worked for 25 years as a mechanical engineer for some of the world's biggest oil field contractors, including SLB and NOV Inc. Rosenthal is also familiar with the state legislature as he's wrapping up a fourth term as a state representative from the Houston area. One of his main priorities is beefing up the commission's ranks.

"I am going to strongly advocate for increased funding, not just for ramping up well plugging, which clearly needs to happen, but also to hire some more folks at the agency to raise their pay scale so that we can be more competitive," said Rosenthal, who served on the legislature's Energy Resources Committee, which oversees the Railroad Commission. "There's some new leadership that my existing relationships I think will be helpful to our effort as a commission."

Since the US midterms, Rosenthal said he's met with Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick as well as outgoing Commissioner Jim Wright, a Republican who lost to French in the primary. Rosenthal said he plans to meet with the other sitting commissioner, Wayne Christian, in about a week.

"We do our best work in the legislature and in these agencies when we seek common ground with our colleagues from across the political spectrum," said Rosenthal. "I just literally cannot wait to get into this role."
