finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.headline: VIX Hits Highest Level Since 2025 Tariff Turmoil as Volatility Warning Signs Flash
finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.author: Bernard Goyder

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:22 PM MST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- The stock market's main volatility gauge jumped to its highest level since April 2025 as the S&P 500 capped its worst week in seven months.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Cboe Volatility Index, better known as the VIX, touched 40 late in the session as stocks extended their slide late in the day, the highest level for the gauge of expected S&P 500 price swings since the tariff turmoil. But while traders are having to pay up for option contracts to protect against bigger swings, there's little sign of panic in the broader market.

The rise in the VIX was more of a mechanical response to the 3.6% fall in the S&P 500 than because of a desperate rush to buy more protection, according to Mandy Xu, head of derivatives market intelligence at the Cboe Global Markets Inc., which created the gauge. "There's a lot more uncertainty in the near term, but not necessarily a lot more fear."

She said that more than four-fifths of the move was due to the drop in the S&P 500 and the knock-on effect that had on the pricing of longer-dated options, rather than because of demand for downside protection.
While the VIX moving into the 30s is a signal of market stress, such events typically happen several times a year, and rarely for more than a few days at a time.
Still, some investors are betting that volatility will persist.

"Conditions may be ripe for a big right tail move in the VIX," Matthew Thompson, managing partner at Thompson Capital Management, said in a call around noon New York time on Friday. The VIX added nine more points on Friday afternoon to briefly touch 40.
The firm is now long index volatility using VIX futures contracts.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.headline: AT&T can phase out California copper landlines, FCC says
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.author: Meg James

paragraphs.text: California’s long-running battle to save traditional telephone landlines has suffered another blow.

The Federal Communications Commission on Friday gave AT&T a green light to discontinue copper landline service to an estimated 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers in California beginning in June.

The Dallas phone giant has struggled for years with California regulators, who have prevented the company from phasing out its copper wires in areas where customers have few other options. Residents and some lawmakers have long advocated for copper lines, saying they are the most reliable form of communication during a power outage, earthquake or wildfire.
Advocates insist traditional landlines are a matter of public safety.

AT&T appealed to federal regulators, arguing that California’s requirement that it continue providing copper landline service was a burden. AT&T separately filed a federal lawsuit against California’s Public Utilities Commission and the state attorney general’s office, requesting a court order declaring the state cannot stop AT&T from hanging up on its landline service.
Those cases are pending.

But, on Friday, the FCC weighed in, saying it had the authority to set communications policy, and that AT&T should be allowed to discontinue its legacy copper service at 360 wire centers in California.
FCC rules “preempt specific state legal requirements” that had kept California’s landline service in place, the FCC order said.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said Friday in a statement. “Those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”
The agency reaffirmed its June decision to allow AT&T to wind down the landline service, despite a California order that it must continue offering it.

“We appreciate Chairman Carr’s leadership and the FCC’s continued focus on modernizing our nation’s communications infrastructure,” Rhonda Johnson, AT&T executive vice president for federal regulatory relations, said Friday in a statement.
AT&T has said that about 3% of households it serves in California use the copper system, and that maintaining those lines costs an estimated $1 billion a year.
Increasingly, copper thieves have become a problem. Replacing stolen copper lines significantly adds to maintenance costs for providers.
“AT&T spends tens of millions of dollars annually responding to copper theft in the state,” FCC Commissioner Olivia Trusty said in a statement, joining Carr in supporting AT&T’s petition.
The company sought the FCC’s ruling, arguing that ending its legacy service would free up resources to provide additional homes with advanced fiber and wireless technology.
The FCC’s lone Democrat, Anna M. Gomez, cast a dissenting vote, saying customers depend on landline service and California regulators should be given time to develop a transition plan.

“I welcome modernizing our networks,” Gomez said. “The question in front of us today is how to do that while keeping consumers at the center, and whether this Commission should override California’s rules before California has finished deciding how to update them.”
The Utility Reform Network advocacy group vowed to continue the fight to preserve landlines.

“Today, the FCC handed AT&T, and every other provider in California, hope that the telecommunications industry will be relieved from state oversight,” Mark Toney, the group’s executive Director, said in a statement.

“If sustained, this Order will result in California Residents losing their legal right to phone service, access to first responders and emergency services, to family and loved ones, and to reliable connectivity,” Toney said.
The California Public Utilities Commission was not immediately available for comment.
“No customer will be left without access to voice or 911 service, and we’re committed to working with our customers every step of the way during this transition,” AT&T’s Johnson said.
Staff writer Jennie Jarvie contributed to this report.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmjeqv89egylo.headline: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmjeqv89egylo.author: Madeline Halpert

paragraphs.text: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.
Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.
The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

latimes.com/sports/story/2026-11-20/man-.headline: Man dies days after falling during fight with fan at 49ers-Cowboys game
latimes.com/sports/story/2026-11-20/man-.author: Chuck Schilken

paragraphs.text: Police are investigating the death of a man who fell during an altercation in the stands during Sunday’s game between the San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.
Mario Narro died in the Medical City Arlington intensive care unit Wednesday at 11:30 a.m., according to the Tarrant County Medical Examiner’s Office website.

“On November 17, we were contacted by the family of a 36-year-old man who had been admitted to a local hospital. They wished to make a report,” an Arlington County Police Department spokesperson said in an email Friday.

“They told officers the man attended the Cowboys game on November 15 and fell during an altercation with another fan around kickoff time. The man stayed and watched the full game. A friend who was with him said he began complaining of pain – and so after the game, they flagged down paramedics at the stadium. The man was then transported to the hospital.”
The department was notified on Wednesday that the man had died at the hospital, the spokesperson said.

Narro’s niece, Claudia DeLara, told CBS News Texas that her uncle suffered internal bleeding after striking his abdomen and underwent emergency surgery. Doctors said Narro suffered internal injuries to his intestines and liver, DeLara said.
A business owner who lived in New Mexico, Narro was a lifelong Cowboys fan who had attended four or five games before Sunday, DeLara said. He sent the family a video from the stadium before the game.
“He was so happy to be there,” DeLara said.
She added: “He loved big events like Cowboys games, UFC fights, boxing, a lot of that stuff. He just really enjoyed being out, being social, being around people, making new friends.”

latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-20/l.headline: A year after catcalling me on Larchmont, he asked if I was single
latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-20/l.author: Ann Nguyen

paragraphs.text: He called out to me from his car. He drove a ubiquitous, white Tesla. “Hey. Hey!” he said.

I never expected to be catcalled on Larchmont Boulevard between coffee shops and high-end boutiques. I was trying to get to Rite Aid for potato chips. I ignored him, pretending I couldn’t hear over the audiobook playing in my earbuds.
But I ran into him in front of FedEx. I knew it was him right away; he was striding toward me with such intentional steps.
“Hi. Are you single?” he asked.
“Yeeess …”
“May I have your number?”
Normally, I would gently refuse. However, my full moon reading said I should “Release: closing off emotionally” and “Affirm: it is safe for me to connect with others.”
“Sure ...”
“I’m Nick.” We shook hands.
“Ann.” I introduced myself out of habit.
“Nice to meet you. What are you up to today?”
“It’s Friday, so I’m working from home.” Nick didn’t need to know I went out for potato chips.
“Yeah? Me too. Had this three-hour block free. I saw you from my car. You’re hot.”
“Thanks.” Also out of habit.
“I’ll text you.”

I got my chips while unable to grasp what just happened. Some rando thought I was hot! I felt flattered, amused and bewildered, but concluded it was all a fluke. I deleted Nick’s number as soon as I got home.
When the texts started arriving the next morning, I was surprised. Was this guy really asking me out? “I can tomorrow, if you’re free?” I offered. We set up a time go for a walk on Sunday.
“Ok see you tomorrow,” he responded.
I texted my friend, Lauren, about what happened. She asked for details about Nick, but I couldn’t offer any. Tall. White. Wore a blue cap. I’d be a terrible witness during a suspect lineup.
On Sunday afternoon, Nick and I met outside his place for a walk. Very soon afterward, he asked my age.
“Does it matter?”
“No. Not at all,” he said.
“How about we guess each other’s age?” I suggested. I thought Nick was 35. He thought I was 29, which is incredibly generous. “I’m 44,” I said.
Nick. Thirty-eight. Tall. Good-looking. Everything great on a dating profile.
After one lap around the block, he asked me to come upstairs to cool off. As soon as we got into the hallway of his building, he pulled me in close. “Come here.”
“Already?”
“How did I see you the other day? You are so hot,” he said, his mouth descending on me like his favorite sandwich from Clark Street Diner (it’s turkey).
The date turned out to be a hookup.
“You didn’t think I wanted to hit that?” Nick asked afterward.
My optimism offered my reply: “No, I thought we were going for a walk.” I mentally strategized my exit. Perhaps out of guilt, Nick began to vent as we continued to “hang out.”

“Why is it so hard to date in L.A.? All the girls I meet are fake. Or they want a serial killer. Like they want someone to take charge,” he said. “Guys in jail are getting married. But then I go up to talk to a girl, and you know the first thing they do? They take out their phone and start filming! It pisses me off. I sometimes want to take their phone and toss it.”

As Nick ranted, I heard his frustration tinged with hopelessness. “Like, I know things are scary, but I’m a nice guy,” he said. “People are telling me I sound jaded, and I hate that. I’m a glass-half-full kind of guy.”
He spoke about his desire for children and to build a family. He meant it. He was serious, and I believed him. More precisely, I believed that he believed it.
“Ten years ago, things felt different,” he said. “It was easier to meet people, be given a chance. Don’t you think so?”

The irony of this moment isn’t lost on me. Here’s a man — tall, handsome, mid-30s career professional — claiming to be available and ready for commitment, who just wants to be given a chance. While I — a single, available, hot (apparently), mid-40s career professional — am just a hookup. It didn’t matter if I had desirable qualities he might find in a committed partner like kindness, patience and reliability.
Because chances were, he had already decided my worth. I was just a body to have sex with.
I was certain this wasn’t the response Nick wanted to hear, so I could only agree.
“Yes, dating in L.A. is hard.”

If this were 10 or even 20 years ago, I would have mistaken attraction for compatibility. I would have been in contact constantly, striving for the attention of someone who clearly had no interest in knowing me. I deleted Nick’s number again, as there was nothing more to pursue. There was nothing there to begin with. We didn’t owe each other anything.

A couple of days later, I was at a girlfriend’s birthday dinner surrounded by girl bosses at least 10 years younger than I was. The birthday star shared her detailed description of “My Person,” a description that read like a prompt for an AI-generated companion.
“At least 5 foot 10, medium-dark skin tone, dark hair. Medium timbre voice. Can’t be too masculine to dominate me, but not too passive that I’m always the one driving the relationship …”

I chuckled, thinking back to Nick’s vents on dating. I watched the nods and affirmations of the young women at the table while I thought, “Where is she going to find this exact person?” But a birthday dinner wasn’t the time for a lecture from a spinster. I was confident my friend would find her “person” in some form or another.

A year later, I was on Larchmont again after finishing my latest Starbucks Rewards mission. Ahead, I saw a white Tesla pull over in front of Bank of America, and I knew immediately who was behind the wheel.
“Hey, are you single?” Nick asked out his window, his expression changing as soon as he recognized me. He got caught.
Looking over, I scoffed, “I already talked to you.”
The author is a producer at a video game company. She lives in Koreatown and enjoys espresso tonics. She’s on Instagram: @annwhatever.

L.A. Affairs chronicles the search for romantic love in all its glorious expressions in the L.A. area, and we want to hear your true story. We pay $400 for a published essay. Email LAAffairs@latimes.com. You can find submission guidelines here. You can find past columns here.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv94d10rwpo.headline: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv94d10rwpo.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?

It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.
"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.
Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Henry Belot

paragraphs.text: The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.
Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.
“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.
But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.
McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.
“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.
Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.
“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.
“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”
On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.
Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.
The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.
Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

latimes.com/travel/story/2026-11-20/sund.headline: How to have the best Sunday in L.A., according to Tatyana Ali
latimes.com/travel/story/2026-11-20/sund.author: Kailyn Brown

paragraphs.text: Although fans of “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” might associate her with the show’s affluent Westside enclave, Tatyana Ali’s favorite Los Angeles neighborhood is undoubtedly Studio City.

“It’s so central to everything,” says Ali, who played Ashley, the spunky, youngest daughter of the Banks family on the beloved ’90s sitcom. She loves Studio City’s food scene as well, especially longtime favorites Daichan and Uncle Andre’s BBQ.
“It’s also really walkable, which I know is strange,” says the Long Island native who moved to L.A. when she was in high school. “Maybe that’s the New York in me.”

For the past two months, the actor and singer has been gracing a different type of TV show: “Dancing With the Stars.” Throughout the season, Ali and her dance partner, Jan Ravnik, have found creative ways to pay homage to “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.” In one standout, heartfelt episode, she teamed up with Alfonso Ribeiro — her former castmate and the “DWTS” co-host — for a Viennese waltz dedicated to the late James Avery, who played their TV dad Philip Banks.

Competing on “Dancing With the Stars” has been a transformative experience for Ali and one that has unexpectedly carried over into her maternal advocacy work. Having spoken candidly about her own traumatic birth experience with her first son, Ali founded Baby Yams, which specializes in handcrafted baby quilts and donates a portion of its sales to organizations funding and training Black and Indigenous birth workers. She’s finding dance to be a powerful way to process her emotions.

“Those things live with you, they stay with you, and we don’t necessarily have access to all the modalities that can heal all of that,” she says of birth trauma. “Somewhere along this journey, because of the partner I have and the man he is, I have cried through the craziest feelings in my body while I’m learning these dances and moving in ways that I’ve never moved before.”
She adds, “And I’m telling you, by the time this experience is over, that s— is not inside me anymore.”

Ahead of the show’s season finale airing live on ABC and Disney+ on Nov. 24 — where Ali and Ravnik will compete for the Mirrorball Trophy — Ali shared her ultimate Sunday agenda. It includes breakfast at Hilltop, exploring museums in Exposition Park with her kids, and an intimate dinner with friends at the iconic Chateau Marmont.
7 a.m.: Attempt to sleep in

I have two kids, a 10-year-old and a 7-year-old, so they are the alarm clock. I naturally would sleep in, but we’re up and at ’em at like the latest 7 a.m. That’s a good sleep-in day. Sundays are the time when we do fun stuff for us as a family outside of all their activities.
10 a.m.: Grab a quick breakfast at Hilltop

I love Issa Rae’s Hilltop. I go there all the time. I like the crispy tater tots, but I do have to control myself. For me, that’s the must must. There’s something about the sauce. I’m a creature of habit, but it changes depending on where I go, so I’d order a vanilla latte with almond milk with an extra shot [of espresso].
11 a.m.: Revisit my childhood stomping grounds

Recently we took the kids to Exposition Park. We haven’t gotten a chance to go to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art yet. But as a kid when I first got to L.A. around high school, the majority of my interaction with L.A. — cause I was working, I was on set — was with my tutors. I had the most incredible on-set teachers and they supplemented all of my education by taking me to museums and landmarks around the city. Exposition Park is a place that my tutor, Portia Adams, used to take me to all the time, so I have a love for that place and the rose garden, the California Science Center, the Natural History Museum and the [California] African American Museum. I love taking my kids there and they love it. That takes most of our Sunday.
5 p.m.: Have an early dinner at Chateau Marmont

I would love to at some point in the evening — not too late — have dinner with my sister and a couple of girlfriends at Chateau Marmont. My favorite thing — and I don’t get to do it enough — is to have a little lunch there. So we’d have an early dinner there. I would get a martini straight up with blue cheese olives. All of their food is so yummy.
7 p.m.: Have bread pudding for dessert

That’s a long day for me already. [laughs] After dinner, I’d get dessert at Aroma Coffee & Tea Co. in Studio City. They make bread pudding, but it’s made with croissant bread instead of regular bread. Oh, my God. It’s a really popular cafe. It’s always packed for breakfast, but they’re open at night too. I would take my dessert to go. I’ve done that before when I wanted a little treat.
7:30 p.m.: Read with the kids before bed

I’d get back home by 7:30 p.m. Then, you know, my doppelgänger has made dinner for my kids so I’m not worried about that [laughs]. No, my husband can cook so he makes dinner for the kids, so I’m right on time for their bedtime at 8 p.m. We get everybody ready for bed, we brush our teeth, all that, and then we read together every single evening. My kids are at the point now where we read chapter books. We read a couple of chapters every night and that’s how we end the kids’ night.
8:30 p.m.: Binge watch ‘The Gilded Age’

Then my routine by then is maybe I get to watch a little something, some good reality or a good show that I’m into. I really liked ‘The Gilded Age.’ Right before I started ‘Dancing With the Stars,’ I was hooked and I binged it. That was the last one that I couldn’t get enough of. I’m watching it in bed, jammies on. A couple episodes. Turn it off. Buenas noches [laughs]. I’d probably go to bed around 10:30 p.m.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-20/de.headline: Despite RFK Jr.'s claim, Arabs do win awards. Getting a visa to receive their prize is harder
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-20/de.author: Lorraine Ali

paragraphs.text: “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields Prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature.”

Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke those words last month while campaigning for Michigan Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right before Rogers lost to an Arab American.

RFK Jr. has never been one for factual accuracy. Plenty of Arabs have been honored by the award bodies he mentioned, but with so much at stake, he wasn’t about to adopt an “Honesty Is The Best Policy” strategy as Republicans faced impending doom at the polls.

But let’s pretend for a minute that he had a flash of conscience and decided to present a more honest picture. “Arabs do win,” he might say. “We just won’t let them in the country to collect their prizes.”

Look no further than last Wednesday, when Abdelrahman ElGendy won the National Book Award for his nonfiction work, “Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming.” He was invited to the ceremony in New York City but couldn’t attend after the U.S. consular office denied the Egyptian author a visitor visa.

ElGendy built a literary career and completed his memoir in the U.S., but left in April 2025 fearing that he would be deported back to Egypt, where he was a political prisoner for more than six years.
His book recounts his experience living through the political upheaval after the military-backed coup of Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. He was just a teen when he was arrested.
ElGendy now resides in exile in the U.K. His editor delivered the author’s acceptance speech at the awards gala Wednesday.

“If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you,” he wrote. “Today, that dream should have come full circle, but like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camp stands ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable.”
He dedicated the award to Palestinians, political prisoners and to the “tens of thousands of souls disappeared into ICE concentration camps.”
ElGendy joins the ranks of other Arabs who have won prestigious honors but have been denied entry into the U.S. to receive their prizes.

Yemeni journalist Maad al-Zikry was part of the Associated Press team that won the 2019 Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting. He was unable to attend the New York ceremony after being denied a U.S. visa amid travel restrictions affecting Yemeni nationals.
Syrian cinematographer Khaled Khatib’s documentary “White Helmets” won the Oscar for documentary short in 2017, but he was refused entry into the U.S. to attend the ceremony.
Syrian director Feras Fayyad was also reportedly denied a U.S. visa to attend the Academy Awards for his film, “The Cave,” which was shortlisted for the 2020 Oscars.
Note to RFK Jr.: Had ElGentry been at the gala for the 77th National Book Awards this week, he would have stood alongside four more writers of Arab heritage being recognized for their work.

They included fiction winner Hannah Lillith Assadi, who was recognized for her novel “Paradiso 17.” The other three finalists were Palestinian American poet Fady Joudah, Cuban Palestinian poet Carolina Ebeid and Syrian writer Samar Yazbek.

Arabs that RFK Jr. chose to omit while attempting to paint the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate — now senator-elect — Abdul El-Sayed as part of a group of people who’ve never contributed to the greater good include Egyptian American scientist Ahmed Zewail, who was awarded the 1999 Nobel Prize in chemistry for his work on femtochemistry.

Omar M. Yaghi is a Palestinian American chemist who won the Wolf Prize in chemistry in 2018 for his work on reticular chemistry and metal-organic frameworks. Tawakkol Karman is the Yemeni journalist, politician, and human rights activist who was a co-recipient of the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize.

RFK Jr. could learn from the Arab or 20 who’ve “produced science” (his words, not mine) and won prestigious awards for doing so. But it’s not the junk science he prefers, such as brain worm fog and 5G cellphone networks altering our very DNA. Is it any mystery why he doesn’t value their contributions?
His promotion of anti-vaccine conspiracy theories and dubious claims that inoculations are linked to autism has directly led to the resurgence of a formerly eradicated disease in the U.S.

It was announced Tuesday that measles is no longer eliminated in the United States, reversing what’s been called one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century. An independent commission of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the nation’s measles-elimination status this week after determining that the virus circulated nonstop for more than a year.

That dubious distinction came within months of Egypt’s Deputy Minister of Health and Population, Dr. Amr Mohamed Kandeel, being awarded the 2026 World Health Organization’s Nelson Mandela Award for Health Promotion. They were honoring his work toward modernizing Egypt’s immunization systems, thereby helping the country achieve certification for eliminating measles and rubella.
Fingers crossed that America catches up to Egypt someday. Meanwhile, Arabs will keep contributing to humanity and winning those awards, despite RFK Jr.’s insistence that they are way, way behind.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm0zlkgrm2o.headline: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgm0zlkgrm2o.author: Robin Levinson-King, Cecilia Barría

paragraphs.text: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
Ankle monitors and debt
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.
Business as usual

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

nytimes.com/article/stock-market-correct.headline: What Is a Stock Market Correction?

paragraphs.text: Stocks have swooned in recent weeks, with investors becoming increasingly wary of the A.I. trade and questioning just how much investment in the technology can scale up. On Friday, the drag in tech pushed the S&P 500 stock index into a correction, a Wall Street term for a decline of 10 percent or more from a recent high.

Investors have digested a spate of news this month that has rattled tech stocks: from the departure of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to midterm election results that triggered fears of a slowdown in A.I. data center build-out. The tech-heavy Nasdaq slumped more than 5 percent on Friday, and suffered its worst week since March 2020, at the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic.
What constitutes a market correction?
A correction is a drop of 10 percent or more in stocks from their most recent high. Since its Oct. 6 peak, the S&P 500 has fallen more than 11 percent.

The 10 percent trigger for a correction is an arbitrary, round-number threshold. But it serves as a signal that investors have turned pointedly more pessimistic about the market. That is particularly the case for technology stocks., with the Nasdaq composite index down 18 percent from its most recent peak, also on Oct. 6.
Are market corrections common?

This is the 14th correction in the S&P 500 since the turn of the century, according to data from Yardeni Research. Of the 13 previous corrections, four turned into bear markets, defined as a more severe decline of at least 20 percent.
Does this mean stocks will continue to fall?
Not necessarily.
Some corrections don’t last very long, like the one in early 2018, which spanned less than two weeks. Others can be more drawn out, generally when they develop into full-fledged bear markets.

That said, one previous bear market, at the start of the pandemic, was severe but relatively short — it erased about 33 percent in value from stocks in just over a month. Less than three months later, stocks had regained their previous peak.

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/science/chinese-s.headline: Chinese-Born Neuroscientist Is Detained by ICE While Traveling From Conference

paragraphs.text: A Chinese-born neuroscientist conducting research at Princeton University was detained on Thursday by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Washington while traveling from an academic conference, university officials and her lawyers said.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, is a third year Ph.D. student who has resided in the United States since 2016. Her visa was expired, her lawyers said, but her pending asylum application allowed her to remain in the country legally.

Via the messaging platform Slack, she informed her colleagues at Princeton’s Brody Lab that she had been detained at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while traveling home to New Jersey. But her lab mates eventually lost direct contact with her.

As of Friday, Ms. Xie was being held at an ICE processing center in Chantilly, Va. She is the latest in a string of foreign-born scientists who have been detained amid Trump administration crackdowns on foreign scientists and on immigrants more broadly.

Those policies have had a chilling effect on American research institutions’ ability to recruit and retain the world’s top minds, creating a strain on fields already struggling to enroll young researchers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” said Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

After Ms. Xie moved to the United States with her family in 2016, she went on to graduate in 2020 from the Bronx High School of Science and in 2024 from M.I.T., where she studied computer science and mathematics. Since then, she has lived in New Jersey while conducting neuroscience research as a Ph.D. student at the Brody Lab.

Earlier this week, Ms. Xie presented some of this research — on the neurons that act as a coordinate system for the brain’s mental maps — at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting in Washington.

“Eva is a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist,” the Brody Lab said in a statement on X. “She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center. She should be home.”
Carlos Brody, who leads the lab, said that as Ms. Xie’s Princeton colleagues worried about her, Ms. Xie seemed concerned about the research.

“Even while in an ICE detention center, she was contacting us to make sure that her experiments could move forward and the grant applications she is part of could be submitted,” Dr. Brody said in an email to The New York Times.

According to Ms. Xie’s lawyers, because her asylum application has not yet been approved and her previous visa is expired, ICE agents were alerted when she passed through an airport security checkpoint.

“In her case, as well as a number of other cases that I personally represent, we’ve seen people being arrested at domestic airports who’ve overstayed a visa but have a pending green card or asylum application,” said Kerry Doyle, one of Ms. Xie’s attorneys.
Officials from ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the grounds for Ms. Xie’s detention or whether she had been moved from the Virginia processing facility.
On Friday morning, Ms. Xie’s lawyers entered a habeas corpus filing, which formally requests that the court review whether a person’s detention is legal.

Princeton confirmed that it had arranged for Ms. Xie to receive legal counsel and would remain in contact with her attorneys, family and colleagues as the situation developed. The Society for Neuroscience said in a statement that it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to offer support.
“Our thoughts are with Eva, her family and her colleagues,” the society said in a statement on X.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Ronny Hallin, TV producer known for ‘Laverne & Shirley,’ dies at 88
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Emily St. Martin

paragraphs.text: Ronny Hallin, a TV producer known for her showbiz family and on-and-off-screen contributions to “Laverne & Shirley” and other popular sitcoms, has died. She was 88.
Her daughter Penny Hallin confirmed the news to Deadline, saying the former producer “passed away peacefully at home” on Oct. 27.

Hallin hailed from a showbiz family. Her professional resume was most notable for projects including the long-running “Happy Days” spinoff “Laverne & Shirley.” Hallin herself appeared in a 1982 episode of the show, portraying Maxine.

Hallin’s sister, Penny Marshall, who died in 2018, played Laverne DeFazio; and her brother Garry Marshall, who died in 2016, created the show. Hallin also worked as an associate producer on the show from 1978 to 1979.

She also made onscreen appearances in a 1974 episode of “The Odd Couple,” as a customer in “Frankie and Johnny” in 1991, an airport cleaning lady in “Exit to Eden” in 1994 and a mourner in “Raising Helen” in 2004.

Behind the scenes, she worked as a producer and casting director for more than two decades, contributing to several hit sitcoms associated with her brother. She served as associate producer and then producer across 148 episodes of “Happy Days” in the late ’70s and early ’80s, and as a coordinating producer on “Perfect Strangers” and “Family Matters.” She also produced 160 episodes of “Step by Step” through the ’90s.
“My aunt Ronny Hallin has passed away. The OG Marshall family is finally all together again, somewhere … out there,” Hallin’s nephew, Scott Marshall, wrote in a tribute on Instagram last month.

He described Hallin as “the unsung hero of the Marshall family” — “the stable one, always on time, never a fuss at every production meeting, run through and post production sound mix for all those sitcoms.”
“Ronny was always there, that’s what I remember,” he continued, “always there with a smile and a hug and always got you exactly what you wanted for Christmas. Always.”
Marshall wrote that his aunt was sweet, kind and “exceptionally cool.”

“She was the first person I ever met who actually surfed. She had been to Hawaii with real surfers and rode the waves! She showed me all the old surf movies like ‘The Golden Breed’ and ‘Liquid Space.’ Incredible early surf docs that she somehow got me copies of on VHS tapes. She took me to the Forum in 1983 to see one of my first concerts. It was David Bowie. Ronny also saw some unknown comedian at the Comedy Store and told my dad he should play the alien on ‘Happy Days.’ That was Robin Williams.”

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/20/u.headline: U.S. stocks slump into correction territory amid tech and AI worries
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/20/u.author: Todd C. Frankel, Shira Ovide

paragraphs.text: U.S. stock markets Friday finished their worst week since worries about President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs caused a global sell-off in April 2025, as investors grew increasingly skittish about AI and tech companies, alongside persistent concerns about inflation and interest rates.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slid into correction territory, moving at least 10 percent below their recent closing records. The S&P 500, a broad index of major companies, was down 3.7 percent for the day, taking it down more than 7 percent for the week. The Dow was off 1.93 percent.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index erased all of its gains for 2026, dropping 5.28 percent on the day.
“It’s a meltdown right now,” said Arun Sundaram, who leads investment strategy for CFRA Research.

The stock market slide occurred despite some encouraging economic indicators this week, such as stronger-than-expected retail sales and gasoline prices that continued their ride under $4 a gallon. The national average Friday was $3.69 a gallon, according to AAA. A month ago, it was $4.28.
Investors’ fears about the future of AI appeared to drive markets, illustrated by two stocks that made ballyhooed debuts in public markets this year.
The AI company Anthropic, which started trading Thursday, was down more than 8 percent Friday. Anthropic shares closed at $88.91 a share after debuting Thursday at $83.
SpaceX — the rocket, telecommunications and AI company led by Elon Musk — saw its stock drop 7.7 percent, ending below the $135 price that SpaceX debuted with during its IPO in June.

Michael Monaghan, who oversees the Founders 100 ETF, an investment fund, said Friday that investors’ mood about AI companies has curdled in recent weeks, despite what he says is evidence of growing business interest in AI technologies.
“In my 25 years-plus investing in the markets, this is the most sentiment-driven sell-off I’ve seen,” Monaghan said.
He attributed the investor vibe shift to a confluence of events.

Big technology companies recently have signaled they planned to spend growing piles of cash building AI data centers, at the same time that the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democratic politicians who are skeptical of AI and data centers.
Monaghan also pointed to the scandal-driven resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, the leading AI computer chip company.
Shares of Nvidia were down about 14 percent Friday.
“The AI-sector’s support for the economy was called into question this week,” Oxford Economics noted in a research report.
Investors turned their attention instead to the steadier consumer-goods segment. PepsiCo’s stock jumped 1.54 percent Friday. Walmart was up 1.52 percent.
correctionA previous version of this article misstated President Donald Trump's name for his 2025 tariffs. He referred to them as “Liberation Day,” not “Independence Day.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/politics/baaja.headline: It’s a Bill on Energy Permits, but Trump’s Pet Projects Are Part of the Debate

paragraphs.text: Cheered on by the Trump administration, lawmakers are moving toward passing a sweeping overhaul of permitting intended to speed up construction of power plants, gas pipelines and other energy projects.

The measure is that increasingly rare species of major legislation with at least some bipartisan support, as backers argue that it could lower energy bills and unleash a wave of new projects in a country they say has made it too hard to build. But as with much in Washington, the bill is also brushing up against the pet projects and mercurial nature of President Trump.

As the legislation advances from the Senate to the House, opponents are warning that its broad implications could accelerate a range of construction projects, including Mr. Trump’s prized triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and a new championship-level golf course in Washington.

“In several of the pending lawsuits there are court orders enjoining parts of Trump’s vanity projects,” said Representative Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, who opposes the bill. “If this legislation were to become law as written, that relief might not exist.”

Chief among the opponents’ concerns: The bill essentially renders toothless both the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to assess the environmental effects of proposed actions, and the National Historic Preservation Act, which establishes a review process to try to prevent historic sites’ destruction or alteration by federal projects.

Provisions in the bill would prevent judges from halting projects for violating those laws, even ones that have nothing to do with energy production. Courts could still block projects that are found to have violated other federal laws and inflict an “irreparable harm to the plaintiff.”
Opponents of Mr. Trump’s arch and golf course have cited those two laws, among others, in their suits.

“There is still going to be a mighty effort to stop them,” Mr. Huffman said of Mr. Trump’s Washington projects. “But NEPA, injunctive relief and the National Historic Preservation Act are critical tools to stopping many of these vanity projects. As written, this bill wipes those tools away.”
Mr. Trump has indicated he would sign the legislation, and praised its provisions on Friday, calling it “one of the biggest things that you’ll see.”
But he has also railed against parts of the nearly 500-page bill. The president recently said he did not like that it could be used to speed up the construction of windmills.
“I will not approve wind turbines,” Mr. Trump said earlier this month, adding: “The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Still, his administration has been working with lawmakers on the bill, and promotes many of its provisions. As more energy projects come online, the cost of energy should drop, administration officials say. One study estimated that the bill would reduce household electricity bills by up to $78 per year by 2040.

The Senate approved the bill on Thursday, 62 to 33. All but two Republican senators voted for the bill, which had the enthusiastic support of business groups, energy developers and labor unions. Democrats were more closely split, though most voted against it. Its fate in the House is less certain.
“It’s going to cause tremendous amounts of new building,” Mr. Trump said on Friday.

Vice President JD Vance called the bill “an amazing bipartisan piece of legislation that will allow the United States to build like we’ve never built before,” acknowledging that the loosening of regulations would reach beyond energy projects.
“That means more homes, more factories, more power plants,” he said.

The bill was the result of negotiations between top Republicans and Democrats on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Republicans pushed for language that could make it harder for environmental groups to sue to block natural gas pipelines, oil drilling, mines and other energy projects. Democrats sought to make it easier to build large power lines, which could greatly expand the use of wind and solar energy.
The bill has generated objections from tribal nations and historic preservationists in addition to some environmentalists.

In a letter to the top Democrat in the House, the founding partner of Cultural Heritage Partners, Greg Werkheiser, laid out what he said were 10 terrible consequences of the bill, including eliminating the public comment process for projects affecting historic sites and no longer requiring agencies to consider visual or auditory effects of new development on historic sites unless they directly diminished the property.
“Under this new bill, which has passed the Senate, if you want to put a Walmart literally right next door to Gettysburg Battlefield, you can do it,” he said in an interview.

A spokeswoman for Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and one of the bill’s main authors, did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement issued after the Senate passed the bill, Mr. Whitehouse promoted its bolstering of clean energy.
“Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit,” he said.

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/science/anthropic.headline: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Solve Riemann Hypothesis With Help From Claude

paragraphs.text: The Riemann hypothesis, often considered the most important unsolved problem in mathematics, may be the latest to be conquered by artificial intelligence.

On Friday, Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on his personal website saying that he had completed a proof of the hypothesis by collaborating with Claude, the company’s A.I. system. He did not include a traditional mathematical paper to describe the proof, but instead linked to computer code that he claimed would verify the result.

“Claude and I have had a great time together, with such breadth in recent months,” Dr. Alpoge said. “But this time, Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

If the claim is verified, it will be the latest remarkable advance by artificial intelligence this year. For months now, mathematicians have been repeatedly stunned to see machines conquer mathematical problems that have eluded human geniuses for years — in the case of the Riemann hypothesis, for more than a century and a half.

“This is the Mount Olympus,” said Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University. He said it seemed clear that Dr. Alpoge had played a central role in telling Claude which mathematical ideas to explore to pull together the proof.
“It is a remarkable thing we might see a lot more of in the future, where there is a very skillful jockey riding a really fast horse,” Dr. Strogatz said.

The Riemann hypothesis was formulated in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician. The problem involves prime numbers (whole numbers greater than 1 that can be divided evenly only by themselves and 1, such as 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and so on) and the question of how they are distributed along the number line as it stretches toward infinity.

As one moves further along the line, primes become rarer: Up to 100, some 25 percent of the numbers are prime, but up to one million, only about 7.8 percent are prime. Riemann hypothesized a formula for estimating, or counting, how many primes exist below any given number.

Other researchers said they were checking Dr. Alpoge’s code, which is written in Lean, a language that turns mathematical statements into a form that can be verified. If there are no errors in the Lean code, that indicates the logic of the proof is solid.
“I think it’s likely to be correct,” said James Maynard, a mathematician at the University of Oxford in England. “I’d be 98 or 99 percent certain.”
Lean is a robust proof checker, Dr. Maynard said, but added, “You have to be a little bit careful about making sure that a Lean verification is proving the thing that you want it to be proving.”

Dr. Alpoge was not the only person working on the Riemann hypothesis. Also on Friday, Alessandro Masullo, an independent mathematician living in Rome, released an incomplete proof that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years.

Brian Conrad, a Stanford University mathematician who was Dr. Masullo’s doctoral thesis adviser, said the proof, which employs a completely different approach than the one used by Dr. Alpoge and Claude, was credible without major gaps.
In a statement, Dr. Masullo said: “The paper is in no way in a state that is fit for submission or dissemination.”

He said he knew there were many imperfections in the draft that needed to be fixed, expanded and improved. “They are a testament to the fact that a human being has been working through it all along,” he said.

Dr. Masullo’s proof did not employ A.I., partly because he, like some other mathematicians, did not fully trust the system with their ideas — a model might produce a proof without giving due credit, Dr. Conrad said.
Dr. Conrad also said that it was “frankly completely outrageous” of Dr. Alpoge to release a proof that he did not fully understand.
Dr. Alpoge did not reply to a request for comment about his proof.

Also on Friday, Dr. Alpoge and Tristan Buckmaster, a professor of mathematics at New York University, revealed a proof of a different variation of the Navier-Stokes problem. The equations involved describe the flow of liquids. In September, OpenAI announced that it had solved a longstanding question: Could the equations produce nonsensical answers in which the liquid could accelerate to infinite speeds? The OpenAI proof found such a case by using a specially designed driving force applied to a liquid.
In their new work, Dr. Alpoge and Dr. Buckmaster claim to show that even without a driving force, a liquid could still reach infinite speeds.

Navier-Stokes and the Riemann hypothesis are among the seven Millennium Prize problems selected in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offered a $1 million prize for each one solved. A century earlier, the Riemann hypothesis was among the 23 most important unsolved problems named by David Hilbert, a German mathematician.
Up until this year, a proof of the hypothesis seemed to be far beyond the capability of generations of mathematicians.
The problem attracted mathematicians not only because it seemed to be the biggest challenge, but also because it appeared to describe something basic yet mysterious about numbers.
“Basically, no one doubted that the Riemann hypothesis was true,” Dr. Maynard said. “We really wanted to know why it was true.”
The new proof “will give us great understanding, and so it’s something to be celebrated,” Dr. Maynard said.

In October, OpenAI released a tranche of more than 350 findings that included a proof of the so-called quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a version with looser constraints that is thus easier to prove. That in itself was a surprise, in that A.I. had been able to crack the problem but also in that the solution had turned out to be a fairly straightforward application of known tools. Indeed, several mathematicians had come close to completing a proof along similar lines.
It seemed that getting from the quasi-Riemann hypothesis to the full hypothesis would require new leaps of understanding. Yet, one month later, the Riemann hypothesis appears to be solved, too.

Alex Kontorovich, a mathematician at Rutgers University, said that after the quasi-Riemann hypothesis proof, he told himself: “Well, that’s it. Now that we know that A.I. can do mathematics at the highest levels, then I can’t be shocked anymore.”
But he said he was still flabbergasted on Friday, adding, “I’m absolutely, absolutely shocked.”

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.headline: D.A. won't charge LAPD officer who shot mentally ill man in Koreatown
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.author: Libor Jany

paragraphs.text: Prosecutors have declined to charge a Los Angeles police officer who shot and killed a knife-wielding man in his parents’ Koreatown apartment more than two years ago, a case that cast a spotlight on police interactions with people who are mentally ill.

Citing insufficient evidence of criminal wrongdoing, the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office concluded that the officer, Andres Lopez, reasonably believed that his life was in danger when he fired three rounds at Yong Yang, who ignored repeated commands to drop a knife.

The decision was swiftly condemned by Yang’s family, which has filed two separate lawsuits — in federal and county courts — contending that their son’s death was preventable and caused by police’s unwillingness to consider other options before resorting to deadly force.
The city has denied wrongdoing in both suits, which remain pending.

In a statement released Friday, Yang’s father, Min Yang, said he was “deeply disappointed” by Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman’s office. He said the charging decision was based on “inaccurate” conclusions about what happened in the incident.
The D.A.’s report copied, almost verbatim, from parts of LAPD’s own internal review of the incident, the father said.
“Both agencies could have uncovered the facts had they chosen to do so,” Yang said.

The deadly encounter with Yang in May 2024 began after his mother called the county’s psychiatric emergency response team for help. The clinician who arrived at the family’s second-story apartment in the 400 block of South Gramercy Place claimed Yang’s behavior became too aggressive and requested police.

In their lawsuit, Yang’s parents dispute that their son tried to harm his father or the clinician, and denied that Yang was diagnosed with schizophrenia. They also took issue with Yang being labeled as “violent,” saying that designation provoked a far more aggressive police response.
They also claimed that the clinician took only a few minutes with their son before calling for police.

According to a report prepared by the LAPD chief, Lopez and his police partner were the first two officers on the scene. Body-worn camera footage released after the shooting showed them talking with Yang’s father and explaining their options to him, including whether to put Yang on a 72-hour mental health hold.

The cops tried to talk to Yang, but he had locked himself inside the apartment and refused to open the door. Eventually, the police requested backup and called a private ambulance to transport Yang to a nearby hospital.

After some deliberation, officers decided to enter the apartment. Upon opening the door, they found Yang standing in the middle of the living room with a kitchen knife in his hand. He began walking toward officers, who shouted at him to drop the knife before Lopez opened fire, shooting three times in less than two seconds.

Lopez could still face discipline for his tactics leading up to the shooting, which the department’s civilian oversight body previously concluded violated department policy. But he is unlikely to face serious punishment after the same body, the Police Commission, ruled that he was justified in using deadly force.
