theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/21/.headline: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/21/.author: Fiona Harvey

paragraphs.text: China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probably outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/21/rej.headline: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK strikes deals on trade and young people
theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/21/rej.author: Harry Taylor

paragraphs.text: The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.
The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week.
Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU with similar access for Europeans in the UK.
Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.
Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next.
He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.
However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options”.

Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the so-called “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.
Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.
Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.
“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said.” “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”
On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”.

He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.
“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.
About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers.
Eagle said: “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and export.
“This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvze7de86pk3o.headline: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvze7de86pk3o.author: Jaroslav Lukiv

paragraphs.text: 11 minutes ago
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6043793/stop-th.headline: 5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6043793/stop-th.author: Malaka Gharib

paragraphs.text: Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch.
" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.

Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life, says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.

"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."

That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health. Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.
Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists, shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.
The problem: You can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Take 15 minutes to come up with a solution
Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.

Instead of reliving the issue, which is unproductive, take 15 minutes to convert the situation into a problem you can solve, Winch says. "What's the best way of handling it? Do I have a conversation with them? And if I want to have a conversation, what's the outcome I'm trying to get to?"
This approach allows you to create a plan for how to address the situation. "You should feel an ease in stress. Now it will be much easier for you to let go," he says.
The problem: You still can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Distract yourself with a game or a memory task
If you can't stop spinning your wheels about work, try distracting yourself for two or three minutes, Winch says. It can help you reset so you can focus on something else.
"You need something that takes up your mental bandwidth so there's not enough left over for rumination," he says.
He shares a few ideas: Play a puzzle or game like Wordle. Name all the state capitals. Think of whom you sat next to in elementary school. Picture all the items on the top shelf of your fridge.

When you're done, instruct yourself to reengage in whatever you're doing, he says. You might tell yourself, "I really want to enjoy this show now," or "I really want to watch my kid [so I can] talk to her after the game."
The problem: You still feel like you're at work when you're home
The fix: Create boundaries between work and home with immersive rituals
Rituals can train your brain to "shift gears from the mindset of being at work to the family gear, the partner gear, the friendship gear," Winch says.

Your ritual should include as many of your senses as possible, he says. Take a warm shower or a hot bath. Listen to music that puts you in the mood for whatever comes next. Shift the lighting — maybe turn off the bright lights you use at your workstation and light a candle.

One of the most effective things you can do is change your clothing, Winch says. "Clothing makes us feel a certain way. That's why power suits make us feel powerful and leisure wear makes us feel relaxed."

If you work from home and are already in your comfy clothes, change into a different set of comfy clothes when your workday is over, Winch says. It should be something "that your brain can distinguish you wear when you finish working."
The more you repeat these rituals, the more your brain knows when it's time to go from work mode to "being more relaxed and open to engaging with what you're doing when you're home," Winch says.
The problem: You feel drained after work
The fix: Do something that energizes you

One of the mistakes people make after work is they err on the side of relaxing because they feel drained, Winch says. But the things we tend to do while resting, like watching screens or doomscrolling, won't recharge us.

"You have to do something that makes you feel energized, and that's a personal thing," Winch says. If you're an athlete, head to the gym. If you're a maker, create something. If you're an extrovert, get a drink with a friend.

It's a "mental battle to force ourselves" to do these things, especially after a long day at work, he says. But "we're going to sleep better that night and have more pep in our step the next day because of that."
The problem: Work feels like your whole life
The fix: Try this thought experiment
It's OK for work to be a part of your identity, but it shouldn't be the only thing that defines you, Winch says.

If you're losing yourself in your job, try this thought exercise, he says. "If your work disappeared tomorrow, what's left? How would you describe yourself? How would you describe what your life is about?" You may find that your worth likely doesn't come from your job title or salary.
And don't forget what it's all for. If you've got the choice between working for a couple of more hours or watching your favorite TV show with your partner, pick the TV show.
"The only reason why I'm working is to be able to have a life in the first place," Winch says. "And if I end up not having one, then what's the point of it all?"

Here's a look at the stigma around mental health at work, how to spot an issue and what to do about it.

Do less, ask for more: How to make life easier as a working parent. Going back to work after having a baby can be overwhelming. You're juggling all the emotions of being a new parent while getting up to speed at your job. Tips to help you make a smooth transition.
This story was edited by Sylvie Douglis. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter. Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit.

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6044237/elector.headline: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6044237/elector.author: Ashley Lopez

paragraphs.text: It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.
And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.

Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.
The practical and legal hurdles

Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."
Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.
Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.
States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.

"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."
But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.

"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."
But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.

Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."

Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.

"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."
A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.
Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.

And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.
And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.
"We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6048678/anthrop.headline: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6048678/anthrop.author: Katie McQue

paragraphs.text: As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.

"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.

The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.

But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.

The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.

Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.

"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich

Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.

As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.
The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.
That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.

"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.

The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.
Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.

"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.
The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.
"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.
In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.

"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety
Competition between AI companies is fierce.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit this week.
That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."

OpenAI also plans to go public, and filed preliminary IPO paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, shortly after Anthropic. But Altman said in September the company has delayed those plans.
In an essay the same month, Amodei discussed the need for AI companies to carefully "pace" the development of frontier models.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," Amodei wrote. "We have sought a middle way: to show that it's possible to build carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete."

"Anthropic has done a fairly good job of investing in analysis of what its models can and can't do, and the vulnerabilities that it creates, and publishing at least some version of this analysis," Kreps said.

In April, Anthropic announced that it would restrict access to its Claude Mythos model after internal testing revealed its powerful cybersecurity capabilities. The company said Mythos could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, making it a potential tool for hackers.

On June 9, less than three months later, Anthropic introduced Fable 5, a Mythos-class model, for general use with additional safeguards to restrict certain high-risk cyber, biological and chemical capabilities. The original Mythos model remains restricted to selected partners.

"In the past, the fact that the trust and the founders were aligned helped them delay the release of Mythos for several months," said Stavros Gadinis, faculty director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at the University of California Berkeley's law school. "But this was at a moment when they felt they were leading the pack."
Anthropic's decision to enter the defense contracting space has raised questions about how its commercial relationships align with its stated mission, said Kreps.

In November 2024, Anthropic announced a partnership with defense contractor Palantir, whose software is used in military intelligence and targeting operations. Under the agreement, Anthropic made its Claude models available to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform.

However, Anthropic earlier this year resisted allowing the Pentagon to use its technology for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Negotiations broke down in February, resulting in the U.S. government designating Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security."

"It does seem to raise a set of concerns about partnering with Palantir, which is contracting with the Pentagon for targeting. What part of that is AI for humanity?" said Kreps. "A lot of people who work there went there because safety was the guiding light."
AI development is accelerating

Questions over Anthropic's promise to prioritize safety over commercial success are becoming more pressing as the technology itself advances. Anthropic is entering the public markets at a moment when its own research suggests the pace of AI development could be accelerating dramatically.

A November 2026 assessment by AI research nonprofit METR concluded that Anthropic's AI capabilities were improving at about twice the previous rate. Researchers estimate that a majority of this acceleration is now driven by Anthropic's use of AI tools to assist its own researchers. METR found no clear bottlenecks that might slow this progress, such as limits on data and computing power.

This could bring the company closer to a future in which increasingly capable AI systems help build even more advanced systems — a process known as autonomous recursive self-improvement. The prospect has fueled fears that Anthropic and other AI developers could lose control of their most advanced models, with potentially significant consequences for society.

"I'm scared myself, but it's very hard to imagine AI technology stopping or pausing," said Gadinis. "We are in a situation where these companies know better than anyone their models to the extent that someone understands them. So we have to work with them as a society."
A federal regulatory vacuum
Society is left relying heavily on AI company executives to make consequential decisions about the risks posed by their own products, experts interviewed for this story said.
Since there are few government safeguards in place to shape how AI companies make decisions about safety and security, the industry's power is going largely unchecked, they said.

At the federal level, the AI sector remains largely unregulated. Under the second Trump administration, the White House has prioritized a deregulatory approach, seeking to limit federal oversight in favor of allowing AI labs to innovate without being encumbered by red tape.

In June, the White House announced its AI framework, which lets developers submit their newest models to federal agencies for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before release. However, the initiative is entirely voluntary.

"I don't think the government knows enough to regulate AI," said Tallarita. "This is a conversation that we should have as a political community, and probably the most serious conversation we should have right now."
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/magazine/hakeem-j.headline: Hakeem Jeffries Thinks He’s the Man for This Moment

paragraphs.text: On Wednesday, House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House, all but ensuring that come January, he will be the nation’s first Black speaker.

Jeffries, who is known for his careful, disciplined messaging and approach, faces a complicated proposition. He has to hold his ideologically diverse party together, navigate a lame duck President Trump, figure out how to quickly deliver on the promises Democrats made to American voters and not ruin the Democrats’ chances to win the 2028 presidential election.
How will he handle this historic nomination and urgent political moment? I sat down with Jeffries on Friday in Washington to find out.

You had an overwhelming vote for your nomination to be speaker. What was the first thing that went through your mind when it happened? I was just thankful for the support of my colleagues, which came from all across the caucus, every part of the country. The ideological diversity of the caucus is one of our strengths. We have progressives. We have New Dems. We have Blue Dogs. And I was proud to have strong support amongst every group. We have a shared mission and objective, which is to deliver big things for the American people. And I’m humbled.

This is a time, though, when the American electorate is pretty angry. It wants radical change. Democrats have been given a mandate. Can you tell me why you think you’re the man for this moment? House Democrats, over the last several years, have worked incredibly hard to battle Republicans on every single issue, and we’ve done that forcefully and aggressively. Battle them on the One Big Ugly Bill. Battle them on Medicaid cuts. Battle them on the Affordable Care Act tax credits. Battle them on Epstein files and transparency. Battle them on a reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. We’ve battled them on ICE funding — certainly battled them as it relates to the unprecedented corruption that has been unleashed on the American people.

So are you saying that happened because you were leader and you led that effort, and that’s why you’re the man for the moment? No, what I’m saying is that we have a track record of success that I was proud to be a part of in terms of rising to the occasion at a moment where everybody was down on the ability of House Democrats to actually do anything, let alone win a historic election.

But this is a moment for you, and the thing that I would like to understand as we go through this conversation is how you see your leadership. You’ve convinced your caucus, but if you had to tell the American people why Hakeem Jeffries is the man right now, what would you say? Well, when it comes to the pain being felt by the American people — which is extraordinary, because there are far too many people in this country working hard, playing by the rules, but they can’t thrive and they can barely survive — I understand the struggles of working-class individuals, because I grew up in a working-class neighborhood. Both my parents were public servants. My mom worked for the city for 45 years. My dad was a substance abuse social worker who worked in the trenches during some incredibly painful times in the city, both the heroin explosion and the crack cocaine epidemic. I grew up in the Cornerstone Baptist Church and came of age myself in the middle of the crack cocaine epidemic, when most of us weren’t sure we would even be able to survive to the next day, the next week or the next month, because of the violence. So the struggles that the American people are experiencing right now, I’ve lived.
Have you heard from the president since the vote? Not yet.

Are you expecting to? It certainly seems to me that we’re going to have to have a conversation about how we are actually going to respond to the demands of the American people to get things done on their behalf.

Obviously, he is still the president, and he will have a lot of power over your agenda. Do you consider a weaker Trump to be a more dangerous Trump or a more pliable Trump? It remains to be seen how the president is going to respond to the decisive defeat that the American people just dealt to Republicans, to the president and to MAGA extremism. Clearly, the American people want a dramatic change in direction. We’ve indicated a willingness at all times to try to find common ground with the other side of the aisle whenever and wherever possible if it means delivering real results for the American people. That was just done in this Congress on a transformational housing affordability bill, the most meaningful one in a generation. That was done in a Congress where Republicans control the House and the Senate, and the Congress came together to pass this bill. We got it to the president’s desk. He didn’t sign it for whatever the reason, but he didn’t veto it, and it became law. That’s a foundation for the type of things that we should be doing.

We’ve seen Mayor Mamdani find ways to develop a relationship with President Trump. Is that something you’re going to try to do on a personal level? Mayor Mamdani has done a tremendous job. He’s gotten off to a great start in working hard to deliver upon the affordability promises that he made to the people of New York City and has developed the ability to have a working relationship with the president in ways that are designed to serve the City of New York. From our standpoint, we continue to maintain a willingness to work with anyone on the other side of the aisle to get things done. Even if I’m going to strongly disagree with the president, the vice president, members of the administration, on the overwhelming majority of issues, the American people want us to do all we can to deliver for them.

In our brief conversation, I think you’ve said “the American people” like a hundred times, and I know that they are at the center of this, but I do want to understand your particular perspective. You had a controversial meeting with the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner several months ago. You do not get along with Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff. You’ve called him a “stone-cold racist” whom you have “zero interest in working with.” So who is going to be your conduit, practically speaking, to the White House? It could be the vice president. There are cabinet secretaries that we can talk to.

Which one do you like? I wouldn’t say I like any of the cabinet secretaries at this particular point in time. I’ve had conversations probably most frequently with Secretary Marco Rubio. I’ve had a conversation with the secretary of Treasury. Here’s the thing: The Republicans have taken a “my way or the highway” approach over the last two years to jam MAGA extremism down the throats of everyday Americans and the country. That’s what they’ve done. And that approach failed. They broke every promise. This is a group of people who promised to lower costs on Day 1. Costs didn’t go down. Costs have gone up.
Do you imagine sitting down with Stephen Miller? No.

Really? No. I made clear that Stephen Miller’s a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time? This is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine, and there’s cruelty associated with that. There’s chaos. There’s death associated with what’s taking place. Now, to directly answer your question about practical engagement, we understand in prior administrations that it often has been the case that secretaries in the cabinet — Steve Mnuchin, for instance, negotiated a lot with Nancy Pelosi — or that vice presidents, such as then Vice President Joe Biden, was the primary negotiator often with majority leader Mitch McConnell at the time.

Have you heard from JD Vance already? No, I haven’t heard from JD Vance, either. But we have heard from the American people. And by the way, I will consistently use that phrase. You are correct. Because we work for the American people. That shouldn’t be confusing to anybody.

What do you make of your new counterpart on the Republican side, Jim Jordan, who is a very staunch Trump ally? We had a brief conversation yesterday, and we’re going to sit down at some point when the dust settles to see what the opportunities may be to actually get things done.

What signal do you think it sends that the Republicans elected Jordan, who isn’t exactly known as super friendly to Democrats? I mean, listen, I think that’s a question that they’re going to have to answer. The reality is MAGA extremism was completely and totally repudiated by the American people up and down the ballot and all across the country.

Do you see any evidence that Republicans in Congress are willing to break with the president after these elections? It remains to be seen, but here’s what is interesting, and this is one of the things that House Democrats were effectively able to do in this current Congress: We repeatedly forced successful votes on the floor over the objection of both President Trump and Mike Johnson.
So you’re saying you can work around them? Well, what I’m saying is that we’ve repeatedly done it, clearly. We did it on the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We did it on the Epstein files.

Do you think you need them? We have a robust majority. We’re going to have a 260-seat majority. We’re going to move aggressively, as I mentioned, to end the reckless and costly war of choice very early on in the new Congress. We’re going to move aggressively to restore SNAP benefits. We’re going to move aggressively to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We’re going to move aggressively to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We’re going to move aggressively to end these Trump tariffs, which have also increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars per year, and we’re going to move aggressively to ban members of Congress from trading stock. And we’ll see whether a handful of Republicans or more join us.

I want to get to the agenda, but just a few more questions on the situation inside of Congress. Do you have an epitaph of Speaker Johnson’s speakership? How do you view his time there? Not really. I’m sure that Mike Johnson will articulate the story of the Republican accomplishments, such as he believes they are. We’ve tried to have the most communicative relationship possible. At times, certainly very early on when we were in divided government and Joe Biden was president, there was a lot more cooperation, this is what the record shows, in the previous Congress than in the current one. Because Republicans decided to just conduct themselves like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump cartel and serve as nothing more than a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s agenda.

That’s been the criticism of Speaker Johnson’s tenure, that he ceded a lot of power to the executive branch and diminished the role of Congress. Is that the way you see it? Certainly, and the days of the House of Representatives functioning in that fashion are over. We’re going to be a check and balance on an out of control executive branch.

There’s a debate about whether or not Chuck Schumer should be re-elected as Senate majority leader. You’ve had your conflicts with him in the past. I remember one during the shutdown fight of March 2025 in particular. What’s your view? No one has delivered more for the people of New York City and the people of New York State over the last several decades from a legislative standpoint than Chuck Schumer. Those are the facts. I’ve had an opportunity to work with him as the leader in the House over several years. And as you pointed out, there are times that we agree on the course forward, and there have been times that we agree to disagree. That’s just the reality of governing.
But you didn’t answer the question about whether you support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. I’ve said yes, I do. I’ve said that repeatedly.

I think there’s a real concern when you look at Chuck Schumer, not that he hasn’t delivered in the past, but is he the man for the future? Well, listen, the senators are going to have to work that out. I understand the dynamics in terms of the intrigue around the inside parlor game, that these questions are going to be asked.

It’s not the parlor. It’s the American people. I feel like I need to invoke it, too. [Laughs]. I appreciate that. But listen, what I’m saying is that from the House perspective, I can tell you clearly and unequivocally, we don’t like it when the senators start messing around in our stuff, getting involved in our agenda, telling us who our leaders should be, suggesting what bills we should bring to the floor, telling us how they think we should be talking to the American people. We don’t like it. So I think I should hold myself to the same standard in advance of a Senate election. Let them work it out amongst themselves.

Do you think it’s healthy to have the debate, or do you think that it would have been better to just get this majority, a huge victory, and not have the conversation be Chris Van Hollen or Senator Schumer? I think debate is definitively healthy on all things. In fact, that’s the reason why this week, even though my election was uncontested, I called for a recorded vote, a secret ballot recorded vote, to give everybody within the caucus the opportunity to express themselves as to who they thought was best capable of serving in a leadership position of significant consequence.

I’m going to move on, but I guess the question is, can you confidently say that Senator Schumer, who is 75 and about to turn 76, is up for this? Just a yes or a no. What I can confidently say is that I don’t like it when senators get involved in our stuff. And I’m going to answer the question.

Because people are going to hear this and think, “He didn’t answer the question, so that means no.” Of course he’s capable of leading us into the future, but that’s a decision that the Senate Democrats are going to have to make.

OK, I want to talk about the plan, and specifically your first 100 days. As journalists, we always love to have a round number. I’m there with you, by the way. I do think it’s important to contextualize for the American people that we’re going to get off to a fast start.

I want to hear about this fast start. What will be the first bill? Well, we’re going to have that conversation. We just talked about all of us coming together. Here’s what I think we should do very early on in the first week or so of the new Congress: We should aggressively move to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. There’s probably nothing more immediate in terms of being able to provide economic relief to the American people than ending this conflict that should have never started to begin with.

I know Democrats are currently wrestling with whether to demand limits to funding the war in order to vote to fund the government and avoid a shutdown. That’s happening in this Congress. Where is your head on that right now? There are ongoing discussions about what can be done in the appropriations bill in advance of Dec. 11 to make clear that this [war] has to end. It needs to be over. In fact, Donald Trump can end it right now. That doesn’t mean there’s not going to be a lot of work ahead, because Iran is in a stronger position now than they were before this reckless and costly war of choice started.

You’ve been through a few shutdowns. It seems like it’s a hard thing for the country and the Congress to go through. It’s a hard thing for the country and for the Congress. We have made it clear that we’re going to fight for a spending bill that protects the health, the safety, the national security and the economic well-being of the people of this great country.

Are you willing to shut down the government in order to get that? I’m not going to say that one way or the other, because we’ve got to figure out right now what’s possible in terms of the appropriations process. What I will say is that we have made clear repeatedly that taxpayer dollars should be spent to make life more affordable for the American people. And we’ve seen several instances when there was disagreement on the other side of the aisle, including during the 43-day government shutdown, that we were not going to go along simply to get along. That was the longest complete shutdown in American history. And at the end of it, we actually were successful in forcing a vote to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.

A lot of this is psychology, right? You’re just seeing who’s going to blink, where people are at in their relationship with their caucus, etc.? And when you look at President Trump, as you’re going into this, I’m wondering, do you think he cares if there’s a government shutdown that lasts 200 days? Because this is his last term. I think presidents get motivated because they’re worried about the next election. They’re worried about the health of their party. But those don’t seem to be the motivating factors for him anymore. So I’m wondering how you think that this is going to be a tool that he might respond to. It remains to be seen how he’s going to react to what just decisively occurred electorally over the next two years.
I guess what I’m asking is, do you think he cares? I think what I’m saying is that it remains to be seen.

You do have to think about it, because it’s a bit of mental jujitsu here that you’re doing. Well, we certainly think about all these things. It didn’t just come out of thin air that we were able to win a historic majority. It didn’t come out of thin air that we were able to win the narrative around the 43-day government shutdown. And it will not come out of thin air that we will successfully end this reckless and costly war of choice.
But you’re not answering whether you think Trump is actually going to be able to be pressured. I did answer the question.
Do you think he’s going to be able to be pressured? You know what the answer is? It remains to be seen.

That’s not an answer. That’s the answer. Do you think that this is a president who is in any way predictable? This is a president who, in one breath, in a nationally televised interview on “60 Minutes,” said we went too far on immigration and that we need to course correct — on the same weekend that he elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of the violent mass deportation machine.

All right. How are you going to approach investigations and accountability? There’s a danger, which I’m sure you’re aware of, that it can seem like Democrats are looking at vengeance and lawfare, as has been portrayed by the Republican side and by the president himself. How do you get accountability without falling into a trap? The notion that these MAGA extremists are going to lecture anybody around overreach is crazy. These people have weaponized the federal government to go after people they perceive to be enemies of the president, illegitimately and consistently. They have zero standing to talk about overreach. Our perspective has been clear. We are going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may.

You saw when you were an impeachment manager for Trump’s first impeachment trial, it made him more politically powerful. He used that as a messaging device to show that he was the subject of, in his view, unfair prosecution. So there is a danger that the American people might view this as a distraction as opposed to what you are saying it is. I have great trust in the legislative leaders of this effort and every single Democrat who’s on the Oversight Committee. We’ve done accountability in this Congress.

What happened with Pete Hegseth and that impeachment [vote], because there was a real sense that this might be a moment with Thomas Massie’s attempt, and the votes by Democrats fell short. And people blamed you. It was disappointing that a few members were unable to make it to the floor.
Why wasn’t it whipped? It was whipped.
Why didn’t they show up then? Well, we have to talk to them about that.

But do you see that as a failure of your leadership? No, I don’t see it as a failure of our leadership. It’s a collective disappointment. It should never happen again. Now, listen, in the minority, we ran Pam Bondi out of town. She should have never been appointed in the first place, but we successfully, in the minority, ran Pam Bondi out of town. We successfully, in the minority, ran Kristi Noem out of the town, who was a disgrace in terms of what was going on at the Department of Homeland Security. So in the majority, on behalf of everyday Americans and people who believe in accountability in this country, we certainly are going to continue to hold cabinet secretaries who have broken the law accountable.

Are you going to try and impeach Hegseth again in the new Congress? Pete Hegseth should be impeached if Donald Trump fails to remove him. Pete Hegseth abused his power, undermined America’s national security. Of course, he has to go.

In terms of oversight, Elon Musk allegedly throttled Ukraine’s internet connectivity earlier this year. Will you be looking into what happened? Do you think the U.S. government should be in business with Elon Musk? I think we have to look into what happened in Ukraine. We need to look at what has happened with respect to the DOGE assault on hard-working federal employees and civil servants. We need an understanding of what has happened with respect to personal information of the American people.
Do you imagine asking him to come to testify in Congress? That’s going to be in the hands, preliminarily, of soon-to-be chairman [of the House Oversight Committee] Robert Garcia.

Do you think he should? Listen, we have to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and then let the chips fall where they may. And when you conduct investigations — and as you pointed out earlier, I was an impeachment manager — you have to be thorough, and you have to make sure that every step that you take is designed to deliver the outcome that is both comprehensive and consistent with the problems that you are seeking to unearth.

Just this past week, I saw Musk say that he’s suddenly not MAGA. He had said in the past not only was he MAGA but he was “dark MAGA.” Do you think this is political posturing in order to avoid accountability? I don’t know, but —

Because I’ve seen a lot of people now suddenly say that they’re moderates, that they are not MAGA, they’ve found a different political religion. Brutal midterm elections do seem to have a clarifying impact on what people want to say publicly. But we can’t forget what has occurred over the last two years. You had people bending the knee in ways that were inconsistent with their own previously articulated values, pretending as if the era of MAGA extremism was a permanent realignment here in the United States of America. It was not. And the American people clearly and decisively showed that to be the case.

One of the toughest issues in your caucus is the role of AIPAC and what to do about Israel. AIPAC has recently changed the way it’s going to give money to candidates. It’s encouraging individual donations from members because of the blowback it’s gotten. In this most recent cycle, you got money from AIPAC. How much was that, by the way?

You tell me, how much was it? Well, I mean, I get asked the question all the time, and I just want the numbers to be clear. In the last two cycles, I’ve raised — from my own re-election campaign, because there’s been no super PAC involvement in any of my campaign activities related to my own re-election — about $40 million for my own re-election. That’s raised and then spent to help elect Democrats all across the country. The average contribution to my re-election campaign is $29 per donor. I’m proud of that fact. I’m proud to be able to raise money from everyday Americans, not special interests.

The question I have, though, is more about what has become such a very touchy issue, the AIPAC funding in particular. But I presume that the reason why it’s become an issue is because people are suggesting that members of Congress are somehow bought and paid for. When I talk to members of Congress, they’re voting their districts, regardless of who they may be raising money from.
Will you continue to accept support from AIPAC? AIPAC has said they’re no longer contributing the $5,000 per contribution that they can make under the current laws.

But would you accept money from them? They’re not giving money at any point in time in terms of AIPAC as an entity. Now, am I going to continue to raise money in the way that I’ve been raising money? In small dollar increments, $29 per donation? Yes, I will. And I’m going to continue to make the case that I’m going to try to raise money subsequently to help House Democrats now hold the majority. And I’m thankful that we’ve won the majority, but to do it in a principled way and to do it in a way that will hopefully continue to give confidence, all of us, that we’re putting the interests of the people that we represent first. Now, I understand that, from a broader issue perspective, things need to change.

You’ve said about Israel: “The status quo is unacceptable. We need dramatic change.” What do you mean about dramatic change? We have to find a path toward a just and lasting peace between Israel and the Palestinian people. To me, the foundation of that is a safe and secure Israel living side by side in peace and prosperity as a Jewish and democratic state with an independent Palestinian state that provides dignity and self-determination for the Palestinian people. That has to be the North Star. And I think it’s fair to say that the U.S. commitment to the two-state solution has left a lot to be desired for decades. There have been administrations, largely on the Democratic side, that have really worked hard to try to bring that type of just and lasting peace about. It certainly happened under the Clinton administration, and it definitively happened as well under Secretary John Kerry’s leadership within the Obama administration. I think we’ve got to make sure that we revive and renew that commitment with everything we’ve got.

There are bills that are currently sitting in front of Congress, the Block the Bombs bill, which has 82 co-sponsors as we record, and the Stop the Settlements bill, which has 76 co-sponsors. Will you put them up for a vote? What I’ve said is that we have to enact dramatic change in terms of the direction of the way things have been going in both the West Bank and in Gaza. The death, the destruction, the devastation that has been experienced in Gaza by Palestinian civilians is unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American. And the conditions on the ground have to change. That requires a surge in humanitarian assistance, including medical assistance and housing support and ensuring that there’s both clean water and clean air.
Those two bills, do you see them as not addressing that? And do you support them? No, I haven’t articulated a position one way or the other.

I’m asking. With respect to any of these bills, because we’re going to have a conversation about the steps that we need to take together as a caucus, what I have made clear is that within the first 100 days, I think the most decisive step that we can take relative to the situation in the West Bank is to move the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. That is certainly something that I think we’ll have strong support for within the House Democratic Caucus, and I believe we should move on it early in the new Congress as a meaningful step forward to changing the conditions on the ground and hopefully meaningfully improving the relationship between Israel and the Palestinian people in the march toward two states for two people.

Some people see that particular bit of legislation about the West Bank as insufficient. The clarion call in the wake of the Gaza war and the broader conflict in the Middle East is that there needs to be a stop on exporting the weapons from the United States that help enact those wars. What I’ve made clear is that’s a conversation that we are going to have but that the current construct is not sustainable, and it needs to change.

In our last few minutes, I do want to get to your own personal story. We touched on it a bit at the top, but I think people want to get to know you. And I want to ask you about growing up in Crown Heights and how that impacted you. You discussed a little bit about the difficulties that you faced in the community back then. How would you say Crown Heights impacted your sense of justice, political activism and just your own leadership? It’s a wonderful neighborhood to grow up in — a working-class neighborhood, good people, hard-working folks. That’s my parents, but that was our neighbors. That was everybody. I had the opportunity, thanks to my mom, to grow up in a loving environment within the Cornerstone Baptist Church. That certainly has had a big impact on me. What was also interesting to me growing up in Crown Heights is that during the first 12 years of my life, my congresswoman was Shirley Chisholm. I never met her, but it’s an honor to stand on her trailblazing, legendary shoulders and to try to continue the fights that she started in such an unbought and unbossed way, particularly as it relates to the children of the Crown Heights community that she so effectively represented. Black Brooklyn, but all across America. Hip-hop, of course, is also a very important part of my upbringing, because I came up during a golden age where hip-hop artists were telling the story of the streets.

I think you were Kid Fresh at some point? You’ve done some great research. My aspiring hip-hop career turned out to be not too successful. Neither did my desire to be a point guard for the New York Knicks. But playing basketball in the streets of Brooklyn, that was an amazing thing, whether that was in my neighborhood or traveling with my boys from Midwood High School to other neighborhoods to find an outdoor court where we could play ball. It was such an amazing time. It was a dangerous time in New York City. You’re talking about 2,000 plus homicides in the heart of the crack cocaine epidemic. But all of us still grew up in such a loving environment. I think that adversity for everyone who emerged from that time has put us all in a stronger position to deal with the slings and arrows of life.

Can you take me back to a moment, something that you remember that really stuck with you and helped you on your way? Even before the crack cocaine epidemic hit, which was probably around ’84 or ’85, it seemed to me that almost every other week or every month or so, my mother would come home having just been robbed. Now, it can’t have been that frequently, but it happened. She was mugged repeatedly, particularly during the winter months, in my recollection. I’ll never forget: Mom comes home, robbed again, and clearly, my dad, who was a loving man but a tough man, had enough. And I saw him grab a saw and race out of the house, apparently trying to track down the person who had just mugged our mom and his wife. Now, I never found out what happened with the saw or the incident, but it was a searing memory about a dad standing up for his family in the face of all the adversity that was going on. I’m thankful that nothing ever happened from the standpoint of harm being done to Mom.

Is your mom still alive? She is. Dad passed away a couple years ago. He was able to see me transition from being chair of the caucus to this current position that I hold, but passed away at the end of 2023. Mom is still alive. In fact, before the vote, as I often do in connection with any big moment in my life, I’ll call Mom, and I’ll just ask her to pray for me, because she’s a praying woman. And prayer changes things. It doesn’t mean the outcome that I hope for has always been achieved. Everybody faces ups and downs in life. That’s the reality. But the last person I spoke to before I walked into that caucus room on the day of the vote a few days ago was Mom. I just told her I loved her. I thanked her for everything and just asked her to pray for me as she’s always done.
This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6048729/ai-stoc.headline: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6048729/ai-stoc.author: Rafael Nam

paragraphs.text: A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.

AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
What happened with stock markets this week?

Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
What's behind the steep drops?
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.

Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.

Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.

And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.

"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
What are the potential financial consequences?
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.

Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.

Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.

And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.

This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness.
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
What does it mean for the economy if the AI boom falters?
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.

Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.

Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/h.headline: Entitled and out of touch, AI CEOs are heading for a fall
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/h.author: David J. Lynch

paragraphs.text: As a young reporter in Washington, I covered the defense scandals of the mid-1980s, when weapons makers tattooed the words “waste, fraud and abuse” on the national imagination with their $640 toilet seats and $435 hammers and executives charged taxpayers to kennel their dogs.

Two decades later, as a financial writer, I watched bankers put their private interests ahead of their public responsibilities, nearly wrecking the global economy in the bargain. As the federal government mobilized to avert a second Great Depression, the financiers had one priority: ensuring their bonuses were paid on time and in full.
Weapons makers and Wall Street certainly managed to alienate average Americans. But I don’t think I’ve ever seen an essential industry act as entitled and out of touch as the AI gang.

Exhibit A: Just days after resigning in disgrace, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly paused his active dating life long enough to entertain an improbable comeback attempt, backed by some of his equally clueless tech industry colleagues.
Dude, read the room.

Put aside for a moment that Nvidia’s board already has dismissed the idea. Overlook, if you can, Huang’s serial philandering, which allegedly included a Nvidia subordinate, which is a violation of the company’s code of conduct, and a possible Chinese intelligence asset, which is a violation of common sense.
The chip impresario who cultivated an aura of indispensability is no longer the right guy to helm the world’s most important chipmaker. He may not realize it, but he’s damaged goods.

Multiple congressional committees, federal prosecutors and securities regulators are all probing Nvidia’s role in the flow of advanced AI chips to China. The first of what is likely to be several shareholder lawsuits has been filed in the Northern District of California, alleging that Nvidia and Huang violated federal securities laws and misled investors for more than a year about the company’s activities.

On Thursday, Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena asking whether the company’s chips or confidential information went to China and whether Nvidia misled investors.

“He’ll be tied up in knots in eight or nine committees before we get to all of the state-level prosecutions and the shareholder lawsuits. So if Jensen Huang could possibly be in any way exonerated from all this, which is inconceivable, he couldn’t do his job because he’s going to be full-time testifying,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management.

Huang may be an extreme example of the AI world’s image problem. But public sentiment had turned against Silicon Valley even before the ex-CEO set fire to his career. In a Gallup survey this past summer, only 20 percent of Americans said they had a great deal of confidence in large technology companies, down from 32 percent in 2020.
But in a trend that Gallup called “unique” among 14 institutions polled, the share of those expressing very little or no confidence in Big Tech rose from 32 percent to 41 percent in just one year.
The public is recoiling from the industry’s politics, its recklessness and its eccentricities.

Tech titans like Elon Musk acted as if the Trump era would never end, standing center stage at his inauguration and applauding his light-touch approach to AI regulation even as their own warnings of societal risks escalated. The authoritarian-curious politics of some Silicon Valley denizens tilted so far right as to earn the pejorative sobriquet “Nerd Reich.”

Now that the political winds have shifted following the Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections, Big Tech’s rhetorical response has been remarkably clumsy. Musk, fresh from spending half a billion dollars in a failed attempt to elect Republicans, implausibly told the New York Times’s DealBook Summit, “I’m not MAGA,” and defended his philosophy as “ideologically quite moderate.”

Alex Karp of Palantir, which is a key supplier for U.S. immigration enforcement efforts, publicly proclaimed his progressive beliefs. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, who now runs the artificial intelligence start-up Prometheus and owns this newspaper, made a point of disclosing that he calls former president Barack Obama for advice.
These high-profile CEOs belatedly seem to recognize the cost of yoking themselves to a divisive and unpopular president.

Making matters worse: A succession of near-daily tech glitches — Microsoft Outlook, the air traffic network, banks and even the National Security Agency’s computers — rattled Americans who have long been frustrated by the tech industry’s relaxed approach to its own shortcomings. The same people who routinely field buggy software now ask the public to trust them to make intelligent machines that we are told might deliver catastrophe while aiming for utopia.
The AI chieftains’ evident — how to say this? — weirdness doesn’t help.

Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg appeared on social media trying to strike an everyman pose by drinking a pint of Guinness. He double-clutched at the first mouthful, acting like he had accidentally imbibed river water.

SNL’s cold open last week satirized the tech elite — Musk, Zuckerberg, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and Huang — as “bug-eyed little weirdos” who needed “to learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy.”

Until this week, one group retained its affection for the AI crowd. Investors eagerly anticipated Anthropic’s initial stock offering, which turned out to be the largest in history and was heavily oversubscribed.
But after a successful debut on Thursday, the frontier lab’s shares sank 8.5 percent on Friday, dragged down by a broader market plunge that hit all major AI names.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index lost 9 percent this week and has given back all of its 2026 gains. Nvidia has absorbed some of the worst punishment: Its shares fell 14 percent on Friday and have surrendered almost half of their value since early October.

The tech industry’s image problems are taking a toll on their business prospects. Public opposition to construction of additional data centers is mounting, including in formerly welcoming venues such as Texas and Ohio.
When Americans go looking for a villain, their gaze increasingly turns to Silicon Valley.

Only 7 percent of registered voters said the government is doing too much to regulate AI compared with 69 percent who said Washington needs to do more, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll in October. Twenty-two percent said the industry is appropriately regulated.
Democratic lawmakers, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York), already say there will be no bailout in the event that what many regard as an AI investment bubble goes pop.
