But in late 2023, Van Hollen began breaking with his party on Israel, increasingly questioning President Joe Biden’s unconditional support as the war with Hamas devolved into a humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
In early 2025, when Democrats were reeling from Trump’s win, Van Hollen began criticizing Schumer, and taking bold stands on immigration and Israel that clashed with party orthodoxy.

In April that year, he traveled to a notorious El Salvador prison to visit Kilmar Abrego García, a Maryland resident the Trump administration deported to El Salvador despite an order barring his removal there. (Van Hollen was turned away from the prison, but allowed to meet with him at a nearby hotel.) At the time, some Democrats were warning the party should downplay immigration issues and focus on the economy.
“That was about taking a courageous stance in the face of the conventional wisdom that now seems very outmoded,” said Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minnesota), who is retiring.

In September that year, Van Hollen obliquely criticized Schumer and Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries for failing to endorse Zohran Mamdani in New York, after he had won his primary. “That kind of spineless politics is what people are sick of,” Van Hollen told a crowd of cheering activists in Des Moines.
His stances earned him new progressive fans and changed his reputation from insider to rabble rouser.

“For a long time he was seen as a kind of consummate inside legislator,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee. “And now he is seen as somebody fully in the progressive resistance to Trump and a leader on a whole bunch of different things, including immigration and human rights.”

But the substance of that pivot has alienated some longtime supporters. Former state senator Bobby Zirkin, a moderate Democrat, has criticized Van Hollen sharply over Israel since the senator began calling for conditioning military aid to the nation. After Van Hollen announced his leadership plans, Zirkin wrote an op-ed in the Baltimore Sun saying the senator pursued “power over morality.”
“He goes where he thinks the wind is going,” Zirkin said in an interview.
But Edwards, who battled Van Hollen for his Senate seat and mended fences with him, said in an interview that she encouraged him to challenge Schumer over the summer.
“Chris represents the boldness that voters spoke to for this election,” Edwards said.
An outside campaign ruffles insider feathers
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan) has also been urging on Van Hollen’s challenge this year, and on Tuesday made the case again to about 100 online influencers.

“The most important conversation isn’t just a conversation between 56 senators; it’s a conversation between the 56 senators and the hundreds of millions of people who elected us all,” El-Sayed said in an interview.

Van Hollen and his supporters have sought to channel the activist anger with party leadership through groups such as MoveOn and Indivisible, whose leaders have endorsed Van Hollen and whose members are calling their senators to demand they back him, too.

“If you were to have a vote today with the Democratic base and say, choose between Senator Schumer and Senator Van Hollen, I would say that Van Hollen would probably win in a landslide,” said Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who is backing Van Hollen.
The tactic has annoyed some lawmakers. It may also have its limits, given the insular nature of the election.

Van Hollen’s Democratic colleague from Maryland, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, announced this week that she is supporting Schumer, saying he had asked for her support before Van Hollen entered the race. As online anger with Alsobrooks boiled, Van Hollen released a statement Thursday saying he did not want the discussion around her vote to involve “vitriol or hostility.”

Van Hollen has vowed to mostly stay out of Democratic primaries if elected leader, noting that El-Sayed and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota would not be elected if Schumer’s preferred primary candidates had won. Both progressive freshmen are backing Van Hollen. Other newly elected Democrats from more conservative areas worry the dispute could tarnish their efforts to push back on the war, inflation, and other issues that fueled their victories.
Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-South Carolina) compared the leadership clash to two surgeons arguing about a procedure while a patient was bleeding in the trauma bay.
“Really what we need is someone just to stop the bleeding,” she told reporters.
Andrews has not said whom she is supporting.
Theodoric Meyer contributed to this report.

Hello! We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release: version 2.3.1. This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in all prior versions. We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME. Description =========== By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is possible to trigger a double free. This double free can be used exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data. Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't be ruled out. Thus an immediate update is highly suggested. Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557) The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975. This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed by GitLab on 2026-11-12. Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20. The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the status lines and key listings from gpg. Initially a buffer of 1024 bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required. When reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the function. Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to the freed memory. Eventually the context is released and the memory freed a second time. Due to other allocations in between the common double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered. Impact ====== All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected. Examples of software using GPGME are - Gpg4win - GnuPG Desktop - GnuPG VS-Desktop - Most mail clients - Many XMPP clients - Samba - Flatpack Solution ======== Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1. If you need a DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version. For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME 2.3.1. If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to very old versions. There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT. Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19) ================================================ [compared to version 2.2.0] * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM. Add mappings for algos used bei backends. [rMa85fa49236] * Fix a double free in the status line read code. [T8557,CVE-2026-129975] * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ GPGME_PK_DLTHM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLKEM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLDSA NEW. Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427 Getting the Software ==================== Please follow the instructions found at <https://gnupg.org/download/> or read on: The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature are available here: https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k) https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is attached. Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. Debian Packages =============== We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants. See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch to other distros/releases. Windows Installer ================= A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer, including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF reader has also been released. cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-ai-sto.headline: Why Anthropic's blockbuster IPO couldn't escape the market correction
cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-ai-sto.author: Eric Rosenbaum

paragraphs.text: No one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the company. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead.

The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).

"The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday.
And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock.

It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street noting downside risks in research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatements in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.

"It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.

The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge."

"You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said.

Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on their new outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said.

"From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based on Fed policy, geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or the AI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.

Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taking by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.

Khodjamirian said while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as results are released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?"

Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, the single biggest trade in the options market on Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.
And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he said. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.

Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.

As an IPO researcher, she says this "discernment" is a healthy thing for the markets. There are few cases to look to as comps for Anthropic, other than SpaceX, and before that, way back to Facebook's IPO in 2012. And neither example is one of quick recovery. SpaceX shares remain well below their first-day closing price more than five months after its IPO. Facebook (now Meta), meanwhile, "did not do well for the first year after going public and we see where it is now. It's just the nature of these disruptive tech companies that come to market," Marquez said. "They lend themselves to more volatility and a longer period of price discovery for investors."

All eyes will next be on Anthropic's rival OpenAI, which has suggested it will be ready to go public in 2027. Marquez said the reaction to the Anthropic deal may be a signal that it was "a good idea to wait, allowing themselves to build more quarters of better financials and improve fundamentals a bit before taking on a market that is really quite discerning."

Tema does not own shares of OpenAI in any of its ETFs. But, "I can't say it wont be," Khodjamirian said. "They exist out there in the secondary market, and we will look at it, but we haven't made any decision. It depends on the ETF fit and if the portfolio manager wants to invest. We are always looking out for these interesting businesses but never just for the sake of private exposure," he added.
Tema does own Databricks, Stripe, Kalshi and Polymarket across its funds. It also was an investor in SpaceX pre-IPO through its Tema Space Innovators ETF (NASA).

Khodjamirian said demand from public market investors to access these "generational businesses" will continue to be the case, despite the market volatility, and will more often come before IPO day. In fact, he pointed to the filing from the world's largest asset manager and one of the biggest ETF companies in the world, BlackRock, earlier this week. It wants to bring out a new kind of exchange-traded product that would bring the ETF and interval fund structures together as a way to increase exposure to private companies, with shares trading on an exchange while the fund makes monthly repurchase offers.
Sign up for our weekly newsletter that goes beyond the livestream, offering a closer look at the trends and figures shaping the ETF market.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/21/n.headline: A new map, and the fight for Black political power
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/21/n.author: Robert Samuels

paragraphs.text: MONTGOMERY, Ala. — Minutes after his opponent conceded the race for Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, Rep. Shomari Figures weaved his way through a small Italian restaurant where a swell of supporters were cheering for him. He made his way to the stage, still contemplating how he managed to win a seat designed explicitly for him to lose.

Black voters turned out with unbridled enthusiasm. Trade wars and actual wars led to wallet-clenching costs for both the farmers in his district raising cows and the families who wanted to eat those cows. Weekends were spent shaking hands at arts festivals and jamborees and church services. And on the night before the big day, in a state where there was no early voting, Figures headlined a politically oriented pep rally featuring hip-hop star Lil Baby, whose musings about hustle and ambition sent students at Alabama State into arm-waving, hip-shaking mania.
But as Figures looked into the crowd on election night and spotted the woman in the crowd with silver hair and thin eyeglasses, he realized the biggest factor of all.

Sheyann Webb-Christburg was just 8 years old when she walked across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, the youngest person among hundreds peacefully protesting for their right to vote. She had been on her knees praying when police sprayed tear gas and set dogs loose to attack them, which sent her running. The horrifying spectacle of racial violence spurred one of the most transformative pieces of legislation of the 20th century: the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
“Seeing what’s happening with the Voting Rights Act, this [win] means something a little different,” Figures said from the stage. “This one is for you.”

Figures, 41, is the last beneficiary of one of the law’s most powerful planks — that states must draw maps to give minority communities an opportunity to elect lawmakers who reflect their values. He had not even served a full term before the Supreme Court nullified the very law that created his seat, unleashing a new era that threatens the existence of predominantly Black, Asian American and Hispanic districts across the country.
A community’s racial demographics do not guarantee such representation when state lawmakers draw lines for congressional districts. The VRA was their safeguard.
A series on how politics is changing after the Voting Rights Act

Back in 2023, a federal court cited the VRA when it deemed that one more predominantly Black district needed to be drawn in Alabama. Figures, a member of one of the state’s most powerful Black families, won the seat the following year.

Since then, the Trump administration has mounted an unprecedented assault on the achievements of the civil rights era. Black unemployment has skyrocketed as the federal government pushed out scores of employees from what was once one of the most integrated workforces in the country. Civil rights investigations at schools have been frozen. Disproportionate numbers of Black service members are having their promotions blocked by the Pentagon.

But civil rights organizations found none of those policies as catastrophic as the Supreme Court’s decision in April in Louisiana v. Callais, which freed politicians to dilute the voting power of Black communities. Lawmakers in Alabama and elsewhere across the country didn’t waste much time redrawing plurality-Black districts like Figures’s to make them Whiter, more conservative and more Republican.

Figures won his race, this time, riding a wave of an election in which no Democratic incumbent in Washington lost his or her seat. But a broader battle continues to be waged across the country about the meaning, and the impact, of representation in the halls of power. Whose voices should get amplified? Whose should be disregarded?

Those debates will play out in the U.S. Capitol and in state capitals across the country as lawmakers find themselves at an inflection point, reexamining policies and practices of redrawing electoral maps while balancing political opportunity and ethical responsibility.

“Without a Voting Rights Act, without the protections of it, they could draw this district down to be 10 percent African American voting-age population,” Figures said. “And so there’s no floor. And that is the problem.”

In the final months of the election, The Washington Post trailed Figures’s fight to keep his seat and interviewed dozens of residents about the meaning of diverse representation. They repeatedly pointed to the flow of federal dollars into Black neighborhoods as well as a sense of pride and purpose that can be more felt than measured — especially in a city like Montgomery, the birthplace of the civil rights movement.

Figures is 6-foot-3 and lithe, caramel-colored and bald with a small, thin mustache. He carries a cadence and collegiality that is typical of a staffer who grew up in Obama’s Washington, button-downs and slack pants and Nike Air Maxes and “who do you know?” His warmth — a trademark of his mother, state Sen. Vivian Davis Figures — can mask his policy brain, which many of his elders say is reminiscent of his late father, Michael Figures.

Both traits were on display on election night, when he thanked everyone from his chief of staff to his wife to his baby’s caretaker before sliding into discussions about bankrupt hospitals and the cost of fertilizer. Webb-Christburg, now 70, waited for him as he climbed off the stage. She hugged him and thanked him for the recognition. But she did not want him to forget the magnitude of the mantle he now carried as the country wrestles with its civil rights history.
“Congratulations,” she said. “You know, there’s still much more work to do.”

Growing up in a predominantly Black section of Mobile, Figures often thought about a quote from the end of the 1991 movie “Boyz N the Hood.” In the scene, Ice Cube’s character, Doughboy, questions why his brother’s death was not featured on a local news broadcast. “Either they don’t know, don’t show or don’t care,” the character remarked.

Figures felt the same way about lawmakers he saw on television, who never seemed interested in tackling the issues that bothered his friends he met at the community basketball courts and football fields. He can only remember seeing his congressman visit his school once.
“They either don’t know what happens in your neighborhoods because they don’t come [or] because they didn’t grow up in those neighborhoods,” Figures told me.
Figures benefited from seeing a different version of political leadership back home.

He was the second of three children in one of the state’s most powerful Black families. His mother, Vivian, was on the city council. His uncle, Thomas, was an assistant U.S. attorney who helped to successfully prosecute the largest chapter of the Ku Klux Klan for one of the country’s last known lynchings. His father, Michael, had integrated the law school at the University of Alabama and successfully represented the family of the victim, Michael Donald, in a civil suit that left the group bankrupt.
Michael Figures’s biggest preoccupation, though, was electing Black people into state office. He had started back in the 1970s, after police faced few consequences for assaulting Black residents.

“We were protesting, but we realized we needed someone on the inside,” said Merceria Ludgood, a former teacher and attorney who worked with Michael at his law firm and later became a county commissioner.

On weeknights, Figures and Ludgood arranged clandestine meetings with a group of Black lawyers, teachers and postal workers in a small room at the YMCA on the Black side of town. There, they strategized how to get people who looked like them into positions of influence. The Voting Rights Act was their tool. As courts forced local governments to comply with the law, the group would brainstorm local leaders whom they could encourage and support to run for elected office.

“We got our first Black members of the legislature in ’74, and then we got school board members in ’76 and ’78,” Ludgood recalled. “And then also in ’78, we got our first Black senator from this area since Reconstruction — and that was Michael.”

As a state senator, Michael Figures continued to invite Black residents to his house for planning sessions on recruitment over his fried chicken and his wife’s gumbo. They focused on local and state elections, believing a federal seat was out of reach.

There was one local Black candidate that he did not support — his wife, Vivian, when others in the group encouraged her to run for city council in Mobile’s 1993 elections. He tried to imbue what he called the “three B’s” — be there, be on time, be prepared — to his children, but enjoyed the everyday practices of cleaning the yard with them on Saturdays and having lunch at McDonald’s. He feared that council job would lead to Vivian taking work home, disrupting their sense of normalcy.
But he relented when Vivian decided she would run anyway. He helped her strategize, and she sang “I Will Always Love You” to him at the victory party.

In 1996, when Shomari was 11, the family was sitting at the dinner table when Michael, then 48, suddenly lost consciousness and collapsed. He never came back home. Doctors determined Figures’s dad had a brain aneurysm. Two days later, he was pronounced dead.

“My life turned into a whirlwind,” Vivian said. Immediately, friends began to wonder if their push to get her to run for city council was an act of providence, setting her up to run for her husband’s seat. “And here I am, a single mother of three when Michael was such, such a grand participant in their lives.”

On the day of his father’s funeral, Shomari made sure to be at school so he could be marked present. A short time later, Vivian told her children she was thinking about replacing Michael in the state Senate. Shomari was so thrilled that he ran upstairs and grabbed his dad’s old campaign hat and began marching around the house.

Figures graduated from law school and then followed in the political family’s footsteps — working as liaison to the Justice Department in the Obama White House, then as a staffer to Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) and deputy chief of staff to Attorney General Merrick Garland. He was considering moving to the private sector when, in 2023, the political fortunes of Mobile began to change.

A federal court essentially agreed with what Figures and the other Black leaders concluded in the 1970s: It seemed too difficult for a Black person to win a congressional election. Even though 26 percent of the state was Black, there was only one predominantly Black district in the state’s seven-person delegation. In its ruling, the court cited one of Michael’s old redistricting cases, Figures v. Hunt. They mandated the state create a new “opportunity district.”

On paper, the new court-approved 2nd District resembled the tail of a small mammal, stretching from the border through the capital of Montgomery to the rural Black Belt to the historic city of Tuskegee before cresting in the Gulf of Mexico. It would be about 50 percent Black and encompass Figures’s hometown of Mobile.
That meant Figures had a chance to be the congressman that he had wanted to have when he was growing up.

“At the end of the day, pound for pound, the communities that I grew up in, communities where my folks come from historically, they don’t see their members of Congress and because they don’t see them, they’re not top of mind,” Figures said. “I saw the potential in this role.”

He bought a house in Mobile in May 2024, moved back home, and won a crowded primary. Adline Clark, a family friend who represented Mobile in the State House, presumed Figures had a good chance because of how much his family was beloved in the city. Vivian was still a senator and Michael was now something of a folk hero — the nicest community center in the city was named after him; a mural of him and his brothers was painted on a building downtown.
Clark knew she did not need to mention the racial significance of the election if she simply mentioned the last name Figures to voters.
“They just got it,” Clark said.
And then, on election night, Ludgood was coming home when she saw a group of young women racing to get to the Michael Figures Community Center before the polls had closed.
“They are having their Obama moment,” she said.
Figures won the race. But the community’s new political power would be precarious.

When Figures got to Capitol Hill, Rep. Sanford D. Bishop Jr. (D-Georgia), an old family friend, gave him a word of advice and a warning. The advice: Establish relationships. The warning: Do good for your district before it gets taken away.

Since his election to Congress, Bishop had seen his district swing from 56 percent Black to 59 percent White and back to 50 percent Black as his state redrew maps to comply with the Voting Rights Act.

“I have been very much involved with voting rights and the implementation of the Voting Rights Act; I’m a product of it,” Bishop recalled saying to Figures. “But the most important thing is that once an individual is able to get into the arena, it’s your ability to deliver, to use the political process to deliver for your constituents — whomever they are — that keeps you there.”

So Figures worked on his reputation. He started fist-bumping members on the other side of the aisle before taking his seat at committee meetings. Inside his office, a black and silver belt sat on his couch honoring him as the MVP in the Lawmaker vs. Lobbyist basketball game.

“The best part of my game is clearly the ability to pick up the slack left behind from Sho. Just playin’,” a teammate, Rep. Blake Moore (R-Utah), told me. “A shared love of sports uniquely unites people, and it’s especially true in the halls of Congress.”

He hoped those relationships would make it easier to bring money back home. Like many Black lawmakers from the South, he figured his district would benefit from the 2022 decision from Congress to resume the process of setting aside money for community projects, commonly known as earmarks. It was a chance for Figures to provide support for struggling communities that may have been overlooked.

In total, Figures brought in nearly $18 million in federal money to his district during the 2026 fiscal year. The freshman netted more money than about 70 percent of lawmakers in Congress, a Post analysis of earmark data showed, and slightly more than the average lawmaker representing Alabama.

More than the dollar amount, Figures prided himself on how the earmarks were distributed. He got money for a police station in the majority-Black city of Tuskegee and money to upgrade police equipment in Mobile.

He facilitated that department donating three police cars to the cash-strapped majority-Black city of Georgiana. He emphasized the importance of rural hospitals and sent $1 million to a hospital in Clark County and $375,000 to help the city of Eufaula purchase a new MRI machine.

“I’m a Republican, and Shomari has been the one who has kept in touch and kept us informed about things probably as good as any of them,” said Jack Tibbs, Eufaula’s mayor. “Actually, better than any of them.”

Back in Mobile, local leaders had repeatedly asked their lawmakers to attempt to find money to improve Africatown, a historic neighborhood that was settled by Africans forcibly transported here on the country’s last slave ship. Each time, nothing.

But in 2026, Figures framed support for Africatown in a way that would appeal to leery conservative colleagues. More so than focusing on Black history, he made a pitch that asked for money for Auburn University, which could work with a development organization in Africatown, to rebuild housing. He found them $2.5 million.
“For all of these years, we’ve been declined, declined, declined, declined,” Ludgood recalled. “And things were changing.” Four months into 2026, things changed again.

After the Supreme Court erased the heart of the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais, President Donald Trump hoped to use the ruling to build his party’s majority. He pressured Republicans to take the unusual step of redrawing districts in the middle of the decade, abandoning the conventional practice of rethinking congressional boundaries every 10 years.

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey acceded to his wish, and the state legislature reshaped Figures’s district to make it more difficult for him to win. His district now resembles a mitten, wider and more stout than before. With Montgomery at the center, the district now enveloped a new military base and communities of White peanut farmers who lived in a conservative area known as the Wiregrass. The Black population in the district dropped from 50 percent to 40 percent.

State Rep. Marcus Paramore, a Republican who hails from the Wiregrass, argued that the issue with the previous map went beyond race. When Figures’s district was created, it was then tied to the interests of cities on the Gulf Coast. “It’s a different culture over there,” Paramore said.

But what comprises the culture of a congressional district? For Figures, there was a culture threading the places he represented. From Africatown, where enslaved people settled, to Tuskegee, where the airmen flew, to Montgomery, where a seamstress started a movement — there was a rich legacy of Black history, and then Black disenchantment, that tied them together.

“There’s certainly more symbolism to this race than I think any other race in the country,” Figures told me. “And so for them to redraw the district in a way that aims to eliminate someone who was a beneficiary of the Voting Rights Act — which came about because of the efforts, the struggles, the violence, the protests, the marching, the organizing in Montgomery, Alabama — then yes, this is a centerpiece of the pushback because this district is a centerpiece of the racial struggle for equality in this nation.”
Figures’s state senator, a Democrat, tried to push back against the Republican plan. His state senator was also his mother, Vivian, who had to balance maternal comfort with political fury.

“If you were a minority, how would you like to be treated? Wouldn’t you want representation?” Vivian recalled saying to her Republican colleagues. “I just couldn’t see how people who call themselves Christians, and laugh in your face every day or give you a hug here and there, could do this.”

Before the state Senate took its final vote on the measure, a strong storm blew over the capitol that caused the lights to dim and sirens to blare. “God doesn’t like ugly,” warned Vivian Figures as she and her colleagues evacuated.

Her vote was an “oh, hell no!” when approval of the new maps came up. She lost, 27-8. When the vote was tallied, her breathing got heavy and she needed to be escorted out. “It was my first panic attack,” she recalled.

The district would no longer include Mobile, Figures’s home, “the reason that I was elected in the first place,” he said. It severed Clarke County, “which sentimentally was very important to me because that’s where both sides of my family came from, going back to slavery.” It was a “disheartening” response from a state that Figures argued too often belittled the contributions of its Black residents.
“We deserve, as Black people, a fair opportunity on more than just the football fields of Tuscaloosa and Auburn,” he said during a state legislative hearing, in a room named after his father.

But then he tapped into his father’s analytical skills. He and his staff calculated that the redrawn district had 60 percent of the same residents, so he was not starting from scratch. He reviewed the election data to discover that the last Democrat elected statewide, Doug Jones, had won the district by 12 points in 2018 against a scandal-plagued Republican candidate, and lost the district by one point in his reelection bid against Tommy Tuberville.

He realized he had an advantage over his opponent by being an incumbent and felt confident he would get support from national organizations who were angry about the Trump presidency and the destruction of the Voting Rights Act. If he could excite Black voters in Montgomery and young voters while appealing to fed-up White conservatives, Figures said, he thought he would have a path.
“They are saying it’s over, but they haven’t seen what I see,” his wife, Kalisha, recalled him saying.
In August, Figures leased a new home in Montgomery so he could live in the district he wanted to represent.

“I watched my father drop dead at a dinner table a week after I turned 11,” he told me. “Ever since then, it’s just like you squeeze out every positive element of everything you can. You don’t have time to sit here and continue to argue and cry about the district. The district is set. It is what it is right now.”

His opponent, Rhett Marques, was born and raised in the Wiregrass, a former tire shop owner who became state representative. He championed his relationship with Trump, who campaigned for him, and lambasted Figures for being new to his own district.

On the trail, Figures focused on his track record and the high price of gas. He dared young people and Black people to defy stereotypes of not wanting to vote. Rarely did he dive into the details of the contours of the district — national organizations and allies were doing it for him.
In Tuskegee, Mayor Chris Lee decided he needed to do everything he could to help Figures defy the odds and win back the seat. His city depended on it.

The city had an outsize impact on Black history. It’s where Booker T. Washington theorized about racial progress and George Washington Carver ran groundbreaking experiments at Tuskegee University. Decades of disinvestment led to its blight, and the downtown was now a rustic collection of empty storefronts. Since 1980, its peak population of 13,000 has declined by almost a third.

Figures got the city the money to help build a new police station, but Lee most appreciated the additional help that had nothing to do with legislation. A few months ago the city’s only dialysis center abruptly gave its clients a 30-day notice of its closure, Lee said. He said he was glad he finally had a lawmaker in Washington who could call the company and flex his influence. Just through reaching out, Lee realized the tangible impacts of the VRA on a community that was often politically ignored.

Figures called the company and explained that such an abrupt closure would be devastating in an area in which 1 in 5 residents are diabetic. The nearest facility was more than an hour away. After Figures’s call, the center agreed to stay open for 60 more days.

Lee rejoiced and Figures visited the center a month later to see how everything was going. There was an affable receptionist at the front desk, but no medical staff. No patients were actually being served.

Figures was apoplectic. But the company’s promise, and then its recanting, showed Lee and Figures both the problems and the possibilities that can come with a member of Congress getting involved. Companies listen, but they also need to see a track record of impact to have a representative’s force feel recognizable and formidable.
“We were really getting started with his real impact,” Lee said. “They’re trying to take it away.”

On a Saturday in early October, Figures and his family tried to find new voters. They drove down a highway that faded into a two-lane state road scaling up and down the bluffs of Alabama, past Dollar Generals and Julia’s Homecooking restaurant and gas stations where the price was $4.09. And then deeper still, to places where the gas stations had gone out of business and then there were vast expanses of grass and cotton. And then, 81 miles and a world away, Figures and his family found a parking space in a nearby bank in Ozark, population 14,000, for a local arts and crafts festival.

This city was one of the biggest in the Wiregrass. Sixty percent White, 30 percent Black in a county where 76 percent of voters in 2024 backed Trump — a place that was new to his district and that could doom his electoral prospects.

A local pop-punk band crooned songs of teenage longing from the amphitheater, while smoke from the grill of a local Black church wafted through the air. The local lodge was selling raffle tickets for a gun giveaway, and, at the far end of the festival, the Sons and Daughters of the Confederacy manned a booth wearing battle flag T-shirts that said “Keep Our History Alive.”
The local mayor was waiting for Figures as he entered and offered a piece of advice. “Every time you see a person, talk to them,” he said. “Otherwise, people here will get offended.”

As goes Congress, so goes a street festival. He walked by the men at the lodge who shook his hand and asked that he join the raffle to win the Ruger 10/22. Figures offered them $5 for one ticket. He headed to the local Republican Party’s booth. “Good to see y’all out here,” he said, as he extended his hands to them, before moving on.
Figures never made it to the Sons and Daughters of the Confederacy table at the other end of the festival. He kept on being stopped by people who wanted to meet him. Almost all of them were Black.
“I’ve seen you on TV,” Alexandra Bean, 37, told him. “You know I’m going to vote for you. It’s good to see someone different running for office.”
“Take God with you,” another woman told him. “Don’t change, be who you are.”

The sky soon became gray, and thick raindrops began to pour. It was only then, as Figures and his family made their way to their car, that for once, a White person stopped him. But she had no apparent interest in politics.
“What a cute baby,” she said, pursing her lips at his 11-month-old, Ezrah, while cooing and shaking his little hand.
On the day that would determine his political future, Figures woke up before sunrise, minutes before now 1-year-old Ezrah started his early morning cry.

Disciplined about wearing his sneakers when campaigning, he put on the wrong shoes — Cole Haan ZeroGrands — and forgot to drink his coffee before he, his wife and their youngest son jumped into the Ford Expedition to carry out his plan to touch every part of the district. He wore a pair of jeans and a white “Figures for Congress” T-shirt.

He cast his ballot at his new precinct at a church in the town of Pike Road — a bedroom community where John Lewis had been born to sharecroppers. He drove past cotton fields and then past an old movie theater turned nightclub turned abandoned, blighted eyesore.

Across the street, the mayor of Tuskegee waited for him. It was about 10 a.m., and there were no lines. One 21-year-old woman who walked up said she was voting for Figures after she had heard his desire to make life less costly at the Lil Baby concert. “I mean, I would have voted for him anyway, but I felt more inspired,” Shakayla Washington, a 21-year-old security guard, said.

Minutes later, a thin young man in a black sweatshirt riding a scooter sailed to the front of the building. It wasn’t very dramatic, but the mayor took it as the best sign he had seen all morning. “When I see a young guy pulling up on the scooter, that’s when I know,” Lee said to Figures. “We’re going to break records.”

Figures stayed for about 20 minutes before jumping back into his car and driving past the colonial homes of Eufaula, where the MRI machine was on its way, and then to a community center in Phenix City. It was sleepy there, too, and Figures and his staff began calling election officials to see if they were having better luck in Montgomery.
“They are saying they’re voting at Obama levels in Montgomery,” said Figures, which is what he wanted to hear.

He then went deeper into his district, traveling more than two hours, to Dothan, in the Wiregrass. He stopped at a community center with a large pavilion and shiny playground equipment and mostly White voters headed to the ballot.
Virtually no one paid him attention, so he got back in the car and crossed the railroad tracks and stopped at a community center on the Black side of town.

“Hey Ms. Doris!” one of his staffers said to a woman hustling inside. Another woman drove past in an old sedan with her windows down and honked her horn. One man with a gray beard and a baseball cap got on Facebook Live using one of his two cellphones.
“Everyone come out and vote here!” he told his followers. “We are going to be out. Someone is going to break out the grills. There will be music!”
A woman jumped out of her car just next to Figures, who waved and smiled at her. She ignored him.
“I don’t need to meet the man; I need to vote for the man,” she said, running into the polls. “And then I gotta go back to work.”
And then, to another community center, where Black residents’ cars were filing into the parking lot, each of them honking at Figures.
“Everyone knows you because you’re always on TV here,” said an old family friend.
“Yeah,” Figures said. “I hate to spend all that money, but that’s what you have to do to get things done.”
“It’s going to happen,” she said. “Have you seen the lines in Montgomery?”

It was close to 4 p.m. when Figures finally saw the lines in Montgomery. The local Hyundai plant had just gotten out and the parking lot was full at City of Refuge church. A man, walking with his 5-year-old son, gently patted Figures on the shoulder.
“Don’t worry,” he said, “we got your back.”

The sun fell, and Figures changed into a light-blue button-down and headed to an office space down the street with paper bags covering the doors and windows. Inside, a staff of 30 people or so had built a war room for him to track numbers.

All but a handful were Black and young, and he thought about what a blessing it was to be building that kind of political leadership in Alabama, no matter what happened. As they shouted “Keisha!” when Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms became the country’s first Black woman governor and saw Democrat after Democrat win their races, Figures barely cracked a smile. He stared at a laptop screen, making sure his staff remembered the task.
“Did anyone check on Montgomery?!” he yelled.

One person who was checking on Montgomery, at a small restaurant in the Wiregrass, was his Republican opponent. Rhett Marques had looked at the numbers and decided that Figures had cut into his lead so much in the Wiregrass that he could not overcome the overwhelming support that Figures was having in the city.
A little after 9:15 p.m., Marques called to concede. “I’m praying for you,” Marques said.

Figures nodded and hugged his family. The room cheered, and he walked a block and a half around the corner to the Italian restaurant where people were eating skewers and sliders. His wife and their four children followed behind him. And there was Vivian Figures, who stood behind her son, applauding a victory that felt as personal as it did political.

Sometimes, it was hard for Figures to disentangle the specific problems of his local district from the national implications of his race. Not just for him, but for his family and his people, whose existence in the United States had always been connected to how they should be represented at the ballot box.

Even in victory, that challenge didn’t disappear. His mind was preoccupied with thoughts of what might come next. Of the ways he might help Mobile, and the rural Black Belt, even if he no longer represented it. Of a new hospital for Tuskegee. Of how a new Democratic majority could pass a new version of the Voting Rights Act that the Supreme Court wouldn’t be able to rip apart so easily. Of Webb-Christburg’s sacrifice for voting rights, which offered both a hope and a challenge. Of his father, who had taught him about the three B’s, and of himself, who now was living a political career that was beyond his dad’s political imagination.
Chris Hacker and Clara Ence Morse contributed to this report.
This story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.
Methodology

To analyze Figures’s community project funding, The Post used a large language model, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, to extract the data, then checked the extracted data against the text of the original documents to verify that the results were accurate. To further check the accuracy of this process, The Post hand-transcribed more than 10,000 values from 125 pages into a spreadsheet and compared them to the extraction process. In this test, the automated extraction process had an accuracy rate of 100 percent; differences in capitalization, punctuation and spacing were not counted as errors.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/americas/me.headline: Top Drug Kingpin Is Captured by Mexican Army as Gunfire Erupts

paragraphs.text: A Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the F.B.I.’s 10 most-wanted fugitives was captured in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican government said on Saturday, in an operation that unleashed chaos as cartel henchmen and military forces clashed.

The arrest on Friday night of the drug trafficker, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro, was a major victory in Mexico’s campaign against its largest criminal organizations. Mr. Meza Flores was among the most powerful traffickers in Sinaloa, where a war between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel has killed thousands and plunged the state into relentless violence.

Mexico’s defense ministry said in a statement on Saturday that the operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores had been carried out in coordination with U.S. intelligence agencies. Representatives for the State Department, the F.B.I. and the Drug Enforcement Administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Meza Flores was a key target for the United States. He was the “dominant crime boss” in northern Sinaloa, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in the state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars for decades. Mr. Meza Flores was the top fentanyl trafficker to the United States, drawing the attention of U.S. law enforcement agencies.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw the northern city of Guasave into turmoil on Friday night as federal forces were attacked, according to a post on X by the state’s public security agency, which urged residents to shelter in place and avoid a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state.

Trucks burned across major roads and gunfire rang out in several neighborhoods, local news outlets reported. In footage shared by Mexican TV networks, helicopters flew overhead, one appearing to fire toward the ground.

A professional baseball game was suspended as gunfire rang out. Videos posted by spectators showed fans streaming into the stadium’s corridors for shelter and players suddenly running off the field. In another recording shared by a Mexican TV network, a reporter covering the clashes ducked between two cars as shooting broke out.

Mr. Meza Flores was the leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, originally part of the Sinaloa Cartel, before starting his own group, which is known as the Meza-Flores criminal organization, in Sinaloa.

The U.S. authorities describe the group as a heavily armed and violent organization that controls drug production and distribution in parts of Mexico. They accuse it of trafficking large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States.

Mr. Meza Flores was first indicted in U.S. federal court in Washington, D.C., in 2012, and a superseding indictment and arrest warrant were issued in 2019. The State Department had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.

Mr. Meza Flores’s group, previously a bitter rival of the Sinaloa Cartel, recently allied with a faction of the cartel called Los Mayos, according to Mr. López. Los Mayos has been fighting another faction called Los Chapitos for control of the cartel since 2024, after one of its founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was taken into U.S. custody.
Earlier on Friday, President Trump said he had told President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico at a summit this week in China that cartels were running her country.
“I told her that,” Mr. Trump said at a news conference. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbor.”

Ms. Sheinbaum has publicly rejected that characterization and repeatedly ruled out U.S. military intervention on Mexican soil, even as her government has deepened security cooperation with Washington. Mr. Trump has vowed to “dismantle” the cartels and repeatedly raised the prospect of sending U.S. military forces into Mexico.

Under pressure from Mr. Trump, Ms. Sheinbaum’s government has intensified its nationwide crackdown on criminal groups. The Mexican authorities have arrested tens of thousands of people, seized hundreds of tons of drugs and destroyed thousands of clandestine labs and other sites used to make drugs. Mexico has also transferred dozens of drug trafficking suspects into U.S. custody.

politico.com/news/2026/11/21/republican-.headline: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
politico.com/news/2026/11/21/republican-.author: Andrew Howard and Aaron Pellish

paragraphs.text: Republican leaders grappling with how to recover after their devastating midterm losses agree on one thing: President Donald Trump isn't going anywhere in 2028, even if some wish he would.

Interviews with more than two dozen GOP state and county officials from red, blue and purple states across the country conducted since Election Day revealed a party still processing their election drubbing and at a loss for how to move forward. Some want to move on from Trump entirely. Some are eager for his involvement. And others are just resigned that he’s going to do whatever he wants, regardless of their preferences.

All of them are worried about the party’s chances of retaining control of the White House in two short years, but they also recognize its current occupant is going to continue to exercise a huge role in the future of the party.

“President Trump is going to be part of it, whether we want that or not,” said Arkansas GOP chair Joseph Wood. “His voters are still going to be Republicans that we need to have come out in this election in two years.”

That leaves the party in a precarious position. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval rating at 32% overall, and at 70% among Republicans — down from 91% on inauguration day last year. A POLITICO Poll taken after the midterms found 56% of Trump’s 2024 voters believe the Republican Party needs to distance itself from him and his agenda. But no one in the party expects that to happen. And Trump has already taken steps to maintain his grip on the GOP, endorsing Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters for another term and ordering his powerful super PAC to continue fundraising ahead of 2028.
A handful of Republican grassroots leaders were openly critical of Trump.
“I don't know how much he really has to offer,” said Vermont GOP chair Paul Dame. “I think most people are ready to move on in a new direction.”
Added Michael Bub, the chair of ruby-red Taylor County, Wisconsin, Republican Party :“He should stay out of it. Look at the people he endorsed: They lost.”
In a statement, RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassare said “President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party.”

“Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our voters and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028,” she said. The White House demurred, pointing to the RNC’s response.
Many party officials are resigned to Trump doing whatever he wants, given his domineering personality and strong sway over the party base.
Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper said “Donald Trump's going to play whatever role he wants to play.”
“He's the president,” Truemper said. “I look at things as they are and not as I want them to be.”
That’s leaving some state-level Republican leaders wanting the president to take on a more constructive role and be willing to let other candidates and ideas rise.

“I hope he becomes kind of the mentor grandfather, and not the godfather,” said Kansas GOP chair Danedri Herbert. “In America, we hope and expect our presidents to not keep a tight grip on the party, to recognize that now it's time for me to mentor the next generation.”

Added outgoing Minnesota Republican Party Chair Alex Plechash: “We need to capitalize on what he brought to the party and do what we can to retain that. But there has been a definite turn in the political landscape.”
Virtually every GOP official cited the poor political environment caused in part by the president’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran as the reason for the party’s midterm meltdown.
But many stopped short of laying the blame directly at the president’s feet, a sign of how criticism of Trump is still verboten within the party.
“I don't want to play the blame game, because I just don't think it's productive,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein. “But I do think that it was more economics than it was anything.”

Many GOP chairs praised the president’s ability to bring in new voters to the party and credited him for working to turn those voters out on behalf of other candidates. Still, some said they hope Trump’s generation-defining tenure at the top of the party comes to an end, allowing Republicans to choose the nominee without his influence.
“Republicans should embrace whoever we decide we're going to get behind as a new president, and let the Trump era be gone by the time we're in 2028,” said Oklahoma GOP chair Charity Linch.
Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, said he is focused on what he and the RNC can control ahead of 2028 — and wants to make sure the organization stays neutral.

“We shouldn't put our hand on the scale,” he said of the 2028 primaries. “I think Republican primary voters are pretty savvy and pretty smart and can figure out who our best candidate is going into the ’28 election.”

Trump still has plenty of defenders. Even some chairs who are bucking Trump’s endorsement of Gruters and backing RNC co-chair KC Crosbie’s challenge to him, like Kentucky chair Robert Benvenuti, think Trump should continue to be heavily involved in 2028.

“He won't take a back seat and should not take a back seat,” Benvenuti said. “I think he's been a tremendous leader for our country. … I think his message will still ring true and will be very helpful as we go into 2028.”
Samuel Benson, Lauren Fedor and Jason Beeferman contributed to this report.

theatlantic.com/international/2026/11/ho.headline: The Houthis Are the World’s Problem

paragraphs.text: In late October, I met a Yemeni military officer at a high-end mall in Riyadh. He wore a dishdasha and had the gruff, weary manner of an aging career soldier. His unit had been fighting the Houthi militia in southern Yemen, more than 800 miles from the immaculate, marble-floored refuge at the center of the Saudi capital where we ordered coffee.

He was mapping the battlefield on the table with his hands, describing how the latest round of fighting had played out, when cellphones began beeping simultaneously all around us: an incoming-missile warning. Moments later, loud booms echoed through the mall, followed by audible gasps from nearby tables and a child’s cry of fear. Shoppers froze in their tracks, some glancing anxiously toward the glass dome above us.
The Yemeni officer looked at me without speaking. A grim smile played on his lips, as if to say: They are all learning about the Houthis now.

The missiles were intercepted, but the moment stayed with me. A new reality was intruding on a population coddled for years by visions of a frictionless post-oil future, when new technologies would keep everyone happy and entertained.

Saudi Arabia is at war. The Houthis have demonstrated, by means of recurring missile barrages, that they can shut down much of the country’s economy at will. A deadly strike on the main airport in Riyadh killed at least 14 people in mid-October and injured hundreds. More than a month later, few flights have resumed.
“The kingdom today faces the most dangerous crisis in its history, the Saudi journalist Abdulrahman al-Rashed told a Saudi podcaster last month.

That kind of candor is extremely hard to come by in Saudi Arabia. None of the Saudi or Yemeni officials I met in Riyadh in October would speak with me on the record. They told me that the monarchy is now taking the Houthi threat far more seriously than in the past. Riyadh has struck deals to bring thousands of soldiers from Pakistan and Syria to help defend the country’s border with Yemen. But these efforts may not be enough. The Houthis are building up their forces too, with help from Iran, China, North Korea, and Russia.
[Graeme Wood: The only thing the Houthis have done successfully]

The Houthis are no longer the rebel upstarts of a decade ago. They are well on their way to becoming the North Korea of the Arab world: an insular, well-armed, and fanatical statelet that poses a threat to the entire region. They have an AI-assisted weapons industry and have studied the Ukraine war; their information operations are way ahead of their Saudi and Yemeni rivals’. The Houthis could soon become more dangerous than Iran, their long-standing patron.

The Saudi military was not designed for this kind of war. The country’s rulers have long been reluctant to build an army that could one day pose a threat to the monarchy. Even now they have dismissed the notion of sending their own troops, apart from elite special forces already deployed in Yemen, to fight the Houthis. But they may soon find that you cannot rely on foreigners when your country is facing a very real threat of invasion.

The current Houthi military offensive began in September, when the group captured the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia’s leaders believe that this plan was largely devised by Iran. In October, I met with a senior Saudi official who described a strategy coordinated by Tehran and its allies in the “Axis of Resistance” over the past several months. The latest chapter, the official said, began in the spring, when President Trump ordered the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. That left Tehran with limited options to retaliate, so Iranian officials met with their Houthi allies and persuaded them to launch an offensive on the Bab el-Mandeb.

The Iranians, the official said, agreed to help make it happen. A Houthi delegation attended the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran in July, he told me, and when it returned, the Mahan Air flight that carried it also conveyed a whole team of Axis military technicians and commanders, including two North Koreans, a Syrian who had been part of the Assad regime, and members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and of Lebanese Hezbollah, the Shiite militia. The plane was loaded with cash and weapons, including drone parts and missile-guidance systems, the Saudi official told me. (Some details of the Mahan Air flight have been reported previously, including the weapons and Iranian officers on board.)

The Saudis had gotten word of the plane’s cargo and bombed the runway of the airport in the Yemeni capital to prevent it from landing. But the flight was diverted to Hodeida, a city on the Red Sea coast that is also under Houthi control, and landed there. Separately, the Saudi official told me, Russia delivered a large shipment of weapons and technology, concealed under thousands of tons of wheat.

If the Saudi official’s account is accurate, it would suggest that the Houthis are receiving more international support than ever. Even if the report was exaggerated for the benefit of an American journalist—Saudi officials are desperate to get more military assistance from the United States—it still points to a larger truth about what the Houthis have become.

The Houthis are the world’s problem. They have proved that they can block a waterway that carries about 15 percent of the world’s trade. They now control about a third of Yemen’s territory and most of its population, and aim to conquer it all. Their use of child soldiers has been well documented for a decade, as has their frequent use of torture, arbitrary detentions, and disappearances. Their rule is rooted in a revolutionary ideology that does not stop at Yemen’s borders and that thrives on constant war. They have challenged Saudi control of Mecca and Medina, Islam’s holiest cities, and they often boast that they will liberate Jerusalem.
[Thomas Wright: The price of defeat in Iran]

These are not empty ambitions. The Houthis are constantly expanding their missile and drone production, using fiber optics and other materials supplied by China. Evidence recently came to light that they have used the AI tool Claude to improve their guided-missile technology. They have developed pragmatic relationships with al-Qaeda and the al-Shabaab terrorist group, despite sectarian differences (the Houthis adhere to an offshoot of Shiite Islam; the other two groups are Sunni). And, in a show of political dexterity and ideological fervor, they have been recruiting and providing training to ethnic and tribal subgroups throughout the Horn of Africa, in Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Sudan. These outreaches appear to be modeled on Iran’s efforts to build up regional allies, and could add more tinder to an already volatile region of Africa.

For now, Saudi Arabia lies on the front line of any effort to contain the Houthis’ power. The United States is too deep in its war with Iran to provide anything more than minimal help, and the Europeans are focused on Ukraine. The other Gulf countries have good reasons to fight the Houthis, but for various reasons, they will not.

The Omanis have been hedging their bets for years—allowing the Houthis to smuggle arms across their border with Yemen and providing some intelligence—in case the Houthis end up as the winners. The United Arab Emirates fought the Houthis inside Yemen for years alongside the Saudis, but late last year, long-running tensions between the two countries reached a breaking point, and the Saudis ordered the Emiratis to withdraw. The Emiratis’ absence has damaged the broader war effort.

The Saudis, who have long backed the internationally recognized Yemeni government in Aden, organized a counteroffensive after the Houthis captured the Bab el-Mandeb. They embedded Saudi commandos with Yemeni government forces across the country. Some were killed in a devastating Houthi strike on October 19. The Saudi official I met in Riyadh told me that the near-term goal is to recapture all of the territory that was lost in September, and then secure some kind of truce. The Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have not yet achieved that, and it is not clear that they will. “I don’t see a way out unless the U.S. agrees to provide direct air support,” Nadwa al-Dawsari, an associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, told me.

Even if the Saudis are able to achieve a respite from the fighting, the Houthis will retain the whip hand in the conflict, because they will still be able to strike the kingdom’s airports and oil facilities. And they will surely use any truce to continue expanding their military, as they have in the past. The Saudi official told me that the kingdom’s long-term plan is to build a larger and more unified Yemeni military that is capable of pushing the Houthis back and “eliminating their military capabilities.”

That is a tall order. The Yemeni military officer I met in Riyadh last month described a fighting force that is hamstrung by clashing political and regional loyalties. “There are forces loyal to Islah”—the Yemeni Islamist party—“and they hate us,” he said, referring to his own more secular faction. (He did not need to add that the feeling is mutual.) In the south, many of the soldiers are more interested in creating a separate state than in fighting the Houthis. “The Houthis know all about the divisions on our side,” the officer said, “and they take advantage of it.”

The Saudis bring problems of their own to the conflict. One is the kingdom’s culture of entitlement and corruption, which has bled into its behavior in Yemen. For decades, the Saudis maintained their influence in Yemen through a patronage system of stipends paid to tribal sheikhs and military figures, and they took a quasi-imperial view of Yemenis as primitive underlings. They had a reputation for paying their proxy soldiers so poorly or so late that some had to sell their weapons in order to feed their children.

This pattern of behavior generated deep resentment, partly because the Yemenis got a glimpse of a different approach. The Emiratis spent decades fostering a culture of discipline and accountability in their own country, and in Yemen, they had a reputation for training their allies, paying them higher salaries, and demanding results in return. The Emiratis—who run a small but highly effective military of their own—therefore had far more success with their Yemeni recruits. The Saudis say they are reforming their system, but that will take time.

The Saudis and their allies are now struggling to relieve the month-long Houthi siege of Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities. If the Houthis capture it, nothing but open roads will separate them from Aden, the base of Yemen’s internationally recognized government and its military headquarters. “There is nothing going on to defend Aden,” Henry Thompson, a Yemen expert who has worked with the United Nations, told me. (Just in the past few days, the threat to Aden has grown, and some signs of defensive preparations have become evident there.)

The Houthis, meanwhile, have taken measures in the territories they control that could pull Yemeni troops into protracted conflict even if they succeed in retaking ground. Some recent seizures of cargo destined for Houthi ports have intercepted equipment for digging tunnels, including excavation tools and ventilation systems. The Houthis appear to have successfully imported large quantities of this kind of gear in recent years.
[Robert F. Worth: Saudi Arabia is running out of options]

“In Hodeida, the Houthis have built a city underneath the city,” Mohammed al-Basha, a Yemen analyst and the founder of the Basha Report, a geopolitical-risk advisory firm, told me. “For anyone trying to capture that place, it would be like going into Gaza.”

For the moment, the war is not going well. After making some gains in October, the Saudi-backed forces announced on November 15 that they had been forced to withdraw from the area around the Bab el-Mandeb. I met several members of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in Riyadh—their rear base—and they tried to put on a brave face, with varying degrees of success. Some seem resigned to deeper losses. “The Houthis will take Aden, and they will keep going,” one told me.

The current battlefield is in southern Yemen, but everyone I spoke with agreed that the Houthis will eventually open a new front in the north and attempt to invade Saudi Arabia. That would make it impossible for the Saudis to deny that they are at war. Until now, they have held firmly to the claim that this is an intra-Yemeni conflict, and that Saudi Arabia is a third party. But the Houthis have made clear for years that they consider themselves to be at war with Riyadh, and they frequently mock Yemen’s internationally recognized government as a Saudi fig leaf.

Almost no one in Saudi Arabia wants to acknowledge the possibility that they could soon be forced to defend their country. “Why should we send our young men to defend the Bab el-Mandeb?” one official asked me in Riyadh. “The conflict is inside Yemen.” He went on to describe the Houthis as nothing more than an “annoyance.”

None of the ordinary Saudis I spoke with in Riyadh, whether old friends or people I approached in cafés, seemed comfortable talking about the war. Saudi Arabia is an autocratic society where dissent can land a person in jail—but the reticence may also reflect the dissonance people feel between the war and everything their ruler has been telling them for the past decade. Saudi Arabia’s problems are supposed to be solved through technology and innovation. Being dragged into a bloody war with a radical militia is not part of that plan.

It is not part of America’s plans, either—especially not since the Trump administration waged an expensive and largely futile air war against the Houthis lasting seven weeks in early 2025. But that could change. The Houthis, like their Iranian allies, believe that they are waging a metaphysical battle against America, and they are determined to topple every outpost of American influence in the region.
