cnbc.com/2026/11/21/us-airlines-first-cl.headline: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/us-airlines-first-cl.author: Leslie Josephs

paragraphs.text: The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.
The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.
A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.
"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."
There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.
A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.
American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)
Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."
No soup, no olives
Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.
On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.
First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.
"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."
Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.
American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.
Carving up business class
Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.
There's more to come.
"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."
First class still flies globally
Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.
Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.
British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.
Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.
"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

The Thanksgiving table can feel like the dance floor of a throbbing nightclub. “Play the hits!” the crowd roars. This is not the time for experimental synths or clunky transitions. “Tradition” — that fraught and flimsy word — sets the tempo. But who gets to control the D.J. booth?

Often, it’s the host, determined by age or authority — and bedroom-to-bathroom ratio. Certainly my cozy apartment looks cramped in the shadow of Thanksgiving, its quaint four-seat dining table shy about half a dozen place settings.

So my fellow single 30-somethings — members of a generation struggling to afford a home, child care, even a wedding — dutifully pack our bags, board our flights or fill up our gas tanks, and exercise power where we can.

“We’re in a changing-of-the-guards period,” one friend told me when I asked about her holidays. She has been given more jurisdiction over the menu, which she described as “half staples” and “half experimental vegetables,” which she cooks with her dad. But though she loves to host, she must still decamp to the suburbs. “When you have a baby,” she joked, “everyone will come.”

A Gen Z friend told me his dad “is very serious about Thanksgiving” and “refuses to deviate.” So he found opportunity in lack, pleading to make mac and cheese, a dish absent from their table. Given a green light, he scoured YouTube for inspiration and has made little adjustments over the past decade to arrive at what he believes is perfection. When he suggested bucking convention with a second contribution, though, his dad’s response was like a D.J. mouthing “Sorry, no requests” over a pulsing bass.

As an editor at NYT Cooking who gets to develop recipes, I would love nothing more than to labor over a feast’s worth of new dishes each year and see what sticks. I’ve been itching to introduce a bit more acid to our menu, for example, and break out Alexa Weibel’s roasted mushrooms with smoky pomegranate sauce. But to unseat my father’s beloved wine- and cream-braised mushrooms — which, I gotta say, he always makes far too much of — would have me excommunicated. Even putting that in writing scares me to bits.

My mother hosted her first (albeit small) Thanksgiving when she was 29. She and my father had just moved from Manhattan to Atlanta and were joined at the table by her brother. She labored over the turkey, something she and my grandmother had learned to cook from neighbors when they immigrated from Cuba some 20 years before. She made sweet potato soufflé with Calvados, using a recipe from Gourmet magazine. And she made stuffing dotted with Italian sausage and green bell peppers, of which Dad was not a fan. So went stuffing from the rotation — until, at a far less established 29, I saw my opening. A different stuffing, with challah I make from scratch, has been my contribution to the meal going on five years.

Last year, I developed this recipe for vegan salted maple ginger pie and hoped to squeeze it onto the menu. Alas, dessert is the domain of Uncle Peter, a former pastry chef, who, for nine of us last year, made two whole cakes, including a divine black velvet with Lambeth piping. I should have known better.

Tradition is a comforting anchor when uncertainty swells. But it can be just as soothing to up-anchor and drift. Doing so can serve our appetite for newness (and control). It can also make for a more inclusive meal.

Enter: the vegetarian centerpiece. A mushroom Wellington competes with no aunt’s turkey or ham, offends no one and pleases far more guests than one can imagine. A maple-lacquered pumpkin, stuffed with jeweled rice and lentils and showered with crispy shallots and sage, makes any meatless guest feel like a priority, not an afterthought. The pumpkin is the ideal vessel for such a mission, a symbol of abundance and a critical link in the establishment of Thanksgiving. It’s not just for pie, folks.

At worst, a vegetable preparation envisioned as a main dish will be treated as a side. At best, it is a conversation starter that becomes a hit in its own right. And for the cook who made it, perhaps it grants a sliver of holiday autonomy when so many other markers of adulthood feel out of reach.
See all our Thanksgiving recipes on NYT Cooking.

THE LATEST NEWS

• The stock market had its worst week in more than a year, with the S&P 500 ending more than 10 percent below its recent high. Tech stocks fared poorly despite Anthropic’s blockbuster I.P.O. as investors showed wariness about the A.I. boom.
• President Trump threatened to ban American tech companies from building data centers outside the U.S., suggesting he could impose a “tremendous tax” or other penalties on violators.
• The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, according to people briefed on the matter.
• Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia spy scandal, has extensive ties to China’s defense industry, The Times found.
• Times Exclusive: ICE went too far last year in loosening its training standards to hire more officers, an internal government watchdog found.
• Federal watchdog lawyers opened an investigation last year into possible fraud surrounding Trump’s memecoin. Then they backed off, convinced the government would kill the inquiry.
• Since losing his Senate bid, Texas’ Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, has dropped a number of high-profile lawsuits against his political opponents.
Around the World
• British and European leaders agreed to remove some of the barriers introduced by Brexit, a decade after the U.K. voted to leave the bloc. Here’s what to know.
• Mexico captured a drug kingpin who was one of the F.B.I.’s 10 most-wanted fugitives, the Mexican government said.
• Polish officials said three Russian objects, including at least one missile, had crashed into the country’s territory. Poland’s prime minister called it an “intentional provocation.”
• An Anthropic mathematician claimed to have proven the Riemann hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, with help from A.I.
• A Missouri state court approved a $7.25 billion nationwide settlement that will end tens of thousands of lawsuits claiming that Bayer’s weedkiller, Roundup, caused cancer.
• ICE agents detained a Chinese-born Princeton neuroscientist while she was traveling from an academic conference.
• The number of new Ph.D. students studying the sciences at major U.S. research institutions has fallen substantially, according to a new federal survey.
ASK THE MORNING
Will the new Democratic majority in Congress be able to limit the war with Iran? | Mark Vezzola | San Diego, California

The Democrats will have a few levers to restrict Trump’s ability to continue the Iran war. They can pass legislation requiring that it end, restrict funding for combat operations or place new restrictions on the Department of Defense. But Trump could veto any of those moves, and Democrats won’t have enough votes to override the president. Even if they refused to approve new defense funding (which could risk a government shutdown), the Pentagon has many ways to shift money around. Democrats’ best chance may come through negotiations where they win concessions on the war in exchange for funding other administration priorities. — Robert Jimison, who covers Congress
THE WEEK IN CULTURE

• Grand Theft Auto VI, which took more than a decade to create, contains a remarkably complex digital world. To illustrate that point, Times reporters examined the myriad options available to players in a single convenience store.
• In the video above, Zachary Small explains how the G.T.A. series evolved to reach this point. Click the video to play.
• The new game is set in Vice City, a fictionalized version of Miami. It is, at its core, about America. Yet the game originated in Scotland.

• Jonathan Yardley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning book critic, died at 87. He reviewed more than 3,000 books, sometimes turning a sharp eye on canonized writers like Steinbeck and Salinger. Read his Times obituary.
• Jan van Eyck, the 15th-century Flemish artist renowned for intimate portraits, helped define a genre. See his genius in three surviving works.
• “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” follows the early years of Haymitch Abernathy, originally played by Woody Harrelson. This new prequel is both bloated and limited, our critic writes.
RECIPE OF THE WEEK
Cranberry Orange Muffins

Most muffins are just cupcakes without frosting, but Yossy Arefi’s cranberry orange muffins are more like tea cakes at heart. These adorable golden-domed treats, made with buttermilk for tang, are topped with a fragrant, orange-zest-flecked glaze. Make them this weekend with any extra cranberries you have on hand. They work equally well with fresh or frozen berries, and they freeze well, too. — Melissa Clark

The Hunt: After a breakup, a Baltimore woman paid off her debt and set off to buy a house alone. What did she find? Play our game.
What you get for $330,000: A Colonial Revival in Enfield, Conn.; a 1914 Craftsman in Lynchburg, Va.; and a Tudor revival in Pittsburgh are all on the market.
Stone by stone: This architect is making a new house look centuries old, one rock at a time.

Cake architecture: See the creations from a baking competition for building nerds.
To dim, or not to dim: Your home lighting choices say a lot about you.
Stretchy status symbol: These $60 tote bags have become the ultimate if-you-know-you-know accessory.

ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
Our most essential travel tips

Heading out of town for the holiday? The right gear and some expert-vetted hacks can make your journey less arduous. For instance, try the 3-to-1 packing method — three tops for every bottom — to avoid overpacking. (By the way, there’s no clear winner in the debate between rolling or folding your clothes.) Bluetooth trackers are great, but don’t overlook the classic luggage tag — it’s the first line of defense against a lost suitcase, and it can help you spot your bag on the carousel. A simple adapter can connect your wireless headphones to the plane’s audio system. And if you’re looking for a great gift for the traveler in your life, our favorites help make flights a bit more comfortable. — Maria Adelmann
GAME OF THE WEEK

Minnesota Vikings vs. San Francisco 49ers: This is one of the most intriguing games of the N.F.L. season. First, there’s the matchup itself: The 49ers have the league’s best offense. The Vikings have the toughest defense, allowing fewer points than any other team. According to The Athletic’s projections, these two teams are the most likely N.F.C. champs. (Here’s a deeper breakdown, plus experts’ predictions.)

And then there’s the venue: Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, which sits at around 7,300 feet above sea level — far higher than even Denver’s vaunted mile-high stadium. The Athletic’s Alec Lewis wrote about the Vikings’ preparations for playing in such extreme altitude, which involved working out in a high-tech environmental chamber. The Niners, for their part, spent the week training in Colorado Springs. Sunday at 8:20 p.m. Eastern on NBC. — Tom Wright-Piersanti

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/s.headline: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/s.author: John Csiszar

paragraphs.text: If you haven’t looked at your investment accounts over the past two months or so, you might be in for an unpleasant surprise. As of early October, the S&P 500 was up more than 14 percent for the year. But after an 11.6 percent decline from its peak, those gains have nearly vanished. As of Friday’s close, the index was up less than 1 percent for 2026, excluding dividends. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite has turned negative, down 2.7 percent on the year.

The S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq are all now in corrections, meaning they’ve fallen more than 10 percent from their recent highs. With the artificial intelligence-fueled stock boom petering out, many investors are concerned just what it means for the overall market and what they should do with their portfolios now.
What’s happening?
Investors have poured money into AI-related stocks, while the companies themselves have spent billions of dollars on data centers, advanced computer chips and other infrastructure.

Recently, however, investors have begun questioning whether all that AI spending will generate enough profits to justify the lofty stock prices. Some of the same companies that helped push stocks higher earlier this year are now pulling the market down.
Corporate earnings, meanwhile, have remained strong. According to FactSet, S&P 500 companies are reporting third-quarter earnings growth of 32.9 percent compared with a year earlier.
The problem, according to Dustin Wigington, founder of wealth management firm Rulicent Investments, is that investors expected even more.

“The success of artificial intelligence as a technology and the success of AI stocks as investments are two entirely different things. A company can be enormously successful while its stock disappoints. The price you pay matters,” Wigington said.

Persistent inflation and the prospect of additional interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve have added to investors’ concerns. But even with all of these worries overhanging the market, Wigington cautioned against assuming the recent downturn will become a prolonged market decline.
In an interview, he pointed to the sharp sell-off in late 2018, when the S&P 500 fell nearly 20 percent from its September peak before rebounding strongly in 2019.

Wigington described the current downturn as a classic, healthy correction, although there’s no guarantee of a quick recovery. And some financial commentators have warned that the AI-driven boom in the stock market has set the stage for a much deeper bust, predictions the markets have defied for much of the past two years.
Avoiding panic

Investing can be emotional, especially when the markets are in turmoil. The key, many financial advisers say, is to avoid disrupting long-term investment plans while still paying attention to what’s going on.

“Staying the course is one of the most powerful things an investor can do. Market volatility is inevitable, and it’s not wise for investors to change their strategy in response to short-term market moves,” said Alex Michalka, vice president of investment research at Wealthfront, an automated investment management and financial planning firm.

Michalka recommends reviewing your portfolio at least annually to make sure it still matches your financial goals — both in terms of your investment objectives and risk tolerance. Making small adjustments in line with your original investment strategy is a better move than making wholesale changes based on the latest headlines, he said.

Check how you’re handling the market volatility as well. If the recent market turmoil makes you lose sleep at night, Michalka said, it’s possible that your asset allocation was riskier than appropriate for you personally.

Your timeline also plays an important role. Michalka said investors in their 60s and nearing retirement usually have different risk profiles than younger investors and should think carefully about how much risk they can tolerate, including how they’d handle another substantial decline.
Similarly, money needed for short-term expenses shouldn’t be exposed to the same stock market risks as long-term savings.

Corrections may be a normal part of investing, as Wigington pointed out. But that’s probably of little consolation to anyone who’s watched nearly a year’s worth of gains disappear in a matter of weeks. For those investors, the more pressing question is whether their portfolios are prepared for what comes next.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy0qj7w5zqo.headline: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy0qj7w5zqo.author: Sarah Rainsford

paragraphs.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders met in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys to discuss Ukraine.
That meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

Hollywood earned its cultural monopoly by absorbing radical technologies that it first resisted: sound, color, computer graphics. People in the industry initially feared that Pixar’s computer animation would replace human actors with “digital doubles.” Similarly, most of the conversation about AI today revolves around cost savings and artist displacement. These issues are important, but they miss an even bigger shift that AI is accelerating. Ask a teenager where their favorite characters come from, and the answer is as likely to be a creator platform—YouTube, Roblox, TikTok—as a Hollywood studio. Unless moviemakers evolve, they risk losing their place at the center of culture. Those who combine new technology with storytelling, and who bring audiences into the creative process, will define the next century of entertainment.

Silicon Valley and Hollywood went through a version of this before, during the early partnership between Pixar and Disney that was crucial to Pixar’s success. Disney storytellers gave Pixar pointed feedback on early Pixar characters, leading John Lasseter, Pete Docter, and the rest of the brain trust to take screenwriting classes. Pixar didn’t believe that technical people were any less creative than artists. Every discipline mattered. The result: Toy Story.

Disney didn’t produce Toy Story by hiring more CGI artists into its 2-D pipeline. Instead, it partnered with Pixar, whose mission was to make movies with the new technology, and eventually acquired it. Pixar had tech that worked, artists who were intimate with it, and a culture of mutual admiration among its artistic and technological creators. Disney had marketing, distribution, major capital, logistical know-how, and a glorious legacy. Neither could build what the other had.

Something similar needs to happen now. Hollywood has an opportunity to partner with studios built for AI, but the rise of creator culture will make the transition harder. During the shift to computer animation and graphics in the 1980s and ’90s, the distribution formats stayed the same—theaters, home video, and broadcast. Today, format, distribution, and production technology are changing all at once.
[Read: The corner of Hollywood that’s most susceptible to AI]

YouTube made more than $60 billion last year, about $15 billion more than Netflix brought in. To keep up, Hollywood studios are adapting properties from creator platforms. They found success with Backrooms (which cost about $10 million to make but collected more than $400 million at the box office) and Obsession (less than $1 million to make; more than $520 million at the box office), and are now rushing to find more YouTube properties and talent. Though this is smart, these audiences were formed and cultivated on other platforms. The Minecraft movie made almost $1 billion, a fraction of the game franchise’s $10 to $12 billion. The movie was effectively a marketing event for the game.

AI didn’t cause the shift to creator platforms, but it will accelerate it. MrBeast, who has more than 500 million YouTube subscribers, built an empire without AI, but the technology allows would-be creators to realize their visions, and it enables existing creators to work more efficiently.

But what about the ethics of using AI models that were trained on artists’ work without their permission or payment? Artists should be compensated for the work that was used to train models. These issues need to be settled in court and through regulation and licensing. The technology won’t go away, so we need artists to help set its terms.

But rejecting AI altogether is not the answer. Across Asia, creators face many of the same concerns, but the technological and cultural shift is further along. In China, microdramas—scripted series typically filmed in portrait mode and designed for smartphone viewing, with episodes lasting one to three minutes—have compressed the distance between creation, distribution, and monetization; generative AI fits naturally into an industrial ecosystem built around rapid iteration, low production costs, and huge volumes of content. In Korea, webtoons and web novels move across streaming, games, music, and other formats. In India, a multilingual audience creates especially strong incentives for AI-assisted dubbing. It is a misperception that creators in the Global South care less about copyright, labor costs, or artistic integrity—if anything, Asia’s creator industries are quickly converging with the West on these questions. The difference is that much of the experimentation is happening within entertainment industries that have been more entrepreneurial and are more willing to embrace new technology.

The first “Toy Story moment” for both AI and the new formats it enables—a work whose artistic and cultural appeal makes the technology itself almost beside the point—may not be far away. The companies and countries that achieve it first could change perceptions of AI in creative work and accrue outsize cultural reach. In that sense, the U.S.-China technology competition is also becoming a competition over who builds the tools, platforms, and creative communities that shape global culture.

Hollywood has defined mainstream culture for a century, and storytelling remains its greatest asset. However, treating YouTube, Roblox, and TikTok as farm systems to feed traditional distribution misses that audiences are on the farm.

Netflix recently laid off 1,000 employees; Disney laid off roughly 1,500 this year and has said more layoffs are coming. Skydance’s co-CEOs have told staff to expect layoffs too. Studios have focused on cutting costs, but Hollywood needs to build for new formats, not just make old ones cheaper.

Hollywood needs to fundamentally shift the way it operates, moving from producing finished products meant for passive consumption to developing stories and characters using input from their audiences. Instead of performing autopsies in hindsight, every major studio could put out drafts and iterate with audiences, the way creators do. Kane Parsons started Backrooms with one YouTube short and expanded it into a series when audiences responded positively. Vivienne Medrano released a fan-financed YouTube pilot of Hazbin Hotel; A24 ordered a full series after it drew a huge following.

Refining work using audience input doesn’t mean asking fans to vote on every creative choice. Strong directors have always filtered feedback, taking notes that tighten their narrative and discarding what dilutes their core vision. Borrowing a page from tech, studios could also be much more rigorous with data sourcing, A/B testing, and analysis to understand their audience’s behavior.

This audience-centered approach can be applied to all parts of moviemaking. Films that perform well after an inexpensive tease, such as an animatic (storyboards that are cut together), can secure financing quickly, because financiers aren’t being asked to gamble many millions of dollars on an untested idea. Marketing happens in parallel with production. Your audience becomes not just fans but ambassadors, because they feel they are part of the process. The production becomes part of the story. Markiplier, a YouTuber whose real name is Mark Fischbach, created and financed a film, Iron Lung, which he planned to release in a small number of independent theaters. His fans emailed exhibitors until national chains picked it up.

Vision is not replaced by data; instead, data can help studios find the audiences for visionary work, position it well, and understand which ambitious projects have real demand before committing hundreds of millions of dollars to them. If Orson Welles could have shared his early ideas with audiences in the 1940s, while making Citizen Kane, data wouldn’t have diluted the ambition of his deep-focus shots, broken timeline, and montages. Analyzing the public feedback could have helped him find his audience faster.

Hollywood has a finite window to make these changes. Creators who already operate this way, such as MrBeast, are building their own production studios and will have less incentive to partner. Others will follow.
[Rose Horowitch: The film students who can no longer sit through films]

Studios are experimenting by launching short phone series on YouTube and TikTok, signing deals with top creators, and hiring creator-platform experts into executive positions. This is smart, but these initiatives still prioritize bringing existing franchises to new screens over developing stories alongside audiences. Dropping a digital executive into a traditional, risk-averse studio pipeline doesn’t change the entire studio’s culture. The business model, people, and creative culture that make a great film studio differ from those that are best for building a YouTube series or Roblox game.

Hollywood doesn’t need to become a tech company, and Silicon Valley shouldn’t arrogantly assume that tech is superior to a story’s ability to move culture. Legacy studios still have what many creators need: capital, global marketing, distribution know-how, and deep story expertise. Just as Disney secured its future by partnering with and acquiring Pixar, today’s legacy studios need to collaborate with a new class of studios, ones that know how to build on creator platforms, are rooted in Hollywood storytelling, and treat technologists and artists equally.

The Disney-Pixar relationship worked because Bob Iger gave Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull real power over Disney Animation. Other Hollywood acquisitions of gaming studios or creator talent have struggled when the acquired company lacked similar authority. A real partnership would allow legacy media to originate ideas on new platforms instead of being licensing arms for new players.
AI will have its Toy Story moment. The studios that achieve it will know how to reach audiences on newer platforms, in formats that bring the audience along for the ride.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fermi-year-sky-bri.headline: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
phys.org/news/2026-11-fermi-year-sky-bri.author: Andy Tomaswick

paragraphs.text: edited by Robert Egan

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The "gap" comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower-energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray Observatory, that can capture radiation at the X-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma-ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher-energy gamma rays.

But why are low-energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies—around 1 gigaelectronvolt (GeV)—the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, in the lower 20–200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from.

Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide—more than 40 times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data, there's some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years' worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, cataloged in what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects—325 of them—are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consists of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nucleus. FSRQs represent a type of "blazar"—a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy in this 20–200 MeV spectral window.

Closer to home, the catalog includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars—the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time it's ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, is the 73 sources that don't have a clear counterpart at other energies. Sixty of those appear to be brand-new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the data set awaiting follow-up observations.

One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data from this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008.

However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASA's Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2–5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades' worth of Fermi data might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.
A. Adelfio et al., The Second Catalog of Low-energy Fermi-LAT Sources, The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series (2026). DOI: 10.3847/1538-4365/aeb54d

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/20/denmar.headline: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged Moscow link to attempted killing of rapper
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/20/denmar.author: Donna Ferguson

paragraphs.text: Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.
“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.
Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

“We must take concrete actions that project European strength and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”

The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.
One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.
Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia.
“We believe that the case is important for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted by Russian hybrid attacks. She said the bloc would soon propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.
The Russian embassy ⁠in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with proof.

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/warren-buffett-quadr.headline: Warren Buffett quadruples Thanksgiving gifts: A breakdown of how much wealth he's giving away
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/warren-buffett-quadr.author: Alex Crippen

paragraphs.text: (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as his Thanksgiving gifts soar
Warren Buffett, 96, more than quadrupled his Thanksgiving donations to four family foundations this year to $5.5 billion.
The gifts consist of Berkshire Class B shares that have been converted from his roughly $160 billion of Class A shares.

The increase is in line with his new goal, announced last July, to give away all of his Berkshire Hathaway shares "within about eight years," with no additional annual donations going to the Gates Foundation.

Around $2.2 billion of shares goes to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named for his late first wife, with the three foundations run by his children, Susie Buffett's Sherwood Foundation, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and Peter Buffett's NoVo Foundation each getting $1.1 billion each.
In July of last year, Buffett gave shares worth $4.6 billion to the Gates Foundation with another $1.4 billion going to the family foundations.
This July, the family foundations received $5.9 billion in stock, bringing the year's total to $11.4 billion, an increase of almost 55% from last year, even as the Gates Foundation received nothing.

In comments included in the Berkshire news release this week announcing the new gifts, Buffett reaffirmed his confidence in his children's ability to disburse his fortune over time, saying they "have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity."
He also said his confidence in Berkshire is "as strong as ever."

Recalling that in last year's lengthier Thanksgiving message he had said, "Kindness is costless but also priceless," Buffett wrote, " A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie [Munger] and I ever bought."

"Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.
"Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I'm grateful to every one of them.
"This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."
Berkshire rally stalls but it's not as bad as S&P's AI selloff
Berkshire Hathaway's fourth quarter rally that had produced a string of record highs cooled this week as both classes of its stock posted five straight daily declines.
That sent them down 3.9% for the week.
Last Friday, Berkshire was up 19.1% since October 1. Now that gain has been cut to 14.5%
The S&P's decline of 8.6% this week, however, was even bigger than Berkshire's 5-day drop, as investors sold to lock in profits from AI-related stocks.
The benchmark index, along with the Dow Industrials, are in a correction after falling 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq Composite has erased all of its year-to-date gains.
Berkshire's smaller decline increased its year-to-date outperformance of the S&P to 12.5 percentage points.
One Wall Street firm, however, thinks Berkshire's run-up has run its course.
Argus Research downgraded the B shares to hold from buy Friday, saying the stock is "fully valued" at about 25 times next year's estimate for operating earnings per share.
Berkshire buys Delta, sells BofA in quiet quarter

As foreshadowed by its 10-Q financial report released almost two weeks ago, Berkshire Hathaway's Q3 13F portfolio snapshot filed with the SEC on Monday showed it wasn't doing much buying and selling of equities this summer.
And the two largest additions, Lennar and Bending Spoons, had been previously disclosed, along with additional purchases at the start of the fourth quarter.
The most notable change we didn't expect was a 12% increase in Berkshire's Delta Air Lines position, bringing it just short of a 10% stake, now valued at $5.2 billion.
Exceeding 10% triggers a number of regulatory burdens, including the requirement to promptly disclose new buying or selling, so we may not see additional purchases going forward.
Delta's return to the portfolio after Warren Buffett sold all of Berkshire's airline stocks in 2020 has been something of a surprise given his bumpy ride with the industry over the years.
As expected, Berkshire continued to trim its Bank of America stake. After nine consecutive quarters of sales, it's been cut by 56% but remains the fifth largest portfolio holding at $21.4 billion.
Berkshire also cut another financial, Capital One, by almost 62%, although it was already a relatively small position, now worth $207 million.
Also notable are two positions that didn't change.
After adding $17 billion in Q2 to the Alphabet bet that had only been initiated last summer, Berkshire defied some expectations by keeping the holding unchanged.
Its 106 million shares are valued at $28.1 billion.

And for the fourth consecutive quarter, Berkshire's largest equity holding, Apple, didn't change. With a big boost from the stock's year-to-date gain of 26.1%, the position is now valued at more than $78 billion.

Why Buffett doesn't worry about what he eats (2001)

Warren Buffett loves to eat what many would call junk food and drink a lot of sugary beverages. A quarter-century ago, when he was 70, Buffett explained why he still thought a life insurance company would rate his life expectancy "considerably better than the average."
AUDIENCE MEMBER: Every time I hear what you like to eat, Warren, it makes me wonder what your cholesterol level is — (laughter) — or if you even worry about it...

WARREN BUFFETT: I do know the number, and I don't remember it. My doctor tells me, "It's a little high," but if he says it's a little high, it means it isn't that high, or he would — because he always tries to push me into making a few changes in my life.

But he — I've got a wonderful doctor. And I was lucky last year, because I hadn't been in to see him for about five years. And — (laughter) — due to — those guys cost a lot of money, I mean. (Laughter)

And due to purely an accident, a reaction to some other medicine I was given when I was out of the city, he got a hold of me, and then he shamed me into having a physical. And it was extremely lucky, because I had a polyp in the colon that would have probably caused trouble, you know, within a couple of years.
I would say that if you ask my doctor, he would want me to make a few changes, but he would also say that my life expectancy is probably a lot better than the average person of 70.
You know, I have no stress whatsoever. Zero. You know, I mean, I get to do what I love to do every day. You know, and I'm surrounded by people that are terrific.
So that problem in life just doesn't exist for me. You know, and I don't smoke or drink or, well, we'll end it right there. (Laughter)
And so, you know, if you were an underwriter for a life company, you would rate me considerably better than the average. You'd rate Charlie better than average, too.
And I'm sure that, you know, I could change it slightly, perhaps, on the probabilities, you know, if I change my diet dramatically or something. But it's very unlikely to happen.
