The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrational fear of having no mobile phone service–although, given all the recent cyber-struggles, why would that be irrational?

The Cambridge 2026 World of the Year is … human. As in us. And perhaps humanity could stand some recognition in times when people see Artificial Intelligence seep into our lives the way ancient dinosaurs may have watched the asteroid plunge through the atmosphere, and think, "They're coming for us!" though I suspect a few T-Rexes might have said, "Hey, don't worry! We're too big to fail!"

Cambridge defines "human" as: "(h)aving the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines," but they don't specify much about what those qualities, faults and feelings are.

I'd say that humans have a sense of responsibility. We can say, "I'm sorry, that's my fault," when we screw up or fall short, as opposed to screens that just flash, SYSTEM OVERLOAD or UPDATE IN PROGRESS, 12% COMPLETE.

Humans seek joy, not just continued existence. Laughter, tears, love, spice, poetry, and all that jazz, not just code or text. Humans like jokes and prayers. We're driven by feelings, not just steered by algorithms. Love, fear, anger, desire, joy, and courage, excited by events, nerves and hormones – combine to make us unpredictable, irreverent and unreliable. But our experiences can also instill judgement; an appreciation for what's important; what endures; and what makes the lives we have worth living and savoring.

Making human the 2026 Word of the Year may remind us that we human beings, unlike any robots we have yet devised, have a sense of our own fragility. We know we don't last forever. And so it is important to strive, laugh, and love while we have the chance. The Cambridge dictionary leaves what human truly means to us.

blog.tymscar.com/posts/studiodisplayethe.headline: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
blog.tymscar.com/posts/studiodisplayethe.author: Oscar Molnar

paragraphs.text: Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.
I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦
The setup#
• MacBook Pro M3 Pro
• 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
• UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display
• UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post
What I thought was interesting#

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.
The driver and flow control#

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.
But the upload was always fine#

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.
Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.
OK, well, what now?#
I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!
With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:
Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:

$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])" # old adapter (RTL8156B) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3 # new adapter (RTL8157) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7 # bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.
Final thoughts#

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?
See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/11/fals.headline: The False Comfort of Online Shopping

paragraphs.text: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

Between Black Friday deals, holiday gift guides, and the endless stream of targeted ads, it’s hard to avoid the temptation to buy something right now. And with just a few taps on our phones, we can purchase almost anything without having to leave the couch. Shopping has never been easier—or more solitary.

In a new essay, Lily Meyer revisits Sophie Kinsella’s Confessions of a Shopaholic, 25 years after its publication in the United States, to explore how shopping has become an ever more isolating activity. The novel’s protagonist spends much of her time wandering through stores, accumulating debt. But at least her shopping takes place in the company of other people. Today, much of that experience has moved online, where influencers recommend products with the familiar tone of a friend, even as their relationships with followers remain fundamentally commercial. Meyer argues that modern shopping doesn't just isolate us from others; it can also create the illusion of companionship, blurring the line between genuine connection and consumption. Her essay offers a reminder that shopping can’t substitute for human connection.
The Loneliness of Buying Too Many Things
Confessions of a Shopaholic, 25 years later, suggests that the way we buy things has gotten too isolated.
Read the article.
It’s never been more exhausting to buy stuff.
It’s Too Easy to Buy Stuff You Don’t Want
Online shopping is too fast for good decisions. (From 2023)
Still Curious?

• If you are still looking for something to delight the people in your life, explore the 2026 Atlantic gift guide, where The Atlantic’s editorial team shares its gift recommendations for this holiday season.
• Black Friday nostalgia: If we’re going to worship consumerism and consumption, we should at least do it together, Annie Joy Williams wrote last year.

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. Last week, Jennie H. from Aitkin, Minnesota, shared a picture from January 1, 2024, of an ice bow over her farm, which “doesn’t happen often. It was well below zero that morning.”
We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.
— Rafaela

cbsnews.com/news/marine-corps-hero-brad-.headline: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
cbsnews.com/news/marine-corps-hero-brad-.author: James LaPorta, Julia Kimani Burnham, Eleanor Watson

paragraphs.text: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."
The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."
Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.
Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.
Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.
When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."
Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"
Daniel Gillan, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillan said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillan said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillan said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillan also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.
"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillan said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."
One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."
"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.
The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.
Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.
When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.
Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."
When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.
His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.
The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.
James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article misspelled former JROTC cadet Daniel Gillan's name. The article has been updated.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:28 p.m. on Nov. 19, 2026.

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/emergency-prep-spend.headline: Tech outages are fueling a new doomsday economy
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/emergency-prep-spend.author: Alex Harring

paragraphs.text: Americans are shopping like there's no tomorrow.

A spate of high-profile technology outages that grounded planes, halted email access and slowed bank transactions have left many people worried about artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks and the state of the U.S. energy grid.

Government officials have dismissed rumors and speculation circulating online that there could be a nefarious culprit for the series of malfunctions. Despite those assurances, consumers like Sabrina Cepeda are readying for a larger-scale technology blackout or other emergency event.

In recent days, the Houston resident has purchased propane and lighter fluid for cooking and heating equipment that can be used without electricity. The mother of three also replenished her backup stockpiles of non-perishable foods, hygiene products and allergy medicine in the event that her family is homebound for several days.
"I have a way to keep my family fed, clean, hydrated, warm and safe," said Cepeda, 39. "You want to have these things and not need them, rather than need them and not have them."
The doomsday economy is catching a bid. Wall Street and retailers are taking note.
Emergency prep buying

At least half a dozen major technology outages took place in the U.S. between Nov. 12 and Nov. 17. In that time frame, spending at brands specializing in emergency products spiked about 400% compared with the same period a year prior, according to card data analyzed exclusively for CNBC by Consumer Edge.

At Ready America, which sells products like emergency survival kits, prepackaged water and high-calorie food bars, sales through e-commerce platforms have seen a roughly five-fold increase in recent days. In addition, corporate customers who keep the Vista, California-based company's supplies in their offices in case of emergency have called in to order more.

The company has rarely seen this much demand since the Covid pandemic sent Americans into lockdown more than six years ago, said Ready America President Trevyn Reese. As a result, Ready America asked its suppliers to scale up production. The family-owned business has faced a shortage of water purification tablets, and redirected shoppers to alternative offerings like prepackaged water pouches.
"With everything going on in the news right now, we've seen a large spike of people wanting to get prepared," said Reese.
While the string of outages brought power-related concerns to a boiling point, data shows that worries had been bubbling under the surface for weeks.

Shoppers began significantly ramping up buying from emergency preparedness brands late last month, according to Consumer Edge. Around that time, Fox News reported that the Pentagon was preparing U.S. military bases to operate for at least 90 days without external support. Exacerbating those fears was the ongoing war with Iran that President Donald Trump signaled could ramp back up.

Firearm trade group NSSF said that gun sales rose about 8% in October from the same month a year prior. Retailers and gun manufacturers have anecdotally reported that demand has remained elevated into November, which NSSF said can be attributed to a combination of uncertainty tied to the midterm election and the recent outages.

"If people are investing in firearms and ammunition, they're telling you very directly, with their wallet, what their priority is," said Mark Oliva, NSSF's managing director of public affairs. "You're literally investing in a product that's going to be able to protect your life and protect the lives of your family."
'Apocalyptic concerns'
Now, the doomsday talk has begun making its way to Wall Street.

Mizuho told clients on Monday that consumer worries about the outages — coupled with what the bank called "apocalyptic concerns" swirling on social media — drove shoppers to stock up on emergency supplies at Costco. As a result, Mizuho said it expects a key measure of non-fuel sales growth for Costco in November to rise above 10% for the first time since 2022.

And RBC said so-called doomsday prepping has had a "real impact" on buying behavior around the globe over recent weeks. Still, the Canadian bank reported that the trend has so far boosted sales for only a small basket of items, such as shelf-stable proteins, water purification products and dry-pantry foods.

Clients of Richard McWhorter, a private wealth advisor at SRM, have been rushing to Costco to buy goods in bulk and splurging for power generators. McWhorter said he's also fielded questions about how to prepare for a situation in which the financial system goes down.

"I've never seen anything like this in my life," McWhorter said. "There's the financial side of what I do, and then there's the psychological side. And the past two weeks have been much more psychological."

Metal dealer American Hartford Gold reported an uptick in customer inquiries this week. Company president Max Baecker said he heard from some customers that their interest in products like gold — long considered a safe-haven asset during times of turmoil — was driven by newfound concern about being overly reliant on digital financial networks following a glitch at JPMorgan Chase that affected customer transactions for several hours.

Vice President JD Vance abruptly canceled his appearance at a New York Times summit on Wednesday to attend meetings about the technology outages. A day prior, Jay Clayton, the U.S. director of national intelligence, told CNBC that the recent outages were not a cyberattack or a coordinated effort by a foreign nation.

Still, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., told CNBC on Wednesday that people were "freaked out" by the outages. Warner, who acts as the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that the U.S. was "lucky" to have not yet seen a major AI-generated cyberattack or crisis due to AI agents going rogue.

Investors may begin pushing companies to accelerate their cybersecurity spending out of an abundance of caution around rogue AI agents following the outages, according to Macro Hive CEO Bilal Hafeez. Such a situation would be reminiscent of the antivirus software push seen during the dot-com boom, he said.

The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) has climbed about 2.5% over the past two weeks, bucking the downtrend seen among AI stocks and the broader technology trade. The Nasdaq Composite on Friday fell into negative territory for 2026, putting the tech-heavy index on track for its first losing year since 2022.
The 'old-fashioned way'

To be sure, not everyone on social media has bought into the idea that they should be prepping for a doomsday scenario. In satirical videos posted on TikTok, users joked that they were gearing up by placing orders in the Starbucks drive-thru or purchasing significant quantities of alcohol.

Still, the topic appears to be on the minds of a growing number of Americans. U.S. Google searches for the term "prepping" have more than doubled when comparing the past month with the same period a year prior. On YouTube, queries for videos about "survivalism," a term describing the practice of preparing for emergencies, have soared by more than 5,000% over the same time frame.

Cepeda, the Houston mom, sees emergency prep efforts as a way to be safe rather than sorry. She's previously tapped into backup food stashes during extreme weather events like Hurricane Harvey in 2017 and Winter Storm Uri in 2021.

But this year is the first time that she's felt she needed to be prepared for a potential emergency caused by technology outages, she said. Cepeda and her husband have ensured they have enough cash on hand and fuel in their cars if there's a broader hit to the U.S. power grid, she said.
"We rely so much on technology," Cepeda said. "You need to be able to do these things the more traditional, old-fashioned way."

cbsnews.com/news/house-ethics-committee-.headline: House Ethics Committee aims to speed up sexual misconduct investigations
cbsnews.com/news/house-ethics-committee-.author: Caitlin Yilek

paragraphs.text: Caitlin Yilek is a politics reporter at CBSNews.com, based in Washington, D.C. She previously worked for the Washington Examiner and The Hill, and was a member of the 2022 Paul Miller Washington Reporting Fellowship with the National Press Foundation.
November 20, 2026 / 4:03 PM EST / CBS News
Washington — The House Ethics Committee on Thursday approved several changes aimed at improving how the secretive bipartisan panel handles sexual misconduct investigations.

The pace of the committee's investigations has come under scrutiny after several members were accused of sexual misconduct this year. Two lawmakers — Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell of California and Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas — resigned before the committee could complete its work. Other members under investigation by the committee for sexual misconduct either ended their campaign or lost their reelection bids.
The panel met briefly Thursday afternoon in a rare public meeting to discuss the proposed changes, which were detailed in a news release Friday.

The committee delegated subpoena authority to the chairman and ranking member, instead of requiring that the full committee vote on subpoenas. The change should "significantly expedite" its investigations, the committee said.

The committee also codified its longstanding policy of publicly disclosing when a member has been found to have engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct, while protecting the identity of victims.

It also consolidated duplicative procedural steps and simplified the process, which it said should "accelerate the conclusion of investigations by several months or more while still providing for important due process protections."
Another change includes "expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered as appropriate sanctions."

"The House of Representatives must have a zero-tolerance policy for sexual harassment and misconduct and the Committee on Ethics is committed to ensuring that its practices and processes sufficiently hold perpetrators accountable and deliver justice for survivors," Rep. Mark DeSaulnier of California, the top Democrat on the committee, said in a statement Friday.

A bipartisan initiative aimed at addressing how sexual misconduct claims are handled within the House was formed earlier this year to propose reforms. The group, led by Reps. Kat Cammack, a Florida Republican, and Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, has yet to release its recommendations.

npr.org/2026/11/21/g-s1-154922/anthropic.headline: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
npr.org/2026/11/21/g-s1-154922/anthropic.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.

"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.

"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/21/i.headline: International talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/21/i.author: Frances Mao, Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control on the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am on Saturday morning, after all night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the Review Conference on Conventional Weapons at the UN in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate simply asks countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using uniquely obstructive stalling tactics from the opening day, other military powers who have all invested heavily in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law is sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges.
European and Nato states, including Ukraine, as well as China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons was discussed in the meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

The CCW is a particular UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said the world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week.
“Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

Diplomats inside the negotiations said that Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

Speaking at a different conference, organised by Atlantic magazine, the former US national security adviser John Bolton said: “We are moving closer and closer to almost totally unmanned warfare in the battle field. I am not sure we need manned aircraft anymore if we have the right drone technology.
“The boundaries western civilisation tried to draw between war and civilian life are disintegrating.”

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that the states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years already, and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.

Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, told the Guardian that autonomous weapons needed binding law.
She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months, and dismissed the US’s proposal for five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

“These are not weapons of the future that are being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems,” Brazil’s delegate told the floor on Wednesday.

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/prediction-market-re.headline: State and federal battle over prediction markets regulation heats up after midterms
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/prediction-market-re.author: Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia

paragraphs.text: The turf war between states and the federal government is intensifying after Democrats secured control of Congress and key governorships on midterm elections night.

While it was widely expected Democrats would step up oversight of the emerging, multibillion-dollar industry if they won control of Congress, the actions after the elections have come from primarily Republican-led states.

At the same time, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets — has ramped up its oversight of "mention" markets, where traders speculate on what individuals will say during a speech or broadcast. It's a type of event contract the agency has said is susceptible to manipulation.

CNBC first reported on Tuesday that the CFTC placed a hold on the certification of markets related to President Donald Trump's words in mid-November. Kalshi said it was complying with the order, but CEO Tarek Mansour said at an Axios event on Tuesday that the company disagreed with the regulatory decision.

On Thursday, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill that would ban CFTC-registered entities from listing contracts involving terrorism, assassination, war or military operations. The measure also bars contracts that are "reasonably expected" to resolve based on an individual's death.
Criminal charges, restraining order, lawsuits

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, on Oct. 28, asserting the company violated a state law that prohibits gambling.
Kalshi's founders are expected to appear in person at Utah's Third District Court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.
"This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona," said Kalshi's spokesperson Dani Lever.
In a separate, civil complaint on Oct. 20, Utah also named institutional market maker Susquehanna International Group as a defendant, along with Kalshi.
Though Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes filed a criminal complaint against Kalshi in March, a federal judge blocked the case from proceeding in April.

Louisiana's Republican attorney general also filed a complaint to ban multiple exchanges from operating in the state on Nov. 12. A state judge ordered a temporary restraining order against the prediction market companies that same day.

"Who would have thought that these red states, that were reluctant to jump into the litigation arena, ended up having the most boldest and most innovative solutions," said gambling attorney Daniel Wallach, noting that Louisiana and Utah's latest lawsuits were led by Republican attorneys general.
In response, the CFTC sued Louisiana on Nov. 13. Separately, the federal agency filed suit against Arkansas after that state pursued civil enforcement against Kalshi.
The CFTC has sued 12 states as it tries to defend what it views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets.

Meanwhile, the CFTC may soon add commissioners. President Donald Trump sent bipartisan nominations to the U.S. Senate on Nov. 12 to fill two of the four open seats on the commission. Chairman Michael Selig has been the only member since his nomination was approved by the Senate in December 2025.

Nathan Anonick, a Republican, and Matthew Rowland, a Democrat, appeared before the Senate Agriculture Committee on Tuesday. Multiple senators questioned them on the issue of prediction markets. Both demurred when asked whether they viewed sports-related event contracts as gambling.
Kalshi loses in Maryland

The CFTC's position faced another setback in a complicated decision by the Fourth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals this week. The court ruled 2-1 that Maryland can enforce its state gambling law against Kalshi, though the judges disagreed on the reasoning.

"Judges can't agree with each other on why we're wrong," Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said in a statement about the decision. "This splintered decision, including three separate contradictory opinions, demonstrates there is no unified coherent legal argument against prediction markets."

Overall, prediction markets have now seen three losses and one win at the circuit court level. It's widely expected the question of whether states or the federal government can regulate sports-related event contracts will be decided by the Supreme Court.
Donald Trump Jr. parts ways with Kalshi
Kalshi on Nov. 12 ended its advisory relationship with Donald Trump Jr. The prediction platform pointed to his venture capital firm 1789 Capital having a stake in rival platform Polymarket.

Though 1789 Capital announced its holding in Polymarket in August, Kalshi and the president's son ended their relationship after Democrats secured a majority in the House and Senate. Democratic lawmakers are expected to probe companies with relationships to the Trump family.

Nine Democratic senators, led by Adam Schiff, D-California, on Monday sent a letter to the CFTC asking it to reverse a directive to platforms not to geofence their offerings when they receive unfavorable court rulings stopping exchanges from operating in certain states.
Geofencing involves the use of location technology to block users in certain jurisdictions from participating in events contracts.
"Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed," the senators wrote.
Meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, has called for Congress to ban sports-related prediction markets entirely.
"Kalshi, a $40B company, lets 18 year olds bet on sports. They call it a 'prediction market.' It's gambling," he wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. "Investigate and ban sports prediction markets."
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: Body pulled from L.A. River following powerful storm
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: Iris Kwok

paragraphs.text: A body was found Friday on an island in the Los Angeles River between the Los Feliz Boulevard Bridge and the Colorado Street Bridge — a day after a powerful storm soaked the area, according to authorities.
The Los Angeles Fire Department responded to a report about the body shortly before 11 a.m. Friday.

Lyndsey Lantz, a department spokeswoman, told The Times that the body matched the description of a person who reportedly fell into the river on Thursday, per initial reports. Lantz said she had no further details about the person’s identity as of Friday evening.
In a statement, the fire department said it received a report at 8:04 a.m. Thursday of a person in the river near Roscoe Boulevard and Brimfield Avenue.

Crews searched for 50 minutes and positioned units at downstream rescue points, the statement said. They searched by ground, air and water, but could not locate anyone, according to a department alert.
The sites where the person was reportedly spotted in the river and where the body was recovered are more than 10 miles apart.
The L.A. County medical examiner’s office will determine the cause of death, and the Los Angeles Police Department will lead the investigation, according to the fire department.

“We urge everyone to stay out of the river and away from its banks, especially during and after rain,” the fire department said. “Swift water is far more powerful than it looks. If you see someone in the water, call 911 immediately and do not go in after them.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/anthropic-ipo-tech-s.headline: Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/anthropic-ipo-tech-s.author: Jordan Novet

paragraphs.text: Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his home in Silicon Valley. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar.

"This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company.

Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.

It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge, which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020.

Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence.

That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX.
With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits.

After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025.
When going public was 'not worth it'

Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar.

"There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said.

Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus.

For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said.
Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to."
"At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that."

Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation."

That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic were to miss its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money."

Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to also use alternatives from Amazon and Google. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier.

"It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics showed it was "going to be a very high-quality business."
IPO pipeline?
Anthropic isn't the only big win for VCs this year.

Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz.

SpaceX and Anthropic alone will turn 2026 into a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other in terms of IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering.

IVP's Dash said that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027.
The macro picture, however, is ominous.

Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the company already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board.

In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would lead Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range.
Narasin said he wasn't even sure the company would get that far.
"I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin said.
That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering.

"This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin said. "There was a company that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: Dogs recovered in Pasadena need fur-ever homes. How you can help
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: Iris Kwok

paragraphs.text: The passel of pooches was discovered after Pasadena Humane, responding to repeated complaints about barking, entered a home on a large lot on the northwestern side of the city, organization spokesperson Kevin McManus told The Times.
The owner initially was unwilling to cooperate with the center’s animal control investigators, according to McManus, and they later obtained a warrant to enter.
They were surprised by the sheer amount of dogs inside. “We didn’t think it was this many,” McManus said.
The dogs, which occasionally were kept in a fenced-off yard, appeared to be in good health, McManus said, and there was “no evidence of abuse or neglect.”
A physical exam found that the four oldest dogs, believed to be around 10 to 12 years old, had some age-related health issues.
The number of dogs in the home had risen exponentially because the dogs were not spayed or neutered, McManus said. It did not appear to be a breeding operation.
The dogs were “clearly loved,” McManus said. “But there were way too many of them.”
On Thursday night, the owner surrendered the dogs to Pasadena Humane, meaning they could be rehomed earlier than expected.

Nearly 30 dogs, which shelter staff named after various fruits, are up for adoption. There are Chihuahuas and Chihuahua mixes as well as Belgian Malinois puppies. One dog named Pear already had found a temporary home as of Friday afternoon, according to McManus.

The dogs’ owner has indicated they plan to reclaim four of the pooches — the maximum allowed by Pasadena city ordinance — and a family member intends to adopt another four. Pasadena Humane, which is holding those eight dogs, said there will be a vetting process before they are returned.
Each dog will be spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped before it is released to a new home, according to the organization.

“Many of the dogs are undersocialized, unfamiliar with walking on a leash, and may have limited experience living indoors,” the organization said in a statement. “They are looking for patient, understanding adopters who can give them time and space to adjust. After so much change, these dogs need stability, patience and a place to call home.”
Pasadena Humane is open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. at 361 S. Raymond Ave.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/opinion/trump-xi-.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin’s New World Order

paragraphs.text: President Trump left a summit in China with no deal for the American people but lots of love for Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. In this episode, the Opinion writer Michelle Cottle talks to the columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French about Trump’s affection for autocracy, the hubris of A.I. power players — like Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang — and how Democrats plan to go after corruption in the new term.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.
The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Michelle Cottle: So today, which is Thursday for us, Donald Trump held the U.S.’s first ever trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir V. Putin. Ahead of the meeting, the president had said he wanted to discuss nuclear nonproliferation, along with the wars in Ukraine and Iran. At the end of the day, there were no major diplomatic breakthroughs, although Trump did greet Putin with a big old smile and called him his friend. So what did everyone get out of this? Was this meeting a win, guys? And if so, for whom? David, you want to go first?

David French: Well, sometimes me and the boys just kind of get together, Michelle. That’s what it felt like, quite honestly, that he sort of sees that Xi and Putin are his only true peers on the world stage; that the rest of the entire Western alliance, that those are his subordinates; that all of those people are just the people who do what he wants.

And that when he’s meeting with Xi and when he’s meeting with Putin, he’s meeting with the people who are at his level — the other key nuclear and military powers around the world. This fits his spheres of influence worldview very well — that we divide the world up into these various zones, and you get to control your zone, I get to control my zone.

And this is part of the root of the way he approaches the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Ukraine is to Putin what Canada is to the United States — the 51st state. And so, nothing is surprising about a summit like this. And it’s also not surprising at all that there would be no productive diplomatic breakthrough in any way, shape or form. But it is an interesting illustration of the way he sees the world, and it’s also an illustration of part of the reason he has seemed, and his administration seems, to tilt more toward Russia, incredibly, in the conflict. So, I thought this was a perfect symbol of his second term.
Cottle: Jamelle?

Jamelle Bouie: Yeah, I mean, I think that’s exactly right. The president, he has, firstly, a might-makes-right, the-strongest-always-has-the-right-to-dominate-the-weakest worldview. And this conference is — to the extent that you can call it a conference — it’s two autocrats and a would-be autocrat coming together and, like, commiserating over their various desired territorial acquisitions. I don’t know. It’s worth saying that this view — this might-makes-right, we-have-our-own-sphere-of-influence view — has not produced a world of greater stability.
French: No.

Bouie: It has done the exact opposite. Leniency, for example, toward Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not actually going to make it less likely that a war is going to break out elsewhere. It’s going to make it more likely, right? If you establish, as the rule for international affairs, that the biggest and the strongest country gets to take what they want, then that’s what’s going to happen, and it’s not going to be a world of reduced conflict.

Cottle: So I have a question about the conference itself, and I like your “if we could even call it a conference” remark, because some people dubbed this summit Yalta 2.0, which is a reference to the 1945 meeting, where the soon-to-be World War II victors were meeting to essentially discuss the fate of Europe and divvy up the world. But Yalta lasted days and was coming at the end of this monumental war.

This was, like, an hour: You stop by, you smile for the photos, and then you move on. I can’t imagine that anything productive could have even begun to be discussed. But if you’re Putin and what you’re looking for is legitimacy on the world stage and have a signal sent that you’re back in the fold of sorts or whatever, it seems like, from a P.R. perspective, this actually could be very useful to Putin but not really so much to Trump. I mean, has Trump once again been used on some level?

French: I think there’s very little question that he’s been used here, and there’s very little question this is helpful to Putin; just as there’s very little question that when Trump tried to strike the diesel deal before the midterms, that was also very helpful to Putin. There’s been thing after item after item after thing after item that has demonstrated, in essence, that Trump is essentially moving America toward switching sides.

And if we think we’re being unfair about might makes right, let’s remember that just in the last week or so, we’ve seen Marco Rubio say — and Pete Hegseth really amplify it — this old Roman quote: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords,” which, I can think of few better formulations of “might makes right.”

I mean, that’s saying “might makes right” without using exactly those words. But it is perfectly illustrative of the worldview that Hegseth has of his use of the military; that Trump has of the United States on the world stage. Cottle: Jamelle, do you want to throw something in?

Bouie: I have basically two thoughts that relate to the various history references we’ve made so far. The first is just the comparison to the Yalta Conference. And part of what makes Yalta, in the American view, often considered a great tragedy was that the goal was not divvying up Europe for spheres of influence but how do we have European self-determination, right?

Like, how do we restore something like self-government in Europe? And what happens is, Stalin takes this as an opportunity to actually expand the Soviet sphere of influence and, in particular, gobble up Poland again. So, because Churchill and Roosevelt are there, kind of like, “How do we protect free Europe?” And Stalin has these ulterior motives. I’m not sure it’s, like, the best analogy. What’s a better analogy is the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, when European colonial powers divvied up Africa as part of their spheres of influence, right? So kind of deciding we’re going to colonize Africa, and here’s who gets what. That, to me, is a much better analogy for thinking about how Trump views the world and how he views his peers — who he views as his peers.
Cottle: You just need a pithier title for that. Yalta 2.0 versus ——

Bouie: Sure. I think I’ve said this before on this podcast of ours. I don’t think that Chuck Schumer is a wartime consigliere, you know? I just don’t think he’s right for the moment. And with that, we are going to land this plane. Guys, it’s been magic!
French: Michelle, your transition from Tennessee girl to The New York Times elite is now complete.
Cottle: Don’t you mock me. I’m not taking any guff from you. You just go play your video games. I’m not taking any abuse from either of you. Thank you, though. Thank you for coming to play.
Bouie: Always happy to do it.
French: Thanks Michelle.
