I had never called my sister at midnight.
But the minute John Mulaney, the impish host of last week’s “Saturday Night Live,” uttered the word “sister,” I picked up the phone.
“Are you watching this?” I asked Peggy.
“Yeah, it’s not funny,” she replied. “It’s hitting too close to home.”

We hung up to experience a flashback to a decade engulfed by caring for our mother. In the sketch, Mulaney plays a man mulling how to care for his aging dad without a nursing home or a costly private health aide.

“That’s when I heard about ‘Sister,’” Mulaney says brightly. “‘Sister’ is a live-in 24-7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister. Now I don’t have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”
“I love my mom more than anything,” another man says. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t, either, but she will, whereas I won’t.”
A third man says “Sister” won’t affect your inheritance: “You’ll still get 50 percent of the house she’s currently deep cleaning.”

It’s also a good bonding opportunity for father and son, Mulaney’s character says. He agrees with Dad that Sister’s a “bitch” after she tries to curb Dad’s salt intake to help with his high blood pressure.

When I tried to curb my mom’s salt intake, she gave me a withering look and said, “I’m 97,” before shaking the saltshaker so hard the top flew off. She kept eating because she liked a little food with her salt.

The “S.N.L.” sketch sparked a million palavers about the fact that America’s strategy for elder care often defaults to the kindness of daughters. As we’ve been startled to learn lately, a lot of our infrastructure systems are shaky and stitched together haphazardly. (Fixing one router in Arkansas should not shut down America’s whole airspace.)

The viral hit surprised me because I thought things would have changed by now, 20 years after my mom died, with a couple of generations of men raised by working women less prone to live by outdated gender roles. But, as I always say, men are evolving a lot slower than women.

“We give little girls baby dolls to play with, to train them to be caregivers, where we don’t do that for little boys,” said Jessica Calarco, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin and the author of “Holding It Together: How Women Became America’s Safety Net.”

“Women are making less than men in most fields and so it becomes sort of easy to assume that it’s not only natural but also logical for women to be the ones doing this kind of work when care becomes this hot potato.”
I was a bad nurse. I focused on making Mom look stylish and pretty, with eyebrow tints and pedicures and silk and velvet jackets, working on the premise that if you look good, you feel good.

“You treat her like she’s a doll,” my brother Kevin said with an accusatory look. But my mom was beautiful, with porcelain skin and snowy hair, and she loved looking good. She was blind the last seven years of her life, so she asked me to put on her red lipstick.

“You’re not doing it right,” she complained. “You’re not doing it like Max Factor.” It turned out that she had actually once had her lipstick applied by Max Factor, himself, when he was just starting out and exhibiting his new makeup line in a Washington drugstore.
Just as my three brothers had fewer household tasks growing up, they knew my sister and I would take care of Mom.

My brothers were great, but they focused on the less onerous, less “maternal” jobs. Michael brought dinner every week. Martin often came over to take Mom out to lunch, gossip about the family or read fun newspaper clippings to her. Kevin watched “Seinfeld” with her.

Peggy and I didn’t resent their doing less. Mom adored her sons, and they adored her back. But it’s often harder for men to see their parents get frail — and people are living a lot longer now. My mother’s growing helplessness — blind and in a wheelchair — made my brothers feel helpless.

“It’s also expediency with a lot of guys,” Kevin told me. “They have a life and they can’t interrupt a good part of it to alter their schedules. But I was always inclined to tell myself, ‘This happened on your watch and it’s your problem.’”

While more of my mom’s friends who had only sons ended up in nursing homes, some men are amazing caretakers. Kevin and his sons, especially his youngest, Brian, have spent years tenderly caring for Kevin’s lovely wife, Ellen, who has M.S.

When my mom’s health problems grew more severe — she once broke her neck trying to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night — we got round-the-clock help. We lied and told her it was paid for by Medicare so she wouldn’t feel sad about draining her bank account. She was living, after all, on a police widow’s pension.

Peggy and I continued to spend an enormous amount of time with her. We both had demanding jobs that required a lot of travel, and I remember feeling guilty that I couldn’t travel as much as I needed to.

It was stressful and I sometimes gave up on my own grooming; I spent way too much time in black yoga pants. But the way you exit relationships shows character. And my mom was not a whiner. She managed her pain — and sadness about losing her sight — with two bourbon and sodas in the late afternoon. (When I gave her a bottle of Maker’s Mark, she hid it in her underwear drawer; it was too fancy to drink.)
If you read her a book or a newspaper or even just ads about sales on food and fashion, she was content.
One day, I told her there was a sale at Saks on control top panties.
She looked intrigued. “Who do they control?” she asked.

She was so warm and funny, it felt like a gift to spend her last years with her. I was glad I was on hand when she fell or fainted. The Bethesda-Chevy Chase Rescue Squad was there in a flash; she never missed its annual oyster roast. I still shudder, though, when I hear a siren from an ambulance speeding through her old neighborhood.
I was happy to be there when her fading memory scared her.

One night, watching “Gone With the Wind,” she began crying because she couldn’t remember the plot of her favorite movie. I hugged her, knowing that I wouldn’t remember the plot, either, on the off chance I made it to 97.
I was happy to be on hand to straighten her out if she got confused and thought she wasn’t in her own home, or thought, because my dad wasn’t there, that he had left her for another woman.
“No,” I reassured her, “he’s waiting for you in heaven.”
There was one particular moment that made it all worth it. Late at night, when she couldn’t sleep, I held her hand.
“I love you,” she softly said. “Very much.”
At the end, as she had her last dose of morphine, with a bourbon chaser, her three sons huddled around her bed, crying. Then they left and my sister and I curled up with her.

Even though it was July, I played Christmas music because she loved it. When “Sisters,” the Rosemary Clooney-Vera-Ellen classic from “White Christmas,” came on, Peggy and I sang along. “Caring, sharing. … All kinds of weather, we stick together.” We knew all the words by heart.

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- It's been a tough month for the stock market, rocked by back-to-back punches from the stunning ouster of Jensen Huang from Nvidia Corp. and the Democrats' decisive victory in the midterm elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Anthropic PBC's record-breaking initial public offering this week was supposed to provide some relief and change the mood. It didn't. Instead, it raised more questions about the struggling artificial intelligence trade, and tech stocks continued to sell off, led by chipmakers, with Nasdaq 100 Index tumbling 10% for the week, its worst performance since the Covid pandemic hit in March 2020.

Now, with few positive catalysts and a series of obvious risks on the horizon, starting with the Federal Reserve's expected interest-rate hike next month, Wall Street is wondering what will inspire stocks to start climbing again. Instead of finding inspiration to buy, investors just keep discovering reasons to sell, as seemingly every other news headline — from air travel shutdowns to financial hacks — fuels suspicion that technology isn't adapting to the risks posed by AI.

"The market is in limbo-land, especially when it comes to tech and AI," said Paul Nolte, market strategist and senior wealth manager at Murphy & Sylvest Wealth Management. "You need to gird your loins and expect a period of volatility and downside risk."

The Anthropic deal could mark the end of the AI trade, Anna Wong, an economist with Bloomberg Economics, wrote in a report on Thursday. The company's financials show weakening pricing power for frontier intelligence, she wrote, meaning that even with all the demand for AI services, leading providers are having trouble getting customers to pay enough for it to justify their spending.

Of course, in a vacuum, Anthropic's IPO did fine. It was priced over its targeted range, and when combined with a separate private placement of shares, the company raised the most cash for a new issue ever, topping SpaceX's deal in June. The stock even raced higher out of the gate. But it quickly plateaued and then started retreating. By the end of Friday it was less than $6 from where it went public.

The bigger issue is it ushered in more selling rather than giving investors a reason to buy. By the end of Friday, the Nasdaq 100 was teetering on the brink of bear market, defined as a 20% decline from a recent high, while the S&P 500 Index had entered a correction after falling 12% from its October record.
All that selling laid bare the magnitude of the questions swirling around AI more than four years into a bull market powered by huge bets on the technology.

"There was a hope that the Anthropic IPO would provide a sustained boost, but the trading there is indicative of the broader concerns surrounding AI," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors. "Anthropic came to market at a time of more general skepticism surrounding the space, and there are a lot of questions about their ability in the near term to deliver on increasingly lofty expectations."

Democratic victories in the midterms raised the risk that data center construction will slow since many of the party's candidates ran on blocking their development. Meanwhile, the risk of higher interest rates raises the cost of capital as big data center developers increasingly turn to credit markets for funding.

"A lot of the growth in AI is dependent on how and whether companies can fund their capital needs," said Malcolm Polley, director of strategic market analysis at Stratos Investment Management, which has $3.6 billion in assets. "Will they need to fund that through capital or debt markets? Until we know the cost of capital, we can't adequately value the asset, and if the cost of capital is going higher, then valuations need to come down."

But it's the chaos at Nvidia that really has spooked investors. The company ousted Huang on Nov. 12 after he admitted having an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, and the stock has been in a tailspin ever since. Even a strong earnings report featuring a raised revenue forecast for next fiscal year and a $150 billion stock buyback authorization couldn't stop the selling, as the question remained who will be Huang's permanent replacement.
Nvidia shares plunged 23% this week, their worst performance since 2008. The stock is down 48% from an Oct. 6 all-time high.

The turmoil appeared to create openings for Nvidia's competitors, including chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. But that bet took a hit on Thursday when a short seller raised questions about AMD's business in China, which could be hurt by more US chip export restrictions. The shares plunged 20% in the final two sessions of the week.

More broadly, it's the sustainability of the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent to expand computing power that's driving the selloff. That spending has juiced earnings for companies across the AI ecosystem, from chipmakers and networking gear manufacturers to electricity providers and industrial companies. But investors are increasingly skeptical that it can last.

This rapid swing from greed to fear is best seen in the trading of semiconductor stocks this year. Chips are historically a cyclical business, rising with demand and then falling as it dissipates. But the belief was that this history would be rewritten as years of AI demand would break the cycle. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index more than doubled in the first half of the year on that bet. But it has lost 41% in the second half as investors rethink those positions.

Memory and storage stocks, which also are major beneficiaries of the AI spending, have been among the hardest hit over the last few months. Sandisk Corp. was leading the S&P 500 in the first six months of year, soaring 857%. It's the worst stock in the index in the second half, dropping 72%. Western Digital Corp. has tumbled more than 65% from a June record, while Micron Technology Inc. is down more than 50% from its all-time high.

Of course, some optimism remains on Wall Street. In particular the hope is the selloff is nearing exhaustion as investors have used the opportunity to reduce risk, according to Brian Smedley, chief investment officer and head of Cynosure Strategies, the hedge fund division of the Cynosure Group.

"I think investors will gain confidence that AI demand remains exceptionally strong, and that the key players — Anthropic among them — will continue to have very healthy growth prospects," he said. "The market has overshot to the downside, just as it overshot to the upside earlier this year."
One thing investors agree on is that Anthropic's debut will provide a new level of visibility into the business of selling AI services.

"It has been hard to get a real feel for AI demand, and Anthropic is the answer to that question," said Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower. "We will know more about the upside of AI, in terms of demand and the return, at the same time that we will be getting a reinforced view of how crazy wildly expensive it is."
In the meantime, strategists are advising clients to stay nimble.

"It's hard to say what it might take to catalyze gains after this week," said Mark Luschini, chief market strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott. "I want to see whether this selloff metastasizes into something more severe. We're oversold, but not deeply so. We could plumb lower still. I want to see stabilization before I make a strong commitment."

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC's initial public offering drew roughly between $115 billion and $120 billion of demand for shares from retail investors, according to a person familiar with the matter, more than the amount sought by them in SpaceX's debut.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The frontier AI lab's first-time share sale had well over $500 billion of demand from institutional investors, more than double the orders for shares in SpaceX, the person said, asking not to be identified as the information isn't public.

Anthropic's IPO is the biggest of all time, with the $93.5 billion raised by the company and its seven co-founders, including the over-allotment, comfortably topping SpaceX's $86.2 billion offering. Anthropic also raised $26 billion in a private placement, for a total haul of $119.5 billion.

Even as the IPO delivered a record amount to the company, adding to the nearly $132 billion of cash and equivalents it had as of Sept. 30, Anthropic's shares erased much of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors' faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history.

Shares of Anthropic fell as much as nearly 15% on Friday, after the stock gained 17% in its first trading day as a public company. The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about $1.5 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world.

Most of the stock in Anthropic's IPO went to long-only investors and sovereign wealth funds, with venture capital investors receiving a low-to-mid single digit percentage point share in aggregate, the person said. Banks working on the first-time share sale, led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley, allocated fewer shares to investors relative to the size of the offering than those who placed orders for SpaceX's IPO, they said.
Retail investors in Anthropic's IPO received about 15% of the shares available, Bloomberg News reported.

Some of the details of the demand were previously reported by the International Financial Review and the Financial Times. Representatives for Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

Anthropic's IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, with allocations heavily skewed toward US-based investors, Bloomberg News reported. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, people familiar with the matter have said.

The company sold $1.1 billion worth of stock to retail investors in the UK and continental Europe, and raised about $3 billion in Japan and around $110 million in Australia, Bloomberg News has reported.

The 22 banks on Anthropic's IPO earned a record $550 million in fees for their work, more than on SpaceX's IPO. They didn't receive fees for the so-called over-allotment shares, or for the private placement shares, according to its filings.
Demand for SpaceX shares ran to more than $350 billion, with over $100 billion coming from retail, people familiar with the matter said at the time.

Anthropic's listing joins companies linked to AI that have lifted US IPO volume to an all-time high. First time stock sales raised $258 billion this year, beating 2021's $195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-check firms, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualized from a shorter period — to $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.

Claude Code, the company's coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering $100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

Anthropic and its rival OpenAI face mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, and as the debate rages over whether the technology poses what Anthropic called "existential risks to humanity" in its IPO filing. OpenAI has filed confidentially for a listing but isn't planning to go public before 2027.

livescience.com/animals/aquatic-animals/.headline: Meet the science adviser behind Netflix's hit series 'Below'
livescience.com/animals/aquatic-animals/.author: Kenna Hughes-Castleberry

paragraphs.text: In Netflix's new series "Below," an ancient, squid-like creature known as "Mudder" threatens a small coastal community in Newfoundland, Canada, arriving around the same time as a mysterious iceberg that starts causing dangerous hallucinations in the town's residents.

The series blends marine science, horror and environmental themes, harking back to Newfoundland's long-standing connections with giant squid (Architeuthis dux), with the first sightings going back to the 1870s.

Annie Mercier, a marine biologist in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, was brought on as a science adviser in 2025 just before Netflix began shooting "Below." Mercier's research focuses on deep sea organisms, studying their behavior, interactions and how they respond to environmental stressors like climate change.

Mercier's lab at the Ocean Sciences Center was used as a filming location, and she met with actor Mackenzie Davis, who plays the research scientist Dr. Fonda Howander to guide the character. Live Science spoke with Mercier about how she helped bring Mudder — and the scientific endeavour to unravel its mystery — to life.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How did you end up getting involved with "Below" as a scientific adviser?

Annie Mercier: Early in 2025, when they were just about to start filming or were finalizing the scripts, I heard that Jesse Mckeown [the director] was looking for a scientific adviser, preferably someone here in Newfoundland. We heard about it through Memorial University's communications team. They mentioned that there would be something about an ancient cephalopod in the series.

I'm not an expert in cephalopods … But I do have a broad background in marine biology, and I'm here at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I sent back my reply, and they eventually contacted me to ask more about what I was doing and what I'd worked on in the past. My research is centered around strange creatures and trying to understand them through curiosity-driven research, so I guess that resonated with them.

Another factor was that I'd previously worked as a consultant on documentaries and television series. I'd done a little work with the BBC, helping explain video sequences, as well as fiction series back in Quebec. I also write popular articles and books for general audiences, so I'm familiar with navigating between science and fiction and with trying to convey something wonderful about science in language that general audiences can understand. I guess that played a role as well, and they eventually asked me to be the adviser.
KHC: What did the advising process look like?
AM: There were two phases. The main thing was that they wanted to share the scripts early on. That's when I was brought in.

Jesse told me they would send scripts at regular intervals, in sequence, starting with the first episode, then the second, and so forth. They would securely send me each script. We had some preliminary discussions to establish exactly what they wanted, because that was my question: How much detail or what kind of feedback were they looking for?

They told me that whatever came to mind, I should suggest it. Of course, I knew they couldn't take everything into account, but I think they wanted to know how far-fetched or how close to reality some of the things were. They asked me to focus mostly on the scientific aspects.

That included the squid, but also how they portrayed the scientific work and the character involved in it. They had climate change, icebergs, ocean currents and a number of other scientific elements in the story.

I went through every script and provided feedback on all sorts of things. Sometimes it was something as simple as the timing of an event. I pointed out things related to the migrations of marine animals and other details that I knew were a little different from reality.

I provided written feedback and sometimes links to additional information. I'd send it back, and occasionally there would be a follow-up meeting or a remote conversation about certain elements. It depended on the situation.

When they started filming, Jesse wanted to schedule a time for me to go behind the scenes and chat with the crew. It was difficult to coordinate because they were filming on three or more sets around Newfoundland, and I was working. Eventually, I managed to visit on a Saturday when they were filming at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I spent some time in the control room, met Mackenzie [Davis] and got to see what they were doing on-site.
Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind. Annie Mercier
KHC: How much feedback did you end up giving on Mudder, the giant, squid-like creature? What aspects did you think were accurate, and where did the show take creative liberties?

AM: Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind. I was hoping they wouldn't go the route of having the arms come out and a giant squid jump onto a boat, or something like "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea." You see those kinds of things in some of the drawings from the 1800s, too. So I had some fears about that.

But when I read the scripts, I could see they were trying to make it as close to reality as possible. Obviously, they had some freedom because it's portrayed as an ancient, social type of cephalopod — more like a squid but with some octopus-like behaviors as well.

I focused my feedback on biology. For example, the eye was very large. It's well known that existing giant squids have one of the biggest, if not the biggest, eyes in the animal kingdom. So that was definitely something that made sense.

I also cautioned them about how giant squids move. Sometimes, in movies, you see their arms portrayed as very muscular, reaching far out of the water. These are mollusks [cephalopods belong to the phylum Mollusca], and in the water, they have quite a bit of strength. But outside the water, they don't have bones that attach muscles to support that kind of movement. It's a very different type of movement.

I drew their attention to the very few cephalopods that actually go out of the water. There's an octopus you can see on certain reefs, and I sent them some images of it. I explained that its movement is very fluid, the way it's able to advance across reefs outside the water.
I also mentioned the kinds of scars they could leave when interacting with sperm whales, for example.

I was quite happy to see that they kept the creature rather mysterious instead of trying to show too much. I was worried it might look completely funny, but I thought they made good use of keeping the mystery alive for a long time.

I also explained that cephalopods in the ocean have no way of detecting prey on the shore. They can't see it or sense it. So if you're going in that direction, you need to be a little careful. Obviously, that's where we're getting into fiction.
But I think they handled it pretty well. An audience expects some fearsome interactions, and if you don't include those at all, you'll disappoint people. Overall, I thought it was pretty good.

There's a lot of lore surrounding giant squids in Newfoundland. They definitely go together ‪—‬ not just in fiction but also because there have been remains, sightings and other encounters. I think this physical place played a role in the inspiration for the show's topic.
KHC: Did you advise on the hallucinogenic properties of the creature's mucus?

AM: No, we didn't specifically exchange information about that. A lot of marine animals have toxins. That's well known, and it's not just cephalopods; all sorts of marine animals have them. Now, how something like that could become airborne, or how it could be associated with melting icebergs and then ingested through the ice, is definitely fictional.
I'm aware of toxic substances, but I'm not aware of any that produce hallucinations, per se. And again, I'm no expert in that area.
KHC: Overall, do you think the series did a good job portraying science? Was there anything you would have changed?

AM: As I said, I had some fears at first. One downside of being an adviser was that I knew everything about the show before watching it, which was a first for me. It was a little different because I would watch and think, "Oh, OK; they did that. They adjusted this. Oh, they went all out with this one."
I discovered what they had taken into consideration and what they had discarded. It was fun to watch, and I think they did a pretty good job overall.

I always think about this when I watch series about different professions. When you see lawyers or police officers portrayed, I imagine they're probably laughing about how simple things seem. Maybe everything is compressed in time, or maybe it's not quite how it happens in reality. This time, it was my turn to see how they would portray my profession.

I think they avoided some of the common clichés. In movies and television, when you go into a laboratory, you often see colorful tubes and bubbling Erlenmeyer flasks just to tell you that you're in a lab. The fact that they filmed here at the Ocean Sciences Centre, in real laboratories, contributed to the sense of reality. Our labs are eclectic. You have nets, tanks, microscopes and all sorts of things around. They're not perfectly ordered, and I think that helped.

I also appreciated that they were careful about how they portrayed scientists. When you're a marine scientist, you're a marine scientist. You're not all-knowing about everything in science. Sometimes shows portray scientists as knowing everything about everything.

For example, when it came to the substance in the show and its effects on health, I explained that a marine scientist might know how to make a diagnosis about something, but that doesn't mean they can necessarily provide a medical assessment. I think the character even says, "I'm not a medical doctor."

I also thought they did a good job portraying scientific uncertainty. In science, you follow lines of inquiry, but you're not necessarily sure what the answer is. You need confirmation and further investigation.

They also did what they could with the squid to make it fearsome but also lovable, without going too far from what a squid might actually do. And when they took creative liberties, they kept things mysterious enough that everything wasn't spelled out exactly.

I also thought they did a great job portraying Newfoundland. They captured the landscapes, the environments and the spirit of the people. The atmosphere was really well done. I think they aimed to make Newfoundland almost a character in the series, and they did that quite well.

Altogether, I thought the Ocean Sciences Centre and the labs were portrayed very nicely. Some of the students here were around during filming in 2025, and they've had showings of the episodes at the university. It's nice for them to see the labs where they work every day portrayed on screen.
KHC: Beyond the creature itself, were there other scientific details in the scripts that you helped the writers get right?
AM: Yes. I provided feedback on a lot of smaller issues, including the use of scientific tools and how different analyses work.

For example, they were trying to date a block of ice. The process was a little different in the original script, and I explained that these analyses take time. You don't just do something in a lab and immediately get an answer. You sometimes have to collaborate with other people to establish things.

I also cautioned against making one microscope tell you everything about something you're looking at. A microscope is there to provide good magnification. It doesn't give you chemical signatures or anything like that. So I tried to caution them against making one instrument do more than it actually does in reality.

I thought they treated the laboratory work quite well overall. One thing they kept ‪—‬ and I can't blame them for it ‪—‬ was the very nice, almost magical tool they use to check the quality of icebergs. You just stick it into the iceberg, get a reading, and it tells you whether it's a good-quality iceberg.

Obviously, when I saw that, I thought it would be nice if it worked that way! But when you want to know the quality of ice or water, there are a number of different analyses you need to do, and you need to know what you're looking for.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro

In movies and television, it's often the case that you put something into a machine and it spits out exactly what you want to know. But in real science, you have to ask the right question. You have to know what you're looking for so the instrument can tell you whether something has a particular property or not.
I understood that they sometimes needed to take creative liberties to move the plot along. There were a number of comments I made about basic science and what was or wasn't realistic.

One feature of the Ocean Sciences Centre that they took into the fictional realm was the basement, where you go through a door and there's an ocean or water behind it. Obviously, don't look for that here! That's just about the only thing that isn't real. The rest is pretty close to reality.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-rift-reawa.headline: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-rift-reawa.author: Earth Institute at Columbia University

paragraphs.text: edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Andrew Zinin

In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake shook southern Africa from an unlikely place: the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana. Cratons are the ancient cores of continents, and this one is built from blocks of crust up to 3.7 billion years old. Geologists have long considered such regions too cold, too thick and too rigid to tear apart.

Now, a new study led by researchers at the Botswana International University of Science and Technology (BIUST) and the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory shows that the craton is indeed being pulled apart. It also shows that the rift doing the pulling has tried this before. The findings are published in the journal Tectonics. The work challenges long-held assumptions about continental stability, revealing how ancient geological seams can reactivate to fracture even the oldest continental cores.

"The earthquake happened in the middle of the craton, a region where no one expected to have an active fault slipping, let alone an active plate boundary developing," says co-author Folarin Kolawole. He is a structural geologist at Lamont and an assistant professor in the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences within the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The new rift lies at the far southern tip of the East African Rift System, where the African continent is slowly stretching apart. Rifts like these are the earliest stage of a divergent plate boundary, the kind that splits a continent and opens a new ocean if successful. For decades, scientists thought the southern end of this system lay in the Okavango Rift Zone of northern Botswana, first identified in the 1970s by Lamont geologist Christopher Scholz and colleagues. Studies of the 2017 earthquake revealed that it reaches nearly 200 miles (320 kilometers) farther, into the craton itself.

This is a surprise, considering how rifts usually go around cratons rather than through them. Around the world, continental rifts tend to follow mountain belts—the younger and weaker zones where ancient cratons once collided. Only a handful of rifts, such as the one that opened the Labrador Sea between Canada and Greenland, are known to have broken across a craton. "It's counterintuitive," Kolawole says. "It basically challenges age-old thinking."
"Whether rifts do propagate through cratons has been a really big question in geoscience," says the study's lead author, Boniface Kgosidintsi of BIUST.

To understand how the rift is breaking into the craton, the team focused on the Khurutshe Fault, which cuts a 50-mile-long (80-kilometer-long) scarp, or step, across the flat Kalahari landscape about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of the 2017 earthquake. In places, the land on one side of the fault sits as much as 400 feet (120 meters) higher than the other.

The researchers dug trenches across the scarp alongside Botswana's A1 highway and examined deeper excavations dug for a government water pipeline. They imaged the rock below with electrical resistivity tomography, which Kolawole likens to a CAT scan of the fault. And they analyzed records from 20 groundwater boreholes drilled across the area.

All three lines of evidence told the same story. When a fault slips, the land on one side drops, and sediment piles up in the low spot, forming a wedge that thickens toward the fault. The team found that both the modern Kalahari Desert sands and much older rock layers from the Jurassic period form such wedges against the same fault. That means the fault was moving in the Jurassic, roughly 180 million years ago, and is moving again today.

The trenches the researchers dug revealed more details about the fault's past. Beneath reddish-brown, windblown Kalahari sand, the team hit hard, highly cemented Jurassic sandstone shot through with white veins of calcite, "a spider web network of whitish lines through the rocks," Kolawole says. The calcite was deposited by hot fluids, like those that build mineral terraces at Yellowstone's hot springs, rising through cracks opened by the fault. Some rock surfaces were polished and scored by slip along the fault.

The team concludes that the rift first opened during a period of continent-wide stretching in the Jurassic, then failed and went dormant until the East African Rift System began pulling on it again. Exactly when it reawakened isn't known, but the fault has offset the young Kalahari sands, which were laid down mostly within the last 2.6 million years. "We believe Khurutshe is one of the failed Mesozoic rifts within the craton and is reactivating," Kgosidintsi says. The rift is in its earliest stage of development, but it is not new.
Flaws in the armor

The researchers also found that faulting began before volcanic activity reached the area during the Jurassic, suggesting that magma alone did not weaken the craton enough to start the rift. Instead, the rift appears to have exploited existing weak spots. The active rifts in eastern Botswana follow an ancient seam where the Kalahari Craton's oldest pieces fused together billions of years ago.

"While cratons are regarded as strong old continental blocks, they do have inherent zones of weakness that can localize a new plate boundary," Kolawole says. And breaking one may take persistence: "Maybe you need to reactivate the rift multiple times. You need to try multiple times before it actually succeeds."

The findings also have implications for how southern Africa's tectonic plates should be drawn. Some scientists have proposed that the region south of the Okavango Rift forms a single, stable microplate, called the San Plate. But an active rift with large earthquakes and fresh fault scarps sits squarely inside it. "We cannot assume that the plate is coherent," Kolawole says. The researchers propose that the San Plate may be slowly breaking into two smaller plates, which they call the North San Plate and the South San Plate.

Any breakup will unfold over millions of years, if at all. According to GPS measurements, the rifts in southern Africa are opening far more slowly than the more mature segments in Malawi, Kenya and Ethiopia, and slow rifts can stall and fail. But Kolawole notes that plate boundaries "often start slow and then they accelerate later in their life."

Studying this rift as it begins offers a rare look at how new plate boundaries form, and where Africa may eventually split. "These systems are like cracks breaking through continents, and they will determine the location and the axis of a future ocean," he says.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/europe/mald.headline: Maldon Salt’s Authenticity Is Questioned, Leaving Foodies Shaken

paragraphs.text: What makes a box of flaky, artisanal seasoning worth its salt?
Culinary connoisseurs are mulling that question as scrutiny is directed at the credentials of a cult-favorite brand of salt.

Maldon Sea Salt, a popular flaky variety found in pantries around the world, was at the center of the shake-up. Fans of the brand, which include Nigella Lawson and Ina Garten, have lauded its taste and pyramidal shape, finishing fancy dishes or desserts with a sprinkle.

Contributing to its popularity was Maldon Salt’s story as a homegrown business, founded some 140 years ago in the English town of Maldon in the county of Essex that was once a site for an Anglo-Saxon era battle. Its salt flakes, the company said, are hand-raked from the town’s River Blackwater estuary.

An investigation published Sunday by the British newspaper The Observer has complicated that image. Maldon, according to the report, was not made only with sea salt from local seawater. Trucks with rock salt imported from mines in Germany were spotted at a production facility — a fact that Maldon had not widely publicized on its packaging or its website.

The company said in response to The Observer that the imported salt came from an ancient sea, and that its “100 percent sea salt” labeling was accurate. Food regulators, including in Britain, where there is no strict definition for artisanal sea salt, approved the product.
Still, the revelation that one of Britain’s most popular artisanal brands included imported German salt rocked aficionados of seasoning.

Some took it with a pinch of salt, adding that the raw material — the inorganic compound sodium chloride — was at least authentic. Others, including food influencers, said they felt deceived, and raised questions about whether the product lived up to its premium, artisanal branding.

Then, there were those amused or exasperated by the newly nicknamed “Saltgate,” with several outlets calling it a “posh” scandal over a brand that some perceive as a status signaler. People online joked about the “salty comments.”

Salt can come in many forms: Table salt, kosher salt, sea salt, Himalayan rock salt. While common forms are industrially produced and inexpensive to buy, manufacturers of more traditional salt brands, which rely on age-old methods, can command higher prices because of their distinct texture, taste and methods.

Maldon Salt, founded in 1882, has in recent decades built a passionate following by influencers and chefs alike who often sprinkled it as a finisher over steaks, in breads or atop chocolate chip cookies. The company made about 39 million pounds, or $51 million, in revenue in the financial year that ended March 2025. (An 8.5-ounce box of salt costs about $13 at Walmart.)
Days after the investigation published, the company said it would review packaging and be more transparent about its process.

“Our previous information focused on the finished flakes and the craft of our salt makers, without giving enough detail about how we prepare our brine,” the company said on its website, adding that it took responsibility for “not sharing that story openly on our packs and website sooner.”

By Friday, Maldon’s website had been updated to include details about its “salt-on-salt” method, which it said was behind the success of the product. Seawater from salt marshes near Maldon is filtered over pure rock salt from Germany, the company said, making a concentrated brine. The mixture is then evaporated in salt pans and harvested by hand.

A spokesman for K+S, a German miner of rock salt whose trucks were spotted at a Maldon Salt facility, declined to comment on specific deliveries. But he said the supplier used rock salt deposits derived from the Zechstein Sea, an inland body of water that evaporated 250 million years ago.
The filtering process was an “essential step” to achieve the product’s signature flake, Maldon Salt said in an emailed statement on Friday. “There is no Maldon sea salt without pure rock salt.”

In Britain and in the United States, there are no specific regulations that define “sea salt” when used on labels. Other countries, such as Canada and France, have stricter rules around such labeling.
Other artisanal salt brands, perhaps seeing a marketing opportunity, posted on social media to suggest alternatives for discerning sea salt users.
“Our sea salt is made from 100 percent Anglesey seawater,” Halen Môn, a Welsh artisanal sea salt company, posted on social media Friday. “Absolutely nothing is added.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/theater/joe-keery.headline: From ‘Stranger Things’ to Broadway, Everyone Knows Joe Keery

paragraphs.text: Joe Keery reached high to grab a package of nori for a woman standing nearby.
“Should I get one of these?” he asked her sweetly. “Are they good?” He took another package for himself.

On the first Tuesday in November, Keery, 34, a star of the Netflix fantasia “Stranger Things” and a chart-topping solo musical artist, had blocked out the afternoon for errands. On the agenda: a frame shop, a florist’s for soil and a tiny houseplant, a Japanese grocery for mochi rice, part of a resolution to cook more. (A bandage covered a recent zucchini-related burn.) Then he would walk the 30-odd blocks to the Hudson Theater, where he is starring in a revival of the Jon Robin Baitz play “Other Desert Cities.”

That afternoon, Keery, who has an apartment nearby, had dressed casually in dark jeans, a denim jacket and a red-and-blue baseball cap, matching the “I Voted” sticker pasted to his shirt. It wasn’t the most camera-ready look. That didn’t deter the half-dozen fans who stopped Keery for selfies or several paparazzi. The woman in the grocery was the rare person who seemed not to recognize him.

Keery was gracious throughout, effortlessly decent. If there were Geiger counters to measure kindness, they would go crazy around him. He posed when asked and made time for a couple of student journalists outside a polling site. Asked about voting, he told them, “It’s invigorating and exciting to do and it makes you feel like you’re taking an actively participating role as a citizen.” At the frame shop, where he is a regular, he gave the owners his personal phone number, so that he could arrange discount Broadway tickets for them. I followed the man into traffic and didn’t think twice.
“Everyone who meets him falls in love with him,” Matt Duffer, a co-creator of “Stranger Things,” said.

Keery is ambivalent about this adulation. On his most recent album, “The Crux,” a song includes the lyrics: “I don’t want your money / I don’t care for fame / I don’t want to live a life where that’s my big exchange.”

So it’s a paradox that just about everyone thinks they know and love Keery, just at the moment when he is trying to complicate how people perceive him as an artist. That complication is why he put himself on Broadway, despite not having done a play since college.
“I really wanted to do something that felt like getting back to why I started doing this in the first place,” he said.

Keery has the problem and the gift of being associated with a single role, one he played for about a decade. He was 23 when he was cast in “Stranger Things” as Steve Harrington, a high school bully with unusually good hair. Matt and Ross Duffer, the creators of the series, watched plenty of audition tapes. Only Keery’s lofted Steve beyond stereotype. “He brought a humanity to him, a charisma,” Ross Duffer said in a recent interview.

Steve was meant to die at the end of the first season. Instead he survived, becoming a hero. He also became a lot more like Keery. “Joe’s charm was undeniable,” Matt Duffer said. “We just started to really lean into that.”

In between the show’s five seasons, many of his co-stars took on other jobs, diversifying their résumés. Keery didn’t do much. “Truly not for lack of trying,” he said. He wasn’t interested in roles that too closely resembled Steve, and casting directors turned him down for others. “Just because you have this thing on a silver platter doesn’t mean you get everything else,” he said.

Still, he kept making music, psychedelic synth pop that unpacked personal experience. A musician since his college days in Chicago, he’d had to part from an early band, Post Animal, when “Stranger Things” first aired. (Filming interfered with touring and fans started showing up to gigs in “Stranger Things” merch, which messed with the vibes.) But as a solo artist, who performs and records under the name Djo, he could make his own schedule. One bittersweet song, “End of Beginning,” which seems to reference his life before and after fame, has reached the top of several global charts.
As we sat, post-errands, in Union Square Park, a man stopped to tell Keery that he had his latest album on vinyl. “Oh, thank you, man,” Keery said. “Thank you. Thank you so much. Enjoy the day.”

As “Stranger Things” neared its final season, Keery made moves. He reunited with Post Animal. He starred in a season of “Fargo” and made a couple of movies. And he began looking for a play to appear in, as a way to reconnect with the actor and the person he had been before he was famous. He struggles to remember how people treated him back then, how he felt in his own skin. “Which is a little scary for me,” he said. “But I try not to get negative about it. Otherwise, I feel like it could be easy to spiral or feel trapped.”

He hadn’t heard of “Other Desert Cities,” a 2010 drama, set in 2004, that drops in on a prominent California family as they celebrate a fraught Christmas in Palm Springs. But he was invited to participate in a workshop of it last winter, opposite Allison Janney and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and he found that he loved it. John Benjamin Hickey, the play’s director, loved him, too. “Joe was just so remarkably self-possessed and took such ownership of the part that it was sort of a no-brainer,” he said.

Rehearsing the play this summer and fall was daunting, especially as tour dates necessitated that he start a week late, but he enjoyed the luxury of working a scene again and again, going deeper each time. And thinking about what makes and breaks a family — he remains close to his parents and four sisters — was a pleasure, too.

Keery plays Trip, the family’s youngest child. Helen Shaw, in The New York Times, wrote that Keery, “a real discovery, manages to be droll with a heart.” For most of the play, Trip serves as a joker, a peacemaker. But in the second act, he delivers a monologue that concludes with the lines, “I am California! And California is not happy!” It’s a big, emotive speech. He delivers it with the naturalness and grace of someone who has been onstage all his life.

“Joe brings such ease,” said Lily Rabe, who plays his older sister in the play. She noted that Keery, who has the dressing room next to hers, was easy offstage, too: “He just does not carry himself at all like someone whose first job rocketed him to lightning-strike superstardom or someone who has women waiting in droves for him at the stage door.” (Several of Keery’s “Stranger Things” co-stars, including Charlie Heaton and Maya Hawke, have also come to see the show.)

Keery has never chased superstardom. He doesn’t want to seem ungrateful, and he isn’t. But he would live less publicly if he could. He seemed most joyful at the Japanese grocery, sincerely congratulating a new cashier on his first day on the job. “And on voting day, too!” he said. His face lit up when he talked about his family, about making music, about finding roles that show he is more than his charisma and wavy hair.
“I can surprise people a little bit,” he said. “Attractive to me in any piece of art is something that is shocking or subverts my expectation. I’m looking for ways to be able to do that.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/nyregion/brooklyn.headline: 10 Days After Fatal Building Collapse, a Brooklyn Block Is in Limbo

paragraphs.text: Ciahola Lawrence became a U.S. citizen in 2014, after years of living in New York City as an unauthorized immigrant. Few possessions are as precious to her as the papers, like her Social Security card, that prove her legal status.
Ms. Lawrence, 54, tucked them carefully in a folder under the couch in her third-floor Brooklyn apartment, along with other mementos, like her junior high school diploma.
She might never see those items again.

Last week, the building next to hers collapsed, leaving eight people dead and 18 others injured, and displacing Ms. Lawrence and more than a dozen of her neighbors in Flatbush, a bustling working-class area that is home to many immigrants. As officials investigate what went wrong, other residents of the block have been kept from returning, left to wonder about their futures and whether their homes are also in danger.

The collapse, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, sheared off a wall of the adjoining building, leaving its apartments open to the air. City officials say they now must demolish that building, 1323 Flatbush, where Ms. Lawrence and her husband had lived for six years.

To make matters worse, nobody — not even city officials or engineers — will be allowed to enter the building, because of potential asbestos contamination and structural instability, the city’s Buildings Department said. That means that Ms. Lawrence’s immigration papers, and everything else in her apartment, may be lost forever.
“I want people to know that my home was special,” she said. “I want people to know that I worked hard for everything that I had in there.”

It is not clear when 1323 Flatbush will be torn down. But to prevent a possible domino effect on the block, where several aging buildings stand side by side, the city said it was installing supports in the next building over — 1325 Flatbush — this week. Both that building, which currently has no tenants, and the one on its other side, 1327 Flatbush, remain under vacate orders.

The city is working to assist the people who have been displaced. Thirteen households have been relocated to hotels, according to the city, until at least the end of the month. The city’s housing department is helping to find permanent homes for residents of the collapsed building and the one next door. City officials said that displaced residents and the families of those killed or injured in the collapse had been given a total of $60,000 in gift cards to help pay for food and other necessities.
Still, residents said they felt like they were in limbo.
“There was no time to get belongings back,” said Moussa Keita, 44, another resident of 1323 Flatbush. Mr. Keita was at work in New Jersey at the time of the collapse.
He said he was frustrated that he could not return to his apartment to retrieve his wife’s passport, family photos and important paperwork before the building was demolished.
“Why do they care about safety now?” he said of buildings officials. “Why didn’t they care about safety before?”

Ahmed Tigani, the buildings commissioner, said in a statement this week announcing the demolition plan that the “entire administration will continue to support the tenants displaced by this incredible tragedy and help the neighborhood, and our entire city, recover.”

While neighbors contend with the aftermath of the disaster, officials are conducting safety sweeps at some 160 sites across the city associated with people or companies that have ties to the collapse.

A visual analysis by The New York Times this week found that 1321 Flatbush — a three-story, century-old, mixed-use building — most likely fell because the excavation at a construction site next door weakened its foundation.

The nature of the collapse made it extremely likely that the building next door, with its peeled-off wall, would have to come down, said Chris Cerino, a structural engineer and former president of the Structural Engineers Association of New York.
“You were looking into it like a dollhouse,” he said. “There’s no way to save that.”
What wasn’t immediately clear at the time of the disaster was that the building was in such bad shape that residents would not be able to retrieve their belongings.

Andrew Rudansky, a Buildings Department spokesman, said the condition of the building had deteriorated in the days after the collapse and that the city had begun informing residents on Tuesday that it was not safe to enter.
Before the building is torn down, though, the department must shore up its other neighbor, 1325 Flatbush.

That is because the two structures share load-bearing walls called “party walls,” a common type of construction in New York City, Mr. Cerino said. Securing the stability of 1325 could involve separating the floors of 1323 from the shared party wall. Then, the city would need to monitor vibrations and movements along the entire chain of buildings on Flatbush before, during and after demolition.
“They are very brittle buildings,” Mr. Cerino said.
The deadly collapse has prompted a criminal investigation and citywide alarm about the stability of buildings near construction sites. The displaced Flatbush residents have more immediate concerns.
Michael Williams, 50, a resident of 1323 Flatbush, said he was worried about where he would live when the Red Cross stopped paying for his temporary housing.
“Don’t put us in your shelter,” he said.

DeAndre Finley, 28, was forced to leave 1327 Flatbush after the collapse and has been living in a hotel. He said he was told that if he was not allowed back into his apartment by the end of the month, he would be moved to a shelter.

But the situation has created a conundrum, he said: He doesn’t want to move back into his building, but the landlord doesn’t seem keen to let him out of his lease. And he worries that even when the building has been deemed safe, it might not remain so.
Why, Mr. Finley asked, would I want to live next to a building that collapsed and another that is about to be demolished?
“And we’re the last building that isn’t?” he said. “No way.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/nyregion/flatbush.headline: Before a Fatal Building Collapse, Officials Signed Off on a Dubious Plan

paragraphs.text: The diagram was small, barely filling one corner in a set of engineering drawings for new construction near Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn.

Still, engineering experts said, it laid out a plan to protect a neighboring apartment building that should have prompted skepticism — or outright rejection — from the New York City Department of Buildings officials who reviewed it in March.

Instead, they stamped their approval, and excavation began at 2625 Bedford Avenue, where, months later, the neighboring building would collapse amid the work, killing eight people and displacing dozens more.

The apparent lapse in oversight raises concerns about not just the city’s handling of the ill-fated project in Brooklyn but its ability to oversee similar work across the city, a New York Times examination has found.

It also raises questions about the officials’ decision nearly a decade ago to effectively disband a special unit in the Buildings Department that was dedicated to reviewing the type of work that was occurring in Flatbush when the building fell.

Andrew Rudansky, a spokesman for the Buildings Department, said in a statement that the city has “robust safeguards” for excavation and that the agency still proactively conducts construction site inspections.

At a City Council hearing on Friday, the department’s deputy commissioner of enforcement, Yegal Shamash, said that officials were still investigating the collapse, but he added that he believed the city’s construction safety standards were “the most rigorous in the country, if not the world.”

Robert Fischman, a real estate investor tied to the limited-liability company developing the project, did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did representatives of the general contractor, Townhouse Builders, or LMW Engineering, which drafted the excavation plans, including the diagram.

In the wake of the collapse, at least four lawsuits have been filed by eight construction workers who said they were injured when the building fell and accused the developers and contractors of unsafe working conditions and ignoring warning signs.

City investigators have yet to determine what caused the building to fall, but a Times visual analysis found that the apartment building most likely collapsed because the excavation had weakened its foundation.

The excavation diagram filed as part of the construction project showed the property line dividing the site from 1321 Flatbush Avenue, the three-story apartment building that toppled, and a plan to dig near its foundation before erecting a new mixed-use building next door.

The plan called for using an excavation technique, sometimes known as berming, that involves digging out soil near the base of the building and pouring a series of concrete steps that slope away from its foundation, with the goal of preventing soil from shifting and destabilizing.

The method is legal and has been safely used for decades across New York, building officials have said. But several building experts who reviewed the plans at the request of The Times said the approach was inappropriate for the site, especially given that the plans lacked details on how to ensure safe excavation.

A chief reason they cited was the composition of the ground beneath the apartment building. It was made up of rough fragments of stone and debris known as rubble, which is weaker than a base of poured concrete. Such conditions often require adding a system of steel columns, beams and a concrete base to shore up the building. No such system appeared to have been in use across a crucial portion of the Flatbush building before it fell.
Even before it submitted the excavation plans to the city, the developer had been advised to use a different approach.

In a report prepared for the developer in November 2025, months before excavation began, engineers hired by the development team said the builders would need to use underpinning, an often costlier support technique that involves pouring concrete beneath the existing foundation of a neighboring building, one small section at a time, to prevent movement. A separate report prepared in March 2026 noted that the nearest wall of the apartment building, which was at least 96 years old, was in “poor condition” and had visible cracks.

Steve Bongiorno, a structural engineer with experience in forensic analysis, said the recommendation to use underpinning should have been followed. But he and four other engineers who reviewed the plans at the request of The Times said they saw no evidence the technique was used on that part of the property.
More troubling, Mr. Bongiorno said, was the lack of detail in the plans as to how to support the wall during the excavation.

“There is no way to achieve this picture without exposing that adjacent building to destabilization,” Mr. Bongiorno said, referring to the diagram and the documented poor condition of the apartment building. “You’ve got to be nuts to try to do something like this.”

Pat Arnett, a principal at TYLin, an engineering and advisory firm, said the berming technique can be performed safely by, among other things, digging farther away from the neighboring building’s foundation and using a less severe slope. Those added precautions, however, can take up more land during construction, he said.

Allyn Kilsheimer, another forensic engineering expert who has spent decades examining major disasters, said any number of things might have gone wrong at the site, even if the excavation plans were perfect on paper. Inaccurate assumptions can sometimes appear on planning documents, he said. And even if everything was accurate, work crews don’t always follow directions.

The developer’s plans for the new construction at 2625 Bedford Avenue called for a nine-story, mixed-use building with 64 apartments and a grocery store. But as the workers were excavating the site, the city had yet to approve a project of that size, having signed off only on earlier plans for a smaller, three-story building.
The distinction meant that the project was not subject to stricter on-site safety requirements.
In past years, such work was closely monitored by an excavation unit within the Buildings Department that had been created under the administration of Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg.

In 2008, less than a year after it was formed, the team conducted 2,772 inspections on 1,685 sites, forcing half of those with active excavation to stop work at least temporarily. Conditions at about 300 sites were so bad that a full engineering audit was ordered; only two passed.

But in 2018, the excavation unit and other specialty teams were reorganized, and the unit’s oversight functions were moved to other divisions of the department. A new compliance unit was made responsible for inspecting excavations.
Philip Mezzatesta, who worked for the Buildings Department for 16 years, including as a chief inspector, said the dedicated inspection team might have made a difference at the Flatbush site.
“If the excavation unit was in effect right now, this would have been caught,” said Mr. Mezzetesta, who now works as a private consultant.
Mr. Rudansky, the buildings department spokesman, disputed that claim, saying that construction-related incidents have fallen 63 percent since 2018, when the excavation unit was reorganized.

Even without such a dedicated unit, the city has ample means to make sure buildings don’t collapse, said Anil Agrawal, the chairman of the civil engineering department at the City College of New York. But, he added, the Buildings Department has to ensure that its inspectors are top-notch.
“The question is about skill levels available in compliance units to review and approve plans and drawings,” he said. “A drawing signed by a professional engineer is not necessarily safe.”
Mr. Mezzatesta, the former building official, said that too often, line-level workers at the department do not possess that high skill level.
“This city has hired people with two, four, five years experience that know absolutely nothing and made them supervisors,” he said. “That’s a problem in itself.”
Luis Ferré-Sadurní contributed reporting. Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/well/rfk-jr-uspst.headline: Powerful Health Panel Has Tumultuous First Meeting With RFK Jr’s Appointees

paragraphs.text: After a year and a half of paralysis, the United States Preventive Services Task Force reconvened on Thursday and Friday for the first time with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s newly appointed members.

It quickly became apparent that a bumpy road lies ahead for the task force, which plays a critical role in Americans’ health care by informing what screenings clinicians recommend and what preventive services insurers are required to cover. It considers topics including mammograms, colonoscopies, H.I.V. prevention medications and much more.

The 16 task force members — eight appointed by Mr. Kennedy in September, and eight predating the current administration — aired significant disagreements on whether they should continue to evaluate evidence through the task force’s traditional processes.
At various points, some new members made comments that suggested they were unfamiliar with those procedures, and with the types of questions the task force seeks to answer.

One, Dr. Louis Wilson, asked what the task force normally did in the virtual meetings its internal work groups hold between its three annual in-person gatherings. And in discussing whether to make a recommendation about screening adolescents for unhealthy alcohol use, two — Dr. Ronald Karlsberg and the new chair, Dr. Seth Corey — made comments that suggested they believed the question at issue was whether teen drinking was healthy, rather than whether there was enough evidence to support the benefits of screening.
In a significant departure from past practice, the task force spent Friday morning listening to presentations from outside experts with financial conflicts of interest.

Conflicts of interest also required three new members to recuse themselves from discussion of a long-delayed cervical cancer screening recommendation. All three were among those who received waivers to serve despite owning stocks in large pharmaceutical and biotech companies, whose products are affected by numerous task force recommendations.

In the past, people with such conflicts were not appointed to the panel to begin with. Very occasionally, someone had to recuse because of a narrow conflict on a single topic, said Dr. Michael Silverstein, the chair of the task force until March. But he could recall that happening only twice in roughly a decade. Three recusals on one topic suggest a body of members “for whom conflicts of interest are going to be a very big problem,” he said.

This was the first in-person meeting since March 2025, after the health department canceled four in a row. While members continued to meet virtually in the intervening time, political appointees prevented them from posting drafts for public comment, voting and publishing final recommendations. Guidelines on at least 18 topics stalled.

On Thursday, Carrie Patnode, a behavioral epidemiologist at Kaiser Permanente, presented the findings of a systematic evidence review her team completed last year for a pending recommendation on lifestyle changes and cardiovascular disease. But she noted that it didn’t incorporate more recent evidence published since the review was completed. Evidence reviews on many topics that stalled over the past year and a half are likely to be similarly out of date.

Perhaps the tensest part of the meeting came when the members discussed edits that Dr. Roger D. Klein, a political appointee leading the federal agency that oversees the task force, had requested to the cervical cancer screening recommendation. These included objections from Dr. Klein to mentioning racial disparities in cervical cancer.
During that conversation, Dr. Sei Lee, a member whose tenure predates Mr. Kennedy, said he wanted to “call out the elephant in the room.”
“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the top line may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Dr. Lee said.

Ultimately, the task force went into a private session to discuss whether to ratify the recommendation, along with the one on alcohol abuse screening and a third on screening for perinatal depression. The task force’s press office said the vote tallies would be made public, but didn’t say when.

A person who was in the room, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that after arguments in which Dr. Klein heatedly defended his removal of the mentions of racial disparities, the task force approved the recommendation with its original language. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling, Mr. Kennedy has the authority to overrule the task force’s decisions.

A lot of NFL games this time of year are as appealing as day-old oatmeal. By late November, half of the teams in the league have a losing record and muddle around at midfield. Coaches call plays that seem calculated to keep their job, soothe critics, and justify their run-pass and go-or-no-go decisions to their owners. Sunday night’s matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and the Minnesota Vikings, however, will be genuine must-see TV for anyone interested in artful, inventive football—and for anyone who cares about leadership.

Kyle Shanahan, the head coach of the 49ers, and Brian Flores, the Vikings’ defensive coordinator, are the two most nonconformist minds in the NFL, and each has been punished at times for high-risk unorthodoxy. They will bring the No. 1 offense and the No. 1 defense, respectively, to the game—a meeting that promises to be revealing for each of them. These guys take chances, and they are worth watching to see how comfortable they are with the consequences of their decisions.

Both go all-in with their play-calling. According to a CBS Sports analysis, Shanahan leads the league in sending all five eligible receivers downfield, declining to hold anything back for extra quarterback protection. The same analysis found Flores leading the league in blitzing—sending at least five men rushing headlong at the passer—at risk of leaving gaps on the field. “There’s going to be a lot of hit and miss both ways,” Shanahan said at a press conference this week.
[Read: The Los Angeles Rams are trying to defeat time]

Shanahan has lost the Super Bowl three agonizing times as a head coach or deputy. In 2017, he was blamed for surrendering the biggest comeback in the game’s history as the play caller for the Atlanta Falcons, who at one point had led the New England Patriots 28–3, only to be defeated in overtime. Shanahan’s own quarterback, Matt Ryan, openly second-guessed his decisions in the aftermath. Three years later, Shanahan was back in the game with the 49ers and lost a 10-point lead to the Kansas City Chiefs. In 2024, he lost another Lombardi Trophy to the Chiefs in overtime, 25–22. “Everyone talks to me about How do you live with what happened in the Super Bowl?” Shanahan told me a few years ago. He said that if he makes a wrong call, “I never regret it. I’m like, Fuck it. Maybe I didn’t make the right call.”

As for Flores, he won four Super Bowls as an assistant coach with the Patriots before becoming the Miami Dolphins’ head coach, and then was fired in 2022 despite having gone 10–6 and 9–8 in his final two seasons. When he couldn’t get another head-coaching job, he risked retaliation and career immolation by filing a racial-discrimination class-action suit against the NFL, which is headed to court.

His creative defense has carried the 7–2 Vikings all season by blitzing at a rate of more than 70 percent. “The only regrets I ever have come when we didn’t blitz,” Flores said at a press conference this month. To put the numbers in context, no other team in the league blitzes much more than 40 percent of the time, avoiding it for fear of giving up foolish-looking big plays. “Usually, people get got, if you do it too much,” Shanahan told journalists this week. “That’s what’s been so impressive.” The Vikings have allowed 12 touchdowns all season, but have sacked opposing quarterbacks 37 times.

One reason Flores’s strategy has been so successful is that he is a master of disguise. He gives his players discretion to make on-the-fly adjustments, so opposing teams have trouble knowing who is coming and frequently hesitate or are thrown into confusion. The Vikings’ 37 sacks have come from a dozen different players, which means quarterbacks often don’t know where to look.
[From the July 2026 issue: As American as the forward pass]

But the Vikings will meet an equal and opposing force in the 49ers, who are 8–1. Most teams regularly commit at least one receiver to help protect the quarterback. Not these guys. Shanahan fans out an array of versatile, sticky-handed speed burners, including Christian McCaffrey, who runs like a downhill boulder, and the human streamer kite George Kittle. Opponents wrench their necks trying to cover 11 players who have caught five or more passes. According to the CBS Sports analysis, the 49ers play “five out” on 80.1 percent of their passing plays. They don’t attack for the sake of attacking; instead, they deploy a coherent design that creates vertical and horizontal states of emergency for the other team. “It’s thought out,” Flores said at a press conference this week. “There’s a rhyme and reason behind it all.”

Shanahan and Flores are not flinchers. In a 2022 podcast, Shanahan explained his play-calling philosophy: “It’s not ever going to be based off of, Yeah, this is probably a little risky to do this. I totally believe it’s right, but I’m not going to do it, because it’s risky, perception-wise, and this could get me blamed,’” he said, and added, “That’s not what you want from a play caller. That’s not what you want from a leader.”

This will be one game that doesn’t need Carrie Underwood’s “Waiting All Day for Sunday Night” power-yodeling to amp it up. On exhibit will be two strong decision makers who have prepared as thoroughly as possible, make their calls clearheadedly, and don’t worry about appearances.

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6047916/killer-.headline: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6047916/killer-.author: Imogen Foulkes

paragraphs.text: GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
Algorithms making life-and-death decisions

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
A "nothing burger"

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
