But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: Red Cadillac, rock 'n' roll, ice cream and cookies. They got to 100 by staying young
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: Steve Lopez

paragraphs.text: The centenarians arrived one at a time, ranging in age from 100 to 107, traveling by scooter, walker and wheelchair to the dining hall at the Hillcrest retirement community in La Verne.
As Thanksgiving approaches, they’ve got a lot to be grateful for.
And what a ride they’ve had.

“From horse and buggy, to today’s cars,” said Sharon Wulfensmith, a fellow resident and author who introduced the nine centenarians and compiled a 30-page history of their lives. “They … lived through the Great Depression, World War II, the Holocaust, the civil rights era and much more.”
Ruth Kurtz, at 107, could easily pass for 25 years younger. She wore a ruby red sweater and a lovely string of pearls. Her hair was perfectly coiffed.
“I love red,” she told me in a low voice, looking out at roughly 150 fellow residents and family members who had come to honor the centenarians, a Hillcrest tradition.
Graham Lovelace, Lena Ott Coffman and Margery Spillman are 103.
Joseph Clair Hanawalt is 102.
Four others joined the 100 club this year — Mickey Deutsch Kommel, Annie Eloise Wallis Greene, Bob Ratliff and Carl Beckwith.

A 10th centenarian, Margaret Coston, recently left Hillcrest to live with family, but she was honored as well. As were recently deceased residents, including Atala Bravo (who died at 111), Imogene Porter Hanawalt, Joseph Schechter, and Charles Sterling Pratt.
“I thought he was going to live forever,” one staffer whispered to another when Pratt’s photo was shown.
Pratt was 105 at his passing.
“You would never know it,” the staffer whispered again. “Never.”

Making it to 100 used to be rare. When I was born in the 1950s, there were only about 2,500 centenarians in the United States. By 2024 there were 101,000, and the number is expected to quadruple by 2054 due to boomer birth rates, medical advances, affluence and other factors. As of 2024, 78% were women and 77% were white.

Some of the secrets of a long life are not so secret. Good genes can help; good luck is even better. There’s a big difference between age span and health span, and enjoying the years rather than enduring them means being able to handle the rising cost of suitable housing and quality supportive care, both of which are out of reach for many.

We know from geriatric science, and from author Dan Buettner’s studies of longevity Blue Zones, that social connectedness and a sense of purpose and belonging are big pluses. I visited the Seventh-day Adventist community in Loma Linda three years ago, where faith, vegetarianism and community causes were part of what led to Blue Zone recognition.

Hillcrest was founded in 1947 by Church of the Brethren, and many of the residents have been members of, and even ministers in, the church. Some of the honorees mentioned faith and family connections as key to their long lives.

Kurtz told me she never touched a drop of alcohol, which pretty much ruined my day. But she lifted me back up by saying she doesn’t turn down any sweets, especially cookies and cake. (Neither does Hanawalt, who told me he has cookies and ice cream most days with his lunch.)
“I can’t see very well and I can’t hear very well,” Kurtz said. “But otherwise I’m well physically.”

She said a good day is made better with classical music, and she loves sitting on her porch and taking in the sun. She also has a neighbor she’s particularly close to. That would be her son, Donald Kurtz, 81, who also lives at Hillcrest. Donald had a quick explanation for his mother’s longevity.
“She’s somebody who doesn’t get upset about anything and never has anything but kind words to say about people,” Donald said, delivering yet another blow to my hopes of a long life.
But getting old, as they say, is not for weaklings. It’s one compromise after another, and deteriorating health is unavoidable, as is the pain of loss. Of spouses, of relatives, of friends.

“I don’t know if I want to turn 100 or not,” said Jacki Gingrich, 85, a Hillside resident who attended the ceremony. “It depends on if my friends are still around. … I’ve already lost my husband, so i don’t want to lose all my friends.”
Annie Greene had tears in her eyes when she told me about her departed husband, but she was all smiles when she told me how she met him.
She was a nurse’s aide at a Palm Springs hospital. The year was 1948, and a World War II Navy veteran, working as a cop, brought in an unruly gent who needed medical attention and physical restraint.
“I’d get one arm and one hand down, and I’d start on the other one,” said Greene, and then her patient would break free of the first restraint.
“The police officer … came over to me and he said — I’ll never forget this — ‘I think you need a guy that knows how to tie a knot. That’s me.’”
The cop, Ted Greene, died in 2006. He and Annie were married for more than half a century, and their son and daughter attended the Hillcrest celebration.

Kommel, who got a college economics degree in New York when that was extremely uncommon for women, later went back to school for a teaching degree in California. She went parasailing in Hawaii to mark her 85th birthday, roots for the Dodgers, and her musical tastes range from classical to rock and modern genres, because, as she explained to me, that keeps her connected to her grandchildren.
In Wulfensmith’s biographical sketch on Spillman, I came upon this:

“Who is that classy lady, with the red high heels, emerging from that bright red Cadillac in the parking lot? Oh, that must be Marge. Some people just seem to be born to stay young for a long, long time.”
Spillman told me she had to park the Cadillac, for now, after breaking her leg in a fall. I asked where she sported off to when she was behind the wheel.
“Everywhere,” she said. “I got my hair done. I played bridge. I went to the Covina women’s club.”
I asked if she intends to keep driving once she heals.
She wasn’t sure.
But she noted she’s got three years left on her current driver’s license.
steve.lopez@latimes.com

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/21/dro.headline: Emergency medical services could be delivered by drones
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/21/dro.author: Margaret Hetherman

paragraphs.text: Five years ago, a 71-year-old man with a history of heart failure went into cardiac arrest while shoveling snow outside his home in Trollhattan, Sweden.

A doctor passing by began CPR as Sven’s wife called emergency services. In just over three minutes after dispatch, according to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, a drone arrived with an automated external defibrillator (AED), which analyzes heart rhythm and can deliver an electric shock to restore a normal heartbeat.
A neighbor retrieved the AED, which had landed just 33 feet from the victim. The first shock was delivered shortly before emergency responders arrived.
The man regained consciousness after three more shocks in the ambulance en route to the hospital. He survived and made a full neurological recovery, according to the case report.

Once just a dream and a pilot program, AED-carrying drones are now integrated into many emergency response systems in western Sweden, covering 15 percent of the region’s population, according to regional officials. As of February 2025, drone operator Everdrone reported about 300 successful AED deployments.

In parts of Florida, local emergency services have been following in Sweden’s footsteps since May 2024, dispatching drones carrying AEDs, part of a slow-going effort in the United States to provide emergency medical services via drone.

Since the program’s launch, Archer First Response Systems, the company that runs the drones, has made 15 emergency deployments between the two counties, said Gordon Folkes, ArcherFRS’s founder and CEO.
Prepackaged payloads can contain Narcan for overdoses, epinephrine for severe allergic reactions, albuterol for asthma attacks, tourniquets and an AED.

In one example, drone’s-eye video captured the drop-off: The aircraft cruises 2.8 miles over swaths of trees, then hovers 200 feet off the ground to lower a package to the wife of a man who had collapsed.
“And then she got the AED pads on the chest about four minutes before ground units even arrived on the scene,” said Folkes, whose company operates through contracts with emergency-response agencies.
In this case, the device didn’t advise a shock, as the heart was in “a non-shockable rhythm,” Folkes said, and the man died.

Still, “in cardiac arrest, getting a defibrillator to someone quickly is absolutely crucial.” said Robson Gilmour, a resident doctor in the United Kingdom who researches drone-based organ transportation.
The American Heart Association estimates a victim’s chance of survival decreases by 7 to 10 percent for every minute after a cardiac arrest without defibrillation.

Despite successful pilot programs and emerging real-world applications — including a first-of-its-kind Cleveland Clinic prescription-delivery initiative launched in July in partnership with drone delivery company Zipline — medical drone service has still not gained much traction across the United States.
Obstacles include aviation regulations and infrastructure needed for reliable delivery. Some applications — like organ transplantation — face more hurdles than others.

“Blood products, pathology samples and medications are probably more likely to become routine before organ transportation,” Gilmour said. “I think these applications make sense as a starting point, because they’re generally more frequent and easier to integrate into existing health care systems. They also help build the infrastructure and confidence needed for more complicated deliveries later on.”
Now, ArcherFRS is moving into delivering blood by drone.

Described by the county as the first of its kind in the nation, the system will initially cover 70 square miles. Folkes expects operations to go live in a few weeks, when paramedics can request temperature-controlled whole blood — which contains red and white blood cells, platelets and plasma — via mobile app. The system is designed to get blood to the scene in 3½ minutes or less.

“Paramedics could be responding to a traffic crash, postpartum hemorrhage, medical or trauma patients, or shooting or stabbing victims whose loss of blood is so significant that waiting to get to the hospital for a blood transfusion might be too late to save a patient’s life,” Hillsborough County said in a release.
Transporting organs

In April 2019, the first unmanned delivery of a kidney took off, propelled by eight rotors. The flight to the University of Maryland Medical Center took just under 10 minutes. Trina Glispy, then 44, had spent eight years on dialysis and was the recipient of the kidney.

Project leader Joseph Scalea was on the surgical team that performed the successful transplant. The physician’s support for the new kind of transportation was fueled by frustration with the logistics of getting organs to dying patients.
“Fifty people touch the organ from the time that the donor goes to the operating room, to the time that organ arrives and is transplanted in a recipient in a different hospital,” he noted.
Those handoffs are necessary, he added. “I just thought, wouldn’t it be amazing if you could just hit the easy button on your cellphone, and the drone lands on my hospital?”
Transportation delays can compromise organ viability. The clock starts ticking from the moment the donated organ is chilled until it begins rewarming in the recipient’s bod
Despite the successful pilot program, the process hasn’t taken off more broadly.

In an October review, Scalea and colleagues concluded that organ transplantation has advanced in immunosuppression, surgical techniques and organ preservation, but the infrastructure of organ movement remains stagnant.

Federal Aviation Administration rules are among the biggest hurdles in the U.S., said Gilmour, the U.K. doctor. Drones generally must remain within the pilot’s visual line of sight. In Glispy’s kidney-transplant case, officials obtained a waiver for the milestone 2.8-mile flight over Baltimore. Such waivers aren’t necessarily a straightforward route to running a large, routine delivery network, Gilmour added.
He added that the FAA is working on measures to allow for these types of operations, but the timing is unclear.
Gilmour also cites reliability considerations: weather, battery life, range and airspace restrictions.

“You can’t really afford a delivery to be delayed or canceled when you’re transporting an organ,” he said. “We know drones can physically carry organs, but what effect do vibration, movement and the forces during flight have on the organ?”

Gilmour and Mekhola Hoff, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, are conducting a large-animal pilot study examining how flight conditions affect organ tissue compared with conventional road transport and storage.

“The Baltimore kidney delivery was a massive milestone because it showed that you could actually transport a human kidney by drone and successfully transplant it,” Gilmour said. “I do think we’re getting closer.”
Signs of progress
On Oct. 21, the University of Michigan announced a pilot with drone company Blueflite to test the delivery of donated organs by drone, with an eye toward developing flight infrastructure.

In June, NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, teamed up with the United Network for Organ Sharing to study transporting human kidneys by drone beyond the pilot’s visual line of sight; preliminary findings showed no negative impact to the organs.

More routine medical drone deployment can be found in countries where challenging topography and bad roads make transportation challenging. A September review in the journal Global Health Action highlighted sub-Saharan Africa, where drones transport blood products, antimalarial medicines, vaccines and diagnostic samples. Researchers found significant reductions in drone delivery times compared with ground transport.

California-based Zipline has made medical drone deliveries to thousands of health care facilities in the region, partnering with Rwanda in 2016 to deliver blood, vaccines and medicines. The company has worked with Ghana since 2019, making over 4,000 blood deliveries last year.

“I think having governments properly commit to these programs has been a big part of their success,” Gilmore said. “There’s a difference between running a few successful trials and having a service that hospitals can actually rely on every day.

“These programs have been particularly useful in areas where road journeys are difficult or take a long time,” he said. “I’d imagine there are plenty of similar situations in rural parts of the U.S. where drones could make a real difference.”

npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6049625/palisad.headline: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6049625/palisad.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire's origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: UC signs deal for ChatGPT at all 10 campuses. Faculty object
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: Jaweed Kaleem

paragraphs.text: The University of California has signed a systemwide deal with OpenAI to provide ChatGPT and other artificial intelligence tools to hundreds of thousands of students, faculty and staff across its 10 campuses, becoming the latest California university to partner with the tech giant, joining Cal State and USC.
The announcement comes amid growing national concern about the rapid advance of AI and after California’s attorney general sued OpenAI this week, alleging it endangered the public.

The university will pay $1.2 million a year for OpenAI’s technology, which will roll out at campuses in the coming weeks. The tools include ChatGPT Edu and Codex, OpenAI’s coding tool. The fee covers basic models, while campuses and users can buy access to more advanced models at a discount. The deal covers UC’s academic programs and operations but not its hospitals or clinics.
The purchase expands a looser 2024 agreement under which UC campuses could buy ChatGPT Edu licenses and credits on their own. Each paid its own costs.
UC President James B. Milliken said the deal would give students and faculty stronger privacy protections than they get through personal accounts.

“This purchase will help ensure equitable access to these widely used tools while providing stronger data protections and lower costs,” Milliken wrote in a letter to faculty leaders Thursday, which said the decision had buy-in from chancellors.

In an interview, UC San Diego Chancellor Pradeep Khosla praised the deal for letting his campus offer OpenAI’s tools for free. “As an educator, my view is I should give equitable access to all my faculty, students and staff,” he said. Khosla said AI “conjures up images of euphoria and fear simultaneously” and that both sides have “legitimate reasons” for their views, but that “it is here to stay.”

UC moved ahead with the purchase despite pleas from faculty leaders in its Academic Senate to slow down. In an Oct. 30 letter to Milliken, UC’s Academic Council — an executive body made up of Academic Senate leaders — said it did not oppose AI but had questions about the deal.
The group said it learned of the pending deal Oct. 21 and asked UC to delay the purchase.

In an email to The Times on Friday, Academic Senate chair Susannah Scott said the concerns remained unresolved. “Foundational decisions about UC’s educational environment are being made without sufficient involvement of its educators,” said Scott, a UC Santa Barbara chemistry professor.
In his letter, Milliken said that offering the tools “in no way mandates their use by students or faculty, nor does it establish academic policy.”
Some faculty members disagree.

“The University of California’s purchase of OpenAI licenses for all of its students, faculty and staff is a significant new academic policy masquerading as a procurement issue,” said Greg Leazer, an associate professor of information studies at UCLA.
“ChatGPT reduces learning, and substitutes homogenized slop in place of the productive struggle of careful reading, discussion and writing.”

Research on whether AI helps college students learn is limited. A Harvard study published last year in Scientific Reports found that physics students learned more with a custom-built AI tutor than they did in class. But other studies have found little benefit when students use AI. Concerns about AI-assisted cheating are also widespread.
Miguel Craven, a UC Davis graduate student who serves as a student regent, said the deal could narrow a divide he has seen among students when it comes to AI.

“There are students who have access and have been paying for the premium subscription models for quite a long time,” Craven said. Other students “can’t afford to purchase those models. So the free resources are what they rely on, and it has led to an equity gap.”
An April Lumina Foundation-Gallup survey found that 57% of college students used AI for coursework at least weekly.

Camille Crittenden, executive director of CITRIS and the Banatao Institute — a UC research center that develops technology for social benefit and studies responsible AI — also expressed support for the purchase. “It’s important for UC to continue to be a leader, especially among public higher education systems, and to be able to offer these cutting-edge tools to be able to recruit and retain faculty and students,” Crittenden said.

Van Williams, UC’s chief information officer, said the deal makes UC users safer because their data won’t be used by OpenAI for use in improving its technology, which is what happens to much of the data absorbed through AI that is offered free to the public.

It’s hard to assess usage-based AI costs because because charges vary by model and the amount of information processed and generated, but UC said that under the agreement, it gets a 20% discount on OpenAI credits. OpenAI also has waived its $10 monthly per-user fee for Codex. Users get unlimited access to the ChatGPT base models. Access to more advanced models will require paid credits.
The deal does not stop UC campuses from using other AI tools, including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot.
Williams said UC’s contract also is supposed to give the university legal recourse if OpenAI causes harm.

The UC purchase comes after Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday in San Francisco Superior Court over a July incident in which hundreds of AI agents running on experimental OpenAI models escaped their testing environment and launched a two-day cyberattack on Hugging Face, a New York-based company.
OpenAI said the lawsuit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

The deal lands as UC seeks a larger public role in AI. On Wednesday, UC regents approved asking the state for $200 million to start an AI institute. It would test advanced AI models for safety and give state agencies, colleges and universities access to high-performance computing.

The institute is part of a $2.62-billion state funding request that also covers campus operations, building repairs and expanded medical training. UC typically receives only a fraction of what it requests.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/21/wid.headline: A widower lost his wedding ring. A used-car sale brought it back to him.
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/21/wid.author: Dan Simmons

paragraphs.text: Roger Reese and Fred Ambuehl are both 85 years old. Both served in Vietnam. Both live in Bemidji, the small northern Minnesota town known for it giant statues of Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox.

They had never met until early November, when Ambuehl and his wife, Vickie, approached Reese as he set up chairs for a concert by the Ambuehls’ country band. Reese regularly volunteers at community events.
“Do you know a Roger Reese?” one of them asked.
“I’m Roger Reese,” he replied with a chuckle.
The strangers had something that belonged to him: the wedding ring Reese had worn since marrying his late wife, Joan, in 1962 — and thought he’d lost forever months ago.
One day earlier this year, Reese drove his Ford Escape to Walmart to pick up some medication. It was his usual routine. What wasn’t usual: His wedding ring slipped off.
He’d heard a clinking sound and realized his ring was no longer on his finger. Joan died 17 years ago, but Reese never stopped wearing the ring.
He searched the parking lot and the car, but he found nothing.
“I realized it was gone,” Reese said. “But my wife was also gone, and I didn’t want to be without my wedding band.”
So he went to a local pawn shop, where he bought a gold ring similar to the one he lost. But it was never quite the same.
Not long after losing the ring, Reese decided to move to a senior center and sell his Ford Escape.

The SUV had only been at the Bob Lowth Ford dealership in Bemidji for a day when the Ambuehls saw it. It hadn’t even been cleaned out yet, but the couple immediately put an offer down. The 2024 model had only a few thousand miles on it. Vickie Ambuehl had turned 80 the day before, and the SUV was her birthday present.

While cleaning it later, Vickie found a ring in a door panel compartment. Her husband, who once worked at a pawnshop, confirmed it was real gold. They checked the glove box, which still had documents with Reese’s information. But because Reese had moved, the address was outdated.

The Ambuehls, whose four-person band regularly performs at senior centers, began asking at gigs if anyone knew Reese. On Nov. 3, as they prepared for a performance that would include country and western standards, they finally found the man they’d been looking for.

Vickie had the ring in her purse and returned it to Reese as other residents cheered and took photos. The lead singer in the band, Dennis Doeden, is a former publisher and longtime writer for the Bemidji Pioneer newspaper. He wrote up the story.

Reese met Joan in the early 1960s, when she was in nursing school. They married before he deployed to Vietnam. Reunited with his wedding ring more than six decades later, Reese was overcome with gratitude.
“That day when [Vickie] found the ring, it looked like my wife was smiling at me” in a picture he keeps of her in his residence, he said.
He decided to gift the pawnshop ring to Vickie. She said she only wanted a hug, which she got.

The Ambuehls sold the replacement ring to a local jeweler and will donate the $500 in proceeds to Bemidji Veterans Home, near where Reese lives, at a ceremony on Monday. They’ll play a concert there, too.

“That’s the entire story, and none of it’s nonsense,” said Reese, who spent 36 years with the U.S. Air Force’s Office of Special Investigations, traveling the world and often administering lie-detector tests.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: Desperate to curb drugs and crime, L.A. is building a fence around MacArthur Park
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: Ruben Vives, Hannah Fry

paragraphs.text: The problems plaguing MacArthur Park have spanned generations.

Los Angeles officials have battled waves of gang violence, homelessness, drugs and deaths in a picturesque green space surrounding a lake in the heart of one of America’s most densely populated neighborhoods.
But sustained improvement has proved difficult, and in recent years the park has seen a new surge in drug dealing and addiction. So now, Los Angeles is trying a new approach.

Officials are beginning to build a $2.3-million fence that they say will allow them to close the park at night and perform maintenance and other improvements. Construction crews began erecting a temporary chain-link fence on Tuesday, with an 8-foot-tall green barrier expected to be completed next year. The gate will be closed from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. and police will patrol the park to clear it out before closing, according to the city’s plans.

The fence is expected to alter the look of the grand park, built as an urban oasis that graced generations of L.A. postcards and was once the pride of Los Angeles. Supporters argue the barrier could be a major step in making the park a place people feel safe visiting again.
But some residents are skeptical.
Isaias De Leon, 41, who was entertaining his 3-year-old daughter by pushing her on the swing set at MacArthur Park on Friday, doesn’t see it as enough.
“A fence isn’t what we need, what we need is more security to keep us safe,” he said, adding he sees people use and deal drugs just outside the park.
The barrier is not intended to be permanent, Mayor Karen Bass said, and city officials will “evaluate its effectiveness over time.”

“In recent years, the park has faced significant challenges, including drug activity, crime, vandalism, graffiti and sanitation issues,” she said in a statement to The Times. “The city has responded with increased LAPD patrols and enforcement, enhanced sanitation services, improved lighting, and continued efforts to connect individuals experiencing homelessness with available resources and supportive services.”

On Friday, much of the park was empty aside from unhoused individuals who were sitting or napping on the grassy knolls near Park View and Wilshire Boulevard. The vendors who for years had operated on the corner of Alvarado Street selling food and other wares were gone.
An occasional breeze carried the scent of marijuana across the open space. A group of men smoking out of a pipe used to ingest methamphetamine were gathered at the park’s southern entrance.

Felipe Ruiz, 61, was among the unhoused individuals at the park on Friday. He became homeless four months ago after he lost vision in his left eye, lost his job as a cook at a Chinese restaurant and couldn’t make rent. Since then he’s made his way from Hollywood to MacArthur Park, spending just a few hours to get free meals.
But he quickly learned something about the park. “It’s not a safe place,” he said while eating a slice of Hawaiian pizza.

Nearby, more than 30 men and women stood in line to pick up a slice and some fruit. Seagulls and pigeons fought over scraps tossed their way. Ruiz said that when he visits the park, he rarely sees families with children and the playground is often empty.
A fence around the park made sense to him, he said, if it meant keeping people out at night when it gets even more dangerous.
“I don’t like to stay here too long because of the drugs and because people aren’t right,” he said.
The five-member Board of Recreation and Park Commissioners approved final plans for the fence last month, which will be funded in part by $1.6 million from the state budget.

Other improvements have already been completed or are underway, including new signage, LED fixture upgrades, security cameras, improvements to the restrooms and upgrades to the playground, including new surfacing.

Officials are looking to restore pedestrian access through the tunnel connecting the north and south sides of the park, improve accessibility, and add Wi-Fi access, solar lights, irrigation repairs and other landscaping improvements. There’s also a push to bring back pedal boats by fall 2027, said Jimmy Kim, general manager of the city’s Department of Recreation and Parks.
“The department has done a tremendous job doing improvements here,” he told commissioners at a meeting last month.
But similar previous undertakings to improve the park haven’t lasted.

In early 2022, the park reopened after a $1.5-million makeover that included new plants and shrubs, irrigation, lighting, an asphalt walkway, park benches and planters. Then-City Councilman Gil Cedillo said at the time the park was reopening “clean, safe and secure” for parents, seniors and children to enjoy.
Homelessness, crime and drug activity quickly returned.

Bright blue concrete benches were strewn with trash and marked with graffiti. Artists’ murals were left unrecognizable, covered with large bubble letters and other markings. Trash covered parking lots and grassy spaces, and debris was left floating on the 8-acre lake on the south end of MacArthur Park.

Police made 694 arrests at MacArthur Park and the 350 feet surrounding it in the first eight months of 2026, down slightly from the 781 arrests during the same period in 2025. The majority of the crimes were aggravated assault and robbery, though two rapes were also reported, according to data provided by the Los Angeles Police Department.
At smaller Lafayette Park nearby, which is fenced and closes at night, 36 arrests were reported between January and August of this year, LAPD data show.

Last summer, MacArthur Park became a topic of national discussion when President Trump sent masked immigration agents to storm the location in armored vehicles and on horseback. While it’s unclear how many people were detained in the operation, city officials saw the move as a blatant intimidation tactic in a public space at the center of a dense immigrant community.

Barry Milofsky, president of the city’s Cultural Heritage Commission, wrote in a letter to the parks commission in August that they were “apprehensive about the concept of closing off a civic monument to the public.” He urged them to consider other options before installing a fence.

Echo Park, which had faced similar challenges to MacArthur Park, had a temporary chain-link fence installed in 2021 while city officials cleared out a massive homeless encampment, cleaned and restored the park. That barrier was removed in 2023.

Efforts to revitalize MacArthur Park date back more than a half-century. In the park’s heyday, the surrounding neighborhoods were dotted with celebrity homes and fancy department stores. But the area declined, and beginning in the 1970s it became a first stop for generations of immigrants from Latin America.
In the late 1980s and ’90s, the LAPD battled the crack cocaine trade with a series of enforcement actions that yielded mixed results.

A decade later, crime concerns sparked a new effort to “take back” the park. New playground equipment and security cameras were added. A few years later, LAPD Chief William Bratton picked the park as a testing ground for stronger police enforcement efforts.
In May, federal agents and local authorities arrested more than a dozen people as part of a sweep called “Operation Free MacArthur Park,” targeting what authorities called an “open-air drug market.”

Norm Langer, the owner of Langer’s Deli, has been been among the most vocal business owners urging officials to clean up the park through efforts that include suspending the needle exchange program that operates there.
He said on Friday that the fence is “just one of several ingredients that are needed to secure the park and make it safe for our families and their children.”
“The ongoing actions by law enforcement are another,” he said.
Staff writer Dakota Smith contributed to this report.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/21.headline: A fixture behind the plate for two teams and part of ‘baseball’s first family’
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/21.author: Paul Duggan

paragraphs.text: For 80 years, baseball has been the Boone family business.
First, there was Ray Boone, a Navy veteran who joined the Cleveland Indians as an infielder after World War II and spent all or part of 13 seasons in the major leagues.
Next, his son Bob Boone, a rugged catcher who seemed impervious to pain, was a fixture behind the plate for the Philadelphia Phillies and California Angels in the 1970s and ’80s.

In the 1990s, Bob’s sons Bret and Aaron Boone, both infielders, debuted with the Seattle Mariners and Cincinnati Reds, respectively, and went on to have solid careers. Bret, a three-time all star, leads the clan in home runs with 252. Aaron, now manager of the New York Yankees, authored a legendary moment for that storied franchise in 2003, belting a walk-off homer in Game 7 of the American League Championship Series.

In the history of the sport, five families have had three generations of players in the big leagues. The Boones were the first and, many believe, the best. All told, they appeared in nine all-star games (Bret and Aaron faced each other in 2003), won 11 Gold Glove Awards for defensive excellence (seven for Bob, four for Bret) and earned two World Series rings (Ray in 1948, Bob in 1980). “Baseball’s First Family,” they’re called.
As Bret put it in a family memoir, “RBIs in your DNA.”

Bob Boone, who died Nov. 9 at 78, was the most accomplished of the bunch. Starting in the mid-1970s, when the Phillies were stocked with young talent and rising from cellar-dwellers to pennant contenders, Mr. Boone, the starting catcher, was the sturdy defensive backbone of those teams. He guided top-notch pitching staffs with exceptional skill while enduring the grueling physical toll of his position with remarkable toughness.

“Gramps used to tell Dad how special it was to be a ballplayer, and Dad told his sons the same thing,” Bret Boone wrote. “‘Never forget you’re playing the best game in the world.’ That’s something none of us ever forgot.”

In 1978, his sixth full season in the majors, Mr. Boone, who was only a so-so hitter in his career, collected his first Gold Glove as the National League’s top defensive catcher, ending the great Johnny Bench’s 10-year grip on the award. Mr. Boone won it again the following season. And in 1980, he was like a poised, rock-ribbed quarterback behind the plate as the Phillies erased decades of hardball heartbreak, winning the franchise’s first World Series title.
“He was a man of great integrity,” Bret Boone said in announcing his father’s death on social media. “He was a great dad, husband, and patriarch. … Baseball lost a great one today.”

By the end of 1981, Mr. Boone, a three-time all-star with Philadelphia, had caught 1,095 games for the team, then the second-most in Phillies history. But his once-passable hitting had fallen off sharply, and the organization, fearing he’d soon be washed up as a catcher, sold his contract to the Angels. This turned out to be a mistake.

Rejuvenated in California, Mr. Boone improved his hitting while his defensive skills and durability made him arguably the best catcher the Angels ever had. In seven seasons, he won four more Gold Gloves, appeared in his fourth all-star game, led the American League in games caught five times and threw out would-be base-stealers at well-above-average rates, leading the league in that category three times.

Mr. Boone, who holds the Angels’ record for games caught with 961, signed a free-agent contract with the Kansas City Royals before the 1989 season and promptly won his seventh Gold Glove. Only three catchers have more. And only two caught more games than Mr. Boone’s career total of 2,225. In 1990, at 42, he retired after 18 full seasons.

At 6-foot-2 and about 200 pounds, Mr. Boone credited his longevity to staying in shape. He pumped iron and practiced a martial art in clubhouses, where he could win a bet by doing hundreds of sit-ups uninterrupted.

“It’s an attitude,” he told Sports Illustrated in 1988, when he was 40. “The kung fu helps because you reach a level beyond pain, beyond exhaustion, and you always know you can do more. I tell myself it’s only pain. Can I play, or can’t I play? It’s just pain. I can play.”

Robert Raymond Boone (a direct descendant of Daniel Boone) was born in San Diego on Nov. 19, 1947, when his father, Ray, was a minor leaguer. Ray debuted with Cleveland late in the 1948 season and rode the bench as the Indians won the World Series. After he arrived in the majors for good in 1949, his firstborn son grew up playing in clubhouses, chatting with big league superstars and shagging batting-practice balls in the outfield.

Mr. Boone attended Stanford University on a baseball scholarship and earned an undergraduate degree in psychology in 1969. The Phillies drafted him that summer. After a stint in the minors, he spent a few weeks with the Phillies in 1972 and became the starting catcher the following spring.
In time, young Bret and his little brothers, Aaron and Matthew, were hanging around the Phillies batting cages or chasing flyballs before games.

“My kids had a bat in their hands before they could walk,” Mr. Boone told author Kevin Cook for his book “The Dad Report: Fathers, Sons and Baseball Families.” He said, “They were raised with the game in their blood, like me.”

Although he posted terrific numbers in the 1980 World Series, reaching base 11 times in 22 plate appearances, Mr. Boone might be better remembered by some fans for a crucial freak play that lives in Philadelphia lore, a miracle witnessed by 66,000 spectators in the Phillies’ old Veterans Stadium.

Leading the Royals in the series, three games to two, the Phillies were ahead, 4-1, in the ninth inning of Game 6, three outs away from a championship. But their weary relief pitcher Tug McGraw loaded the bases with one out. Then the Royals’ Frank White sliced a foul pop up to the right side. Mr. Boone, with a sprained ankle tightly wrapped, raced toward the arcing ball, as did first baseman Pete Rose.

What happened next, when the two converged at the lip of the Phillies dugout, would become a staple of blooper reels. As Rose looked on, Mr. Boone lifted his glove to make the catch, but the ball clanked off his mitt. He said he felt a jolt of terror as it caromed toward the ground — before Rose, reacting in a flash, reached down and speared it for the second out.
“I wanted to kiss him,” Mr. Boone recalled. McGraw struck out the next batter, and the Phillies finally celebrated a World Series title.

Starting in 1995, Mr. Boone managed the Royals until he was fired in 1997. Four years later, when he became manager of the Reds, son Aaron was about to begin his fifth season with the team. Aaron was named to the 2003 National League all-star team, while Bret, playing for the Mariners, was voted onto the American League squad. Ray Boone, nearly 80 and fighting cancer, and son Bob trekked to Chicago’s U.S. Cellular Field to see them play.
Two weeks after the game in July 2003, the Reds fired Mr. Boone and traded Aaron to the Yankees.
Besides his three sons, Mr. Boone is survived by his wife of 59 years, Susan Boone, and several grandchildren.

After his abortive managing career, Mr. Boone worked as a front office adviser for the Washington Nationals for 16 years. He resigned as a vice president in 2021 rather than comply with the organization’s covid-19 vaccination mandate.
In his elder years, he enjoyed relaxing at home in his memorabilia room with a row of TVs on a wall, watching manager Aaron Boone’s Yankees from his leather recliner.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.headline: Honeymoon over? Controller Mejia accuses L.A. Council of trying to sabotage Raman
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-21/.author: David Zahniser, Melissa Gomez

paragraphs.text: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman and members of the City Council made a public display of post-election unity last week, offering remarks that were designed to put the hard feelings of the campaign behind them.
It didn’t last long.

City Controller Kenneth Mejia, one of Raman’s fiercest advocates during the mayoral campaign, has gone back on the offensive, accusing council members of trying to undermine her authority before she even takes office.

Mejia, who serves on Raman’s transition team, assailed the council in recent days for placing two proposals for rewriting the City Charter on Friday’s meeting agenda, saying they were setting the stage for a last-minute power grab. Those proposals would weaken Raman’s authority as mayor, Mejia said on Instagram.
“The Council is trying to radically change the balance of power in City Hall without any public debate,” Mejia said.

One of the two proposals, authored by Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, would let the council remove a city department head by a two-thirds vote, a move that would reduce the mayor’s power to hire and fire top managers. The other proposal, written by Councilmember Monica Rodriguez, would give the council the power to overturn a mayor’s executive directive by a two-thirds vote.

Jurado and Rodriguez said their respective proposals were focused not on Raman but on other issues facing the city. Both were drafted in May — before Raman had made the top two in the primary election — at a time when the council was weighing a long list of charter revisions for the Nov. 3 ballot.
Neither proposal made the cut for this month’s ballot.

On Friday, the council sent the two proposals to a new council committee that was recently set up to vet charter reform proposals for the November 2028 ballot. No decisions have been made on any of those ideas, said Councilmember Tim McOsker, who heads the committee.

McOsker said the public will have many opportunities over the coming year and a half to weigh in not just on the Jurado and Rodriguez proposals, but on expanding the size of the council, lowering the voting age, creating a borough system and many other topics.
Any proposal endorsed by the committee will be presented to the council in 2028 for possible inclusion on the ballot, he said.

“This is a 2028 question,” McOsker told his colleagues. “And I do not want to be in the position that we were in in the last cycle, where all of this stuff, including analysis, either wasn’t done or was coming to us at the last minute.”
Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson offered a tougher assessment, saying it was not true that the proposals were written to target Raman.
“I’m loath to criticize any other elected member,” he said, “but when you tell a bold-faced lie [when] you know better about your colleagues, it has to be called out.”
Mejia responded hours later, saying the council’s handling of the matter was “evidence of a broken system in which the public is left in the dark.”
“These are bad proposals that would greatly weaken the Mayor’s executive power, essentially removing the Mayor’s ability to be the CEO of the city,” he said.

Raman spokesperson Liz Garcia said the mayor-elect’s team didn’t communicate with the city controller about his various statements criticizing the council. She said her boss also has strong doubts about the proposals.

“The Mayor-Elect has — for many years — also expressed concern that eroding executive authority makes city government less efficient, less accountable, and ultimately less effective in delivering services to residents,” Garcia said in a statement.

Jurado said she wrote her proposal last spring out of concern over the Los Angeles Police Department’s treatment of protesters and journalists at demonstrations against federal immigration raids. Those events have raised “urgent questions” about the council’s limited authority over the department’s leaders, she said in a statement.
“This was never about undermining the mayor,” Jurado said. “Mayor-elect Raman has made clear she intends to change LAPD leadership, and I have confidence she will address these concerns.”

Rodriguez said her motion was focused on the dozens of executive directives that have accumulated from different mayors over the last 20 years, dating back to the administration of former Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa.
“We have layers upon layers of these,” she said. “So are we going to clean things up or not?”

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-21/zo.headline: Zoox launches its first robotaxi rides in L.A. County
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-21/zo.author: Caroline Petrow-Cohen

paragraphs.text: The Bay Area-based robotaxi company Zoox put its first purpose-built autonomous vehicles on the road in Los Angeles County.
The pill-shaped vehicles rolled out Thursday in Santa Monica, where they will serve company employees and their friends and families. The wait list for public riders will open next year.

Though several companies are competing to scale robotaxis, Zoox vehicles are unique because the company built them from the ground up. Waymo, which leads the robotaxi race, uses existing vehicles retrofitted with autonomous technology.
Zoox taxis lack a steering wheel and gas pedal and feature interior seats facing each other. The vehicles can also roll in either direction without turning around.

The futuristic taxi is already common in parts of San Francisco and Las Vegas, where Zoox has served the public since last year. Public service is coming next to Atlanta, Miami and Austin, Texas, the company said.

“We’re excited to begin driving our purpose-built robotaxi in Santa Monica as we continue to grow in California,” said Ron Thaniel, senior director of policy and regulatory affairs at Zoox. “Great transportation starts with trust and transparency, and we’ve designed our operations to complement the way this community already moves.”
Zoox has been testing in the region since last spring, using a fleet of retrofitted Toyota SUVs. The SUVs will not be used to serve riders.
Zoox’s expansion into Los Angeles County comes as Waymo rapidly grows across the state, operating now in San Diego, swaths of the Bay Area and much of L.A. County.
Waymo, owned by Google’s parent company Alphabet, took a hit this week when the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned Waymo taxis from operating on the state’s freeways.
In response, Waymo voluntarily paused all its freeway operations until safety issues have been resolved.

Tesla is also entering the robotaxi market with the Cybercab, a golden two-seat self-driving vehicle operating in Austin. The launch of the Cybercab in September prompted an investigation from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
Zoox has surpassed 1 million riders in San Francisco and Las Vegas and has plans to expand its service area in Los Angeles County beyond Santa Monica.

“As Santa Monica continues to innovate, our priority remains the safety, accessibility and trust of our community,” said Santa Monica City Manager Oliver Chi. “We appreciate that Zoox is taking a measured, collaborative approach to its rollout.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/europe/prin.headline: Catherine, Princess of Wales, Documents Life With Cancer in BBC Film

paragraphs.text: Catherine, Princess of Wales, documented her life since being diagnosed with cancer in a new film that will air this month on the BBC, Kensington Palace announced on Saturday.

Called “Heal,” the film follows the princess as she participates in the National Three Peaks Challenge, which involves hiking up the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales. Her challenge supports the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

“Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” Catherine, 44, says in a trailer for the film, which will be released in Britain on Nov. 29 and the next day in the United States. “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The princess revealed in a video in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer and begun chemotherapy, only a month after King Charles III had disclosed his own cancer diagnosis and treatment. The back-to-back announcements were a severe blow to the royal family, which has not said which cancers the princess and the king have.

Windsor Palace has said the king is still undergoing treatment, but at a scaled back pace. Kensington Palace announced in January 2025 that the princess was in remission. The cancer was detected after she was hospitalized for abdominal surgery.
The new film shows Catherine “exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness,” palace officials said on Saturday.

“The princess reflects on her own experience alongside individuals navigating their own health journeys,” the palace said in a news release. “Together, they explore the profound impact serious illness can have on the whole person, and the people, places and experiences that can help us heal.”

Catherine withdrew from public life after her diagnosis, making her first appearance several months later. At the time, in the summer of 2024, she said that “as anyone going through chemotherapy will know, there are good days and bad days.”

Since then, however, she has slowly returned to a more normal schedule for a working royal. In early 2025, she met with other cancer patients at a hospital in London. In May, she made her first official overseas trip since the diagnosis, traveling to Reggio Emilia, Italy, where she was greeted in the town’s main square by a throng of people.
The trailer for the new film shows the princess dressed in outdoor wear and a baseball cap as she hikes up the mountains.

“It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone,” she says. “Things can renew and grow. You’re nearly there. Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-19/.headline: Why Erewhon's $749 Thanksgiving feast highlights a holiday grocery divide
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-19/.author: Karen Garcia

paragraphs.text: The “K-shaped economy” is coming to the Thanksgiving table.
When it comes to pre-made holiday feasts from supermarkets, there is one part of America trying to save as much as they can and another segment willing to pay big for the luxury experience.
The average cost of a Thanksgiving meal for 10 people is an estimated $58.63, up 6.3% compared to 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation’s 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner survey.
But retailers are also offering pre-made meals for under $100, with the Vallarta Supermarkets leading the way with an $89.99 feast that serves eight, and Ralphs is not far behind.
Then there is a meal for the other half. For $749, Erewhon shoppers can preorder the “ultimate organic feast,” which includes a free-range cooked turkey as the main and all the fixings.
The entire feast is estimated to feed between eight and 10 people, about $74.90 per person.
Erewhon is famous for its organic gourmet food, cult-like following and high prices. So the market’s newest meal is generating the usual snickers.

Brandon Hau, a digital creator in Northern California, called the meal a social experiment in a video on Instagram. “Erewhon has to be out of their ... minds because what do you mean their Thanksgiving feast is $749,” he said.
But food experts say it underscores a larger economic divide.

For Ralphs and other conventional grocery stores, “it’s incumbent upon them to have food that is at a price point that is affordable for all quintiles of U.S. households in terms of earnings,” said Ricky Volpe, a professor in the agribusiness department at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. “Erewhon and Whole Foods are in a different position because of the demographics to which they’re appealing.”

“The Erewhon meal is sort of an interesting anecdote, and it exists because there’s a demand for that sort of thing, but that’s not in any way reflective of affordability in the United States,” he added.
Whether a person is buying the “ultimate organic feast” or another ready-made meal, it’s a choice.

Pre-made or ready-made options will always cost more than buying ingredients and cooking a meal yourself. That’s because consumers are paying for the labor, the staff who are cooking the meal, packaging and the convenience on top of the food product, said Jeffrey Dorfman, professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics at North Carolina State University.
It’s certainly possible to spend less than $100 on a full meal, Dorfman said. But some people want to splurge.
“There are people who do spend hundreds of dollars, maybe even $1,000, if they buy some nice wine and three or four different pies for desserts,” he said.

When the American Farm Bureau Federation surveyed the average price of serving a Thanksgiving meal, researchers weighted the cost of the complete menu, including the fixings, which includes the following ingredients: a 16-pound turkey, whole milk, carrots, celery, cranberries, cubed stuffing, dinner rolls, frozen green peas, sweet potatoes, pumpkin pie mix, frozen pie crusts, heavy whipping cream, ham, frozen green beans and russet potatoes.
Here are several ready-made options offered by Southern California grocery stores.
Vallarta
Vallarta Supermarkets is promoting an $89.99 fully cooked meal estimated to feed about six to eight people — an estimated $11.24 a plate.
What’s on the menu: A butterball turkey, creamy mashed potatoes, homestyle gravy, stuffing and cranberry orange relish.
Ralphs
Ralphs is offering a Kroger-brand-inspired pre-made meal for $95, enough to feed about six to eight people for $11.87 each.

What’s on the menu: A bone-in turkey served with Kroger-brand sides including homestyle stuffing, green bean casserole, maple pecan mashed sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes, and classic gravy.
Sprouts
Sprouts is promoting an organic turkey meal that serves six for $129.99, which comes to $21.66 per person.
What’s on the menu: An organic turkey, organic sourdough stuffing, Yukon gold mashed potatoes, turkey gravy and cranberry sauce.
Bristol Farms
For about eight to 12 guests, Bristol Farms’ offering is $279.99, an estimated $23.33 per person.

What’s on the menu: An organic turkey alongside turkey gravy, mashed potatoes, traditional stuffing with Italian sausage, cornbread stuffing, cranberry relish, green bean Almondine, roasted Brussels sprouts with Applewood bacon and fig balsamic glaze, creamed corn and brioche dinner rolls.
Whole Foods
Whole Foods Market’s “Thanksgiving Extravaganza for 12,” costing customers $599.99, which comes out to $49.99 a head.

What’s on the menu: Two entrées, a roasted turkey with turkey gravy and a maple bourbon ham with brown sugar citrus glaze. The sides include sea salt and cracked pepper green beans, velvety creamed spinach, roasted koginut squash with dried cranberries and walnuts, creamy mashed Yukon Gold potatoes, classic holiday herb stuffing, zesty cranberry-orange sauce, aromatic butternut squash soup, Brussels sprouts, beet and butternut harvest salad, brioche dinner rolls. It also comes with not one but two desserts: apple pie and pumpkin pie.
Erewhon
Erewhon’s “ultimate organic feast” can be pre-ordered for $749. The serving size is for eight to 10 people, about $74.90 per person.

What’s on the menu: A free-range cooked turkey as the main showstopper served with sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, Brussels sprouts, garlic mashed potatoes and turkey gravy. The meal also comes with dessert, a deep-dish pumpkin pie.
When it comes to Erewhon’s Thanksgiving meal, one commenter on Hau’s Instagram video said, “8-10 people in Los Angeles, 4-5 people in the real world.”
“I don’t know who is buying this, but props to you,” Hau said in his post.

livescience.com/space/winter-stargazing-.headline: Winter stargazing 2026: The best skywatching sights this winter (and how to see them)
livescience.com/space/winter-stargazing-.author: Kimberley Lane

paragraphs.text: Winter is an incredible time for stargazing. With the long hours of darkness and an impressive variety of celestial objects on display, it's easy to fall in love with the night sky during the winter. Whether you have binoculars, a telescope, a smart telescope or are just observing with your eyes, there's something for everyone to enjoy over the coming months.

We've listed all the best sights to see this winter, including the supermoons, star clusters, galaxies and deep-sky nebulae that are best placed in the sky in December, January and February. We see the return of Orion and the Pleiades, with Jupiter and Saturn also making their way back into the night sky, while December also has one of the best and brightest meteor showers of the entire year — the Geminids.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of everything you can see — we'd be here until July — but just a collection of some of our favorite winter sights. Some, like the supermoons and planets, are specific to 2026/2027 timings, but the constellations and deep sky objects we see over the winter are something stargazers look forward to all year. Something to get us through the cold, dreary weather, and a reassuring sign that we made it through another year.
Lunar & planetary
Three winter supermoons

This winter is host to three consecutive supermoons (in addition to the supermoon we had in November, making four in a row). The first, and the most festive, is the Christmas Eve supermoon, peaking on December 24, 2026, at 01:28 UTC (which works out as late evening on the 23rd in North America). This last moon of the year is traditionally called the Cold Moon, and this supermoon will look up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than a normal full moon.

The first full moon of 2027, known as the Wolf Moon, peaks on January 22, 2027 at 12:17 UTC. Finally, the super Snow Moon peaks on February 20, 2027 at 23:24 UTC, coinciding with a penumbral lunar eclipse. This is when the sun, moon and Earth line up loosely during a full moon, causing the moon to pass through the Earth's faint outer shadow — the penumbra. During this type of eclipse, the moon only dims slightly, so it won't be nearly as dramatic as a blood moon eclipse.
Annular solar eclipse

Observers in South America and Africa will witness an annular solar eclipse on February 6, 2027, peaking at around 16:00 UTC. It will appear as a "ring of fire" in the sky, as an annular solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between Earth and the sun when the moon is near or at its farthest from Earth, known as apogee. Unlike a total solar eclipse, the sun isn't totally blocked, and the sky doesn't turn dark.
Saturn in the evening sky

Since Saturn made its return to the evening sky in the fall, it rises earlier and earlier over the winter months, making this a great time to observe Saturn at a reasonable hour. There are still a few years before we will see the rings at full tilt again, but in 2026/2027 we can start to see more details in the rings after the planet appeared edge-on last year.

To get a good glimpse of Saturn this winter, you'll need a telescope with at least 4 or 5 inches of aperture and a good eyepiece that gives you at least 100x magnification. Smart telescopes and binoculars don't have the reach, so this is a job for an observational telescope. But that's all right; the hill we'll die on is that there's nothing that'll take your breath away quite like seeing Saturn's rings with your own eyes.
Jupiter at opposition

Jupiter will reach opposition on the night of February 10-11, 2027, when it will be at its brightest and closest to Earth, making it appear its largest in the sky. This is the perfect time to observe it with your telescope to see the bands and the Great Red Spot, as well as its four Galilean moons. You'll be able to see the moons with a pair of big astronomy binoculars (we can see them with our 15x70’s), but you'll need a telescope to make out any of the finer details on the planet itself.
Mars at opposition

After almost a year of absence, Mars made its return to the evening sky in November (albeit quite late in the evening) and will reach opposition on February 19, 2027. Despite being one of our closest neighboring planets, Mars is notoriously difficult to get any meaningful observations with via a telescope, so its opposition is the best chance you'll have.

You'd be forgiven for thinking that because Mars is technically closer to Earth than Jupiter, Saturn and deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy or the Orion Nebula, viewing it through a telescope would be a breeze, but that's not the case. Mars is very small, with low-contrast features, and only comes observably close to Earth for a few months at a time around every 26-27 months, so it demands quite a lot from a telescope. Even with larger telescopes, it'll only show up as a fuzzy orange dot most of the time.

If you want to try viewing Mars with a telescope this opposition, you'll need 4-6 inches of aperture minimum, depending on what kind of telescope you have. However, for Mars, it's arguably more important to have good seeing (unfortunate with the nearly full moon on this day), excellent quality optics, a stable (preferably motorized) mount, a good focuser and an eyepiece with good eye relief that gives 100x magnification or more to observe any of the planet's finer details.
Alternatively, if you're more of a beginner and are just starting your stargazing hobby, you can head outside with just your eyes and go "Hey look, there's Mars. Cool!" and be done with it.
Meteor showers
Geminids

The Geminids meteor shower is active from December 4-20, peaking on the night of December 13-14, 2026. The waxing crescent moon sets early, leaving dark skies after around 9 pm for prime meteor viewing, and this is one of the few meteor showers that very kindly peaks before midnight.

The Geminids are one of the strongest meteor showers of the year, and this year’s show is expected to have around 120 to 150 meteors per hour under clear, dark skies — making it an exciting opportunity for astrophotography.

Unlike most meteor showers, which come from icy comets, the Geminids originate from a rocky asteroid called 3200 Phaethon. The debris from this asteroid is much denser than the dust from comets, making it able to survive deeper into the atmosphere before burning up. This results in brighter, stronger and more colorful fireballs than the other meteor showers.
Ursids
If the Geminids left you hooked on meteor showers, you'll only have a few weeks to wait until the Ursids peak on December 22-23, 2026.

However, there are a couple of hurdles here. First, the activity rate is usually quite low — between 5 and 10 meteors per hour. Second, the nearly full moon will hinder visibility and limit sightings to only the brightest meteors. However, as they originate from Ursa Minor, which is circumpolar, the peak viewing time of 21:00-22:00 UTC is much friendlier than the showers that peak in the middle of the night, so it won't require an unreasonable amount of commitment if you do want to catch them.
Quadrantids

The first meteor shower of 2027, the Quadrantids, is active between December 28, 2026 and January 28, 2027, peaking on the night of January 3-4, 2027. The thin waning crescent moon won't interfere with viewing conditions, and we could see up to 100-120 meteors per hour. The best time to view will be from midnight through to the pre-dawn hours, when the radiant point, Bootes, is highest in the sky.
Constellations, asterisms and star clusters
Sirius and Canis Major

Canis Major (the "Greater Dog") is visible over the winter months through until spring, and is easily recognisable by Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's one of the closest stars to our solar system, sitting 8.6 light-years away, and due to its distance and apparent magnitude, its twinkling and flashes of color are particularly noticeable. This is known as scintillation, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bends starlight as it passes through different layers of air. It's especially noticeable when Sirius is low in the sky, as the light has more atmosphere to pass through.

You don't need any specialist gear to spot Sirius — it's easily visible with the naked eye. However, if you do have a pair of binoculars, you can even try to spot it in the daytime at certain times of the year.
Canis Minor

Look above Canis Major, and you'll find Canis Minor — the "Little Dog". It primarily consists of two bright stars: Procyon and Gomeisa, the former making up a key part of the Winter Triangle and Winter Hexagon. Canis Minor is a fairly faint constellation, but a pair of binoculars will give you a better view.

Canis Minor and Canis Major are most famously known as the loyal hunting dogs of Orion, who spent seven years pursuing the Pleiades sisters to no avail. He should have just led with the fact that he had two dogs.
Orion's belt

Speaking of Orion, one of the most recognizable sights in the night sky is Orion's belt, consisting of three bright stars in a straight line: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Because of its prominence in the winter sky, Orion's belt has served as a universal celestial marker for navigation, timekeeping and mythologies across human history. The entire Orion constellation is a favorite among stargazers because there's so much to see, both with the naked eye and through binoculars or a telescope.

Another prominent feature of the Orion constellation is Betelgeuse. This red supergiant is easily visible to the naked eye, and astronomers expect it to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. When that eventually happens, it will become visible in broad daylight and shine as brightly as the full moon for a few months. Betelgeuse, Sirius (Canis Major) and Procyon (Canis Minor) make up the Winter Triangle.

There's also Rigel, the brightest star in the constellation, which marks the hunter's foot, and Orion's Sword, a hanging line of stars just below the belt, which contains the Orion Nebula (more on that later).
Taurus, the Bull (and the Pleiades)

Although Taurus returned to the evening sky in the fall, winter offers the best viewing time because it sits higher earlier in the evening. The brightest star in the constellation, Aldebaran, is easily recognizable as an orange-red star that marks the bull's eye.

With a pair of binoculars, you'll be able to see two beautiful star clusters — the Pleiades (M45) and the Hyades. The former is a bright open star cluster consisting of seven stars (also known as the Seven Sisters) that you can just about see with the naked eye under very dark skies, and the latter is a V-shaped open cluster that forms the face and head of the bull.
The Pleiades is an ideal first target if you're thinking of buying an entry-level smart telescope, and it's also easy to pick out in wide-field iPhone photos of the night sky.
Auriga
Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation high in the sky between Taurus and Gemini, and is home to a few star clusters to observe this winter.

M36, the Pinwheel Cluster, contains around 60 to 100 stars and is located north of the star El Nath in Auriga. M38, known as the Starfish Cluster, contains over 100 stars, with its brightest forming an X shape, giving it a starfish-like appearance. Finally, M37, known as the Salt and Pepper Cluster, is the brightest and richest cluster in the constellation and contains over 500 stars.
Gemini, the Twins

Not only is Gemini the radiant point of the Geminids meteor shower, but its two most prominent stars, Pollux and Castor, are a very recognizable winter target in the night sky. Pollux is an orange giant star and the constellation's brightest point, while Castor appears blue. Although Castor looks like one star to the naked eye, it's actually a complex multiple star system, consisting of three distinct binary pairs: Castor A, Castor B and Castor C. With a small telescope, you can split Castor into its two main pairs, Castor Aa and Castor Ba.
Gemini also contains M35, a large open cluster also known as the Shoe Buckle Cluster, which you can easily view with binoculars.
Winter Hexagon

It’s not an official constellation, but the Winter Hexagon (also known as the Winter Circle) is a recognizable pattern of prominent stars in the winter sky. It consists of Rigel (Orion), Aldebaran (Taurus), Capella (Auriga), Pollux (Gemini), Procyon (Canis Minor) and Sirius (Canis Major).
Once you spot all of the stars that make up the Winter Hexagon, it provides an easy way to navigate your way around the night sky with your binoculars or telescope.
Deep sky nebulas and galaxies
Orion Nebula (M42)

Probably everyone's favorite nebula, largely because it's very easy to spot. It's located in Orion's sword, just below Orion's belt, and when conditions are dark enough, you can even see it with the naked eye and identify it in smartphone photos. Binoculars reveal it as a faint smudge, while telescopes give you a better view of the bright, glowing gas. It's also a wonderful target for smart telescopes with a wide field of view.

While you're there, you can find the Running Man Nebula, a bright reflection nebula complex located just north of the Orion Nebula — and it can be captured in the same frame if you're photographing it. If nebulas are your thing, Orion is absolutely packed with them, including the Casper the Friendly Ghost Nebula (M78), the Monkey Head Nebula (NGC 2174) and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118), although many of Orion's nebulas are quite faint and tricky to capture, requiring long integration times.
Another great target in Orion is….
Horsehead (IC 434) and Flame Nebula (NGC 2024)

The Horsehead and Flame Nebula in Orion is another popular target for smart telescopes, as it takes up a big portion of the frame and doesn't need a super-long integration time to get a decent, web-ready image (although we'd always recommend shooting for as long as you can).

The Flame and Horsehead are technically two separate entities, but are often paired together due to their close apparent proximity, often fitting inside the same frame. The Flame Nebula is a bright, vibrant emission nebula that gets its name from its fiery network of dark, dense dust lanes. The Horsehead Nebula, on the other hand, is a dark nebula. It's composed of a dense cloud of molecular dust and gas that blocks the light from the emission nebula and stars around it. As the name suggests, this dark nebula takes on the form of a horse's head and neck.
Rosette Nebula (NGC 2237)

The Rosette Nebula is a vast, star-forming region in the constellation of Monoceros and is a fantastic astrophotography target. Its large, flower-like appearance comes from stellar winds and radiation from the central cluster of young stars. The best time to view and photograph the Rosette Nebula is from January, when Monoceros climbs higher and higher in the evening sky.
California Nebula (NGC 1499)

The California Nebula lives in the constellation Perseus and gets its name from its resemblance to the U.S. state. This famous emission nebula is made up of ionized gas from the nearby Xi Persei, giving it its vibrant red and pink appearance. It has an apparent size of approximately 2.5 degrees, making it a great target for astrophotography and smart telescopes, as it appears quite large in the frame. Peak visibility of the California Nebula is from now until February.
Tadpole Nebula (IC 410)

12,000 light-years away, in the constellation Auriga, you'll find the Tadpole Nebula — a beautiful emission nebula and active stellar nursery. It spans 100 light-years across and makes for a stunning smart telescope target. It gets its name from the distinct, prominent gas and dust pillars that resemble cosmic tadpoles swimming through space — only these tadpoles are around 10 light-years long.
