If you're using a smart telescope or astrophotography camera, you'll typically need an integration time of 2-3 hours to bring out more structure in the nebulosity, although longer sessions will yield better results.
Flaming Star Nebula (IC 405)

Also in Auriga is the Flaming Star Nebula, although this nebula is much closer to Earth — around 1,500 light-years away — and spans about 5 light-years across. Despite being "smaller" than other targets, it appears quite big in the frame of a smart telescope due to its distance from Earth. It's best seen throughout late autumn and winter when Auriga is climbing high in the sky.

The Flaming Star Nebula is an emission and reflection nebula, with each type of nebulosity responding to different filters. In this instance, capturing two sets of data to stack in astrophotography software can help reveal more detail and colors. Broadband filter exposures capture the full range of visible light, including the blue light reflected by dust, as well as natural star colors. Narrowband or dual-band filters isolate specific emission wavelengths, such as hydrogen-alpha (Ha) and oxygen-III (OIII). By using these filters for separate sessions, your final image will show the red glow from the emission nebula and the blue tones from the reflective dust.

theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/21/brit.headline: British man recalls ‘despair’ over son’s death after fall from Cyprus window
theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/21/brit.author: Patrick Daly

paragraphs.text: A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel & Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.
The 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster said: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.
“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”
The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he said. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

The charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.
At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.
The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.
Foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.
Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.
“It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/21/t.headline: White House seeks to limit information contractors should share with Congress
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/21/t.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump has issued an executive order ordering federal contractors to inform the White House about any congressional requests for information about their work with the government, and withhold any information the government considers confidential or protected by executive privilege.

It is the White House’s latest move pushing back against congressional oversight as it prepares itself for an aggressive fight against planned investigations from a Congress that will be led by Democrats in January.

Friday’s order said that “certain congressional leaders” had been “seeking confidential executive branch information from agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the Federal Government.”
Contractors who fail to comply with these requirements could see their existing contracts canceled and potentially be barred from future federal work, said the order, which was issued late Friday.

“The executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without fear that confidential information will be released to unauthorized third parties,” the order added.

Legal experts have previously told The Post they expect the issue of whether the Trump administration’s communications with outside figures could be covered by executive privilege to be fiercely debated, and likely to wind up being tested in court.

The White House has taken several steps to prepare for clashes with Democrats over congressional oversight and legislative probes next year. Meanwhile, private companies have been scrambling to prepare for subpoenas as the next Congress is expected to focus more than usual on the private sector and companies that had dealings with the Trump administration.
On Monday, White House counsel Will Scharf issued an internal directive requiring federal agencies to seek White House approval before any personnel testify before Congress.

And on Nov. 11, the White House released a letter from Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California), who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee in the new Congress. That letter accused Democrats of “abusive and capricious threats” and said the administration would resist congressional subpoenas on the grounds that they lack a “legitimate legislative purpose.”
Garcia described the letter as an intimidation tactic, telling The Post: “We’re not going to be intimidated, and the president’s not going to stop us from investigation.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/rmd-deadline-penalty.headline: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/rmd-deadline-penalty.author: Kate Dore, CFP®, EA

paragraphs.text: Every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec. 31.
Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty, experts said.
"One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," said certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon.
Most retirees must start RMDs from pretax accounts at age 73. The withdrawal is based on the previous year's account balances on Dec. 31, your age and an IRS "life expectancy factor."
The first annual RMD deadline is April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and future withdrawals are due by Dec. 31. If you wait until April 1 for the first one, you'll need two RMDs that year.
RMDs also apply to certain inherited IRAs if the original IRA owner reached RMD age before their death.

In 2023, more than 14.8 million taxpayers age 70 or older had a traditional individual retirement account, according to the latest IRS data. The average year-end market value of the accounts was about $330,000.
Don't miss the RMD deadline
Deferring RMDs until the last minute raises the likelihood of mistakes, such as overlooking certain retirement accounts or making withdrawal calculation errors, Canellopoulos said.

Some 7% of Vanguard investors at RMD age missed their yearly withdrawal in 2025, up slightly from 6.7% in 2024, according to a Vanguard analysis of about 400,000 RMD-age retirees with IRA balances published in December 2025.
One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute.Alex CanellopoulosDirector of wealth at Vista Capital Partners
Among those investors, the average missed RMD was $10,500 in 2025, Vanguard told CNBC.

Investors who don't take RMDs by the annual deadline may owe an excise tax to the IRS, worth up to 25% of the amount they should have withdrawn. For example, the excise tax could be up to $2,625 for a $10,500 missed RMD.
How to reduce the IRS penalty for missed RMDs
Mistakes happen, of course.
If investors miss a required withdrawal, they could reduce the penalty to 10% if they "timely corrected" the RMD within two years and file Form 5329, according to the IRS.

In some cases, the IRS could waive the penalty entirely due to "reasonable error" if investors take "reasonable steps" to fix the shortfall, according to the agency. Investors can file Form 5329 with a letter of explanation to request the waiver.

"If you don't ask, you're not going to get it," said certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird. "I've never heard of anybody being denied the waiver."
Charitable transfers could cover RMDs
Investors who give to charity may be skipping a specific donation strategy that can reduce or eliminate their annual RMDs, according to Lawrence Pon, a CFP and CPA based in Redwood City, California.
They can use a so-called qualified charitable distribution, or QCD, Pon said.
A QCD has a dual tax benefit: It doesn't count as taxable income and may also satisfy at least part of an investor's yearly RMD, Pon said.

The move requires a direct transfer from an investor's pretax IRA to an eligible nonprofit organization. They can donate up to $111,000 in 2026. While QCD eligibility begins at age 70½, transfers won't start counting toward RMDs until an investor reaches their RMD age.

Generally, taxpayers only get a tax break for large charitable donations if they itemize deductions on their tax returns. But QCDs still provide a tax benefit for charitable gifts when investors use the standard deduction.
QCDs "provide a real benefit if you are not itemizing [tax deductions]," said Pon.

While there's no tax deduction for QCDs, the transfer won't increase a taxpayer's adjusted gross income, or AGI. Raising AGI can cause other tax consequences, such as higher premiums for Medicare Part B and Part D.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/alaska-your-ne.headline: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/alaska-your-ne.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.

Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.

Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.

“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.

Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.
“Ha, yes, that’s me,” he replied.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

Amanda Silberling is a senior writer at TechCrunch covering the intersection of technology and culture. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261120.headline: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

paragraphs.text: Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/21/never-wanted.headline: I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/21/never-wanted.author: Cepee Tabibian

paragraphs.text: I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas. My manager was only a few years older than me, and while my coworkers seemed motivated by the idea of working their way up to his position, I felt no desire to follow that path.

It all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb. I wanted to work, but I couldn't wrap my head around building my whole identity around a job.

I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve. For a long time, I wondered if something was wrong with me. It wasn't until I finally made a long-term move abroad about a decade ago that I realized it was okay to want something different.
I never dreamed about traditional milestones
After college, I got a job in travel sales. I was good at it. Talking about travel all day suited the wanderlust I'd carried since my first trip abroad in my teens.

I continued working in sales, marketing and the odd temp role for years. But they were always just jobs. I didn't feel like they defined me or feel a calling to an industry or title the way people around me seemed to.

Of course, I wanted financial stability, but I was unwilling to sacrifice my time and well-being to get it. I just didn't connect with the version of ambition that meant grinding toward a corner office. What I wanted the most wasn't status; it was freedom, growth and new experiences.

The wanderlust eventually caught up to me, and at 26 I moved to Spain to teach English. Even though I was working, people saw it as taking a year off from my career and warned me it could damage my resume. I simply didn't care. Living for my resume had never made sense to me.

Looking back, I think being abroad offered an escape from the pressure to chase the traditional path of the American Dream. There, I felt free to enjoy life and figure out who I was without worrying about what box I needed to tick next.

I wanted to stay in Spain, but I couldn't find a visa that would let me live there long-term, so I returned to the U.S. I became a serial job hopper for almost 10 years, quitting a job every year to spend summers visiting friends in the Netherlands, the U.K. and Switzerland or solo traveling in Spain on the money I'd saved up.

On the personal side, I wasn't in a rush to get married or have kids. In my 30s, single and childfree, I felt like I was failing at adulthood, even though deep down, I didn't actually want the things I was supposedly behind on. Settling down just because everyone else was doing it never felt right to me.

And I couldn't shake the dream of living in Europe. In my 20s, people mostly assumed my desire to travel was a phase. By my 30s, the conversations had shifted and I was getting pulled aside. Friends, family and colleagues all had some version of the same message: It was time to get serious and build a life in Texas.
But my gut said to try one more time. So I did.
Moving abroad helped me redefine success

In 2015, on my fourth attempt, I finally made it to Spain for good. It was scary to shake things up when everyone around me was settling down, but deep down I knew at 35, this was my chance to stop trying to conform and start building a life that felt right for me.

In my new home, the pace was slower. I quickly noticed that people actually took their vacations. Strangers at a dinner party didn't immediately ask me what I did for work. Adults in their 30s, 40s and beyond were out living full social lives. Single, childfree women my age didn't feel like an anomaly.

Living abroad didn't solve everything overnight. I still had to figure out how to support myself. But having the space to define myself professionally without constant judgment changed what felt possible.

In 2017, I launched She Hit Refresh, where I help women over 30 figure out how to move to Europe and build new lives for themselves. It's not something I could have created from anywhere else, with any other experience than my own.

In the process, I've met so many others who left corporate America behind to create something different for themselves. I've seen more women asking the same questions I spent years asking myself. Burnt out, disillusioned with hustle culture, realizing that checking all the boxes of the American Dream they grew up on didn't deliver the feeling they were promised.

We're all figuring it out together; each of us writing a version of a life that didn't fit a standard template. Moving abroad helped me understand that success, for me, was never about earning more or owning more. It was always about more ease, more time, more space, more life.
For years, I thought I was behind. I felt like something was wrong with me for wanting a different kind of life. Looking back, I just hadn't found my place yet.

Cepee Tabibian is the founder of She Hit Refresh, where she's helped over 24,000 women age 30+ plan their move abroad. Grab her free Move Abroad After 30 Guide to start planning your own move. The daughter of Colombian and Iranian immigrants, Cepee grew up in Houston, Texas, before becoming an immigrant herself in Spain. Follow her @shehitrefresh.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/c5v.headline: Lewis Moody: Ex-captain joins England side to face New Zealand's haka before Nations Championship match
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/c5v.author: Mike Henson

paragraphs.text: Former England captain Lewis Moody joined the current team to face New Zealand's haka in an emotional start to Saturday's Test match at Allianz Stadium.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) last year, stood at the centre of England's line-up - between captain Maro Itoje and one of the team's vice-captains, Ellis Genge - as they faced up to the traditional pre-match challenge.

Led by Genge's fellow vice-captains Ollie Chessum and Jamie George, England then advanced to form a V shape, similar to the formation they took before last year's victory and the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final win against the All Blacks.
Moody, who was embraced by most of England's team in the aftermath of the challenge and its acceptance, also delivered the match ball.
With Twickenham energised, England started the match fast, with Henry Slade getting on the end of a Fin Smith grubber kick to score the first try after just four minutes.
All of England's players are wearing boots emblazoned with the logo of Moody's Front Up to MND campaign, to which signed warm-up and match-worn shirts will be donated.
The campaign's first fundraising drive is a mass-participation coastal walk in June, which aims to raise more than £1m to fund research into the disease.

A statement from England Rugby said: "As a hugely respected former England captain, it was important to the England men's team to show their support for Lewis and to involve him in many areas of the match day, including on the pitch.
"Supporting Lewis and Front Up reflects the game's commitment to standing alongside those affected by MND, and to help raise awareness and funds for research."
Moody delivered the match ball before England's victory over Australia last autumn, a few weeks after he revealed his diagnosis in an interview with BBC Breakfast.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.headline: Armed with guns and sword, owner of squatter removal company cleared out a home. Now he faces felonies
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-20/.author: Salvador Hernandez

paragraphs.text: The owner of a squatter removal company is headed to court, where he faces multiple felony charges alleging his company used guns and swords to remove people from a San Bruno home.

ASAP Squatter Removal claims on its website that it has a 95% success rate and touts the use of “professional-grade tactical gear,” including firearms, ballistic armor, flash bangs, tear gas and custom ammunition, to remove squatters. The company doesn’t make any mention of using samurai swords but its owner, James Jacobs, appears in a picture on the website wielding a long sword.

Now Jacobs faces seven felony counts in San Mateo County, where he and contractors with his company are accused of storming into a San Bruno home on Jan. 6 wielding swords and guns, and ordering people inside the home to leave. The charges include first-degree burglary, two counts of assault with a semiautomatic firearm, and four counts of false imprisonment by violence. Jacobs is set to appear in court on Dec. 3, according to court records.
Jacobs has pleaded not guilty. He did not immediately respond to requests for comment through his company, and his attorney also did not immediately respond.
In a recent interview with the San Francisco Chronicle, Jacobs described himself as a “moral crusader” and embraced the reputation he has earned as a vigilante.
“If you’re calling me a vigilante, then you’re admitting that basically there’s an issue with the system,” he told the Chronicle.
But prosecutors allege Jacob’s company crossed a line.

After criminal charges were filed against Jacobs in March, San Mateo County Dist. Atty. Stephen M. Wagstaffe said the use of weapons to evict squatters raised the possibility that the incident could have gone violently wrong.
“Anytime weapons are brought into a circumstance, there’s a danger,” Wagstaffe told KTVU Fox 2 at the time. “How do they know the people inside didn’t have their own firearms?”
The Chronicle reported that Jacobs has since also filed a claim against San Mateo County, alleging that Wagstaffe has made comments that have defamed him.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261120.headline: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

paragraphs.text: We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.
Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times."

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.
A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times

The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times."

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.
A New Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics."

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz749ey0r75o.headline: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz749ey0r75o.author: Tara Mewawalla

paragraphs.text: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261120.headline: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

paragraphs.text: Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.

Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing."
How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion

For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.
The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!"

Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space."
A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome

This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.
As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.
For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.
But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

These surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.
Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.
Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb
To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.
Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao."

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.
At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.
Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.
Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.
The merger has left astronomers with another important question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.
Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs
One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.
The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.
Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

The telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.
Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

Scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.

Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.
A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars
The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.
Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.
The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.
NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.
With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.
"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.
The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.
Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/business/used-car.headline: The Used Car Industry Is Booming. This N.J. Campus Is Setting the Price.

paragraphs.text: Car dealerships and Super Bowl ads are the most visible part of the auto industry. But arguably the real action is in places like this vast rectangular building near Trenton, N.J.
Hundreds of vehicles change hands on sale days at this auction center owned by Manheim, a division of Cox Automotive. It is among the largest of about 80 U.S. auction hubs Manheim operates.

The center has 17 lanes, each with its own entrance and exit. Manheim workers, many of them retirees earning a few extra bucks, drive vehicles slowly through garage-style doors, past auctioneers calling out prices from podiums, then out the other side. The din is overwhelming.

The site, in Bordentown, N.J., sells about 4,500 vehicles a week, part of a $730 billion market for used cars. Measured by the number of vehicles sold, the used car market is now more than double the size of the new car market. The vehicles might be trade-ins, coming off leases, older rental cars or repossessed from owners who fell behind on monthly loan payments.

Most Americans can’t afford new cars and have to buy used vehicles. In October, the average sale price for a new car was more than $51,000, according to Cox, a record. Automakers have discontinued many affordable models, like the Nissan Versa and the Ford Escape, because they were less profitable than big pickups and sport utility vehicles.
“You don’t see a lot of cars under $25,000,” said Lenny LaRocca, who leads the U.S. automotive industry practice at KPMG.
That has only made places like Manheim’s Bordentown hub more important. Auctions play a large role in setting prices for used cars, affecting the finances of millions of Americans.

Used car prices have been following the new car market higher. The average retail price of a three-year-old used car was $33,000 in October, up 2 percent from a year earlier. But there were big differences among categories.

Prices for electric vehicles and fuel-efficient compact cars rose more than 6 percent in October as buyers looked to save money on fuel. Prices for less efficient luxury cars, pickups and sport utility vehicles slipped, according to the Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, a closely watched benchmark that is based on sales at Bordentown and other auction centers.

So far this year, wholesale prices for the least fuel-efficient cars have fallen 15 percent while prices for the most efficient vehicles have risen 10 percent. “Gas prices matter,” Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told several reporters during a tour of the center.
Sixteen of the 25 fastest-selling used cars are electric, according to separate data from iSeeCars, an online shopping site.

On a recent sunny day, car dealers, typically men dressed in jeans or sweatpants, roamed the auction lanes, stepping carefully to avoid the moving vehicles and indicating bids with a nod or a raised hand.
A blue Mercedes-Benz wagon with a badly dented right side went for $9,800. A 2023 Subaru Outback went for $14,800. A top-of-the-line BMW sport utility vehicle sold for almost $60,000.
“There she goes,” shouted an auctioneer, declaring the winning bid for the BMW by banging a length of rubber hose like a gavel. The vehicle disappeared through a door back into the sunlight.

Most of the bidding, about 70 percent, is done online. Before vehicles go on sale, they are driven through a brightly lit tunnel where 40 cameras capture detailed images that bidders can scrutinize. Manheim’s employees also inspect vehicles and flag problems.
“Unlike a new car, every used car is unique,” said Grace Huang, president of Cox Automotive’s Inventory Solutions group, who oversees the auction centers.
The New Jersey site has body and repair shops where vehicles can be spruced up. Manheim offers software to help sellers decide whether to make fixes or sell vehicles as they are.

Thousands of cars and trucks wait in parking lots that cover most of the 350-acre site. More than once, gangs of thieves have broken through the high fences, topped with barbed wire, and made off with valuable vehicles.

A growing percentage of cars at the lot were repossessed from owners who are struggling financially. Rising prices are forcing buyers to stretch their budgets, often to the breaking point. In October, 18 percent of car loans were subprime, meaning they were taken out by buyers with poor credit histories, according to Cox.

Signs point to a used car market that will continue to be lively. The average car on U.S. roads is 13 years old — older than they’ve ever been. Many people who have been putting off replacing their ride may not be able to wait much longer.
“Most vehicles are not made to last longer than 13 years,” Mr. Robb, the chief economist, said.

The used-car market is also becoming an important source of revenue for carmakers. They have discovered that they can make good money selling parts like floor mats or subscriptions to features like adaptive cruise control.
“A little known secret,” Mr. LaRocca of KPMG said, is that carmakers “actually make a lot of money in their aftermarket business.”

livescience.com/archaeology/americas/lik.headline: 'Like walking the plank': For 3,000 years, Indigenous people herded bison off a unique cliff in Texas, study reveals
livescience.com/archaeology/americas/lik.author: Kristina Killgrove

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.
Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.
"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.
"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/is-selling-an-.headline: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/is-selling-an-.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”

Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”

How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”

For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

thehill.com/homenews/house/6235202-nancy.headline: Pelosi reflects on decades-long political career: ‘They made me the villain’
thehill.com/homenews/house/6235202-nancy.author: Suryatapa Chakraborty

paragraphs.text: Rep. ) reflected on her decades-long political journey this week as she gets ready to retire from Congress in 2027. “They made me the villain,” Pelosi said while discussing how her political career weighed on her family in an interview with “Tea&Vodka” hosted by Ebs Burnough.

“You always have to have a villain; they created me as a villain.” Pelosi also talked about the many difficulties and challenges women face in politics including false narratives, accusations of overspending and portraying women in a “ridiculous” light. “The impression was that women were more ethical and so what they would want to do is to cut that down right away,” Pelosi said.
She is a two-time House Speaker and the only woman to hold the role in American history. Democrats secured a House majority in the 2006 midterm elections for the first time in more than a decade. S.

history. “Now, we have so many women that it’s a little bit different,” she said, however, “it’s still a challenge for women.” Earlier this month, Pelosi announced that she would retire from Congress at the end of the term in January 2027.

In a video addressing her constituents, she said, “With a grateful heart, I look forward to my final year of service as your proud representative.” Over the years, Pelosi has had her notable moments. In 2019, months into her second term as second tenure as Speaker, Pelosi, along with her Democratic colleagues, attended a meeting at the White House with President Trump.

The meeting came after House Democrats, led by Pelosi, launched an impeachment inquiry into Trump. Less than an hour after the meeting started, Pelosi and her colleagues walked out.   During her recent interview, looking back on her career, Pelosi noted, “We really never accomplished what we needed to do … on gun violence,” calling it, “an unfinished business.”
She added that there is a bipartisan community safety bill, but what is needed is background checks, saying, “American people support that but not the Republicans in Congress.”

cbsnews.com/news/kate-princess-of-wales-.headline: Kate, Princess of Wales, announces she's in remission from cancer
cbsnews.com/news/kate-princess-of-wales-.author: Alex Sundby, Haley Ott

paragraphs.text: Alex Sundby is a senior editor at CBSNews.com. In addition to editing content, Alex also covers breaking news, writing about crime and severe weather as well as everything from multistate lottery jackpots to the July Fourth hot dog eating contest.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, said Tuesday her cancer is in remission, about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.

"It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery," she said in her post on Instagram after visiting the Royal Marsden Hospital in London. "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
The princess had announced last March that cancer was discovered following an abdominal surgery and she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy.

In September, she said she had finished chemotherapy. She spoke about receiving the cancer treatment during her visit Tuesday. "It's really tough,'' she said, according to the Associated Press. "It's such a shock."

Kate spoke with patient Katherine Field about the chemotherapy port that's used to deliver the treatment, saying, "I got so attached to it," and joking that she was almost reluctant to have it removed, according to the AP.
On social media Tuesday, Kate said she visited the hospital to thank the staff "for looking after me so well during the past year."

"My heartfelt thanks goes to all those who have quietly walked alongside William and me as we have navigated everything," she said, referring to her husband, the Prince of Wales. "We couldn't have asked for more. The care and advice we have received throughout my time as a patient has been exceptional."
Kensington Palace also announced that she and William have become patrons of the hospital.

"My hope is, that by supporting groundbreaking research and clinical excellence, as well as promoting patient and family wellbeing, we might save many more lives, and transform the experience of all those impacted by cancer," Kate said on social media.

Since 2007, William has held the role of the hospital's president. His mother, Princess Diana, also held that position, according to the palace. The hospital is known as a world-leading cancer center with three sites in London.
Kate spoke with other patients as well as doctors and nurses during Tuesday's visit, according to Britain's Press Association news agency.
"The body is amazing at telling us 'you need to take time out,'" she said after learning about a man's diagnosis.
She also talked about receiving her cancer diagnosis, according to the news agency.

"It's the uncertainty of that initial diagnosis," she said. "It's such a wealth of information. Understanding the diagnosis, it's a massive amount of information to take on as a patient. Having that continuity, in the clinical setting and outside in the home setting, is so important."

phys.org/news/2026-11-babies-ancient-gre.headline: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
phys.org/news/2026-11-babies-ancient-gre.author: Sandee Oster

paragraphs.text: November 21, 2026 feature
by Sandee Oster, Phys.org
edited by Sadie Harley, reviewed by Robert Egan

Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

A new study published in the European Journal of Archaeology analyzed the chemical signatures in Himera children's bones and found that babies began eating solid foods at just 3 months but were not fully weaned until around 3.8 years old. That's much longer than ancient writers suggested and sheds light on how mothers in a diverse society like Himera approached child care.
Laurie Reitsema, a biological anthropologist at the University of Georgia and a mother herself, said, "It was exciting to see 2,500-year-old evidence of mothers' responsiveness to infant needs."
Growing up in a Greek colony

Himera was an ancient Greek outpost located in Sicily between the seventh and fifth centuries B.C., the study authors wrote. It was founded by Dorian and Chalcidian colonists before growing into a large city home to a diverse multicultural population.
According to the study, archaeologists have uncovered over 13,000 burials. Many of these are of adults. Infant and child mortality appeared to be surprisingly low.

Children born into such a diverse world likely experienced different cultural realities than their parents and would become the seeds of cultural change across generations, the study reported. However, what these childhoods may have looked like remains unclear.

Weaning is one crucial cultural and biological milestone every child experiences. To better understand how that practice played out in the ancient city of Himera, Reitsema and her colleagues looked at the carbon and nitrogen chemical signatures preserved in some of its inhabitants' bones.

Nitrogen told them how long a baby was breastfed, because its values rise during nursing until a baby's chemical signature looks like a carnivore's. Carbon told them what plant-based solid foods babies ate once they stopped drinking only milk.
"Breastfed babies look different than weaned babies, isotopically, because their diets consist of milk, which differs isotopically from other foods (babies are top carnivores!)," Reitsema said.

According to the study, the team examined 58 children's and 27 adult women's bones. What they found was that children at Himera began weaning early, around 3 months, around 2 to 3 months earlier than ancient physicians like Galen and Soranus recommended.

Meanwhile, breastfeeding continued far longer than in most modern preindustrial societies, for around 3.8 years. Soranus recommended weaning at just 1.5 years, and Galen suggested breastfeeding should stop at 3 years.
The study suggests this long period of breastfeeding may explain why Himera's infant mortality was so low.
"Breastfeeding is well known to support infant survival," Reitsema said, "especially in places without reliable access to clean, safe drinking water, which describes most of human history."

On the other hand, the study focused on children who died young, despite being breastfed for years. "Would a baby with an optimal weaning trajectory be dying at age 2 or 3?" Reitsema asked. "It's possible that the weaning behaviors we see in this study reflect a specifically unsuccessful strategy."
The study found that Himera, despite its cultural diversity, had weaning practices that were echoed in another Greek colony, Apollonia Pontica, on the Black Sea in present-day Bulgaria.

The study authors wrote that this suggests even far-flung Greek communities shared a similar approach to breastfeeding. That differs from other studies in Roman cities, which found weaning practices were far more varied and diverse.

"Child care is deeply personal, and practices within households are often difficult to see in historical records or the archaeological record," Reitsema said. But Himera, as a diverse melting pot, offers a rare glimpse into differences and similarities. "This can help us ask how people lived together: whether traditions blended, remained distinct or coexisted. It offers a glimpse into cultural interaction at an intimate, everyday level."
Next, the authors want to study Himera's adults. "Adults are children who lived, and they may have had very different childhoods than those who died young," Reitsema said.
