fortune.com/2026/11/21/snl-sister-sketch.headline: The $120,500 cost of being ‘Sister’: SNL sketch puts a face on America’s caregiving crisis
fortune.com/2026/11/21/snl-sister-sketch.author: James LaForge

paragraphs.text: On the Nov. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live, host John Mulaney starred in a parody drug ad for “Sister,” “a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.”

The sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it. Its jokes land on real pressure points in American caregiving: who does the work, what it costs them, and how much more of it is coming.
63 million Americans now provide ongoing care

A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability. That is 45% more caregivers than a decade earlier.

The work has also gotten harder. More than 40% of caregivers provide high-intensity care, and more than half perform medical and nursing tasks such as giving injections and managing catheters. Only 22% have been trained to do them.

An aging population is the main driver, says Geoff Gross, founder and CEO of Medical Guardian, a Philadelphia-based medical alert and connected-care company. But strains on the broader care system are pushing more Americans into the role.
“What we’re also seeing is pressures on in-home care and labor overall,” Gross said. “There’s a burden on caregivers right now that is not scalable.”

Paid help is scarce and expensive. As gerontologists Jane Tavares and Marc Cohen wrote for Fortune, a home health aide runs a median of about $6,688 a month, while the direct care workforce remains underpaid and short-staffed.
The bill comes due in lost wages and retirement savings

The sketch opens with Mulaney’s character weighing a nursing home against a private aide who “could cost thousands a week.” For real families, the costs keep compounding long after the caregiving ends.

A report published Nov. 4 by the AARP Public Policy Institute modeled the lifetime income losses of working caregivers born between 1981 and 1985. The typical caregiver in that group stands to lose about $120,500 in earnings, workplace retirement income, and Social Security, including roughly $15,400 in retirement and Social Security income alone.

Across that single five-year birth cohort, the losses add up to an estimated $2.3 trillion. Only 3.4% of working caregivers in the model lost no work hours to care. Chandra Bozelko, who cares full-time for her parents, ran those numbers on her own family in a recent Fortune commentary.
For some, the strain reaches the basics. In the 2025 AARP survey, 1 in 5 caregivers said they couldn’t afford necessities such as food.
Women give three more years of care than men, and the gap is growing

The sketch’s sharpest line comes from a doctor, played by Mikey Day, who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours.”

Research from the University of Michigan published in October suggests the gap behind the joke is widening. If current rates hold, U.S. women can expect to spend seven years of their lives caring for older family members or friends, up from six in 2011. Men’s lifetime total held steady at four.

The difference isn’t in caring for spouses, where men and women spend about the same time. It shows up in care for parents and grandparents. Edward Jones managing partner Penny Pennington has called it “the elder daughter phenomenon,” arguing that eldest daughters are quietly propping up family finances.
“Women still bear disproportionate financial burden, time burden, and energy burden,” Gross said, adding that any progress on the issue “isn’t happening fast enough.”
Demand for care will only grow. The U.S. Census Bureau projects that in 2029, Americans 65 and older will outnumber those under 18.
“Caregiving is really a societal crisis, but it isn’t designated in that way as much as it should be compared to other things we read about each and every day,” Gross said.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/21/aft.headline: After a rough start, Commanders’ new coordinator has the defense taking charge
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/21/aft.author: Tashan Reed

paragraphs.text: With more Washington Commanders bearing down on him than the New York Giants could possibly block, quarterback J.J. McCarthy had no choice but to chuck the ball downfield. The pass ended up near its intended target — but cornerback Rasul Douglas was right there to make the interception and seal the 24-21 win Nov. 12.

The Commanders’ defense dictated the terms of engagement. They play a sport where it’s widely accepted that the offense forces the defense to react, but they came into this season aiming to flip that notion on its head.

“It’s really a privilege to be able to play offense on the defensive side of the ball,” outside linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson said before the season. “You dictate what plays you’re going to see on the offense.”

To start the year, however, Washington’s defense was reeling. Through the first five games, the Commanders gave up 29.8 points per game (30th). Even after General Manager Adam Peters invested a stockpile of resources on that side of the ball and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones introduced a new scheme, they looked helpless.

Then, suddenly, everything changed. The defense morphed into an aggressive, attacking, playmaking unit. Since their narrow Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, they’ve allowed just 18.5 points per game (tied for eighth).

“One thing that happened in that game — and it kind of led over to the others a little bit — is the belief of the guys,” Jones told The Washington Post. “That’s a huge attribute that can go unnoticed if you’re not paying attention. It has to be our ability as coaches to piggyback on that belief and ask more of our guys.”

Jones’s scheme has played a major part in that turnaround. He heavily utilizes deception. He constantly works in disguised coverages, simulated pressures and exotic blitzes. He substitutes players frequently and deploys unique alignments along the defensive front and in the secondary. It’s all creating confusion and hesitation for offenses. When that happens, mistakes tend to follow.

The Commanders’ defense isn’t perfect, but it’s much closer to what it set out to be. That’s happened despite Washington losing defensive tackles Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw and linebacker Leo Chenal to season-ending injuries.

They’ll face their toughest challenge of the season when Washington (3-5-1) hosts the Cincinnati Bengals (7-2) on Monday. Quarterback Joe Burrow and wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins lead arguably the best offense in the NFL.
That doesn’t intimidate the Commanders.
“They feel like they can play with anybody,” Jones said. “That leads into, ‘Okay, in that case, we can do this, we can be that, we can move forward from here, we can continue to grow from here.’”
‘Hard for them, easy for us’

Across a decade as an NFL assistant with four different franchises, Jones has learned from different coaches. None had a greater influence than Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, under whom Jones worked as the defensive backs coach from 2023-25. His biggest takeaway: Learning how to think outside the box.

“We’ve been trained almost in this profession to think of rules and not going outside of the norms,” Jones said. “And Flo, his courage to not even be in the box, right? There’s no box with him at all. You don’t know what thought he may come up with.”

When Commanders Coach Dan Quinn interviewed Jones this offseason, he was impressed by his forward-thinking mindset. Among Jones’s core principles was forcing offenses to adjust to the defense — often through pre-snap manipulation.

“He’s on the front edge of some things,” Quinn said in August. “Often at the line of scrimmage, offenses can have the pen last … What I like in the system that we have now is we are also into some of the checking to make the offense have to adjust.”

The deception game continues after the snap. A strategy Jones frequently uses is disguised coverages. There are times when it looks like the Commanders are playing man coverage but they’re actually playing zone and vice versa. On other plays, Washington will have players appear like they’re about to blitz before dropping back into coverage.
“It’s hard for them, easy for us,” linebacker Sonny Styles said.

Jones also often uses simulated pressures. On those plays, traditional pass rushers (such as defensive tackles) drop back into coverage while nontraditional pass rushers (such as cornerbacks) are sent on blitzes.
“It’s giving the offense a lot to think about in a short amount of time,” defensive end Charles Omenihu said. “They have to snap the ball and decipher after the snap. It can be difficult.”

The Commanders blitz a lot. Nobody blitzes as often as Flores — the Vikings blitz on an absurd 69.2 percent of their opponents’ drop backs — but Jones outpaces most defensive play callers. Washington has blitzed on 40.4 percent of opponents’ drop backs (third).

“Who made that rule to say four-down [defense] is a four-man rush and if you bring five, that’s a blitz?” Jones said. “When you think that, it’s like, ‘Well, five, six, they’re just numbers at the end of the day.’”
There are a lot of moving parts in Jones’s scheme. That complexity can easily lead to confusion throughout the defense, which defeats the purpose. Having strong communication is paramount.
Players credited Jones for his ability to teach effectively in the offseason, but there’s no replicating in-game action.

“We’re not asking guys to just be plug-and-play players,” Jones said. “Just to say, ‘Hey, this guy can be that in this scheme,’ well, no, he can’t. Everyone learns differently. And so, you can only move as fast as the slowest learner or the guy who’s the furthest behind because we’ve got to all move in one direction.”

Additionally, Jones had to be adaptable. He cut things within the scheme that weren’t working. When Washington hired longtime NFL coach Steve Wilks as a consultant during its Week 7 bye, Jones accepted his game-planning help.

“Honestly, that level of thinking of what you’re asking the players has to be what you are asking everyone,” Jones said. “So the open-mindedness of players and staff allows that thought process to grow.”
‘Comfortable being uncomfortable’
During the Commanders’ recent success, the structure of the defensive approach hasn’t changed much. Their early struggles didn’t lead them to abandon their principles.

Through the first games of the season, they blitzed on 43.2 percent of opponents’ drop backs (second), used a nickel package on 53 percent of their snaps (22nd) and played zone coverage on 76 percent of opponents’ drop backs (16th). Since then, they’ve blitzed on 36.6 percent of opponents’ drop backs (fifth), used nickel on 57.5 percent of their snaps (22nd) and played zone coverage on 80.1 percent of opponents’ drop backs (11th).

The biggest change: The Commanders have used 3-4 fronts less frequently. In the first five games, they used a 3-4 front on 34.9 percent of their defensive snaps. That’s down to just 17 percent since, but that’s largely because they have less depth at defensive tackle after losing Kinlaw and Payne.
For Washington, the real difference is the execution. The Commanders have stepped up in more key moments, limiting explosive plays and creating turnovers.

Through the first five games of the season, they allowed opponents to convert 43.3 percent of their third downs (24th), gave up touchdowns on 83.3 percent of their red zone possessions (last) and forced turnovers on just 3.4 percent of their drives (31st). Since then, they’ve allowed a 34.5 percent conversion rate on third downs (10th), given up touchdowns on 57.1 percent of their red zone possessions (14th) and forced turnovers on 11.4 percent of their drives (tied for 16th).

“If you get comfortable being uncomfortable in practice and in the meeting rooms, it starts to breed a level of confidence, right?” Jones said. “Now, that uncomfortable feeling becomes confidence. And then that confidence is what allows you to be able to execute on game day.”

There are still areas where the Commanders are leaving plenty to be desired. They’re generating a pressure rate of just 33.5 percent (24th) and a sack rate of 5.1 percent (26th). They’ve allowed opponents to convert 83.3 percent of their fourth downs (tied for 30th). Although the defense has become more reliable, it still has work to do.

“The sky’s the limit as long as we continue to progress and guys continue to stay grounded and continue to focus on the keys of playing great defense as a unit and togetherness,” Jones said. “As long as that happens, these guys can accomplish whatever they set their mind to.”

marketwatch.com/story/micron-and-sandisk.headline: Micron and Sandisk stocks might look like bargains, but analysts say that's actually a red flag

paragraphs.text: Cheap valuation multiples for memory stocks have historically been associated with peak pricing levels, according to analysts
Shares of Micron fell nearly 14% on Friday.
Memory stocks were among the biggest decliners as the technology sector bled red ink on Friday.
Shares of Micron Technology (MU) closed down 14% on Friday, while shares of Sandisk (SNDK) fell 16%. Western Digital's stock (WDC) sank 12%.
The pressure on these stocks is mounting. Micron shares are down 50.99% from their peak, while Sandisk shares are down 72.85% from their highs and Western Digital's stock has shed 64.97%.

The chip sector in general has been hit hard due to various factors. Those include concerns that politicians could get stricter about data-center construction, leadership uncertainty at Nvidia (NVDA) and the idea that Anthropic's (ANT) IPO might have sucked attention away from the broader tech sector.
Then there is the perennial debate over the price-to-earnings multiples of memory stocks.

Micron and Sandisk shares both trade at meaningful discounts to their recent historical valuations. Micron's stock trades at 3.76 times estimated earnings for the next 12 months, versus a two-year average of 9.10 times. Sandisk's multiple of 3.04 times forward earnings expectations is below its 10.47-times average since the time of its separation from Western Digital in February 2025.

But Brendan Burke, the research director for semiconductors, supply chain and emerging tech at the Futurum Group, says that low price-to-earnings ratios for memory stocks are a "warning label, not a bargain sign."
"Investors have learned over decades to sell memory stocks at peak earnings, because the earnings side of that ratio has historically collapsed when the cycle turns," he said.
"A multiple in the low single digits tells you the market is pricing today's profits as a peak," he added.

Admittedly, there are some caveats. The historical precedent "ignores that AI has changed the shape of this cycle." Some types of memory, like high-bandwidth memory and solid-state-drive storage, are tied to what he called "mission-critical data-center buildouts," as opposed to memory for PCs and handsets. That distinction means the earnings might be "more durable than these multiples imply," Burke said.
William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji told MarketWatch that there's a limit to the usefulness of low P/E ratios as a "valuation support metric."
Memory stocks often see "extreme volatility in pricing," CreditSights analyst Andy Li added, and that can lead to boom-and-bust cycles.
If investors assume the market is still cyclical, a "dramatic price decline may well be in the cards," he said. "The price action reflects that fear."

Li explained that cyclical stocks like memory often top with "very low" price-to-earnings multiples, because that's when their estimated earnings for the next 12 months are "most inflated." Meanwhile, they also bottom with relatively high multiples, following the same logic, he said.
Separately, he added that the fact that monthly options expire on Friday could also be a technical factor affecting the stocks.
See also: Jensen Huang was a 'China salesman' for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/21/mexi.headline: Mexico seizes cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro,’ among FBI’s most wanted
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/21/mexi.author: Diana Baptista, Samantha Schmidt

paragraphs.text: MEXICO CITY — Mexican forces captured a top drug trafficking leader who was one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives, the country’s defense ministry said Saturday, in a dramatic raid that set off an outburst of violence in the kingpin’s Sinaloa stronghold.

Elite Mexican military forces were attacked by firearms and explosives Friday as they entered a building to arrest Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a top cartel leader in northern Sinaloa known as “El Chapo Isidro,” the defense ministry said. Two other top cartel leaders, the second-in-command and financial operator of the criminal group, were also arrested in the operation in Guasave, Sinaloa.

The capture delivers a victory for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum as it faces increased pressure from the Trump administration to show results in its efforts to dismantle drug trafficking organizations.

“These arrests are an important step toward bringing peace to Sinaloa,” said Omar García Harfuch, the country’s top security official. He said security agencies remain “deployed in the state to protect the population.”

The operation was carried out in coordination with U.S. intelligence officials, Mexico’s defense ministry said. Meza Flores faces an arrest warrant in Mexico on organized crime and drug-related offenses and an extradition warrant to the United States for criminal conspiracy to distribute drugs on U.S. soil.
The Mexican military identified Meza Flores as the leader of the criminal group Beltrán Leyva and an ally of the Pacific cartel.

In 2012, Meza Flores was indicted in the District of Columbia for the possession and distribution of drugs, along with other crimes. Since 2017, the U.S. State Department issued a reward for $5 million for any information leading to the capture or conviction of the drug kingpin.

In 2025, Meza Flores was added to the FBI’s list of 10 most-wanted fugitives due to his role as the alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Organization. The FBI wanted him over the alleged possession, distribution and importation of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the U.S.

According to U.S. authorities, the criminal group has operated over 20 years out of Guasave, where it has used planes, maritime vessels and tractor-trailers to transport drugs in the U.S. The group is also allegedly responsible for the deaths of Mexican law enforcement officials, and of other crimes such as kidnapping, torture and extortion.

Meza Flores’s group was identified in 2013 by the U.S. Treasury Department as one of the main rivals of the Sinaloa cartel, whose turf war drove a rise in violent crimes in Sinaloa, including murder, kidnapping and arson.
Meza Flores has a long criminal career in the most violent Mexican cartels. He was considered the “right hand man” of drug kingpin Alfredo Beltran Leyva.
The criminal group disbanded after Beltrán Leyva’s arrest in 2008 and Arturo Beltrán Leyva’s death at the hands of the Mexican military in 2009, and Meza Flores started his own organization.

Since the 2024 arrest of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, who co-founded the Sinaloa cartel with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, Sinaloa has seen an all-time rise in violent crime. The arrests ignited a battle for the control of the cartel, in which opposing groups regularly block streets, burn cars and trade shots in the streets.

fortune.com/2026/11/21/court-pauses-army.headline: ‘An extraordinary and extreme backstop’: Earthjustice warns Army off bypassing paused Iowa permit
fortune.com/2026/11/21/court-pauses-army.author: Molly A. Wallace

paragraphs.text: A federal appeals court has paused the emergency permit authorizing the U.S. Army to blow up nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. But the Justice Department told the court Friday that the Army may be able to proceed without it.

In a notice filed on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency, government lawyers said they would oppose a motion by two environmental groups to keep the permit on hold. The notice added that “in qualifying emergency situations,” EPA regulations authorize the Army, which is not a party to the case, “to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit” when there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

The notice did not say whether the Army plans to go ahead with the detonation, now set for Monday, Nov. 23. An Army Sustainment Command spokesperson did not respond Friday when asked whether the Army would proceed while the stay is in place, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported. On Friday evening, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state, federal, and local agencies ahead of the planned blast.

Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the groups, called the emergency provision “an extraordinary and extreme backstop” and said the groups “strongly urge” the Army not to rely on it.
The standoff leaves residents of southeastern Iowa and western Illinois facing a weekend of uncertainty over whether a plume of lead-laden dust will drift across their towns and farmland on Monday.
A one-sentence order

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued its order late Thursday, pausing the permit the EPA issued to the Army on Nov. 13 after finding the material posed an “imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment.” The pause lasts until the court rules on the groups’ emergency motion, which asks it to keep the permit on hold while it decides the case. The government said it would file its full response by Sunday.

Cody Smith, director of climate initiatives at the Iowa Environmental Council, one of the groups that filed the lawsuit, said detonating without the court’s approval would be unlawful. The council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter argue that the permit lacks adequate protections for health and the environment, that the EPA did not fully consider alternatives, and that it was issued without the public notice and comment they say the rules require.

Hours before the court acted, the Army postponed the detonation from Friday to Monday. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Monday was the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

The 68 drums of lead azide, an explosive used to set off munitions, were stored on site for more than 20 years in a bath of ethanol and water. The Army says the material degraded and recrystallized, leaving it highly sensitive to friction and shock.
Who knew, and when

The blast is expected to release a plume of dust containing lead. Army maps modeled for a Friday detonation projected the dust settling across a roughly 25-mile stretch north of the plant, with low levels of airborne lead traveling farther. The Army asked some residents of Middletown, a town of about 360, to leave their homes during the blast because it could shatter windows.

The permit required the Army to model the plume using conservative assumptions so as not to “under-predict” potential impacts, and it states that EPA and Army experts agree the modeling is “not necessarily representative of actual conditions.”

The Army held a public open house about the planned detonation in mid-October. On Nov. 15, five days before the original blast date, it released the detonation date and plume maps, meeting the permit’s requirement to publish a preliminary forecast at least five days in advance.

Smith said the council began receiving calls from concerned residents on Monday, Nov. 16, and when it contacted state and local officials, “We were telling them for the first time.” Reynolds’ office has said neither the governor nor any state agency was told of the plans before the Army’s Nov. 15 announcement, Little Village reported.
“This lawsuit is largely the outcome of a last resort,” Smith said.

A letter from the EPA paints a different picture. Writing to Reynolds on Friday, Jim Macy, who heads the EPA’s Region 7 office, said the agency issued three emergency permits for the lead azide between April and September and notified Iowa’s congressional delegation, state lawmakers, and local officials each time, and again on Nov. 13 when it approved the detonation.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Illinois Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth, and Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek were among a bipartisan group of officials who wrote to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin urging a delay. “We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives,” they wrote, according to CBS News.
Why the Army chose to blow it up

The Army’s environmental assessment considered chemical neutralization, which would avoid a blast plume, but rejected it. The assessment concluded that the 7 to 22 days of handling it would require created an unacceptable risk of a fatal accidental detonation, with no guarantee that neutralization would work.

Macy’s letter said the Army also weighed building a structure over the material, moving it to the plant’s open detonation unit, and leaving the drums in place, and found each posed “an unacceptable safety risk” because of “advanced crystallization.” The Army, he wrote, “concluded the only viable option was a controlled detonation in place with extensive mitigation measures.”
The environmental groups say the Army chose detonation “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead.”

“It’s not our role to recommend to the Army or the EPA how to deal with explosives most effectively,” Smith said. “As far as we can tell, it’s been stored on site for at least 20 years, and they’ve known about this for at least the last several months. And they decided to wait until the very last minute to issue that permit and make it publicly known.”

In September 2025, the Army posted a federal contracting notice saying it planned to have American Ordnance LLC, which operates the plant, perform “lead azide neutralization.” The notice did not describe the method. The Army’s environmental assessment says the material’s degradation was discovered in March 2026. The Army has not responded to requests for clarification about the notice.
‘Hose that off’

Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa on Nov. 17 that residents worried about lead dust on their property had a simple remedy: “The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone.” The station reported that fine lead particles could reach as far north as Maquoketa.

Smith said that advice, including the Army’s guidance to hose off playground equipment and wash cars, is inconsistent with how lead persists in the environment. The groups’ court filings called the idea that lead can be washed away “absurd, counterfactual, and extremely harmful misinformation to share with the public.” Iowa health officials say no safe level of lead exposure has been identified.

In his letter, Macy said EPA staff have been in Middletown since Nov. 16 testing drinking water and watersheds, and that the EPA and Army will provide filters to homeowners on public water systems if testing finds elevated lead.
“People have really been scrambling for information about what to do,” Smith said.

The court could rule before Monday. If it grants the groups’ motion, the permit stays on hold while the case proceeds. If it denies the motion, the pause ends and the Army is free to proceed under the permit. Whether the Army would invoke the emergency exception if the court rules against it remains an open question.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/21/pola.headline: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a ‘mistake’
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/21/pola.author: Mary Ilyushina

paragraphs.text: Russian missiles and a drone violated Polish airspace and crashed in the country’s southeast on Friday, according to Polish officials, who accused Moscow of a deliberate “provocation” and linked it to major military exercises by allied European countries preparing for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine.

“This doesn’t look like an accident,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. “We know for certain that what fell on Polish soil came from Russia.” Tusk said that foreign partners, including NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, shared that assessment.

President Donald Trump, however, shrugged off the alarm raised by Polish officials, saying that Russian President Vladimir “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake.”
Officials said that one of the missiles was a Kh-101, a cruise missile that typically carries a warhead weighing 400 to 450 kilograms, or about 880 to 990 pounds.

The incident is the latest apparent violation of NATO airspace by Russian drones and missiles. The incursions have drawn outcry from European nations, but the alliance has so far largely followed Trump’s approach, playing down such incidents and refraining from retaliation against Moscow.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into European nations on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fueling tension with the West and raising fears of a more direct conflict between Russia and the alliance. So far, no NATO ally has sought to invoke NATO’s collective defense clause over the incidents.
The military exercise was being held near Nowa Deba, about 60 miles from Poland’s border with Ukraine.

Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in news conference Friday that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight airstrikes on Ukraine, all landing in the southeast.

One unspecified missile came down about 20 miles from where European troops were holding their military exercises, according to officials. The Kh-101 cruise missile crashed roughly 30 miles from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit the ground about 20 miles from the border.
No injuries or damage were reported.
The Kh-101 is among the most capable conventional weapons in Russia’s arsenal — a low-flying, generally hard-to-detect cruise missile launched from strategic bombers.

Moscow has used it extensively against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, and it is built to hit its targets with precision, which means its landing on NATO territory raises more questions than the airspace violations by drones, which more frequently fly off-course.
The incident occurred a day after Putin, speaking at a news conference on Thursday following meetings with Trump and Xi Jinping in China, dismissed the idea that Russia poses a threat to Europe.

“The Americans keep urging us to mend our relations with Europe. But we never damaged those relations in the first place. Honestly, this political diarrhea needs to stop,” he said. “What is this talk about us attacking Europe? Everyone knows perfectly well that we have no desire for a war with Europe. What kind of nonsense is this?”

In China, Trump greeted Putin with a warm joke and called the Russian leader “my friend,” a remark that drew criticism from Western officials, including Poland’s Tusk, who posted on X: “God, protect us from such friends.”
The missiles came down in Poland amid a large-scale Russian air attack on Ukraine, which, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, killed at least eight people and left nearly 30 injured.

“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure — things that literally sustain people’s lives,” Zelensky said.
The strikes on Ukraine came days after U.S.-brokered direct talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi last week — the first such discussions following a nine-month lull.

The two sides agreed only on humanitarian relief and appeared to remain far apart on other issues, as Russia also pressed to widen the discussion to the postwar security architecture in Europe, in line with the hard-line demands Russia sent the West in 2021. Back then, senior Russian officials denied any plans to invade Ukraine, but within weeks Putin ordered his troops across the border.

Europe has been under pressure to name delegates to participate in the talks, as Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, push to bring European representatives into the next round of negotiations.
Russia has so far insisted there is no sense in engaging with Europe, which it describes as a “party to the war” because of its concerted military and financial support for Kyiv.

The Abu Dhabi talks were followed by a marked escalation. Ukrainian forces, in missile and drone strikes, destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Built by Russia after its invasion and illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, the bridge is of huge symbolic importance to Putin, who has vowed to retaliate harshly.

“After the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not negotiate,” Putin said at Thursday’s news conference in China. He claimed the bridge was used only for civilian purposes and that he had been considering agreeing to limited ceasefires in Ukraine until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed.
“We will respond to these attacks,” he said. “Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge.”
On Friday, Russia launched a major attack across Ukraine, targeting bridges and railway stations in Kyiv overnight.

Zelensky has defended Ukraine’s repeated strikes on the Crimean Bridge, the main link between Russia and the occupied peninsula, calling them a “fair response” to what he says were 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges across Ukraine.
Zelensky told the BBC that the intense Russian attacks that followed the damage to the Crimean Bridge were a “signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate.”

fortune.com/2026/11/21/gen-z-workers-ai-.headline: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor says using AI is riskier for them
fortune.com/2026/11/21/gen-z-workers-ai-.author: Bilin Lin

paragraphs.text: The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers.
For younger workers, using AI could come with a different set of professional risks than it does for their more experienced colleagues.

“Because younger workers haven’t had the same amount of time in their career fields to build up their standing as experts, using a technology that blurs their own contribution to their work can feel especially risky,” Jessica Reif, an assistant professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, told Fortune.

The survey of more than 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers, conducted in June through NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel, found that 58% of Gen Z employees use AI in their current roles, compared with 60% of baby boomers, 63% of millennials, and 67% of Gen Xers. Seramount defined Gen Z as workers 29 and younger.
That leaves a puzzle. Gen Z workers, often cast as digital natives, use AI at nearly the same rate as baby boomers but show far less interest in getting better at it.
Younger workers worry AI makes them look less capable
Younger workers are considerably more concerned about what using AI might say about their own abilities.

Some 22% of Gen Z employees surveyed by Seramount worry that using AI could lead others to question their skills, compared with 10% of millennials and Gen Xers and just 8% of baby boomers. Only 27% of Gen Z employees feel comfortable acknowledging their use of AI for a work task, compared with between 47% and 53% of their older colleagues.

Those concerns are not entirely unfounded. In four experiments involving more than 4,400 participants, Reif, then at Duke University, and her co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll found in a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that employees described as receiving help from AI were perceived as less competent, less diligent, and lazier than those described as receiving other forms of help or whose use of help wasn’t specified.

The stigma could also influence hiring decisions. In one experiment, managers who used AI less frequently themselves favored candidates who did not use AI, while managers who were more frequent AI users favored candidates who used it daily.

The penalty in those experiments held regardless of the age of the employee being evaluated. But Reif said its consequences could be more substantial for workers who are still trying to establish themselves professionally.

“A senior employee who uses AI has a more substantial record of results that can offset doubts about their effort or ability, but an early-career employee doesn’t have that record yet so others might weight their AI use more heavily when evaluating them,” Reif said.

The pressure can work in the opposite direction, too. A survey of 3,001 professionals worldwide released Tuesday by the London School of Economics’ Inclusion Initiative and consulting firm Protiviti found that 48% of employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough at work, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it.
For workers at the beginning of their careers, that presents a dilemma: They need to demonstrate their ability to work with AI while also proving what they are capable of doing themselves.
Gen Z is less convinced AI improves its work
Beyond concerns about their professional reputation, younger workers appear less convinced of the benefits of using AI in the first place.

Only 30% of Gen Z employees in Seramount’s survey believe AI helps them work more efficiently, compared with roughly half of their older colleagues. And 41% believe it improves the quality of their work, compared with 56% of Gen Xers.

Young people are also questioning whether the immediate benefits of AI could come at the expense of their long-term development. A survey by Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29, released in April, found that 80% believe using AI tools is very or somewhat likely to make learning more difficult for them in the future.

Among employed Gen Z respondents, 48% believe the risks of AI in the workforce outweigh its benefits, compared with 15% who believe the opposite. Some 69% place greater trust in work completed without AI than in AI-assisted work.
That skepticism, as Fortune has reported, partly reflects how poorly schools, employers, and government have prepared young people for an AI economy.
Gen Z feels less supported by employers
Younger employees’ attitudes toward AI may also reflect the environments in which they are being asked to use it.

Only 27% of Gen Z respondents in Seramount’s survey said their organization provides support to help them integrate AI into their work, compared with 38% of millennials and 43% of Gen Xers. Younger employees were also the least comfortable seeking help from colleagues on how to use AI tools, with only 18% saying they felt comfortable doing so, compared with 34% of baby boomers.
Seramount suggested that junior employees may also have less need for AI in their current roles or more limited access to enterprise AI tools.

The LSE and Protiviti research points to the importance of training in AI adoption across generations: 93% of employees who had received AI training used the technology at work, compared with 50% of those who had not.

Not all research suggests young workers are being left behind on training, though. The LSE and Protiviti study found that 66% of Gen Z employees had received AI training in the past year, compared with 40% of baby boomers. That study polled professionals worldwide, while Seramount surveyed only U.S. workers.

For employers, failing to engage their youngest employees in AI adoption could create a longer-term talent development problem, echoing warnings that automating entry-level roles could cost companies their future workforce.

“If Gen Z falls behind on AI, employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline,” Diana Forster, senior director of research at Seramount, said in a press release. She called on employers to provide clearer guidelines, training, and opportunities for young employees to practice using the technology.
Sam Altman sees an opening for young workers
Despite the challenges young workers face in embracing AI, the technological disruption could also work in their favor.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes that periods of rapid technological change give people at the beginning of their careers a chance to gain a competitive advantage. As AI transforms how jobs are done and opens up new business opportunities, those with fresh ideas and new skills could have an edge over more established players.

“I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open,” Altman said during an interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business in October, as previously reported by Fortune.
He added, “I think people with high potential, drive, ideas, a new way of looking at things, and new skills tend to do relatively well when the ground is shaking the most.”
For workers concerned about being judged for using AI, Reif offered some advice.

“No matter their age, employees are increasingly in a position where they need to demonstrate their value above and beyond what AI can do,” Reif said. “Employees who are proactive in communicating how AI enables them to contribute more or in ways that would not have otherwise been possible may be able to counteract some of these perceptions.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/20/technology/jensen.headline: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine at Nvidia

paragraphs.text: As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.
“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.

Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.

Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Mr. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Mr. Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Mr. Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Mr. Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)

Mr. Huang denied Mr. Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Mr. Fisher said. Mr. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Mr. Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Mr. Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Mr. Huang.
‘It Pained Me’

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.

Mr. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.

Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Mr. Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Mr. Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
But in the eyes of some, Mr. Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.

In September 2004, Mr. Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Mr. Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H.R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Mr. Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.
In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.
That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Mr. Huang said at one point.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”

Mr. Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”

Mr. Winston said he then confronted Mr. Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

That November, Mr. Winston was called into a meeting with Mr. Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Mr. Huang told Mr. Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Mr. Winston sued Nvidia, Mr. Huang said he would make sure Mr. Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.
“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Mr. Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”

In the months that followed, Mr. Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Mr. Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Mr. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Mr. Huang.
But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.
Mr. Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.

In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Mr. Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Mr. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”

Mr. Pettigrew discussed Mr. Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Mr. Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Mr. Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.

Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Mr. Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.
‘Thank You, Jensen’

After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Mr. Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A.I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
Power Plays
Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch, taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to footage of the talk.
“I want to say it in human words,” Mr. Huang said, after Mr. Mensch tried to explain an A.I. concept. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”
Georgia Gee contributed research.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/us/jonathan-mckin.headline: The California Grandparents Accused of Killing Jonathan McKinsey, Their Son-in-Law

paragraphs.text: On a warm Saturday afternoon this fall, Jonathan McKinsey had just finished playing with his three children at a Bay Area park. He dragged a wagon past a baseball diamond and crowded playground and began to load items into the trunk of his SUV.
Then a bullet struck the back of his head, prosecutors say. Within 40 seconds, at least 17 more rounds were fired at Mr. McKinsey.
It was shocking enough that Mr. McKinsey was shot repeatedly in a park filled with children in Dublin, Calif., a Bay Area suburb popular among tech workers.

But the killing, on Sept. 26, reverberated far beyond Northern California after the authorities said the assailants were Mr. McKinsey’s 77-year-old in-laws. And headlines all over the world noted Mr. McKinsey’s role as director of engineering for the department at The New York Times that produces Wordle and other games.

Prosecutors say that the in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, jointly carried out a murder plot amid contentious divorce proceedings and a custody battle between Mr. McKinsey and their daughter, Candice Jang. Mr. McKinsey had been married to Ms. Jang for 15 years and had three children with her before they were recently separated.

Defense lawyers have not disputed that the couple shot Mr. McKinsey, but say that they did so out of fear for their safety as well as the safety of their daughter and grandchildren. They cite child abuse allegations against Mr. McKinsey as well as the ongoing family court proceedings.
“The larger court record is replete with facts supporting both self-defense and defense of others,” Amy Cheng, a deputy public defender who represents Mr. Zhang, said in a recent filing.

The details of the allegations are laid out in court documents that have been unsealed or filed in recent weeks. Mr. Zhang, Ms. Chen and their lawyers could not be reached for comment. The Alameda County District Attorney’s office, which is prosecuting the case, said it would not comment on an ongoing case.
Both Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen have pleaded not guilty and are being held without bail. They are expected to return to court on Monday for a pretrial hearing.
Prosecutors say that they believe Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen planned the shooting, and the murder charge the couple faces includes a special circumstance of “lying in wait.”

Mr. Zhang typically got around by bicycle, prosecutors say, but he rented a car the day before the shooting. His wife of nearly half a century, Ms. Chen, was behind the wheel and wearing a wig as the couple drove to the park. They brought with them two loaded pistols, according to the documents.
The couple, prosecutors say, waited at the park for several minutes until Mr. McKinsey handed off the three children to their daughter, who drove off.

Then, just after 3 p.m. in the Dublin Sports Grounds parking lot, Mr. Zhang shot Mr. McKinsey once in the back of the head, causing him to fall to the ground, police say. Mr. Zhang continued to fire at him while he lay motionless, according to footage captured by a school camera across the street that was cited by prosecutors and defense lawyers.

Seconds later, Ms. Chen left the vehicle and fired a second gun several times at Mr. McKinsey, who remained on the ground, prosecutors say. Mr. Zhang fired at him again, and the couple stared down at Mr. McKinsey, prosecutors said.

After the shooting, detectives found four photo albums in the Dublin apartment where Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen live. Mr. McKinsey’s face was cut out of some of the pictures. On one photo, there were black ink marks on his chest and over his right eye, the very places he was later shot, prosecutors say.

After his arrest, Mr. Zhang was interviewed by the police, through a Mandarin interpreter. According to court documents, Mr. Zhang told the police that he had been thinking about killing Mr. McKinsey all day and that he had rented the car so he could drive to a gun range and practice shooting.

Mr. Zhang, a retired metallurgist, immigrated to Albuquerque from China in 1985. He was joined three years later by his wife and daughter. In 2016, he and his wife relocated to Northern California to be closer to their daughter and her family.

Years later, at the time of the shooting, Mr. Zhang believed that Mr. McKinsey had a “dark soul” and had treated his grandchildren poorly, including physical abuse, he told the police, according to court documents. He also believed his son-in-law had wanted to harm him.

Mr. McKinsey and his wife, Ms. Jang, 46, had each accused each other of verbal, physical and psychological abuse, according to previous court records. Mr. McKinsey was a transgender man and had accused Ms. Jang and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity.
Katharine Tinto, a clinical law professor at the University of California, Irvine, said the outcome of the case could hinge on the defendants’ state of mind during the killing.

Mr. Zhang was diagnosed with memory loss last year, his lawyers said. Ms. Chen’s lawyer said that Mr. Zhang was “in the grips of serious mental deterioration” and becoming increasingly paranoid about Mr. McKinsey.
Those factors or a self-defense argument could throw into question the proof of advanced planning required for a murder conviction, Ms. Tinto said.
“That’s what the heart of this case seems to be: how culpable are these parents, and what was their intention, what was their mental state when they did these acts?” she said.

Mr. Zhang told detectives that he told his wife to drive them to the park and to bring a gun, but that she did not know anything more. They did not discuss killing Mr. McKinsey, Mr. Zhang told detectives.

Ms. Chen’s attorney, Curtis Briggs, wrote in a recent court filing that Ms. Chen could not see clearly what was happening from the driver’s seat of the car when Mr. Zhang was shooting at Mr. McKinsey. She saw what appeared to be her husband doubled over in pain clutching his abdomen, and rushed out to protect him from what she feared was an assault from a “violent and dangerous Mr. McKinsey,” Mr. Briggs said.
But prosecutors argue that Ms. Chen knew of her husband’s plan because she brought a firearm and wore a black wig to cover her normally silver hair.

It remains unclear what, if anything, Ms. Jang knew about their plans. Investigators have searched her home, but she has not been charged with a crime. She declined to be interviewed when reached by phone.
On a recorded jail-line call between Ms. Jang and Ms. Chen, Ms. Chen asked her daughter to return the rental car so that it didn’t accumulate late fees, according to Mr. Briggs’ court filings.
She told her repeatedly to take good care of the children. And, according to the filings, she apologized for “all the stress I’m causing you.”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Crypto Crashes Pile Up as Once-Diehard Fans Chase New Bets
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Vildana Hajric and Emma Haidar

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Every week, crypto gives its diehards another reason to quit as prices sink, trading thins and hacks take their toll.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Bitcoin broke below $57,742 on Friday for the first time since September 2024, heading for its longest weekly losing streak since 2022. ETF investors are cashing out. The crypto market is worth around $2 trillion, about half its peak last year.

A stronger dollar, rising bets on another Federal Reserve rate increase and jitters over the artificial-intelligence trade hit everything from copper to tech shares this week. But the crash in token prices is now more than a year in the making with the record Binance hack adding to the tumult.
From once-solid stablecoins to Bitcoin and altcoins, the retreat reaches across crypto. Trading volumes have dropped off, too.

At a gathering in New York City this week, a group of young professionals pitched friends still hooked on crypto on other ways to spend their time. Collect coins from all 50 states — actual coins. Walk backward through the city. In fact, doomscrolling on X, one pitch went, beats checking the price of Bitcoin.
James Steinberg, who organized the gathering, called the mission "rehome a crypto bro."
"Crypto is leaving the zeitgeist," he said.

Some of crypto's former diehards have already found new homes for their money. They're buying AI stocks on the bet that the technology will make businesses more productive and profitable even after the recent downturn. They're trading election and earnings outcomes on prediction markets, buying tokenized funds or using perpetual futures to bet on stocks and commodities. They haven't quit speculating. They've quit betting on tokens for their own sake.
Ether has plunged more than 60% since last October, and Solana has lost roughly two-thirds of its value.

The retreat is increasingly showing up in investor behavior. Both short- and long-term holders have been throwing in the towel of late. Short-term holders sent more than 700,000 Bitcoin to the five largest exchanges over the month, increasingly doing so at a loss. Just 2.5% of the Bitcoin they transferred on Wednesday had been in profit, down from roughly 60% in mid-October and the third-lowest reading since 2021, according to data from CryptoQuant.

US stocks are coming off a bruising week — the S&P 500 lost 8.6% in the five-day stretch through Friday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 lost even more as exuberance over Anthropic's IPO gave way to renewed fears over inflation and AI spending.

"The broader market has shifted into a sharp lack of confidence, and investors are de-risking due to a wall of expected Fed hikes, post Anthropic-IPO adrenaline crash, and the string of recent tech snafus," wrote Andy Baehr, managing director of asset management at GSR. "Bitcoin is along for the ride here."
Bitcoin has plenty of troubles of its own. But with global markets sliding too, digital-asset traders who used to buy the dip are saving their money for a different bet.

Scott Kantrowitz, a 56-year-old retail investor from New York, said he sold his investments in Fidelity's spot-Bitcoin and Ether ETFs earlier this year — at a loss — and instead put his money toward shares in the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs.
"I got bored of it," he said. "It was just sitting there in my portfolio not doing anything."
--With assistance from Teresa Xie.
