cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/co.headline: College basketball rankings: No. 25 Indiana dominates Kentucky as impressive start for Hoosiers continues
cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/co.author: Gary Parrish

paragraphs.text: Nov 21, 2026 at 11:16 am ET • 2 min read
Indiana started 7-0 last season and still missed the NCAA Tournament with an 18-14 record. So I understand those with a pump-the-brakes attitude.
But doesn't this start feel different?

It certainly looks different. And in terms of the quality of the wins, it's undeniably different following Friday's 90-76 blowout of Kentucky inside Lucas Oil Stadium that pushed the Hoosiers to 6-0 with three victories over schools ranked inside the top 80 at KenPom. Last season's 7-0 start at Indiana featured zero wins over schools that finished ranked inside the top 80 at KenPom -- and five of those first seven wins were over teams that finished ranked 240th-or-worse.

Again, this season's 6-0 start features three wins over schools ranked inside the top 80 -- specifically Arkansas (No. 38), Kentucky (No. 63) and Syracuse (No. 78). For what it's worth, Arkansas and Kentucky -- John Calipari's current school and his old school -- were both in the preseason AP Top 25 poll, meaning the only schools with multiple wins over teams in the preseason Top 25 are Houston, Memphis and Indiana.

Will this be the season the Hoosiers get back to the Sweet 16 for the first time since Tom Crean guided them there in 2016? As always, we'll see. But there's no denying they're off to a nice start, one that has more substance to it than the start IU put together last season.
Indiana is No. 25 in Saturday morning's updated CBS Sports Top 25 And 1 daily college basketball rankings, where Houston remains No. 1 for the third straight morning. As for Kentucky, I mean, yuck.
As I've noted many times on the Eye On College Basketball Podcast, nobody needed an encouraging start to the season more than third-year UK coach Mark Pope.
So far, it's going terribly.

The Wildcats are 4-2 with no good wins, a 20-point loss to Kansas and a 14-point loss to Indiana. They're down to 63rd at KenPom and 64th at BartTorvik. Even worse, when you remove the preseason data from the rankings at BartTorvik, Kentucky drops all the way down to 115th.
And did you see the updated projections at KenPom?

It now has the Wildcats entering the SEC Tournament with a 16-16 record, including a 6-12 mark in the SEC. Needless to say, barring something surprising, that would result in a coaching change at UK, a place that has spent big on rosters each of the past two seasons but is -- to date -- getting a poor return on its investment.

engadget.com/2318247/common-reasons-why-.headline: Common reasons why your iPhone keeps randomly turning off
engadget.com/2318247/common-reasons-why-.author: Roger Fingas

paragraphs.text: Your iPhone can immediately shut off for various reasons, and none of them are good.

Glitches and bugs are to be expected on even the best smartphones. They're complex devices with a lot to handle across many possible OS, app and hardware combinations. And that's part of what makes random iPhone shutdowns feel intolerable: Apple has much more control over every aspect.

Having your smartphone shut off when you aren't expecting it is frustrating and can be a huge problem given how much we all depend on them (at least to entertain ourselves). In some circumstances, you might be worried that your iPhone is gone for good until you're finally relieved to see the Lock screen pop back up.

But it's not just bugs that can trigger these failures. There may be serious hardware issues at play, to the point where a shutdown is sometimes how iOS prevents far worse issues from occurring. Here's what you need to know to minimize or fix the downtime you're dealing with.
Why your iPhone is randomly shutting off on you

When a software problem triggers a reboot, that means it's so severe that it's preventing iOS from operating properly, and the only solution is to start from scratch. On a technical level, there are many potential causes, such as memory access errors. Behind these are usually coding errors, and it's not impossible (though highly unlikely in normal cases on an iPhone) for malware to intentionally exploit vulnerabilities.

A surprisingly common culprit — having experienced this myself — is temperature. If your iPhone reaches an unspecified level of internal heat, it may shut off automatically to prevent component damage. Typically, it will employ other measures first, namely performance throttling until heat comes back under control. You may also see a warning that your phone is too hot and you need to pause use of it. Shutdowns are also possible under extreme cold, but I've never once encountered these despite surviving multiple Alberta winters.

Where the problem starts to get serious is battery health. If your battery is struggling to hold capacity, it may not be able to supply enough power for high-demand activities, and will shut down to prevent damage. It's a problem called battery sag (AKA voltage sag), and I'm quite familiar with it through my electric unicycle (EUC) hobby. As an EUC's battery drains, its top speed (and torque) diminishes, and you ignore the warning beeps at your peril.

Less often, other hardware failures can be to blame. There are, for instance, a number of sensor checks that have to be completed every 180 seconds. If one of these fails, your iPhone will reboot as a defensive measure.
What you can do to prevent iPhone shutdowns

To prevent software-based shutdowns, it's important to keep iOS and your apps up-to-date. Glitches may still happen, but generally, keeping everything on the latest version reduces the odds of a hiccup. Check for iOS updates through Settings > General > Software Update, and apps by opening the App Store, tapping your profile icon and selecting App Updates. Swipe down to refresh the App Updates view.

As for heat shutdowns, your major concern should be keeping your iPhone out of prolonged sun exposure. It's a bad idea to mount it in your window if you're on a long summer road trip, for example. You may also want to avoid running high-demand activities for hours at a time, like 4K video recording or graphically heavy gaming. During the winter, make sure your iPhone gets a chance to return to room temperatures regularly.

To size up battery health, head over to Settings > Battery > Battery Health. If it's reported at 80 percent or higher, you're probably fine. The further you dip below that threshold, however, the more likely you are to run into problems. If you can't get your iPhone to turn back on without plugging it in first, it's definitely time to schedule a battery replacement or buy a new iPhone.

Make sure you aren't running your device at extremely low free space, as that can cause performance issues. Visit Settings > General > iPhone Storage to check how much you have. If you're running with less than a few gigabytes to spare, make room on your iPhone. And if your iPhone has recently suffered physical damage, that could be the source.

If you've ruled out the above concerns, book an appointment at an Apple Store or authorized service center. There's likely internal damage or a defect, and while Apple does offer self-service repair, there's no easy way of diagnosing what's broken — let alone fixing it — unless it's blindingly obvious that a specific hardware feature is involved.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cwm.headline: England 37-12 New Zealand: Hosts run up record win over All Blacks
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cwm.author: Mike Henson

paragraphs.text: England (19) 37
Tries: Slade, Van Poortvliet, Earl, Chessum, Atkinson Cons: F Smith (2), M Smith Pens: M Smith (2)
New Zealand (5) 12
Tries: De Groot, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie
England's revival roared up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody led the hosts' response to the haka.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, stood at the centre of a flying V formation that England had adopted for their victories over the same opponents last year and in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.
In terms of margin, this win trumped both - and the other seven England victories in the teams' 121-year rivalry.
And the hosts were full value for it. They dominated the All Blacks from the start.
Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.
Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men.

England introduced five forwards off the bench in the immediate aftermath of that 55th-minute score and, with Ellis Genge in fearsome carrying form, they had more than enough to see out victory in comfort.
Seb Atkinson took a delayed pop pass from Marcus Smith to stroll in for England's fifth try just after the hour.
The hosts finished the game camped down in the New Zealand 22m in search of a sixth score while choruses of Swing Low rolled around the stands.
For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.
By contrast England, who could still end up in next weekend's Nations Championship grand final depending on results, are riding a wave of confidence.
Moody sets the mood
Moody's involvement in the pre-match challenge ensured New Zealand were met by a wall of noise and relentless pressure from kick-off.
Fast starts have become a feature of England's autumn campaign so far, with Australia and Japan both blitzed in the opening minutes.
New Zealand are a class above those teams, but fared little better against the revved-up hosts.
The game was only four minutes old when Slade, with roars from the stands at his back, won the race to a Fin Smith grubber.
After that initial strike, England maintained a stranglehold on the match.
A brilliant 50:22 from George Furbank bought more territory and England, hitting hard in defence, penned New Zealand back.
Their dominance did not immediately translate into points.
Individual errors - Jack van Poortvliet's fumble at the back of a breakdown, Fin Smith's over-cooked cross-field kick, Alex Coles being held up over the line - meant chances went begging.

After half an hour, England had enjoyed 74% of possession, 82% of territory and made 183 metres to New Zealand's 34. A sense the hosts may ultimately regret those mistakes nagged at fans in the stands.

It proved misplaced. Van Poortvliet plunged over from short range after a Cadan Murley break and then, four minutes later, the excellent Ben Earl thundered off the back of a scrum, trampled through Cam Roigard and went under the posts.
New Zealand prop Ethan de Groot burrowed over to repair some of the damage, but at 19-5 down at the break, the visitors were both reeling and somewhat fortunate to still be in touch.

England started the second half at the same breathless pace that marked their approach to the first. Ollie Chessum, lurking out wide, ploughed through the unfortunate Will Jordan for a try inside two minutes of the restart.
Beauden Barrett's score briefly had the embers glowing for New Zealand, but England's bench stomped out any hopes of a comeback.
Genge, Will Stuart, Luke Cowan-Dickie, George Martin and Greg Fisilau gave the forward brought crunching physicality and line speed.
The starters were not far behind, with Chessum levelling former All Black captain Scott Barrett with a superb tackle.

With victory long since secured, an 81,953-strong crowd could relish those individual duels, reflect on a scoreline that exceeded the famous 2012 win and look forward to next weekend, and a possible rematch with New Zealand or meeting with South Africa, at leisure.
England: Furbank; Freeman, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph; F Smith, van Poortvliet; Baxter, George, Heyes, Itoje, Coles, Chessum, B Curry, Earl
Replacements: Cowan-Dickie, Genge, Stuart, Martin, Fisilau, Pollock, Spencer, M Smith
New Zealand: B Barrett; Jordan, Lienert-Brown, J Barrett, Moorby; McKenzie, Roigard; de Groot, Taylor, Newell, S Barrett, Holland, Vaa'i, Lakai, Sititi
Replacements: Aumua, Bower, Tosi, Segner, Fainga'anuku, Ratima, Mo'unga, Ioane

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/who-is-el-.headline: Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/who-is-el-.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.
Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.
Recommended Stories

The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”
“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”
Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of?
Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.

Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.

US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.
The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.

“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.
He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.
How was Chapo Isidro arrested?
Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.

Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.

It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.
The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.
Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.
Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.
“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

cbsnews.com/news/catherine-princess-of-w.headline: Catherine, Princess of Wales, speaks about healing from cancer in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"

paragraphs.text: November 21, 2026 / 11:01 AM EST / CBS/AP
Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.
Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.

Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.

In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."
She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/3.headline: 3 things to check before choosing a health plan
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/3.author: Christy Bieber

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Christy Bieber1 min

Open enrollment provides the opportunity to buy or change a health care plan. Whether you’re signing up for an employer plan or one on the individual health insurance market, there are three things to check.

• Network size: Some plans require you to go in-network for covered services except in emergencies. Others offer more affordable care from in-network providers. Find out how large the network is and whether your preferred providers are in-network.

• Maximum out-of-pocket limit: This is the maximum you’ll have to pay each year for covered medical services. There are often separate limits for in-network versus out-of-network care. Know them both to understand your financial exposure.

• Deductible: This is the amount you pay out of pocket for covered services before your insurer covers the bills. There’s often a separate in-network and out-of-network deductible. Until you pay your deductible, your insurer won’t pay for most care except an annual exam and some preventive services.

Understanding these three things helps you see what care you can access and how much you’ll spend. Plans with higher deductibles and maximum out-of-pocket limits have lower premiums, but you should be aware of the trade-off that you may spend more on care throughout the year.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: My husband refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with my family

This letter writer tells us that her husband (“Jim”) has a perfectly wonderful relationship with her family. Except for one thing that comes up around the holidays: He absolutely refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with them.

Jim’s issue with these dinners is that the family eschews the bedrock of a traditional Thanksgiving meal: They don’t serve turkey. Instead, the family plates up beef wellington as their holiday main. This is a meal, our letter writer explains, that’s as traditional to their family as turkey is to most people.
So what is this letter writer to do? In this week’s episode of Life Hax, advice columnists Carolyn Hax and Shane O’Neill deeply disagree on what’s appropriate.
Shane suggests the couple could just bring turkey to share with her family. Carolyn says offering up food would be perfectly fine — if only it weren’t the main dish.
Per Carolyn: “Could your husband please lose his ever-loving mind over the mashed potatoes? Or a pie? Please?”
To hear more from Shane and Carolyn, follow the Life Hax show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. If you have your own question to ask, email LifeHax@washpost.com.
Reporter covering travel
When to hit the road for the least-bad Thanksgiving traffic
When it comes to Thanksgiving road trips, the early bird should get the easiest ride.

Traffic congestion in areas around New York City, D.C. and Los Angeles is projected to more than double during early afternoon and early evening drives on certain days before and after the holiday, according to data from traffic analytics firm INRIX.
The best advice from road trip experts: Start driving in the morning to avoid peak traffic jams.

A forecast from AAA using data from INRIX said the busiest driving days are expected to be the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving and the Sunday and Monday after. On the holiday itself, expect “minimal traffic,” the forecast said.

On the far edges of the travel period — Nov. 24 and 30 — drivers should be on the road before 1 p.m. to avoid the worst stretches starting around 2 p.m. and lasting through early evening. On Nov. 25 and 27, it’s best to head out before noon. And on the weekend after Thanksgiving, get driving before 11 a.m. as the worst congestion is expected to start at noon and last until 8 or 9 p.m., depending on the day.
AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel by car at least 50 miles from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.
Visual correspondent covering California and the Southwest
L.A. train heists net thieves more than $22 million in goods, feds say
The freight train was still clattering down the tracks when a masked man using a red Milwaukee angle grinder sawed through the lock of a shipping container filled with Nike Air Max sneakers.

By the time the crew filmed this heist in October 2024, it had already allegedly stolen more than $167,000 in Nike shoes in another train job. According to a federal indictment released Thursday, they were just getting started.

The Southern California crew is charged with breaking into more than 70 shipping containers over 31 months, stealing more than $22 million in electronics, tools, sneakers and other apparel to be sold on the black market.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the indictment. The 14 men were arrested Thursday and a federal grand jury charged each of them with one count of conspiracy, 14 counts of theft and two counts of violence against railroad carriers.

Federal prosecutors say the crew was led by Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, and included his father and two uncles. They allegedly identified trains hauling high-value cargo from overseas and were moving through Southern California rail yards headed to distribution centers out of state. The thieves allegedly climbed aboard and cut air hoses to trigger the emergency brakes at predetermined locations, where they loaded rental trucks and vans with stolen goods.

The indictment comes during concerns about rail heists around the country. According to the Association of American Railroads there were more than 75,000 thefts nationally last year with a 50 percent increase year over year. In Los Angeles, a string of thefts in 2022 left hundreds of boxes strewn on the tracks.
“The images looked like a Third World country,” Gov. Gavin Newsom told reporters at the time. “What you saw here in the last week is just not acceptable.”
Reporter covering Latin America from Mexico City
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
El Salvador’s popular and ironfisted president, Nayib Bukele, formally registered his candidacy for a third term Thursday, setting the stage for elections in February that he is expected to win.

Since entering office in 2019, Bukele, 45, has found widespread support at home and from some quarters abroad for his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and a steep reduction in homicides. But he has been widely criticized for curtailing civil liberties, sweeping up alleged gang members without due process, repressing political dissent and dismantling democratic institutions.

He has successfully consolidated his power in what has become a de facto one-party state. Last year, Bukele’s allies in the legislature changed the country’s constitution to allow a president to serve an unlimited number of terms. If he wins next year’s elections, he would remain president until 2033.
Speaking before cheering crowds Thursday after registering his candidacy at the country’s electoral tribunal, Bukele said that “some international media say there isn’t democracy in El Salvador.”
“I tell them, no, no, no, there wasn’t democracy in El Salvador before,” he said.

Bukele is launching his candidacy as he pursues a gang battle abroad, in Haiti, where he has deployed about 2,500 Salvadoran troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing during a gang ambush while supporting a United Nations-backed international force. This week, large crowds poured into the streets in Haiti to praise and thank Bukele.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
Texas governor-elect and Trump agree to work together on border security
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
“It was a very productive call,” Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa, adding, “I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall.

“He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,” said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. “I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.”

On Thursday, Hinojosa met the state’s border sheriffs and told Fox News, “We need the federal government to put more resources along the border,” noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICE’s violent interior immigration enforcement “needs to end.”
“We have had people killed in the streets,” she said. “I will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Hat had traveled too far into Fiona’s intestines to safely remove, zoo says

A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo who died Thursday, showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff “tried everything they could” after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.

“Open incision in a hippo that size — with an incision that’s that long — would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasn’t enough for her,” Wenninger said in a video Friday.

Fiona’s unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons — a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday — at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.

thehill.com/opinion/healthcare/6233880-c.headline: The blue wave can fix America’s critical food safety and security gaps
thehill.com/opinion/healthcare/6233880-c.author: Lyndon Haviland, opinion contributor

paragraphs.text: When millions gather this Thanksgiving, most won’t question the safety of the food on their plates. They’ll assume our government has strict measures in place that protect our food supply from dangerous contaminants that could cause people harm.

The facts tell a different story. A recent Washington Post investigation found that the Food and Drug Administration has inspected fewer than 8 percent of all major foreign facilities that provide fresh produce to the United States since 2009.

Think about that: Over 90 percent of the largest international plants that sell fruits and vegetables to America have not received an FDA inspection in nearly two decades. It’s a massive public health blind spot for a country that’s become increasingly reliant on produce imports in recent years.

The public health threat this poses to Americans isn’t hyperbole. This summer, a multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis that was linked to iceberg lettuce imported from Mexico sickenednearly 13,000 people, hospitalized over 550 and claimed two lives. The contaminated lettuce came from a Mexican supplier whose operations hadn’t been inspected by the FDA in seven years.

There have been other contaminations. In September, broccoli sprouts and microgreens imported from New Zealand contaminated with salmonella sickened 34 people across six states. In October, frozen blueberries from Chile were recalled due to an E. coli outbreak that caused 17 illnesses and six hospitalizations.

In total, the FDA anticipates over 550 food recalls will take place this fiscal cycle, a number consistent with what the agency typically sees in an average year. However, the increasing severity of these events, combined with cutbacks in personnel, has public health experts worried.

Janet Hamilton of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists says “the scale and magnitude of outbreaks that we’re facing right now are unprecedented. It’s like we’re being eclipsed by the scale and magnitude of these outbreaks with the staffing levels that we have.”

She’s right: The very institutions tasked with protecting the U.S. food supply have been weakened by recent federal workforce reductions. Cutbacks at the FDA — over 4,000 people in just the past two years alone — have hampered the government’s ability to prevent recent deadly foodborne contamination events.

U.S. lawmakers have failed their collective responsibility to ensure the nation’s food regulatory agencies are keeping Americans safe. But a wave of newly elected members to Capitol Hill is expected to bring much needed support for our public health institutions when the next Congress convenes in January.

Two physicians have been elected to the U.S. Senate. They include pediatrician Annie Andrews in South Carolina and physician and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Both will bring a deep bench of medical and public health experience to federal rulemaking in the nation’s capital.

They — along with several other incoming members of Congress with science backgrounds — will help ensure facts prevail and lead the way on health policy. They will be important voices who will hold to account the country’s top health official, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., whose initiatives to date have turned the clock back on public health safety.

These include the removal of 10,000 roles at Health and Human Services, the dismissal of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine advisory committee and the easing of restrictions on unproven therapies that align with Kennedy’s personal lifestyle choices. A Democratic majority in both chambers of Congress will establish important checks and balances to administration efforts that have put public health at potential risk.

The advancement of public health food policy will soon be part of the national legislative agenda. Democrats are already pushing support for important food security initiatives, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, whose mission to help low-income families has been decimated under the current Congress.

Public health institutions have endured a steady erosion of trust in America. Restricting federal resources that make it more difficult for them to protect the safety and availability of our food supply will only make it worse.

Preventing foodborne illness and providing food access for those in need will be a top focus of the next Congress. Whether the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress will work with Democrats to support these important goals to protect the safety of the American people will be up to them.
Lyndon Haviland, DrPH, MPH, is a distinguished scholar at the CUNY School of Public Health and Health Policy.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/us-midterm.headline: US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/us-midterm.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not take power until January.
Election officials are still certifying results, while the newly elected lawmakers are preparing to take office, and the outgoing Congress is continuing its legislative work.
Recommended Stories
So what happens between now and January, and what will change as the 120th Congress takes office?
What has happened so far?
After the elections, officials have been finalising the results and completing the certification process, which varies by state.
On November 9, the existing Congress returned to Washington for what is known as the “lame-duck” session.
A lame-duck session occurs when Congress meets after an election but before the new Congress takes office.
This means the Republicans still have the majority in both chambers of Congress and can continue passing legislation until the new Congress takes office in January.
November-December: New lawmakers prepare to take office
During this time, newly elected members start preparing to take office in January.
They attend orientation sessions in Washington, hire staff, and learn more about how Congress operates day-to-day.

Political parties also choose their leaders in the House of Representatives and the Senate. The party controlling each chamber selects the majority leader, while the other party selects the minority leader. The House will also vote on a speaker, who leads the House leadership.
The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as its Senate leader, entering the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.
The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight.

Among Democrats, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator and current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York to be Senate majority leader, with a vote scheduled for December 1.
Speaking on Al Jazeera’s This Is America, Democratic strategist Roger Fisk suggested that the differences between the two candidates may be more about their methods than their political goals.
“I think the difference would probably come in the how rather than the what,” Fisk said.
Republican strategist Doug Heye said the leadership debate reflects wider questions facing both parties after the midterms.

“Both parties have somewhat of an identity crisis,” he said, referring to the Republicans’ losses and the future of the party but also the divisions in the Democratic Party between moderate Democrats and more progressive ones.
December 11: A government funding deadline
One of the biggest challenges of the current Congress is a December 11 deadline to approve government funding.
Congress passed a temporary spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to keep the federal agencies functioning without approving a full-year budget.
But before the measure expires, Congress must approve another bill to keep the government funded.
If lawmakers do not reach a deal, part of the federal government could face a shutdown.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Heye suggested a temporary funding extension could push negotiations into February, by which time Democrats will control both chambers.
“So that would probably go through February,” he said, referring to a possible continuing resolution.
Heye also said the federal debt ceiling is another challenge for the new Congress.
“These are two things that never come up on the campaign trail, but it can be very important to tell us about the next two years,” he added.
December 17-18: Congress wraps up
The current Congress is expected to finalise its legislative work before the Christmas holidays.
The House’s final sitting day is planned for December 17 and the Senate’s for December 18.
But lawmakers could remain in Washington longer if major issues remain unresolved.
Even if lawmakers finish their work earlier, the 119th Congress’s term does not officially end until January 3.
January 3, 2027: The new Congress takes power
The 120th Congress starts its term at noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, 2027.
But January 3 falls on a Sunday, and Congress could pass a law setting a different date for the first meeting.
When the new House convenes, lawmakers must elect a Speaker before being sworn in. Newly elected senators will also take their oaths.
With Democrats controlling both chambers, they will gain authority over congressional committees, legislative priorities and investigations into the administration of President Donald Trump.
“You’re going to have in the House and the Senate something called committee chairs, and they’re all going to be Democrats, and they’re all going to have subpoena power,” Heye told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned that congressional investigations could complicate negotiations between Democrats and the White House.
What changes politically in January?
Trump will remain president after the midterms, but he will face a Congress controlled by Democrats in both chambers.
This means his administration will have to negotiate with the Democrats to pass legislation, while a Democrat-led Senate will control the confirmation process for presidential nominees.
Democrats will also be able to launch congressional investigations and hold hearings looking at the president’s actions and the actions of those in his inner circle and administration.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has already outlined some of the party’s priorities.
“We need to end the war of choice in Iran. We need to stop the Trump tariffs,” he said.
He also called for reversing Medicaid and food assistance cuts and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.
But Democratic control of Congress does not guarantee those policies will become law. Trump can veto legislation, while overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.

“I would hope that […] each side would at least be willing to give each other 60 to 90 days to see where they might be able to cobble together a couple wins on behalf of the American people,” Fisk, the Democratic strategist, said.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/americas/me.headline: Who Is the Mexican Drug Kingpin Known as El Chapo Isidro?

paragraphs.text: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the United States’ most wanted criminals, has been captured, the Mexican government said on Saturday.

Mr. Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, was among the most powerful drug traffickers in Sinaloa, a state in northwestern Mexico where cartels mass produce fentanyl and other illicit drugs that are bound for the United States and other parts of the world.

The U.S. authorities have described Mr. Meza Flores as a top drug trafficker in the region who leads the Meza-Flores organization, a heavily armed and violent group. He was first indicted in the United States over a decade ago, and he has been on the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list since last year.
Here’s what we know about the drug kingpin.
How did he become so powerful?

Mr. Meza Flores, 44, appears to have worked his way up through the ranks of Mexico’s drug cartels. He was a leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, which split from the Sinaloa Cartel in 2008, according to the Treasury Department.

The Sinaloa Cartel, which was founded and led by Joaquin Guzmán Loera, known as El Chapo, and Ismael Zambada Garcia, known as El Mayo, is one of the world’s largest and most feared crime syndicates. Rivalries among cartels and organizations that splintered off during internal fighting have led to devastating gang wars in Mexico.
(Mr. Meza Flores shares a similar nickname but is not related to Mr. Guzmán Loera, who was arrested in 2014.)

The Beltrán Leyva split set off a bloody regional war, according to the Treasury Department, which issued sanctions against the group. Beltrán Leyva was founded by Arturo Beltran Leyva, a weapons and drug smuggler, and his brothers, and its enforcement arm is considered “one of the most ruthless and brutal in the way they dispose of their enemies,” according to the State Department.
Mr. Meza Flores later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores criminal organization.
What is his group accused of?

The Meza-Flores group has smuggled tons of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States from several places in Mexico, according to U.S. officials. The group has long operated from the northern city of Guasave in Sinaloa, U.S. officials say.

In 2013, the Treasury Department officially designated Mr. Meza Flores and his group as a drug trafficking organization and linked Mr. Meza Flores’s wife, parents, sister and uncles to the criminal enterprise.

Mr. Meza Flores waged a brutal turf war with the Sinaloa Cartel, which saw the quadrupling of drug-related killings between roughly 2008 and 2012, as well as a spike in kidnappings and arson attacks, the Treasury Department said in 2013.

But the Meza-Flores group had recently allied with a faction of the cartel that has been fighting for control, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in Sinaloa’s state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars.
The Meza-Flores group is responsible for the deaths of many Mexican police officers as well as military and law enforcement officials, according to the F.B.I.
How long has the U.S. sought him?

Mr. Meza Flores was indicted in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on charges related to the possession and distribution of cocaine and methamphetamine. In 2019, a federal grand jury issued a new indictment for him with additional drug trafficking charges, and firearms violations.
Last year the F.B.I. added Mr. Meza Flores to its 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List, offering a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his capture.

Federal prosecutors in Washington updated the charges against Mr. Meza Flores two months ago, suggesting that the U.S. authorities were still actively pursuing him. The latest indictment added new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Mr. Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel, and it accused him of abducting and killing a member of the Mexican National Guard in Oaxaca in 2022.
How was he captured?
Mexico’s defense ministry said in a statement on Saturday that the operation had been carried out in coordination with U.S. agencies.

The Drug Enforcement Administration said in a statement that the capture of Mr. Meza Flores “delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization” and “underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders.”
Representatives for the State Department and the F.B.I. did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw Guasave into turmoil on Friday night. Sinaloa State’s public security agency urged residents to shelter in place and stay away from a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state to avoid attacks between gang members and federal forces.

nytimes.com/2026/11/21/business/anthropi.headline: Anthropic’s Debut Shows the Disconnect Between Wall Street and Silicon Valley

paragraphs.text: Anthropic on Thursday celebrated its first day of trading as stock prices surged and the company touched a valuation of $2 trillion. On Friday, its stock deflated, sinking 9 percent.

In the aftermath of its record-breaking initial public offering, Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, has vacuumed up more than $120 billion in investor funds. It also consumed the good will of investors, many of whom were already becoming spooked at the artificial intelligence industry’s trillions of dollars of spending on data centers and other infrastructure to power the technology.

Following the huge investments in Anthropic, rival OpenAI and other A.I start-ups may face new hurdles going public, analysts and investors said. And even more established A.I. companies which need to raise debt or equity to pay for their expansion projects may encounter an uphill battle as the sector loses its glow.

That new hesitation was on full display this week, reflecting the widening disconnect between Silicon Valley optimism over A.I.’s potential and Wall Street’s growing doubts about whether the businesses are financially viable.

“The old-school way of looking at this is: This is the largest I.P.O. in history, late in the A.I. cycle. Psychologically, that could be a topping event,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, which brokers stock sales for hedge funds.

The market was shaken on Friday by some of those fears, ending the week with the worst stock slide in more than a year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 5.3 percent, wiping away the gains it had made this year. And the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent, reaching correction territory, or a drop of 10 percent from its recent high.
Stocks of bellwether A.I. companies including Nvidia, CoreWeave and Advanced Micro Devices fell by double-digit percentages on Friday.

Contributing to the sell-off was last week’s resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, and worries about what that means for the chip maker’s important role financing other A.I. companies. Interest rates are also rising, making it more expensive for some companies to build data centers and buy chips. And Democrats swept into power during the midterm elections, many promising A.I. regulation.

Those developments put the enormous amount of money needed to finance the chips, data centers and electricity underpinning the technology at risk. Companies are planning to spend about $5 trillion between now and 2030 on the infrastructure, said Michael Arougheti, chief executive of Ares Management, a large investment manager, on an earnings call last month.

SpaceX, Meta and others tapped the markets last month for tens of billions of dollars to fuel their A.I. spending. Executives at most tech giants have told investors they are increasing their spending on the technology each quarter. And Anthropic’s initial public offering piled on top, causing fatigue, analysts and investors said.

Many concerns about A.I. spending are easily dismissed in Silicon Valley, which, by nature, lives in a different world. Venture capitalists this year have minted nearly 200 new unicorns, or start-ups worth more than $1 billion, more than in any other year since the private market frenzy in 2021, according to PitchBook, which tracks start-ups.
But a market for the kinds of initial public offerings or mergers to justify the velocity of investments hasn't yet emerged.

Even in Anthropic’s case, the company allowed early employees to sell more than $25 billion of combined stock at the start of trading, an unusually large sum that some investors and analysts viewed as aggressive. Companies and their investment bankers usually limit employees and other shareholders from selling their stock for weeks or months after I.P.O.s to help stabilize the price.

Many hedge fund managers failed to get stock in Anthropic’s offering at the initial price of $83 per share, said Raphaëlle D’Ornano, an A.I. industry analyst who also invests in public stocks. The hedge funds instead paid a significantly higher price for shares when trading opened on Thursday at $111.50.

Those hedge funds would have lost money as the stock quickly sank, closing at $88.91 on Friday. At the same time, funds have been trying to limit how much stock they own in A.I. companies overall, she added.
Friday “was pure panic,” Ms. D’Ornano said.

Wall Street and Silicon Valley largely agree that A.I. tools are certain to upend how people work, use the internet, and maybe even make discoveries in medicine. But no one is confident on how quickly the technology will produce those benefits.

And as the tech companies invest heavily, it isn’t clear how many will bring in enough revenue to become profitable. Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth has depended on businesses that use Claude for automating software engineering work, and the company will need to broaden that customer base in the coming years, analysts said.

OpenAI, which has filed for an initial public offering expected as soon as next year, is hoping for a similar shift into a broader customer base. The company also wants to get more free users of its popular chatbot, ChatGPT, to start paying.
(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Those business realities have led to some criticism from Wall Street fund managers, who feel that many in Silicon Valley are overly optimistic about potential returns. For example, Dylan Patel, a closely followed A.I. industry analyst, has predicted unrelenting growth, saying Anthropic and OpenAI would together surpass a half-trillion dollars in revenue by the end of next year, despite shaky markets.

As Mr. Patel walked onstage at a private San Francisco conference for venture capitalists and start-up founders this month to an upbeat electronic song, “Levels” by Avicii, tech stocks were tanking. “Do you have more depressing music, given what’s going on in the market?” he joked.

Mr. Patel, who runs the San Francisco-based market research company SemiAnalysis, said at the conference that investors’ skepticism about the continued pace of revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic was one big reason for market turmoil. He predicted those companies would generate more revenue from new business lines, like offering cybersecurity tools and designing chips.
“I myself am a little cuckoo, and I think they actually will hit this, just to be clear,” he said. “But I think many people are a bit skeptical.”

Some A.I. start-up executives said they have noticed a pullback from investors as they consider jumping into their next rounds of funding. Those company leaders are starting to openly acknowledge one awkward reality of the A.I. boom: The technology’s growth has been largely powered by a relatively small number of voracious business customers and consumers who pay for it.

“Eighty percent of the revenue is probably coming from 20 percent of the users. It might even be 90 percent,” said Aravind Srinivas, the chief executive of the Nvidia-backed A.I. start-up Perplexity, at a conference last week hosted by the tech publication, Newcomer.
(The Times has sued Perplexity, accusing it of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The company has denied the claims.)
Even as Silicon Valley venture capitalists watched Anthropic’s rocky entry into the public markets, they remained upbeat about the future.

Hemant Taneja, the chief executive of tech investment firm General Catalyst, said he felt relief that Anthropic’s stock price held above the offering price amid “turbulent” markets. Anthropic, he added, was not a one-off example of a venture-funded company that would capitalize on A.I. advances.
“I’m walking away saying: Who’s the next set of founders with the same opportunity?” he said.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/all-the-ai-age.headline: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
techcrunch.com/2026/11/21/all-the-ai-age.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Haven
Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.

According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”
Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.
Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.
Instinct
Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls.
The company remains in private beta.
Iris

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin
Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick
Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.
The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.
Miso
Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.
Ohai
Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.
It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.
Orbits
Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.
Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.
Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.
Pally

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.
There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.
Poke

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.
Rene

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.
Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.
Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.
Skye

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.
The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.
Stanley

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.
Szn

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.
According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.
Tab

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.
The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.
Tomo
The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.
The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.
Town

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.
In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.
Underdog

Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.
The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.
Wajo
Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.
Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.
Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.
