engadget.com/2318404/apple-homeview-cook.headline: One of Apple HomeView's best features will have you cooking like a pro
engadget.com/2318404/apple-homeview-cook.author: Alec Hively

paragraphs.text: As every home chef knows, using a recipe on your phone is a pain. Nothing is less appetizing than trying to unlock your phone and scroll through a 3,000 word preamble to learn when you should take your eggplant parmesan out of the oven. Beyond the inevitable frustrations, the colony of germs teeming over your phone screen make it a hygienic nightmare.

In comes the Apple HomeView, a versatile smart hub that allows you to manage your various apple products hands free. Released on November 13, 2026, the entertainment hub comes with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and a bounty of Siri AI features. One of its most useful tool is its Start Cooking feature, which provides an easy-to-navigate recipe in Safari on your HomeView screen. Eliminating the need to constantly return to your iPhone when making a rice pilaf, the HomeView's smart feature integrations make your culinary creations easy and enjoyable.

Before diving into how the HomeView can facilitate your next meal, let's cover a quick prerequisite: your phone. Owning an Apple iPhone or iPad is essential to unlocking your HomeView's best features, as you can seamlessly handoff music, Safari searches, calendar reminders and FaceTime conversations to your smart hub. To use your HomeView, update your iPhone's operating system to iOS 27.2 or later.
How to use your HomeView's recipe feature

If you are exploring a new recipe on your iPhone's Safari app, you can easily transfer the webpage to your HomeView screen by holding it up to your device. Alternatively, you can browse directly for recipes using your smart hub's Siri AI functions or with an old-fashioned web search. Once your HomeView detects that a recipe page is pulled up in Safari, it will offer you the option to follow a recipe via an icon of a spoon and recipe card at the bottom righthand corner of your screen. Simply tap this Show Recipe button and your HomeView will enter its cooking mode.

Once converted to Show Recipe mode, your webpage changes into an easy-to-follow recipe guide, with each step separated into a swipeable slide so you can easily understand and track every step. Simply swipe left to navigate to the next step. The ingredients, meanwhile, are broken out into a checkable list.

If you need to set a timer, Apple's HomeView will automatically offer you the opportunity to begin a countdown preset to your recipe's specifications. Simply click the orange highlighted timeframe text when you want the timer to begin. Once clicked, the countdown will appear at the top of your HomeView's screen. Simply click on the countdown to navigate to your timer's screen.

In addition to making your recipes more manageable, the HomeView helps makes your cooking experience more enjoyable. Now you can dance to Frank Sinatra, check your doorbell camera and review your latest text messages all without leaving the kitchen. No more burning your soufflé because you got distracted while shewing a solicitor off your doorstep.
Getting your HomeView up and running

The darling of Apple's Welcome Home event in October, the smart hub currently retails on Apple's website for $299. Also available at your local Apple store, HomeView comes in two versions. The first is a a self standing speaker that comes in four colors. You can also purchase it as a wall mounted device in either SpaceGray or Silver. Notably, wall mounted devices require you to purchase a mount to set them up and may require professional installation.

As it stands, Apple currently offers two mounting options. The first is a the $79.95 hardwired AC mount from Schneider Home. Sleek and cordless, Apple suggests enlisting a professional installer to attach your AC mount. A cheaper, easier option is the Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector. Costing $59.99, this mount can be self-installed. However, it also requires a 20W or more power adapter, which is sold separately. While Apple offers a 40W Dynamic Power Adapter when purchasing a wall-mountable HomeView, you can likely purchase a cheaper adapter from favorite electronics retailer. Apple also plans to offer a hardwired power over ethernet (PoE) mount, enabling a direct internet connection. However, this option is currently not available.

Once purchased, setting up your HomeView is easy. First, prepare your iPhone or iPad by visiting the Settings app, connect to your home WiFi network and update your device. Next make sure you are signed in to the same Apple account you plan on using for your HomeView.

Now, make sure that your home is added to your Home app. Next, plug in your HomeView via its USB-C cable and adapter. Once the Hello screen appears, unlock your iPhone or iPad and hold it up to your HomeView and complete the setup by following the onscreen prompts.

washingtonpost.com/the-seven/2026/11/21/.headline: Man convicted of starting deadly Palisades fire in California
washingtonpost.com/the-seven/2026/11/21/.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news
A jury has found a man guilty of starting the 2025 Palisades Fire — one of the most destructive wildfires in California’s history, which killed 12 people and burned through whole neighborhoods.
Former Los Angeles resident Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted of arson and destroying property on Friday, after a previous trial ended in a mistrial. He denied all the charges.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht lit what became known as the Lachman Fire on Jan 1., 2025, while he was alone in a small clearing on Hidden Buddha Hill. Firefighters suppressed that fire, but it continued to burn underground, and resurfaced on Jan. 7, prosecutors said.
That fire rapidly expanded into the massive Palisades fire that destroyed more than 6,800 buildings across Los Angeles and Malibu, with officials estimating the damage bill at $25 billion.
Rinderknecht was arrested in Florida in October 2025.
During the 14-day trial, prosecutors argued that Rinderknecht had been angry and frustrated in the run-up to the fire, and said geolocation data placed him near the fire’s origin site.
Rinderknecht’s lawyer said in a statement to the Associated Press that he would consider whether to appeal.
Rinderknecht is due to be sentenced on March 17, 2027.
3 things to check before choosing a health plan

Open enrollment provides the opportunity to buy or change a health care plan. Whether you’re signing up for an employer plan or one on the individual health insurance market, there are three things to check.

• Network size: Some plans require you to go in-network for covered services except in emergencies. Others offer more affordable care from in-network providers. Find out how large the network is and whether your preferred providers are in-network.

• Maximum out-of-pocket limit: This is the maximum you’ll have to pay each year for covered medical services. There are often separate limits for in-network versus out-of-network care. Know them both to understand your financial exposure.

• Deductible: This is the amount you pay out of pocket for covered services before your insurer covers the bills. There’s often a separate in-network and out-of-network deductible. Until you pay your deductible, your insurer won’t pay for most care except an annual exam and some preventive services.

Understanding these three things helps you see what care you can access and how much you’ll spend. Plans with higher deductibles and maximum out-of-pocket limits have lower premiums, but you should be aware of the trade-off that you may spend more on care throughout the year.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: My husband refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with my family

This letter writer tells us that her husband (“Jim”) has a perfectly wonderful relationship with her family. Except for one thing that comes up around the holidays: He absolutely refuses to have Thanksgiving dinner with them.

Jim’s issue with these dinners is that the family eschews the bedrock of a traditional Thanksgiving meal: They don’t serve turkey. Instead, the family plates up beef wellington as their holiday main. This is a meal, our letter writer explains, that’s as traditional to their family as turkey is to most people.
So what is this letter writer to do? In this week’s episode of Life Hax, advice columnists Carolyn Hax and Shane O’Neill deeply disagree on what’s appropriate.
Shane suggests the couple could just bring turkey to share with her family. Carolyn says offering up food would be perfectly fine — if only it weren’t the main dish.
Per Carolyn: “Could your husband please lose his ever-loving mind over the mashed potatoes? Or a pie? Please?”
To hear more from Shane and Carolyn, follow the Life Hax show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. If you have your own question to ask, email LifeHax@washpost.com.
Reporter covering travel
When to hit the road for the least-bad Thanksgiving traffic
When it comes to Thanksgiving road trips, the early bird should get the easiest ride.

Traffic congestion in areas around New York City, D.C. and Los Angeles is projected to more than double during early afternoon and early evening drives on certain days before and after the holiday, according to data from traffic analytics firm INRIX.
The best advice from road trip experts: Start driving in the morning to avoid peak traffic jams.

A forecast from AAA using data from INRIX said the busiest driving days are expected to be the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving and the Sunday and Monday after. On the holiday itself, expect “minimal traffic,” the forecast said.

On the far edges of the travel period — Nov. 24 and 30 — drivers should be on the road before 1 p.m. to avoid the worst stretches starting around 2 p.m. and lasting through early evening. On Nov. 25 and 27, it’s best to head out before noon. And on the weekend after Thanksgiving, get driving before 11 a.m. as the worst congestion is expected to start at noon and last until 8 or 9 p.m., depending on the day.
AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel by car at least 50 miles from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.
Visual correspondent covering California and the Southwest
L.A. train heists net thieves more than $22 million in goods, feds say
The freight train was still clattering down the tracks when a masked man using a red Milwaukee angle grinder sawed through the lock of a shipping container filled with Nike Air Max sneakers.

By the time the crew filmed this heist in October 2024, it had already allegedly stolen more than $167,000 in Nike shoes in another train job. According to a federal indictment released Thursday, they were just getting started.

The Southern California crew is charged with breaking into more than 70 shipping containers over 31 months, stealing more than $22 million in electronics, tools, sneakers and other apparel to be sold on the black market.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the indictment. The 14 men were arrested Thursday and a federal grand jury charged each of them with one count of conspiracy, 14 counts of theft and two counts of violence against railroad carriers.

Federal prosecutors say the crew was led by Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, and included his father and two uncles. They allegedly identified trains hauling high-value cargo from overseas and were moving through Southern California rail yards headed to distribution centers out of state. The thieves allegedly climbed aboard and cut air hoses to trigger the emergency brakes at predetermined locations, where they loaded rental trucks and vans with stolen goods.

The indictment comes during concerns about rail heists around the country. According to the Association of American Railroads there were more than 75,000 thefts nationally last year with a 50 percent increase year over year. In Los Angeles, a string of thefts in 2022 left hundreds of boxes strewn on the tracks.
“The images looked like a Third World country,” Gov. Gavin Newsom told reporters at the time. “What you saw here in the last week is just not acceptable.”
Reporter covering Latin America from Mexico City
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
El Salvador’s popular and ironfisted president, Nayib Bukele, formally registered his candidacy for a third term Thursday, setting the stage for elections in February that he is expected to win.

Since entering office in 2019, Bukele, 45, has found widespread support at home and from some quarters abroad for his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and a steep reduction in homicides. But he has been widely criticized for curtailing civil liberties, sweeping up alleged gang members without due process, repressing political dissent and dismantling democratic institutions.

He has successfully consolidated his power in what has become a de facto one-party state. Last year, Bukele’s allies in the legislature changed the country’s constitution to allow a president to serve an unlimited number of terms. If he wins next year’s elections, he would remain president until 2033.
Speaking before cheering crowds Thursday after registering his candidacy at the country’s electoral tribunal, Bukele said that “some international media say there isn’t democracy in El Salvador.”
“I tell them, no, no, no, there wasn’t democracy in El Salvador before,” he said.

Bukele is launching his candidacy as he pursues a gang battle abroad, in Haiti, where he has deployed about 2,500 Salvadoran troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing during a gang ambush while supporting a United Nations-backed international force. This week, large crowds poured into the streets in Haiti to praise and thank Bukele.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
Texas governor-elect and Trump agree to work together on border security
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
“It was a very productive call,” Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa, adding, “I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall.

“He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,” said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. “I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.”

On Thursday, Hinojosa met the state’s border sheriffs and told Fox News, “We need the federal government to put more resources along the border,” noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICE’s violent interior immigration enforcement “needs to end.”
“We have had people killed in the streets,” she said. “I will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.”

thehill.com/homenews/senate/6235221-colo.headline: Colom announces town hall in reddest county of Mississippi
thehill.com/homenews/senate/6235221-colo.author: Ford McCracken

paragraphs.text: Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) will hold a town hall next Tuesday in the county where he received the lowest share of the vote in the midterms, he announced earlier this week, aligning with the Democrat’s pledges to be “a senator for all Mississippi.”

“Itawamba County is where I received my lowest percentage of the vote on Election Day. But I promised to be a senator for all Mississippi and I meant it,” Colom wrote in Facebook post Thursday. “No matter where you live or how you voted, your voice matters and I’ll always show up for you.”

Itawamba County is in northeast Mississippi, just east of the city of Tupelo. President Trump carried the county by 80 points in 2024 and received the highest share of the vote in county history for a Republican presidential candidate. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), whom Colom unseated in this year’s Senate race, won Itawamba by nearly 66 points.
The town hall invitation describes the event as “an opportunity to hear directly from Senator-elect Colom, ask questions, and engage in meaningful dialogue.”

Colom defeated Hyde-Smith in a massive upset that took days after the election to call. He is the first Black senator Mississippians have elected by popular vote and the third to ever represent the Magnolia State — the last being Sen. Blanche K. Bruce, who served during the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Although the state of Mississippi is one third Black, according to census data.
The senator-elect made reaching out to Republicans a focal point of his Senate campaign, something he had to do in order to be elected in deep-red Mississippi.

One viral video he posted to social media showed him speaking with voters in line for Trump’s Mississippi rally just days before the election. Colom said in an interview Friday speaking with Trump voters showed him they had a lot in common and were dissatisfied with similar issues.

“I want to represent those people. So, it was my job to go listen to them, and I found out we had a lot in common,” Colom told MS NOW’s Ari Melber. “They were saying the same stuff I was hearing across the state: high gas, high groceries, get out of the war in Iran.”
Even Trump chimed in to Colom’s appearance at his rally, saying in an interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith he gave the Democrat “a lot of credit” for campaigning in his line.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cmx.headline: Nations Championship: Liam McConnell shines as 11-try Scotland dismantle Japan
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cmx.author: Tom English

paragraphs.text: Scotland (29) 67
Tries: Graham 3, McConnell 3, Rowe, Smith 2, Dobie, Hutchinson Cons: Jordan 4, Horne 2
Japan (0) 5
Tries: Matsunaga
A Liam McConnell hat-trick in only his third appearance inspired Scotland in an 11-try Nations Championship rout of Japan at Murrayfield.
The 22-year-old Edinburgh back row was electrifying, not just in scoring three wonderful tries, but on both sides of the ball, attack and defence.

The sparkling Darcy Graham also got a hat-trick - his 39th, 40th and 41st international tries - against Eddie Jones' severely weakened team, blasted to kingdom come by England last weekend, and now on the end of another bruising experience.

They shipped five tries in an opening half that ended with the Scots leading 29-0. Game over. Graham got two of his in that opening spell with McConnell getting his first, with Kyle Rowe and Ollie Smith adding the others.

There's been considerable buzz about McConnell for a long time now and significant frustration among his supporters at his lack of opportunities with Scotland. He got his second and third scores before the hour. Jamie Dobie added a seventh.
Gregor Townsend changed most of his team from the win over the Wallabies last Sunday but the second string, if you can call them that, were at it right from the start.

Dobie's box-kick was spilled by the visitors and the last person they would have wanted to seize on the loose ball was Graham. He hacked on and scored. Tom Jordan, playing 10 instead of Finn Russell, was errant off the tee for much of the day and missed the first of his conversions. George Horne came on later and banged over some extras.
Scotland never relented in the building of their points mountain. Kyle Rowe took the ball in the air and the appreciation of space and speed of execution was too much for Japan after that.

Smith, heavily influential at full-back, was at the heart of so many things and he linked with Graham to put McConnell away. The big back row with his giant stride and his fantastic pace ate up the ground to score.

Rowe scored the third after brilliant running from Graham. Barely a quarter of the Test gone and it was already 17-0. Graham's solo score, following a sumptuous pick-up off the floor, brought up the bonus point just after the hour. The wing sped away to score under the posts.

Japan were reeling at the accuracy and the ambition of the Scotland attack. Getting cut open repeatedly, they had no answers. A fifth try arrived just before the break when Japan kicked, rather unwisely and aimlessly, out of defence - just meat and drink to Scotland.
McConnell's outstanding running put the hosts on the front foot and Japan in the horrors. Dobie and Rory Hutchinson set up Smith in the corner.

You felt for Japan. Rabbits in the headlights. McConnell's second came via more thrilling stuff from Darcy who picked up, chipped ahead and gathered to get in behind Japan. He offloaded to the rapid flanker who sprinted in from distance.

A form of Japanese consolation came when full-back Takuro Matsunaga scored but the Scottish response was swift and brutal. McConnell again, of course. He won the ball in the air and flew away to glory. A statement performance albeit against a broken team.
Dobie got the next after nice work from the quietly impressive Hutchinson and Smith got his second and Scotland's ninth after Blair Kinghorn had entered the fray with impact.
The last thing on earth that Japan needed was two yellow cards in the last 10 minutes but that's what they got.
Hutchinson scored not long after it became 15 versus 14 and Graham completed his own hat-trick when it was 15 versus 13.

A savage day for Japan but an unforgettable experience for the hat-trick men - especially the serial-scorer Graham and the emerging star McConnell. His smile at the end was so bright it could have powered half the city's electricity for the night.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/real-madrid-ou.headline: Real Madrid outpace Bayern Munich in revenue race as both clubs post record figures

paragraphs.text: European football's financial heavyweights are celebrating another record-breaking season. Real Madrid reported operating revenue of €1.221 billion for 2025-26, comfortably ahead of Bayern Munich's €988.2 million.
Real Madrid sets €1.25bn budget after record revenue
Real Madrid president Florentino Pérez announced the record figures at the club's annual general meeting, while presenting a budget of €1.25 billion for the 2026-27 season.
For the first time, the Spanish giants have surpassed the €1.2 billion revenue mark, a figure Pérez described as unprecedented for a sports organisation.

The club also recorded its highest-ever EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation), at €287.4 million. Net profit after tax reached €26 million, an increase of eight per cent compared with the previous season.

Pérez highlighted Real Madrid's international standing, citing Forbes, Deloitte and Brand Finance rankings. According to Forbes, the club is the world's most valuable football club for the fifth consecutive year. Deloitte ranks it first in revenue, while Brand Finance considers it the world's most valuable and strongest football brand.
Pérez said the club's partnerships with companies and technology providers would help it apply new expertise to its operations, particularly its sporting activities.

The figures underline the commercial strength of both clubs, although the Spanish giants remain out in front. Real Madrid's revenue increased by 3.1 per cent compared with the previous season, while Bayern recorded a more modest rise of around one per cent.

The difference amounts to approximately €233 million, although the clubs' published accounting figures are not entirely like-for-like: Real Madrid explicitly excludes player-transfer income from its operating revenue figure.
Real Madrid outstrip Bayern Munich in record revenues
Real Madrid's growth has been driven largely by its commercial operations and the redevelopment of the Santiago Bernabéu stadium.

Marketing generated €539 million, an increase of six per cent, while stadium revenue reached €363 million, up 11 per cent. Television rights and revenue from international competitions contributed a further €319 million.
The stadium's commercial performance is particularly significant: its revenue has more than doubled compared with the final season before the redevelopment began in 2018-19.
Real Madrid have now recorded a profit for 26 consecutive financial years, according to the club.
Bayern close to the billion-euro mark
Bayern Munich are not far behind, having increased their consolidated revenue from €978.3 million to €988.2 million.
The club's sponsorship income was particularly strong, rising by almost €30 million to €268.4 million. Merchandising also reached a record €152.8 million.

However, the financial picture was more mixed when it came to profits. Bayern's operating result (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million, but its profit before tax fell by 16.9 per cent to €35.3 million. The group's net profit declined by 15.9 per cent to €22.8 million.

Bayern explained that the lower profit was largely due to exceptional revenue in the previous financial year from the European Championship and the Champions League final, which did not recur in 2025-26.

CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen nevertheless described the results as another record year(source in German), emphasising the club's financial stability and its continued investment in the men's and women's teams.

Bayern also highlighted a decline in revenue from the Bundesliga's central media marketing, which fell by €10 million to €93 million. Dreesen said German clubs needed to address their competitive disadvantage in international television marketing.
Bayern reach a historic membership milestone
Away from the financial figures, Bayern celebrated another milestone: the club has surpassed 500,000 members for the first time.
According to Bayern, this makes it the largest sports club by membership worldwide. Its membership has doubled over the past 12 years, from around 250,000 in 2014.

The milestone also underlines the difference between the clubs' structures. Bayern is majority-owned by its members' association, FC Bayern München eV, while Real Madrid is entirely owned by its members, known as socios.
At Bayern, members also have voting rights at the annual general meeting, giving them a direct say in the club's affairs.
Two different models of financial success
Although Real Madrid currently have the larger revenue stream, both clubs demonstrate how Europe's leading football institutions are expanding beyond traditional sources of income.

Real Madrid have benefited considerably from their renovated stadium and global commercial reach. Bayern, meanwhile, have built particularly strong sponsorship and merchandising businesses while maintaining a cautious approach to spending.

The substantial difference in turnover does not translate into an equally large gap in profitability. Despite generating around €233 million more revenue than Bayern, Real Madrid reported net profit after tax of €26.3 million, only €3.5 million more than the German club's €22.8 million.

This suggests that higher revenues do not automatically result in significantly higher profits, as operating costs, player salaries, transfer spending, financing and other expenses also play a major role. Both clubs nevertheless ended the 2025-26 financial year in the black, demonstrating their ability to remain profitable while operating on a huge financial scale.
For Bayern, the next major target is clear: breaking through the €1 billion revenue barrier. Real Madrid, meanwhile, have already moved beyond it and are setting their sights on further growth.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/indias-opp.headline: India’s opposition stages protests against Meta over account removals
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/indias-opp.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Youth wing of Congress party issues a seven-day ‘ultimatum’ to the US technology giant, urging it to lift all restrictions.

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party has staged protests outside Meta offices in three cities, demanding that the United States technology company restore the Instagram accounts of its leaders.

The protests took place in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram, near New Delhi, on Friday and led to clashes with police and security guards, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress on Saturday.
Recommended Stories

In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building that houses Meta’s offices and clashed with police. In Mumbai, protesters spray-painted slogans on the walls outside, and in Gurugram they held banners reading “restore Youth Congress accounts”.

The party has alleged that on November 19, Meta illegally withheld the Instagram accounts of the youth wing’s president and the party official overseeing the wing on orders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In a statement accompanied by videos of the protests, the Congress youth wing said, “If Meta wants to do business in India, it must respect the Indian Constitution, not surrender to arbitrary BJP government orders.”
It had also warned Meta on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the accounts were restored.

Manu Jain, who runs the group’s social media, told the Reuters news agency on Saturday that two accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of other accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government are still restricted.
The youth wing issued a seven-day “ultimatum” to the technology giant, urging it to lift all “restrictions on opposition voices, journalists and creators”.

It asked how many Indian accounts were withheld on government orders in the past six months, and how many remain blocked. It also asked Meta to explain what it called the automated blocking of posts that mention Congress leader Rahul Gandhi or criticise Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP.

On Saturday, the protesters also posted a video of workers putting up a banner in central Delhi that mocked Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, as “Mark BJPberg” – suggesting that Meta favours Modi’s party.
Meta has yet to issue a statement on the matter.
Police action and BJP response
Police registered a complaint against four Youth Congress leaders in Mumbai and detained some protesters, Dainik Jagran English reported.
Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the ruling BJP, accused the protesters of vandalising Meta’s Hyderabad office and “flaunting it on social media”.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users.

In February, the government ordered platforms to remove unlawful content within three hours of notice, down from 36 hours. The government issued nearly 195,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July, the Indian Express reported.

Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025, according to its disclosures. It said most were cases in which it was “obligated to proactively restrict content” under local law.

cnbc.com/2026/11/21/trump-fbi-database-h.headline: Trump says there could be a 'positive spin' from the latest FBI database hack
cnbc.com/2026/11/21/trump-fbi-database-h.author: Jeff Cox

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database.
The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.

The hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified and it is unclear what data was extracted.
CNN had first reported on the suspected hack, citing sources familiar with the issue.
In a wide-ranging interview on Fox, Trump said there could be upside from the news.
"Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he said. "I always like to put things on a positive spin."

This would be the second recent intrusion into the FBI system; the previous one came in September, when a group known as "ShinyHunters" broke into an FBI jobs website. The result compromised data on current and former FBI employees and shut down part of the agency's operations until the issue was resolved.
Trump said it's possible there could be information gleaned from the latest hack.

"I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?" he said. "People should hear about it, because it actually put our country in danger, and so maybe we'll learn things that we wouldn't have learned otherwise."
The FBI did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-20/an.headline: Anthropic’s record IPO nets huge windfall for L.A. investors
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-20/an.author: Nilesh Christopher

paragraphs.text: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic’s record-breaking public listing Thursday minted new billionaires and thousands of millionaires.

Some of the windfall from the listing is also enriching longtime Los Angeles investors, including actor Ashton Kutcher, as well as the pensions and retirement savings of teachers, police officers and other residents of the region.

The size of Anthropic’s offering is staggering. It raised more than $100 billion in its initial public offering, smashing the previous record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. It gives the company huge financial firepower to compete with OpenAI and other rivals.
Shares surged more than 17% to close their first day on the market at $97.17. That gives it a market value north of $1.3 trillion, making it bigger than Walmart, Samsung and Chevron.

Anthropic’s performance will be a barometer of Wall Street’s appetite for AI. Investors have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into AI companies, betting that the technology will transform the economy. But much of that money has come from professional investors.

Anthropic develops the Claude family of advanced models that underpin the AI boom. In its prospectus, it highlighted the promise of accelerating scientific innovation, curing diseases, and boosting economic growth. The company’s growth has stunned investors. Revenue reached $33 billion for the first nine months of the year, growing 1,400% from the same period last year.

The company was founded in 2021 by a breakaway faction of OpenAI researchers who were concerned the company was putting commercial incentives ahead of safety. They were viewed as the “doomers” who struck out to build a safety-focused AI.

The product’s initial popularity was contained to a niche group of software developers. But its relentless focus on selling Claude to business users, and the success of its coding assistant Claude Code, supercharged it to eventually surpass rival OpenAI.

Priced at $83 a share, the company raised $107.3 billion from the listing. It will use the money for the physical infrastructure of chips, power and data centers needed to support the explosive growth of its business.

The IPO brings Anthropic to a much wider audience. Its price will reflect whether ordinary stock market investors are willing to pay a premium for a company that loses money as it faces enormous costs and fierce competition.
Its market debut also helps answer a question hanging over the AI boom: Can these companies generate enough profit to justify their high share prices?

The listing’s success sent mixed signals to the market Thursday, as Anthropic seemed to suck money out of other shares. The Standard & Poor’s 500 index fell 2% for its sixth straight loss. That’s its longest losing streak in 2½ years.
Here are some of the local beneficiaries of Anthropic’s stock market success so far:

Sound Ventures co-founders Guy Oseary, who is Madonna’s manager, and actor Ashton Kutcher met with Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei at their Beverly Hills office in 2023. After the meeting, Sound Ventures invested $35 million at a $5.1-billion valuation for Anthropic. The firm followed with an additional $400 million, and has participated in every single fundraising round since building up about a half-a-percent stake in the company.
The $435-million stake is expected to be valued at approximately $7 billion, according to Bloomberg, though Kutcher is no longer with Sound Ventures.
People of Southern California
Yasmin Razavi, a general partner at Spark Capital, was listed as an investor in Anthropic’s IPO filings. Her early bet in Anthropic has now made pensioners in Los Angeles and Orange County richer.
Equable Institute, a nonprofit focused on public retirement systems and pensions, found that at least 18 public pension funds in the U.S. hold Anthropic through private investments.

Its report said California Public Employees’ Retirement System, Los Angeles City Employees’ Retirement System, Los Angeles Fire and Police Pensions and Orange County Employees Retirement System have all invested in funds that have invested in Anthropic.
Spark Capital received commitments from pension plans for public-sector employees in Orange County and Los Angeles, according to the global publication the Information.
Spark’s stake in Anthropic is now valued at $11 billion, Bloomberg reports.

A prolific investor who owns homes in Los Angeles, Schmidt was one of the earliest backers of Anthropic and was brought in as an investor in 2021. Cami Clarke, the wife of Amodei who had dated Schmidt, facilitated the investment. That 1% stake is projected to reach $20 billion.

Some of Anthropic’s biggest backers are the Big Tech companies Amazon, Google and Microsoft, which offered loans for Anthropic to buy their computing chips, will see their investments turn into equity worth tens of billions of dollars. That debt turning into equity accounts for most of Anthropic’s loss of $104 billion for the first nine months of this year.

Thomas Laffont started his career as a talent manager in Hollywood’s influential Creative Artist Agency. His spent his years negotiating deals and packaging talent, and worked with A-list actors including Brad Pitt on the movie “Meet Joe Black.” In 2003, he left to co-found Coatue Management with his brother Philippe Laffont, who had made his name in Wall Street.

The New York-based hedge fund, which previously invested in companies such as Snapchat, Spotify, and ByteDance, manages assets worth $50 billion. Coatue has invested a total of $4.75 billion in Anthropic, that across multiple rounds starting in 2025. Its late but aggressive bet on Anthropic paid off handsomely, with its stake worth more than $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.
Coatue also owns a stake in rival OpenAI. Thomas, the former talent manager turned investor, is a Beverly Hills resident.
Soon after General Motors acquired the robotaxi startup Cruise, engineer Sol Bier cashed in on his modest equity and moved to Southern California to start venture capital firm Factorial Funds.

Working on self-driving cars put him in close contact with AI researchers working on chatbots. In early 2020, he watched a demonstration of a primitive version of ChatGPT by Mira Murati, then OpenAI’s chief technology officer.

“I saw the promise, and it was a huge deal,” Bier said. “When I started Factorial, that was on the top of my mind. So I chased after the companies I thought were the best in the space, and then Anthropic was the one that stood out.”

He leveraged his industry connections to to be able to invest in Anthropic. Although initial rounds came from friends and family, Bier said he began raising money from institutions for subsequent rounds with soaring valuations.

Factorial Funds first invested in Anthropic in 2023 in its Series C, according to PitchBook data, and has since participated in consecutive fundraisers, accumulating about a 0.72% stake. That stake is now worth $10 billion, according to a person familiar with the details.

The Newport Beach-based company has steadily grown its influence over the last five years, investing in SpaceX, Anduril, Mistral and others. Anthropic will be Bier’s second exit after SpaceX earlier this year.
“That was a wild bet, and I hope these two IPOs repay your trust,” Bier wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Lorenzo Esparza didn’t actively seek a potential billion-dollar windfall. His Los Angeles-based wealth management company, Manhattan West, invested $31 million at a $15-billion valuation during a fire sale of Anthropic shares in 2024.

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of disgraced cryptocurrency exchange FTX, owned roughly a 13.5% stake in Anthropic through its $500-million investment in 2021. When the exchange went under, FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold its stake to multiple investors to generate cash for creditors.
Esparza bought Anthropic shares during that sale, which Forbes estimates are now worth over $1 billion.
“It’s been a good investment,” Esparza told The Times. “We came in through Parella Weinberg Partners, the bankers who led the trustee sale of FTX shares.”

Malibu-based Type One Ventures is another benefactor of the FTX divestiture. When a friend reached out in 2024 with the opportunity to invest in Anthropic, Abdo John Hajj was quick to say yes because he’d been looking for AI companies to invest in.
“This is just going to be one in a very few companies. … This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” said Hajj, co-founder of the company.

He said the decision was driven less by negotiating a discount and more by the belief that Anthropic could become a consequential company with broad economic and productivity effect. It made one investment and held the position without participating in consecutive rounds.
Hajj declined to divulge his firm’s exact stake, but said that it was now worth hundreds of millions.

Laguna-Beach-based WCM Investment Management invested when Anthropic was valued at $183 billion in September 2025. The investment firm, founded in the 70s manages $136 billion in assets on behalf of institutions and individuals. PitchBook data show the firm still holds a stake in Anthropic, which is now worth billions.
WCM did not respond to a request for comment.

marketwatch.com/story/the-thought-of-liv.headline: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

paragraphs.text: Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson called Social Security a 'scam' and urged lawmakers to shut it down
Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a constant stream of new unwitting investors.
Fear can lead us to do and say unexpected things.

It can push us toward panic selling, drive us to make wild assumptions about the world, and sometimes force us to take a hard look at our own finances. We are especially prone to these impulses when we are looking for something or someone to blame.

Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson, the chairman of the Committee on the Budget, on Wednesday took aim at Social Security ahead of a hearing on the subject, calling it a scam. "It's grotesque and at this point, there really is no way to fix Social Security," he said. "It is a Ponzi scheme."

Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a stream of new unwitting investors who pay the returns promised to earlier ones. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law, in which payroll taxes fund benefits.

He isn't the only one who's frustrated with Social Security. Experts attribute an expected shortfall in Social Security to demographic factors - older workers retiring, with some claiming benefits early out of fear that the funds will run out.
Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law.

Unless Congress acts, the combined trust funds will run out in 2034, covering just 83% of benefits. A new AARP report said: "The share of gross domestic product subject to Social Security's payroll tax, the program's primary income source, has fallen steadily over the past four decades."

The Social Security taxable maximum is $184,500 for 2026 and $192,300 for 2027, meaning earnings above those limits are not subject to Social Security payroll taxes. In other words, a growing share of national income is excluded, contributing to the expected shortfall in funds.

Like Johnson, a Moneyist reader also used the "P" word. "The thought of living to 100 terrifies me more than dying. For me, the biggest fraud is telling people to wait until 70 to retire just to maximize their Social Security benefits - as if that's the only factor worth considering."

They continued: "I grew up in the 1980s, and the advice to never count on Social Security is sounding more and more like a warning than a prediction. I fear there will be a run on Social Security similar to the bank runs before the Great Depression. Long live the Ponzi!"
Don't miss: Is $1 million enough for a household to retire? The answer keeps changing.
Addressing the criticisms

The reader is essentially asking four questions: (1) Will fear trigger a Social Security crisis? (2) Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? (3) Why sacrifice your 60s to get a bigger check at 70? And (4) Can you really count on Social Security?

(1) As for fear leading to a crisis: Probably not, so do not get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom and gloom. A run on a bank involves a large number of people withdrawing their money and, if the bank cannot meet those withdrawals, even an otherwise solvent institution can fail.

I grew up in the 1980s too, and here's a fun fact about Generation X: The American Institute of Stress says we are apparently more stressed out than other generations. The main reason for that, researchers theorize, is that we are worried about falling short on our retirement goals.

(2) Social Security is a social-insurance program funded by workers and employers to provide support in retirement, prevent vulnerable people from falling into poverty and provide economic stability during downturns. It is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.
Social Security is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.

(3) You can claim Social Security at 62, but doing so reduces your monthly benefit by 30% compared with waiting until your full retirement age (FRA) of 67. Waiting until 70 increases your benefit by 8% for each year you delay beyond 67. That's 24% more in total.

If you are collecting Social Security and remain below FRA throughout 2026, you can earn up to $24,480 before benefits are withheld. Above that limit, $1 is withheld for every $2 you earn. At FRA, Social Security recalculates your benefit to account for withholdings.

Yes, some people do claim Social Security benefits early due to fears about the program's long-term viability. But the program values stability, security and peace of mind over recklessness, madcap investments and promises of riches.

(4) You can count on Social Security, which is not projected to disappear. Payroll taxes and other incoming revenue will keep funding benefits. Under current projections, though, that revenue would cover only 83% of scheduled benefits from the combined trust funds in 2034.
Don't miss: 'I still have horrible memories of the Bernie Madoff scandal': At 63, who can I trust with my $655K retirement fund?
Why we have Social Security

Social Security was created in 1935 in response to the Great Depression and was not intended to maximize investment returns. Today, it provides a social safety net against the financial hardships of retirement, disability and the loss of a family's breadwinner.

There are two separate funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund and the Disability Insurance Trust Fund. Their reserves are invested in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government.

So what about this looming funding crisis? The Congressional Budget Office said earlier this year that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which pays retirement and survivors benefits, is projected to run out of reserves in 2032.

The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, said in a June report that, at that point, incoming revenue would cover just 78% of scheduled benefits from that fund. Without congressional action, those shortfalls would mean across-the-board reductions in benefits.
There is already a demographic 'run' on Social Security.

"The program's long-run outlook worsened significantly this year," it said. "The Social Security Administration (SSA) revised its fertility and immigration projections downward." The 75-year shortfall has risen to approximately $30 trillion - up from $26 trillion last year.

There is already a demographic "run" on Social Security. The Bipartisan Policy Center said "an aging population is a major contributor to the problem." The ratio of workers to beneficiaries has dropped from 5-to-1 in 1960 to 2.6-to-1 in 2025 and is projected to fall to 1.9-to-1 by 2075.

The Social Security Disability Insurance Trust Fund is projected to remain solvent until 2100, the end of the Board of Trustees' 75-year projection period, but the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, under current estimates, won't have enough to pay full benefits in 2032.

We are encouraged to delay our dream life, save more, work longer and maximize our retirement contributions. Still, the price of financial security should not be spending our 60s worrying about our 70s, 80s and 90s, and beyond. For millions of people, however, that worry is a daily reality.
Keep calm and carry on working, if you can, and saving for retirement.

marketwatch.com/story/im-sick-of-flying-.headline: 'I'm sick of flying': I paid for priority boarding, but the overhead bins were full. Was I duped?

paragraphs.text: 'Maybe next time I'll try the other approach: I'll board whenever I feel like it and drop my suitcase in the first open slot I see'
"I wondered what would happen if I put my carry-on in the first-class bin." (Photo subject is a model.)

On a recent flight, I paid extra for priority boarding. When I reached my row, the bin was already full. I looked down the aisle and saw people who were seated much farther back had put their bags in the bins over the forward rows. One man had wedged two bags into a single compartment, and his seat was several rows behind mine.

I asked a flight attendant if there was room for my carry-on. She said I'd have to look farther back or maybe check it at the gate. I told her I'd paid extra to board early and that the space above my seat had been taken by people who hadn't reached their rows yet. She said there wasn't much she could do.

I stood there with my bag, the line of passengers stacking up behind me. I'd done the sensible thing and followed the system as it was explained to me, and I was the one holding up the aisle. It reminded me of being a kid who raised his hand and waited his turn while everyone else shouted out answers. Frankly, I'm sick of flying.

Also, I wondered what would happen if I put my carry-on in the first-class bin. Would the flight attendants be so relaxed about that? I suspect the rules would suddenly matter a great deal. Maybe next time I'll try the other approach: I'll board whenever I feel like it and drop my suitcase in the first open slot I see. What do you think?
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
Related: 'It's good to be old': I've been invited to a dozen free meals that turn into annuity sales pitches. Should I stop going?
Priority boarding and charging for larger carry-on bags are, in part, the result of overzealous hard-shelled wheelie bags being crammed into overhead compartments.
The beauty of priority boarding, when you flight is leaving on time, is that it only works if you use it and board as soon as possible.

That sounds harsh, I know, but the fact is if you had boarded early, I don't think you would have had a problem finding overhead space for your bag. Boarding is generally spaced out strategically: People with disabilities and/or children typically board first, followed by first-class passengers, priority boarders, veterans, seniors and, finally, all the other plebs (that is, people like me who don't pay for assigned seats or priority boarding).

You pay for your seat, not the overhead space. That can lead to disgruntled passengers trying to find space, like yourself, and also "carry-on monsters" who bring so many bags that they squeeze them all in those overhead compartments - sometimes at the expense of their neighbors, who then have to find a space at the back of the aircraft, and wait until everyone else has deplaned before they can retrieve their bag.

Baggage fees have become big business since they were first introduced two decades ago. U.S. airlines make more than $7 billion from baggage fees, according to reports, and while they account for only a small amount of revenue for many major carriers - despite adding to already skyrocketing fuel costs - they can add as much as 20% to revenue for low-cost carriers that enforce their baggage rules with an iron fist.

Priority boarding and charging for larger carry-on bags are, in part, the result of oversized, hard-shelled wheelie bags being crammed into overhead compartments. As writer Ian Bogost pointed out in The Atlantic: "The rabble holding cheap tickets who board last are most affected, but even jet-setters with elite status seem to worry about bag space; they hover in front of gates hoping to board as soon as possible - 'gate lice,' they're sometimes called."
You pay for your seat, not the overhead space.

Regarding priority boarding: Some passengers also have a legal right to go first, even if they have not paid for priority boarding. Under the Air Carrier Access Act, U.S. airlines and foreign carriers operating flights to and from or within the U.S. are legally obligated to offer early boarding to passengers with disabilities, while some airlines allow passengers with young children to board next, even before customers who have paid for priority boarding.

As this bill of rights from Delta Air Lines (DAL) says: "Airlines must allow a passenger with a disability who self-identifies at the gate as needing additional time or assistance to board, stow accessibility equipment or be seated, the opportunity to board before all other passengers. Passengers with disabilities must be provided prompt and timely boarding and deplaning assistance, upon request, from properly trained airline personnel."

"If level loading bridges are not available, a lifting device must be provided to assist persons with limited mobility safely on and off the aircraft at most U.S. airports, except when boarding smaller aircraft (less than 19 seats)," it adds. "For smaller aircraft and nonprimary U.S. airports or foreign airports, airlines must ensure boarding and deplaning assistance by any available means acceptable to the passenger."
Don't turn left when you enter the aircraft with your bag unless you have a first-class ticket.

cbssports.com/mlb/news/mlb-rumors-freddy.author: Dayn Perry

paragraphs.text: Nov 21, 2026 at 11:14 am ET • 2 min read

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.
Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Saturday's supply just below.
Freddy Peralta market picking up steam

Freddy Peralta, who'll be going into his age-31 season in 2027, is one of the strongest free-agent starting pitchers on the market not named Tarik Skubal. As such, there's healthy interest in his services. The Tampa Bay Rays, the Chicago White Sox, the San Diego Padres, the Toronto Blue Jays, and two presently unknown clubs all have significant interest in signing Peralta, the Athletic reports.

Peralta, coming off three straight seasons for the Milwaukee Brewers in which he topped 30 starts and 200 strikeouts, wasn't himself with the New York Mets for the first half-plus of 2027. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form.
Itoh visits Chicago

Right-hander Hiromi Itoh, who's seeking to make the leap from Japan to MLB, was recently in Chicago to visit the Cubs or the White Sox, ESPN reports. Both Windy City squads are in need of pitching help, and Itoh would certainly help them on that front.
The 29-year-old Itoh ranked 26th on CBS Sports' offseason list of the top free agents in the current class. Here's part of our write-up:

"A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters are expected to post Itoh, who turned 29 in August, this winter."
The Cubs have a lot of uncertainty in the rotation, while the White Sox still need help even after adding Dustin May this offseason.
Mets getting calls on Vientos

The New York Mets retained the services of first baseman Mark Vientos leading up to the recent non-tender deadline despite his pattern of decline over the last two seasons. Now, Vientos could be on the move. The soon-to-be 27-year-old has been the subject of trade inquiries, The Athletic reports. While Vientos is coming off a highly disappointing 2026 season, he still has power potential and in his semi-recent past a 2024 campaign in which he hit 27 home runs in 111 games. All of that makes Vientos a fairly compelling change-of-scenery possibility, and the Mets may seek to make that happen this winter.

engadget.com/2318288/why-36-percent-hous.headline: 36 percent of households have ditched a streaming service subscription recently: Here's why
engadget.com/2318288/why-36-percent-hous.author: Erin Carson

paragraphs.text: If you're thinking of unloading one of your streaming subscriptions or have cut off some services in the past few months, you're not alone. Data from consultancy Deloitte shows that more than a third of consumers have cut loose entertainment subscriptions recently. The big reason? Money.

The average household is spending about $76 a month on SVOD, or subscription video on demand, according to the report. For Gen Z, that number is even higher, coming in at $83 per month. Once upon a time, streaming video offered a less expensive alternative to traditional cable subscriptions. As the years have progressed, some consumers aren't seeing the same savings they once did: Prices have gone up and perhaps so have their subscription counts. Now, Deloitte is reporting that about 60 percent of consumers say they would probably cancel their favorite service if the price went up by $5.
Price isn't the only factor motivating people to rethink their subscriptions. From ads to media ownership, here's a look at why so many people are ditching their subscriptions.
Pricing

Deloitte's report highlights that the cost of maintaining streaming subscriptions is one of the biggest grievances consumers have. As of October, 45 percent of respondents said they paid too much for streaming services. About 50 percent of participants said they were looking for ways to bring their streaming costs down, leading some to swap out the apps they subscribed to.

Sixty-four percent of respondents also expressed frustration that prices keep going up. That frustration is not unfounded: A 2025 report from research firm Forrester found that between 2021 and 2025, the average cost of ad-free streaming services rose 54 percent. Major streamers like Apple TV, Netflix, Paramount+, and Disney+ all raised prices in 2026, leading a number of watchdogs to label the hikes "streamflation."

The Forrester analysis suggested that streamers regularly debut with lower prices to attract subscribers, but then raise prices as the pressure to boost profits grows. And meanwhile, consumers aren't necessarily getting any extra perks for their money.
Other concerns

Skyrocketing subscription prices aren't the only motivators for people to take a hard look at their streaming services. For one, Deloitte found that some consumers have been gravitating toward social media for their idle entertainment. About half of Gen Z respondents said that social media content is "more relevant" than traditional content. As part of that, these respondents said they feel more connected to the creators they see on social media than TV actors or other personalities.

Ads could be another sore spot. A survey from Consumer Reports found that while people might opt for the ad-supported tier of a streaming service in hopes of saving money, 48 percent of respondents found them to be "very annoying." Respondents specifically disliked seeing the same ads too often and having to sit through too many breaks throughout the content.

While streaming offers the convenience of deep catalogs of TV shows and movies, some consumers are frustrated that they don't own their own libraries in this setup. A change in a licensing deal could mean a beloved TV show is no longer available on a certain streaming service. Some viewers are turning back to physical media and building libraries of DVDs and Blu-Rays — even VHS tapes, in some cases — as a way to wrest back control and even bypass algorithmically driven recommendations. And if you don't want to commit to shelves and shelves of physical boxes, you can digitize a media collection and host it on your own server.

Whether you're feeling cranky about how much streaming services are costing you, or spending your time on social media, or raiding the thrift store bins for your favorite movies, you're not the only one making major choices about your subscriptions.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/japanese-figur.headline: Japanese figure skater Mao Shimada wins a second Grand Prix in her debut season

paragraphs.text: HELSINKI, Finland (AP) — Mao Shimada of Japan won the Finlandia Trophy Grand Prix on Saturday, making it two-of-two for the 18-year-old in her first senior-level figure staking season.

Shimada entered the campaign after winning four consecutive junior world titles and has kept up her winning streak in skating’s big league. She won Skate Canada International this month and followed that up with another dominant performance in Helsinki.

Already owning a comfortable lead after her short program on Friday, Shimada ran away with it by shaking off an early fall on a quad toeloop early in her free skate to “Waloyo Yamoni” by Christopher Tin. That gave her a total of 229.49 points for the two-day meet.
Niina Petrokina of Estonia, the reigning European champion, was second with 214.06 total points. American Isabeau Levito was third with 207.19, completing a repeat of the podium at Skate Canada.

Japanese women have won all five Grand Prix events so far this season. Olympic bronze medalist Ami Nakai won the season-opener in France and Skate America last week, while Mone Chiba won the Cup of China earlier this month.
The regular season ends with NHK Trophy in Tokyo next week.

The top six performers in the rankings for each discipline will then qualify for the Grand Prix Final in China from December 10-12. Shimada and Nakai are leading the women’s standings, followed by Alexandra Ignatova, Petrokina and Anastasiia Gubanova. Levito is clinging to sixth and the final berth for the final.
Seven Russian skaters were withdrawn from the meet early this week after the Finnish government barred Russian athletes from entering the country due to the war in Ukraine.
